path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 0 — Cloud Foundations/00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On-Prem Pentesting.md
title: 00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On-Prem Pentesting
body: 00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On Prem Pentesting What This Note Covers This note explains what cloud penetration testing actually is, how it fundamentally differs from traditional on premises (on prem) network pentesting, and why those differences matter when you're planning or executing a cloud security engagement. What Is Cloud Pentesting? Cloud penetration testing is the process of simulating an attacker's actions against cloud hosted infrastructure, services, and configurations to identify security weaknesses before a real attacker does. Unlike traditional pentesting where you're looking for exploitable software vulnerabilities (CVEs, buffer overflows, unpatched services), cloud pentesting is primarily about: Misconfigured services — storage buckets set to public, overly permissive IAM policies, open security groups Credential exposure — API keys leaked in code, environment variables, metadata endpoints Identity and access abuse — escalating privileges through cloud IAM roles, assuming other identities, chaining permissions Logic flaws in cloud architecture — trusting relationships between services that can be abused [!tip] Key mindset shift On prem pentesting = "Can I exploit this software?" Cloud pentesting = "Can I abuse this identity, permission, or configuration?" Core Differences: Cloud vs On Prem 1. Attack Surface | Dimension | On Premises | Cloud | | | | | | Entry points | Network ports, exposed services | APIs, IAM keys, storage URLs, metadata service | | What you target | Hosts, services, CVEs | Roles, policies, buckets, functions, secrets | | Lateral movement | Network pivoting, pass the hash | Role assumption, service impersonation, token theft | | Persistence | Scheduled tasks, registry, rootkits | Backdoor IAM users, rogue Lambda, access keys | | Exfiltration | Network egress | Data replication, cross account copy, public bucket | 2. Credential Centric vs Exploit Centric On prem pentesting often relies on exploiting vulnerabilities in software — buffer overflows, RCE, SQLi — to gain a foothold, then move laterally using harvested credentials. Cloud pentesting flips this. Credentials are often the entire attack. If you find an AWS access key pair with broad permissions, you may have full control of the environment immediately. No exploit needed. The "vulnerability" is a misconfigured IAM policy or a leaked secret, not a CVE. [!danger] No CVE, still critical A publicly accessible S3 bucket containing customer PII is a critical finding even though no software was "exploited". Cloud security failures are often configuration failures, not code failures. 3. No Network Perimeter Traditional pentesting assumes a network boundary — firewall, DMZ, corporate LAN. You breach the perimeter, then move inward. Cloud environments don't work this way: Resources communicate via APIs over HTTPS There is no "internal network" in the traditional sense (though VPCs exist) An attacker with valid credentials can operate from anywhere in the world Identity is the perimeter in cloud 4. Everything Is an API Every action in a cloud environment — creating a server, reading a file, adding a user — is an API call. This means: Everything is logged (potentially) via services like AWS CloudTrail, Azure Monitor, GCP Cloud Audit Logs Everything is governed by IAM policies You can enumerate and test permissions programmatically Attackers and defenders both operate via the same API surface 5. Shared Responsibility Changes the Scope In on prem, you own and are responsible for the entire stack. In cloud, responsibility is split between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures what they build on top of it. This is covered in depth in 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model. 6. Blast Radius In on prem environments, a compromised workstation means one machine. In cloud, a compromised IAM role with broad permissions could mean: Access to all S3 buckets in the account The ability to spin up hundreds of EC2 instances (for crypto mining) Full database access Cross account access to other AWS accounts in the organisation [!warning] Blast radius is amplified in cloud A single over privileged IAM key can be equivalent to full domain admin. Always assess blast radius before acting in a cloud environment, especially in production. 7. Ephemeral Resources Cloud resources appear and disappear constantly. Auto scaling groups create and terminate servers. Lambda functions live for milliseconds. Containers spin up and down. This means: Persistence mechanisms must be cloud native (IAM backdoors, not cron jobs on a server that might not exist tomorrow) Logs can be incomplete if resources terminate before logging completes Your enumeration snapshot is stale within minutes in active environments 8. Multi Tenancy Risk Cloud providers run infrastructure shared across thousands of customers. Historically, vulnerabilities like VM escape or hypervisor flaws could (in theory) allow cross tenant attacks. In practice, these are rare and the providers remediate them quickly. Your focus as a cloud pentester is almost always the customer's own misconfigurations , not breaking out of the cloud provider's infrastructure. What You're Actually Looking For in Cloud Pentesting 1. Exposed credentials — API keys, service account JSON files, connection strings in code/config/environment 2. Over permissive IAM — roles and policies that grant more than needed (violating least privilege) 3. Public facing resources — storage buckets, databases, admin dashboards open to the internet 4. Insecure service configurations — logging disabled, encryption off, MFA not enforced 5. Privilege escalation paths — chains of permissions that allow a low privilege identity to gain admin 6. Secrets in wrong places — passwords in environment variables, unencrypted secrets in code repos 7. Cross account trust abuse — overly permissive trust relationships between accounts/tenants 8. Insufficient logging and monitoring — CloudTrail disabled, no alerts on privilege escalation Tools You'll Use (vs On Prem) | On Prem Tools | Cloud Equivalents | | | | | Nmap (port scanning) | ScoutSuite, Prowler (service enumeration) | | Metasploit (exploitation) | Pacu (AWS exploitation framework) | | BloodHound (AD paths) | AzureHound, AWSPX (cloud IAM paths) | | Mimikatz (credential dump) | IMDSv1 SSRF, metadata endpoint harvesting | | CrackMapExec | aws cli + enumerate iam | | Impacket | ROADtools (Azure AD attacks) | Quick Reference Related Notes 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 0 — Cloud Foundations/00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model.md
title: 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model
body: 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model What This Note Covers The shared responsibility model defines who is responsible for securing what in a cloud environment. It's the foundational legal and operational concept that determines the scope of every cloud penetration test. Getting this wrong means either testing things outside your authority or missing the actual attack surface. The Core Concept When an organisation uses a cloud provider, security responsibility is split between: 1. The Cloud Provider — responsible for securing the physical infrastructure, hypervisors, networking hardware, and the services themselves 2. The Customer — responsible for securing everything they build, configure, and deploy on top of that infrastructure [!tip] Simple mental model The provider locks the building. The customer is responsible for what they put inside it, how they configure the rooms, and who has the keys. The exact split depends on the service model being used — IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS. (Service models are covered in detail in 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface.) AWS Shared Responsibility Model AWS describes this as: "Security OF the cloud vs Security IN the cloud" AWS is responsible for (Security OF the cloud): Physical data centres, power, cooling, physical access Hardware: servers, networking equipment, storage hardware Hypervisor and virtualisation layer Managed service infrastructure: the underlying compute that runs Lambda, RDS, etc. Global network backbone The Customer is responsible for (Security IN the cloud): IAM : who has access, what permissions they have, MFA enforcement Operating systems on EC2 instances: patching, hardening, endpoint security Application code running on cloud infrastructure Data : encryption at rest and in transit, classification, backup Network configuration : VPC design, security groups, NACLs, routing S3 bucket policies and ACLs : whether data is publicly accessible CloudTrail and logging : whether audit logging is enabled and protected Secrets management : not hardcoding credentials, using Secrets Manager [!warning] The most exploitable gap The customer is responsible for IAM, data exposure, and network config. These are exactly where 90% of real world cloud breaches originate. AWS will never stop you from making your S3 bucket public or giving a role — that's your responsibility. AWS Shared Responsibility by Service Type | Service | Provider Secures | Customer Secures | | | | | | EC2 (IaaS) | Hypervisor, hardware | OS, patches, apps, networking, IAM | | RDS (PaaS) | OS, DB engine patching | DB config, access control, encryption, parameter groups | | S3 (Object Storage) | Durability, availability | Bucket policies, ACLs, encryption, access logging | | Lambda (Serverless) | Runtime environment, scaling | Function code, execution role permissions, env vars | | DynamoDB (Managed DB) | Infrastructure, availability | Table access policies, encryption, data classification | Azure Shared Responsibility Model Azure's model follows the same principle but is articulated across their service tiers. Microsoft Azure is responsible for: Physical infrastructure: datacentres, hardware, power, cooling Network controls at the physical/infrastructure layer Host infrastructure (hypervisor) Physical security and access to facilities The Customer is responsible for: Azure Active Directory / Entra ID : user accounts, MFA, Conditional Access policies Data governance : classification, encryption, retention Applications : code security, authentication logic Network configuration : NSGs, Azure Firewall, Virtual Networks Identity and access management : RBAC roles, service principal permissions OS level security on VMs: patching, endpoint protection Azure Shared Responsibility by Service Type | Service | Provider Secures | Customer Secures | | | | | | Azure VM (IaaS) | Hypervisor, hardware | OS, network config, apps | | Azure App Service (PaaS) | Runtime, scaling infra | App code, identity, CORS, TLS config | | Azure SQL Managed Instance | Infrastructure, HA | DB config, auth, firewall rules, encryption | | Azure Blob Storage | Infrastructure | Access policies, SAS tokens, firewall, encryption | | Azure Functions (Serverless) | Execution environment | Function code, managed identity permissions | | Microsoft 365 (SaaS) | Entire application stack | Data, accounts, access policies, DLP | GCP Shared Responsibility Model Google Cloud Platform uses similar language: "Google manages security of the cloud; you manage security in the cloud." Google is responsible for: Physical datacentre security Hardware, network infrastructure, storage systems Hypervisor and virtualisation layer Core GCP service infrastructure (the underlying systems running Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, etc.) The Customer is responsible for: IAM : service accounts, roles, bindings, org policies Network design : VPC, firewall rules, private Google access Data : encryption keys (if using CMEK), classification, DLP Application security : code running on GCP Container security : images, Kubernetes RBAC, node pool permissions Audit logging : Cloud Audit Logs configuration and retention Org policies : constraints on what can be deployed Why This Matters for Penetration Testing Scope Definition Before starting any cloud pentest, you must establish which layer of the model you're testing: Testing customer managed resources (IAM, storage, compute configs) — almost always in scope, this is where misconfigs live Testing the cloud provider's infrastructure (hypervisor, physical layer) — this is out of scope and may violate provider terms Testing shared responsibility edge cases (e.g., managed service configurations) — clarify with the client What You're Actually Authorised to Test When a client engages you for a cloud pentest, you are authorised to test: Their IAM configurations Their deployed services (EC2, S3, Lambda, etc.) Their network configurations (VPCs, security groups) Their application code and pipelines Their secrets management practices Their logging and monitoring setup You are not authorised to: Attack AWS/Azure/GCP infrastructure itself Attempt to break out of the hypervisor Test other customers sharing the same cloud infrastructure Perform DDoS or availability testing without explicit written permission [!danger] Provider permission requirements AWS, Azure, and GCP all have policies on penetration testing. AWS requires advance notification for certain activities (load testing, simulated DDoS). Azure has a similar policy. GCP requires a formal request. Always read the provider's current penetration testing policy before engagement. This is covered in 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations. Shared Responsibility Failure Patterns (Real World) These are the most common ways customers fail their side of the shared responsibility model: 1. S3 bucket left public — customer failed to configure bucket ACL/policy (not AWS's fault) 2. IAM user with and no MFA — customer failed to enforce MFA and least privilege 3. RDS database publicly accessible — customer checked "publicly accessible" during setup without understanding the implication 4. EC2 instance with IMDSv1 enabled — customer didn't enforce IMDSv2, leaving SSRF to credential theft open 5. Secrets in environment variables — customer stored database passwords in Lambda env vars instead of Secrets Manager 6. CloudTrail disabled in a region — customer didn't enable audit logging, so attacker activity goes undetected 7. Over permissive service roles — Lambda function role has on instead of just the bucket it needs Quick Reference Related Notes 00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On Prem Pentesting 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 0 — Cloud Foundations/00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations.md
title: 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations
body: 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations What This Note Covers Cloud pentesting has a legal and contractual dimension that doesn't exist in on prem testing. Testing cloud infrastructure without understanding the boundaries can get you — and your client — banned from the platform, or worse, prosecuted. This note covers exactly what you need to know before touching anything. The Fundamental Rule You need two layers of authorisation to legally pentest cloud infrastructure: 1. Written permission from the customer — the organisation that owns the cloud account 2. Compliance with the cloud provider's penetration testing policy — AWS, Azure, and GCP each have their own rules about what testing is and isn't allowed [!danger] No exceptions Having permission from the customer is not enough. If AWS's terms say you need to notify them before load testing, and you don't, you may have your account suspended regardless of what the customer agreed to. AWS Penetration Testing Policy Current Status (as of 2024) AWS has a customer service policy for penetration testing . The key points: AWS no longer requires prior approval for most standard penetration testing activities on services you own You can test without prior approval against: EC2, RDS, CloudFront, Aurora, API Gateway, Lambda, Lightsail, Elastic Beanstalk Prohibited activities (require explicit AWS approval or are never permitted): DNS zone walking via Amazon Route 53 Hosted Zones DoS, DDoS, simulated DoS, simulated DDoS Port flooding Protocol flooding Request flooding (login request flooding, API request flooding) What Always Requires Customer Written Permission (not just AWS policy) Any testing of the customer's AWS account Any data access, enumeration, or exfiltration testing Social engineering simulations Testing in production environments [!warning] Always check the latest AWS policy Policies change. Before any engagement, verify at: https://aws.amazon.com/security/penetration testing/ AWS Rules of Engagement for Pentests Azure Penetration Testing Policy Current Status Microsoft has a Penetration Testing Rules of Engagement document. Key points: Microsoft does require advance notification for certain types of testing You must submit a Microsoft Cloud Penetration Testing Notification form before testing Testing is allowed against resources in your own Azure subscription Multi tenant services (where other customers' data could be affected) are out of scope DoS attacks against Azure infrastructure are prohibited Microsoft's Specific Requirements Notification must be submitted at least 1 week in advance for most testing Notification form available at: https://portal.msrc.microsoft.com/en us/engage/pentest Physical security testing of Microsoft datacentres is never permitted Social engineering against Microsoft employees is prohibited [!warning] Azure notification is mandatory Unlike AWS (which dropped the prior notification requirement for most services), Microsoft still requires you to submit a notification form before testing. Skipping this can result in account suspension. GCP Penetration Testing Policy Current Status Google Cloud's policy: GCP does not require pre approval for security testing of your own GCP resources Testing must be conducted only against infrastructure and services owned by the customer (their project/org) DoS and DDoS testing against Google's infrastructure is prohibited Attacks that could affect other GCP customers are prohibited [!tip] GCP is the most permissive GCP has the fewest restrictions of the three major providers for standard security testing. That said, always document your authorisation and stay within your project boundaries. Scoping a Cloud Penetration Test What Goes Into a Cloud Pentest Scope A proper scope document for a cloud pentest should define: Account/Subscription Boundaries: AWS Account ID(s) in scope Azure Subscription ID(s) and Tenant ID(s) in scope GCP Project ID(s) and Org ID(s) in scope Service Boundaries: Which services are in scope: e.g., "All services in us east 1 except production RDS" Explicitly out of scope services or environments (prod vs dev vs staging) Access Level Granted: Black box: no credentials provided (external attacker simulation) Grey box: limited credentials provided (e.g., a low privilege IAM user) White box: full read only access, IAM policy exports, architecture diagrams Testing Activities Permitted: Enumeration and reconnaissance: yes/no Privilege escalation testing: yes/no Data exfiltration simulation: yes/no (usually a read only proof of access, not actual exfil) Destructive testing: almost never (no deleting resources, no modifying IAM) Social engineering: yes/no (separate agreement usually) Prohibited Actions: No modification of production data No deletion of resources No changes to billing or account settings No adding IAM users or roles (unless specifically testing persistence) No DoS Black Box vs White Box vs Grey Box | Type | Access Given | What You're Simulating | | | | | | Black box | Nothing | External attacker with no insider info | | Grey box | Low privilege IAM credentials | Compromised employee, leaked API key | | White box | Full read access + architecture docs | Security audit, assume breach scenario | [!tip] Grey box is most common Most cloud assessments are grey box. You're given a low privilege user to simulate what an attacker could do after finding a leaked API key. Pure black box cloud testing often yields little beyond public resource discovery. Key Legal Frameworks to Know Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) — US Unauthorised access to computer systems is a federal crime. "Authorised" in cloud means both customer permission AND provider policy compliance. A signed SOW with the customer is essential. Computer Misuse Act 1990 — UK UK equivalent. Unauthorised access to computer material is a criminal offence. Same principle: you need explicit written authorisation. GDPR — EU/UK If you access or handle personal data during the test (which is likely in any real cloud environment), GDPR applies. Your engagement must address: How discovered PII will be handled Whether test data should be anonymised Reporting obligations if you discover a breach Cloud Provider Terms of Service Violating AWS/Azure/GCP ToS is grounds for immediate account suspension, which could take down the client's production environment. This is an engagement ending risk. Always read the provider's ToS on penetration testing. Rules of Engagement Template (Quick Reference) Related Notes 00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On Prem Pentesting 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface 00.8 — Cloud Security Assessment Methodology

title: 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface
body: 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface What This Note Covers IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS are the three cloud service delivery models. Each one gives the customer a different level of control — and correspondingly, a different attack surface. Understanding this is essential for knowing what to test and where to look in any cloud engagement. The Three Service Models — Overview Think of it as a spectrum of control: As you move right, the provider takes on more responsibility and the customer has fewer moving parts to misconfigure — but also fewer levers to pull for hardening. IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service What It Is The cloud provider gives you virtualised compute, storage, and networking. You get a virtual machine (or bare metal), and everything above the hypervisor is your problem. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine, AWS EBS (storage), Azure Blob Storage (when used raw) What the Customer Controls Operating system (choice, patching, configuration) Runtime environment (language runtimes, web servers) Application code Middleware Data Network configuration (security groups, firewall rules, VPC/VNET routing) IaaS Attack Surface | Attack Vector | Description | | | | | Exposed services | SSH, RDP, web servers, databases exposed to internet via misconfigured security groups | | Unpatched OS | Customer is responsible for OS patching — missed patches = CVEs | | IMDSv1 SSRF | Instance metadata service accessible from instance — SSRF can steal IAM credentials | | Instance profile abuse | EC2 instance attached to an over permissive IAM role — compromise the instance, get the role | | EBS snapshot exposure | Snapshots shared publicly — attacker can mount and read the disk | | Userdata scripts | EC2 userdata (startup scripts) often contain credentials or config that's readable | | Public AMIs | Custom AMIs (disk images) shared publicly may contain secrets or sensitive config | | Default credentials | Out of box services running with default passwords | [!warning] IaaS is the broadest attack surface You're responsible for the OS and everything up. One missed patch, one misconfigured security group, one IMDSv1 SSRF — and the whole instance, and its IAM role, is compromised. PaaS — Platform as a Service What It Is The provider manages the OS, runtime, middleware, and scaling infrastructure. You deploy your application code and configure the service. You don't manage servers. Examples: AWS Lambda, AWS RDS, Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, Google App Engine, Google Cloud Functions, Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk What the Customer Controls Application code Data Service configuration (connection strings, environment variables, access policies) Identity and access (who can invoke the function, who can connect to the database) PaaS Attack Surface | Attack Vector | Description | | | | | Execution role abuse | Lambda/Function App has an over permissive IAM/managed identity role — compromise the function, get the role | | Environment variable exposure | Database passwords, API keys stored in function environment variables (visible in console, sometimes in logs) | | Publicly accessible databases | RDS/Azure SQL with "public access" enabled and weak auth | | Event injection | Lambda triggered by SQS/S3/API Gateway — malicious payloads in the event source affect function behaviour | | Dependency vulnerabilities | Application code using outdated libraries with known CVEs (provider doesn't patch your code) | | Function enumeration | Listing all Lambda functions, their triggers, their roles — maps the application architecture | | Misconfigured API Gateway | No authentication on API endpoints, resource policy too permissive | | Container image vulnerabilities | If PaaS uses container based deployment — vulnerable base images | [!tip] PaaS narrows OS level risk, opens IAM risk You don't worry about OS patches with Lambda. But the IAM execution role attached to that Lambda, and what's in its environment variables, is entirely your problem. SaaS — Software as a Service What It Is The provider delivers a fully managed application. The customer uses it — they don't manage the infrastructure, OS, runtime, or (usually) the application code. Examples: Microsoft 365 (Exchange, SharePoint, Teams), Google Workspace, Salesforce, Slack, Dropbox, ServiceNow, GitHub (the SaaS product) What the Customer Controls Data and content User accounts and access control (who can access what) Configuration of the SaaS product (sharing settings, external access, integrations) Authentication settings (SSO, MFA enforcement) SaaS Attack Surface | Attack Vector | Description | | | | | Misconfigured sharing settings | Files/docs/repos shared publicly or with entire organisation when should be restricted | | Weak authentication | No MFA enforced, weak password policies, no Conditional Access | | OAuth app abuse | Third party apps granted excessive permissions to the SaaS (e.g., app with mail read access to all inboxes) | | Account takeover | Phishing, credential stuffing against SaaS login — if no MFA, game over | | Data exfiltration via SaaS features | Legitimate sync features used to exfiltrate data (SharePoint sync, Google Drive sharing) | | API key exposure | SaaS platforms issue API tokens that can be leaked (GitHub tokens, Slack tokens in code) | | Insider threat via SaaS | Over permissioned admin accounts in the SaaS product | | Supply chain via integrations | Third party integrations/plugins to the SaaS with excessive access or vulnerabilities | [!warning] In SaaS, identity is everything The provider handles almost all technical security. What remains is identity, access configuration, and data governance. A compromised admin account in Microsoft 365 can be catastrophic without MFA. Service Model Comparison — Pentester's View | Factor | IaaS | PaaS | SaaS | | | | | | | Pentest focus | OS, network, IAM, CVEs | IAM, env vars, code, event injection | Auth, config, API tokens, data access | | Primary risk | Unpatched OS + over permissive IAM | Over permissive execution roles + exposed secrets | Account takeover + misconfigured sharing | | OS level access | Yes (you own the OS) | No (provider owns runtime) | No | | Most impactful finding | IMDSv1 SSRF to IAM credential theft | Execution role with wildcard permissions | Admin account with no MFA | | Logging | CloudTrail + OS logs | CloudTrail + function logs | SaaS audit log (if enabled) | Serverless — A Special Case Serverless is a subset of PaaS where you write functions that execute in response to events. No servers to manage at all — not even conceptually. The compute is completely ephemeral. Why it matters for security: No OS to harden — that's the provider's problem No persistent environment — can't install a rootkit or maintain a reverse shell the traditional way All persistence must be via IAM backdoors, data store modifications, or function code modification Attack surface is concentrated on: the function's IAM execution role , environment variables , trigger configuration , and function code quality This is covered in depth in MODULE 5 — Serverless & PaaS Attack Surface. Quick Reference — Attack Surface by Service Model Related Notes 00.1 — Cloud Pentesting vs On Prem Pentesting 00.2 — Shared Responsibility Model 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters MODULE 5 — Serverless & PaaS Attack Surface 01.4 — Lambda Attacks 02.5 — App Service and Function App Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 0 — Cloud Foundations/00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters.md
title: 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts Every Pentester Must Know
body: 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts Every Pentester Must Know What This Note Covers Before you run a single command against a cloud environment, you need to understand the foundational concepts that make cloud architecture different from on prem. This note covers regions, availability zones, tenants, accounts, subscriptions, projects, resource groups, and the attacker mindset shift required for cloud engagements. Regions and Availability Zones Regions A region is a physical geographic location where a cloud provider operates data centres. Each major provider has regions across the world: AWS: (N. Virginia), (Ireland), (Singapore), etc. Azure: , , , etc. GCP: , , , etc. Why this matters for pentesting: Resources (EC2 instances, S3 buckets, databases) exist in specific regions IAM policies may be global or region specific CloudTrail, logging, and monitoring can be enabled per region — missing a region means missing visibility Cross region data replication can be a data exfiltration path You must enumerate every region during a pentest, not just the obvious ones [!warning] Region blind spots Attackers love under monitored regions. If a company primarily operates in , they may not have CloudTrail enabled in . Attackers create resources in obscure regions to avoid detection. Availability Zones (AZs) Within a region, cloud providers operate multiple isolated availability zones — physically separate data centres with independent power, cooling, and networking. For example, has AZs: , , , etc. For pentesting: AZs are mostly an architectural concern (high availability). From an attacker's perspective, if you compromise one AZ, you have access to the others in the same region via the cloud's internal networking. Accounts, Tenants, Subscriptions, and Projects These are the fundamental isolation boundaries in each cloud. Everything is contained within one of these. Understanding the boundaries tells you the blast radius of a compromise. AWS — Accounts An AWS Account is the top level isolation boundary Each account has its own IAM, billing, resource namespace Resources in Account A cannot access resources in Account B by default Large organisations use AWS Organisations to manage multiple accounts (dev, prod, security, logging accounts) Cross account access is possible via IAM role assumption — this is a key attack path Azure — Tenants and Subscriptions An Azure Tenant (also called an Entra ID / Azure AD tenant) is the top level directory — it holds all users, groups, and app registrations Within a tenant, there are one or more Subscriptions — each subscription is a billing and resource management boundary Resources live within subscriptions, organised into Resource Groups A large organisation may have one tenant with many subscriptions (prod, dev, test, shared services) GCP — Organisations, Folders, and Projects A GCP Organisation is the root node — tied to a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain Within an organisation, there are Folders (optional grouping, like departments) Resources live in Projects — each project has its own billing, IAM, and resource namespace A large company might have hundreds of projects (one per application, environment, or team) [!tip] Key concept: escalating scope During a cloud pentest, you start in one account/subscription/project. As you escalate privileges, you may gain access to other accounts/projects via trust relationships. Always check: "Can I assume roles in other accounts? Can I access other projects?" Resource Groups (Azure) In Azure, a Resource Group is a logical container for related resources (a web app + its database + its storage account might all live in one resource group). Resource groups: Have their own IAM assignments (you can grant access at the resource group level) Are always in a specific Azure region Are used to organise resources for management and billing Attack relevance: If you gain Owner access to a resource group, you control everything in it. Resource Group level IAM misconfigurations are common. IAM — The Central Concept Every action in every cloud environment is governed by Identity and Access Management (IAM) . This is the single most important concept in cloud security. IAM answers two questions: 1. Who are you? (authentication / identity) 2. What are you allowed to do? (authorisation / permissions) Identities in Cloud (who can act) | AWS | Azure | GCP | | | | | | IAM User | Azure AD User | Google Account / G Suite User | | IAM Role | Service Principal / Managed Identity | Service Account | | IAM Group | Azure AD Group | Google Group | | Root Account | Global Administrator | Org Admin | | AWS Service | Azure Resource | GCP Service | Permissions in Cloud (what they can do) | AWS | Azure | GCP | | | | | | IAM Policy (JSON) | Azure RBAC Role Assignment | IAM Binding (member + role) | | Inline Policy | Azure Policy | Org Policy | | Resource Policy (S3, SQS) | Resource Policy (Storage, Key Vault) | Bucket IAM / Resource IAM | | Permission Boundary | — | — | The Golden Rule of Cloud Pentesting If you control an identity, you can do everything that identity is permitted to do. This is why credentials are so valuable. Finding an IAM access key = finding out what that identity can do. If it can do a lot, you've effectively compromised the environment without exploiting a single CVE. The Metadata Service Every cloud provider runs a metadata service accessible from within compute instances. This service provides the instance with information about itself — and critically, temporary credentials for its attached IAM role . | Provider | Metadata URL | | | | | AWS | | | Azure | | | GCP | | Why this is critical: The metadata service is not accessible from the internet — only from within the instance However, if an application running on the instance has an SSRF (Server Side Request Forgery) vulnerability, an external attacker can use it to reach the metadata service From the metadata service, you can retrieve temporary IAM credentials With those credentials, you now have the permissions of the EC2/VM instance's attached role This is one of the most impactful and common attack chains in cloud security. Covered in depth in 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks. Attacker Mindset for Cloud Engagements Credential Centric Thinking When you find any of the following, treat it as your primary objective to enumerate and exploit: AWS Access Key ID + Secret Access Key Azure Service Principal credentials (client ID + client secret, or certificate) GCP Service Account JSON key file Any token, cookie, or OAuth token for a cloud identity The chain: Find credential → Validate identity → Enumerate permissions → Escalate privileges → Achieve objective Blast Radius Assessment Before acting on a privileged identity, mentally map the blast radius: What services can this identity access? Can it create/delete resources? Can it access other accounts/projects? Can it read secrets, databases, storage? Can it modify IAM (the most dangerous capability)? [!danger] IAM modify = game over If an identity can create IAM policies, attach policies to users, or assume other roles — it can escalate to admin. This is the cloud equivalent of "DA or bust". Always check for IAM modification permissions first. Lateral Movement via IAM In on prem, lateral movement means: compromise one machine, pivot to the next via the network. In cloud, lateral movement means: use one identity's permissions to assume another identity (role assumption), invoke a service that runs as a different identity, or use one service's output to gain access to another. Common cloud lateral movement paths: — assume a different IAM role Invoke a Lambda function that runs as a more permissive role Access a Secrets Manager secret that contains another service's credentials Use EC2's instance profile to interact with S3, then find credentials in S3 The Principle of Least Privilege — Why It's Always Violated In theory, every identity should have the minimum permissions needed to do its job. In practice: Developers grant because it's easier Copy paste IAM policies from Stack Overflow include wildcards Service accounts accumulate permissions over time as features are added and never cleaned up Temporary "emergency" permissions become permanent Your job is to find these accumulations and demonstrate their impact. title: 00.6 — Tool Setup — CLI Tools and Security Frameworks
body: 00.6 — Tool Setup — CLI Tools and Security Frameworks What This Note Covers The core tools for every cloud security engagement — installation, configuration, and first use syntax for AWS CLI, Azure CLI, gcloud CLI, and the major cloud security frameworks: ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, Pacu, ROADtools, Stormspotter, and SkyArk. AWS CLI What It Is The official command line interface for interacting with all AWS services. Every cloud pentester needs this. All AWS API calls can be made through it. Install Configure with Credentials Core Flags Essential First Commands on Engagement Azure CLI (az) What It Is Microsoft's official CLI for managing Azure resources and Azure AD / Entra ID. Equivalent to AWS CLI for the Azure ecosystem. Install Authenticate Core First Commands Google Cloud CLI (gcloud) What It Is Google's official CLI for GCP. Manages compute, storage, IAM, Kubernetes, and all other GCP services. Install Authenticate Core First Commands ScoutSuite — Multi Cloud Misconfiguration Scanner What It Is Open source multi cloud security auditing tool by NCC Group. Connects to a cloud account, pulls config data from all services, and generates an HTML report of security issues. Supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and others. Install Usage What to Look For in the Report ScoutSuite flags findings by severity. Priority review areas: IAM: users without MFA, over permissive policies, unused access keys S3: public buckets, buckets without encryption, buckets without logging EC2: security groups with on sensitive ports, instances without monitoring CloudTrail: disabled regions, no log file validation RDS: publicly accessible instances, unencrypted storage Prowler — AWS/Azure/GCP Compliance Scanner What It Is Open source cloud security tool focused on compliance and best practices. Checks against CIS Benchmarks, PCI DSS, SOC2, GDPR, and more. More compliance focused than ScoutSuite. Install Usage Pacu — AWS Exploitation Framework What It Is Pacu is the Metasploit for AWS. Open source AWS exploitation framework developed by Rhino Security Labs. Contains modules for enumeration, privilege escalation, persistence, exfiltration, and more. Install Basic Usage [!warning] Use Pacu carefully in production Some modules take destructive or high visibility actions. Always read a module's description before running. Use where available during initial testing. ROADtools — Azure AD Enumeration What It Is ROADtools is an Azure AD/Entra ID enumeration and analysis framework. It dumps Azure AD data and provides a graphical interface for exploring users, groups, app registrations, service principals, and relationships. Install Usage ROADtools collects: users, groups, service principals, app registrations, OAuth permission grants, device registrations, role assignments. Extremely useful for mapping privilege escalation paths in Azure AD. CloudMapper — AWS Network Visualisation What It Is Open source tool by Duo Security for visualising AWS account network topology. Helps you understand VPC configurations, security groups, and connectivity at a glance. title: 00.7 — Lab Setup and Practice Environments
body: 00.7 — Lab Setup and Practice Environments What This Note Covers How to build a free cloud security lab, and where to practice cloud pentesting skills legally. This covers free tier account setup, intentionally vulnerable cloud environments, and curated practice platforms. Free Tier Account Setup Before practising against intentionally vulnerable labs, you need cloud provider accounts. All three offer free tiers. AWS Free Tier [!danger] Protect your root account and API keys AWS root account = full unrestricted access, including billing. If compromised, you can face thousands in fraudulent charges. Enable MFA on root immediately. Never generate root access keys. Azure Free Account GCP Free Tier Intentionally Vulnerable Cloud Labs These are deliberately misconfigured cloud environments designed for learning. Legal, safe, and exactly what you need to build practical skills. flaws.cloud — AWS (Attacker Path) What it is: A series of AWS security challenges created by Scott Piper. Each level is a misconfigured AWS resource that you must compromise to find the secret that unlocks the next level. Topics covered: Public S3 buckets and enumeration EC2 instance profile credential theft IMDSv1 metadata service exploitation AWS snapshot exposure IAM role enumeration and assumption URL: http://flaws.cloud Cost: Free Access: No account needed — you interact from your own machine using AWS CLI flaws2.cloud — AWS (Attacker + Defender Paths) What it is: Sequel to flaws.cloud, by the same author. Two parallel tracks: Attacker path: Compromise cloud services to progress Defender path: You're given CloudTrail logs and must answer forensic questions about what the attacker did Why it's valuable: The defender track teaches you what cloud attacks look like from a detection and IR perspective — essential for both red and blue team work. URL: http://flaws2.cloud Cost: Free CloudGoat — AWS (Scenario Based Exploitation) What it is: "Vulnerable by Design" AWS deployment tool by Rhino Security Labs. Creates real AWS infrastructure (in your own AWS account) with specific vulnerable scenarios to practice against. Topics covered (scenarios): — IAM policy version privilege escalation — Lambda execution role abuse — S3 bucket enumeration and data exfiltration — SSRF to metadata service to IAM credential theft — Secrets leaked in CI/CD environment variables — SQS injection and business logic abuse URL: https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/cloudgoat Cost: Free (you pay AWS costs, usually minimal — a few dollars per session) [!warning] CloudGoat deploys real AWS resources These are real resources in your AWS account. They cost real money (usually $1 5 per session). Always destroy scenarios when done. Set up a billing alert. AzureGoat — Azure What it is: INE's intentionally vulnerable Azure environment. Deploys a series of misconfigurations covering Azure services. Topics covered: Azure AD misconfigurations Managed identity abuse Storage account exposure App Service vulnerabilities Function App privilege escalation URL: https://github.com/ine labs/AzureGoat Cost: Free (Azure costs apply, use free credit) GCPGoat — GCP What it is: INE's intentionally vulnerable GCP environment, equivalent to AzureGoat for Google Cloud. Topics covered: Service account key exposure GCS bucket misconfigurations Compute Engine metadata abuse Cloud Function privilege escalation IAM binding weaknesses URL: https://github.com/ine labs/GCPGoat Cost: Free (GCP costs apply, use $300 credit) HackTheBox — Cloud Machines HackTheBox (HTB) has cloud themed machines and challenges. As of 2024, they have a dedicated Cloud category. These are real Linux/Windows machines with cloud misconfigurations or cloud credential based attack paths. Access: https://hackthebox.com Cost: Free tier + Pro subscription (£14/month) for active machines TryHackMe — Cloud Rooms TryHackMe has guided cloud security rooms, good for beginners before tackling CloudGoat. Notable rooms: AWS — IAM misconfigurations Cloud Storage Attacks Intro to Cloud Security Access: https://tryhackme.com Cost: Free tier + Premium (£10/month) for all rooms Recommended Learning Path Follow this sequence to build from zero to capable: Quick Reference — Lab Setup Commands Related Notes 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters 00.6 — Tool Setup — CLI and Frameworks MODULE 1 — AWS Security & Attack Techniques MODULE 8 — Cloud Security Assessment Methodology

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals.md
title: 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals
body: 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals What This Note Covers AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the absolute foundation of AWS security. Every action in AWS is governed by IAM. This note covers what IAM is, how it works, every component type, and how each component maps to an attack surface. What Is AWS IAM? IAM is AWS's system for controlling who can do what across all AWS services and resources. Every API call made to AWS — whether by a human, an application, or an AWS service — goes through IAM for authorisation. IAM answers two questions: 1. Authentication: Are you who you say you are? (Valid credentials?) 2. Authorisation: Are you allowed to do what you're asking? (Permissions?) IAM is global — it's not region specific. An IAM user or role created in one region is available everywhere. IAM Components 1. IAM Users A user is a permanent identity representing a person or application. It has: A username Optional password (for console access) Optional access keys (for CLI/API access) — up to 2 at a time Optional MFA device [!warning] Access keys are the primary attack surface Unlike passwords, access keys work programmatically — no MFA challenge, no browser, just the key pair. A leaked access key gives an attacker full programmatic access as that user, 24/7, from anywhere. 2. IAM Groups A group is a collection of IAM users. You attach policies to groups rather than individual users. A user can belong to multiple groups and inherits all permissions from all groups. Attack relevance: If you can add your compromised user to a group (via ), you inherit that group's permissions — a common privilege escalation path. 3. IAM Roles A role is an identity with permissions, but no permanent credentials . It's assumed by: AWS services (EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks) IAM users in the same or different accounts Web identity / OIDC federated users SAML federated users When a role is assumed, AWS issues temporary security credentials (access key + secret key + session token) that expire (typically 1 12 hours). [!tip] Roles are the gold standard target Roles are attached to services. Compromise an EC2 instance → steal its instance profile role credentials → act as that role. This is the most common cloud lateral movement path. 4. IAM Policies A policy is a JSON document that defines permissions. It states what actions are allowed or denied on what resources under what conditions . Policy types: | Type | What It Is | | | | | AWS Managed Policy | Pre built by AWS, e.g. , | | Customer Managed Policy | Created by the customer, reusable | | Inline Policy | Embedded directly in a user/group/role — not reusable | | Resource Based Policy | Attached to a resource (S3 bucket, SQS queue, Lambda) instead of an identity | | Permission Boundary | Maximum permissions an identity can ever have, regardless of other policies | | Service Control Policy (SCP) | Org level guardrail — restricts what accounts in an AWS Org can do | | Session Policy | Passed at time to further restrict the role's permissions for that session | 5. Policy Structure — JSON Anatomy Key fields: : or . Explicit Deny always wins. : The API action being permitted/denied. = all actions. : The ARN of the resource this applies to. = all resources. : Optional conditions (IP range, MFA required, time of day, etc.) [!danger] Wildcard policies are the root of all evil on = full admin. This is AdministratorAccess. Finding it on any non admin user or role is a critical finding. Identity Policies vs Resource Policies Identity policy: Attached to a user, group, or role. Defines what that identity can do. Resource policy: Attached to a resource (S3 bucket, SQS queue, Lambda, KMS key). Defines who can access that resource. Cross account access requires both sides: For a principal in Account A to access a resource in Account B, both the identity policy (in Account A) AND the resource policy (in Account B) must allow it. Trust Policies A trust policy is the special policy attached to an IAM role that defines who is allowed to assume that role . It's a resource based policy on the role itself. [!warning] Overly permissive trust policies = privilege escalation If a trust policy allows or allows an account you control, you can assume that role. If the role has powerful permissions, you've escalated. Modifying trust policies ( ) is itself a privilege escalation technique. Permission Boundaries A permission boundary is an advanced IAM feature. It sets the maximum permissions that an identity can have. Even if a policy grants , if the permission boundary only allows , the effective permissions are only S3. Attack relevance: If you can remove or replace a permission boundary ( , ), you can escalate privileges even if boundaries were used as a security control. IAM Policy Evaluation Logic When AWS evaluates whether to allow an action, it follows this order: [!tip] The default is DENY Everything is denied unless explicitly allowed. This is the principle of least privilege baked into the system. The attacker's goal is to find identities where "explicitly allowed" includes far more than it should. The ARN (Amazon Resource Name) Every AWS resource has an ARN — a unique identifier. Note: IAM ARNs have no region (IAM is global). S3 bucket ARNs have no region or account. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks.md
title: 01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks
body: 01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks What This Note Covers How to enumerate IAM without credentials, how to validate and enumerate with credentials, how to find exposed access keys in the wild, and how to determine what a compromised key can do. Phase 1: Unauthenticated IAM Enumeration Before you have any credentials, there's still information you can extract about an AWS account and its IAM configuration. 1. Account ID Discovery The AWS account ID (12 digit number) is needed for constructing ARNs and cross account attacks. It's often discoverable without credentials. 2. Username / Principal Enumeration (No Credentials) AWS has a quirk: when you try to attach a policy to a non existent principal, the error is different from trying to attach to a principal that exists. [!tip] User enumeration is low value alone Knowing usernames without credentials doesn't give you direct access. Combine with password spraying against the AWS console login (rare — most orgs use SSO) or focus on finding leaked credentials for those users. 3. S3 Bucket Discovery (Unauthenticated) S3 bucket names are globally unique. Enumeration is possible without credentials. This is covered in depth in 01.4 — S3 Attacks. Phase 2: With Credentials — Validate and Enumerate Step 1: Validate the Credentials The very first thing you do with any found credential pair. Interpreting the UserId prefix: | Prefix | Identity Type | | | | | | IAM User | | | IAM Role | | | Temporary credentials (assumed role) | | | IAM Group | | | EC2 Instance Profile | | | Managed Policy | | | Access Key (long term, IAM user) | Step 2: Enumerate Permissions The challenge: IAM doesn't have a single "list your permissions" API. You have to enumerate policies attached to the user, their groups, and any inline policies. Manual enumeration: Automated enumeration — enumerate iam: [!tip] enumerate iam makes noise It fires hundreds of API calls. CloudTrail will log all of them. In a real engagement, this is noisy. Use with awareness of detection, or reserve for test environments. Automated enumeration — Pacu: Phase 3: Finding Exposed Access Keys This is often the initial foothold. Keys get leaked constantly. Source 1: GitHub / Public Code Repositories The most common source of leaked AWS credentials. Source 2: Environment Variables in Application Code Developers hardcode credentials in: files committed to repos Docker Compose files Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets (base64 encoded, not encrypted) CI/CD pipeline configs (GitHub Actions , Jenkins files) Source 3: EC2 Instance Metadata Service (SSRF) If an application on an EC2 instance has an SSRF vulnerability, the metadata service leaks temporary role credentials. Covered fully in 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks. Source 4: S3 Bucket Contents Misconfigured public S3 buckets frequently contain: files Configuration files with hardcoded credentials Application backups with embedded secrets Database dumps Source 5: Lambda Function Configuration Lambda environment variables are visible in the console and via the API to anyone with . Source 6: EC2 Userdata EC2 instance startup scripts (userdata) are often stored with credentials to bootstrap applications. Phase 4: Using Temporary Credentials When you get temporary credentials (from AssumeRole or metadata service), they come with a session token that must be included in every request. [!warning] Temporary credentials expire Credentials from the metadata service typically expire in 1 6 hours. If you need long term persistence, you need to create permanent credentials (new IAM user + access key) or backdoor a role — covered in MODULE 9 — Cloud Persistence. Quick Reference — Access Key Attack Chain Related Notes 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks 01.4 — S3 Attacks 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation MODULE 7 — Cloud Reconnaissance and OSINT

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks.md
title: 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks (IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2)
body: 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks (IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2) What This Note Covers The EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) is one of the highest impact attack vectors in AWS. This note covers what it is, why IMDSv1 is critical, how to exploit SSRF to steal IAM credentials via the metadata service, and the full exploitation chain from SSRF to account compromise. What Is the EC2 Instance Metadata Service? Every EC2 instance can query a special HTTP endpoint at to retrieve information about itself. This is how applications running on EC2 discover their own: Instance ID, AMI ID, region, availability zone Hostname and IP addresses IAM role name and temporary credentials User data (the startup script) Security groups and network interfaces The address is a link local address — it's only accessible from within the EC2 instance itself. It is not routable over the internet. Until SSRF happens. IMDSv1 — The Vulnerable Version IMDSv1 (Instance Metadata Service version 1) requires no authentication . Any HTTP GET request from within the instance to is served immediately, no questions asked. This means: If any application running on that instance has an SSRF vulnerability, an attacker can use it to reach the metadata service The attacker gets the temporary IAM credentials of the instance's attached role With those credentials, the attacker can act as that role anywhere in AWS Checking if IMDSv1 Is Enabled IMDSv2 — The Mitigated Version IMDSv2 requires a session token that must be obtained first via a PUT request before any metadata can be read. The PUT request cannot be made via SSRF in typical configurations because: It requires a header Many SSRF vulnerabilities only allow GET requests Proxies typically strip custom headers [!tip] IMDSv2 isn't a complete fix If the SSRF can make PUT requests with custom headers (some can), IMDSv2 is still bypassable. IMDSv2 raises the bar significantly but isn't bulletproof. Full Exploitation Chain: SSRF → IAM Credentials Scenario Target: A web application running on EC2 that has an SSRF vulnerability (e.g., a URL fetching feature, a PDF generator, an image proxy). The EC2 instance has an IAM instance profile attached with the role . Step 1: Identify SSRF The application has a parameter that fetches a URL: Test if internal URLs are accessible: If the response contains metadata categories ( , , etc.) → SSRF confirmed, IMDSv1 enabled. Step 2: Get the IAM Role Name Response: Step 3: Get the Temporary Credentials Response: Step 4: Use the Credentials Other Valuable Metadata Endpoints Beyond credentials, the metadata service exposes other useful information: [!warning] User data is a treasure chest The EC2 user data (startup script) is often where admins put database passwords, API keys, bootstrap credentials, and configuration. Always retrieve and examine it. SSRF Bypasses for Metadata Endpoint Some applications have SSRF protections that block directly. Common bypass techniques: Other Cloud Metadata Endpoints The same SSRF to metadata pattern applies to Azure and GCP: [!tip] GCP metadata is harder to SSRF The header requirement means simple SSRF often can't reach it. But if you can control headers or use a blind SSRF that reflects responses, it's still exploitable. Detection and Defences What This Looks Like in CloudTrail Defences 1. Enforce IMDSv2 — set on all instances 2. Disable IMDS entirely if the application doesn't need it 3. Restrict EC2 instance roles — minimum permissions required for the application 4. WAF rules — block HTTP responses containing metadata patterns 5. Fix SSRF in the application — validate and allowlist URLs Quick Reference — Metadata Exploitation Related Notes 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals 01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation 03.3 — GCP Metadata and Service Account Attacks 02.4 — Managed Identity Abuse

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.4 — S3 Attacks.md
title: 01.4 — S3 Attacks
body: 01.4 — S3 Attacks What This Note Covers Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is the most commonly misconfigured AWS service and responsible for more data breaches than any other. This note covers bucket enumeration, public bucket discovery, ACL and policy misconfigurations, unauthenticated access, data exfiltration, and bucket takeover. What Is S3? S3 is AWS's object storage service. You store objects (files) in buckets (containers). Buckets have globally unique names across all of AWS. Access is controlled via: Bucket ACLs (legacy, per object or per bucket) — grant access to AWS accounts or "everyone" Bucket policies (resource based IAM policies) — JSON, define who can do what IAM policies (identity based) — on the calling user/role A bucket can be accessed: Authenticated — via AWS credentials Unauthenticated (public) — if the ACL or policy explicitly allows it S3 Bucket Naming and Discovery S3 bucket names are global and predictable. Companies often name buckets after their products, domains, or environments. S3 URLs — Two Formats Automated Bucket Discovery DNS Based Discovery S3 buckets used as static websites or via CloudFront have DNS CNAMEs pointing to them. During subdomain enumeration, you'll find: Public Bucket Access Checking for Public Access Types of Public Access Misconfigurations 1. Public Bucket ACL (Block Public Access disabled) AWS introduced "Block Public Access" settings (4 toggles) to prevent accidental public exposure. When disabled: 2. Public Bucket Policy 3. Public ACL on individual objects Objects can have their own ACL set to . Even if the bucket is private, individual objects may be publicly accessible if their ACL was set incorrectly. Authenticated Enumeration (with Credentials) With valid credentials (any AWS identity), you can enumerate buckets and try to access data. [!tip] Check versioning for historical secrets If a bucket has versioning enabled and a secret was once stored there but deleted, the old version is still accessible. Check old versions of config files. High Value S3 Targets When you have access to a bucket (public or authenticated), look for: Common high value findings in S3: files with database credentials SSH private keys TLS/SSL certificates and private keys Database dumps ( , ) Application backups containing configuration CloudTrail log files (attacker activity in other services) Access logs (internal URLs, user tokens in request logs) Terraform state files ( ) — contain resource IDs, sometimes secrets [!danger] Terraform state files files stored in S3 are extremely high value. They contain the current state of all infrastructure including resource IDs, and sometimes plaintext passwords for RDS, secrets passed as variables, etc. Bucket Takeover If a subdomain CNAME points to an S3 bucket that no longer exists, you can create a bucket with that name and serve content from it. This is a subdomain takeover via S3. This can be used for XSS, phishing, cookie theft, CSP bypass, etc. S3 Cross Account Access S3 resource policies can grant access to other accounts. When combined with weak conditions, this leads to cross account data exposure. CloudTrail: S3 Logging Blind Spots S3 data events (object level access: GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) are not logged in CloudTrail by default. Only management events (creating/deleting buckets, changing policies) are logged. This means: if data event logging isn't explicitly enabled, your S3 data exfiltration won't appear in CloudTrail.
