path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation.md
title: 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation
body: 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation What This Note Covers IAM privilege escalation is the process of using a low privilege AWS identity to gain higher privileges — ultimately admin. AWS has 25+ documented privilege escalation paths. This note covers the theory, the most impactful techniques with exact commands, and how to scan for them. The Core Concept In AWS, privilege escalation doesn't require exploiting a CVE. It requires finding IAM permissions that allow you to modify your own or others' permissions , directly or indirectly. The key insight: any permission that lets you affect IAM, or lets you execute code as a more privileged identity, is a potential escalation path. [!tip] The attacker's question For every permission you have, ask: "Can this permission — alone or combined with others — let me do something that grants me more permissions?" Automated Detection First Before manually reviewing permissions, run automated tools: Technique 1: CreatePolicyVersion (Set as Default) Permissions needed: If you can create a new version of an existing customer managed policy, you can replace it with one that grants you , then set it as the default. Technique 2: AttachUserPolicy / AttachRolePolicy / AttachGroupPolicy Permissions needed: (or role/group variants) Directly attach the AWS managed policy to yourself. Technique 3: PutUserPolicy / PutRolePolicy / PutGroupPolicy (Inline Policies) Permissions needed: (or role/group variant) Create or overwrite an inline policy on yourself granting admin. Technique 4: AddUserToGroup Permissions needed: If a group has admin permissions, add yourself to it. Technique 5: UpdateAssumeRolePolicy (Modify Trust Policy) Permissions needed: Modify a role's trust policy to allow your identity to assume it. Technique 6: iam:PassRole + Lambda (Create Function + Invoke) Permissions needed: , , Create a Lambda function, pass it an admin IAM role as its execution role, then invoke it to execute code as that role. Technique 7: iam:PassRole + EC2 (Instance Profile) Permissions needed: , , access to the instance (SSH or SSM) Launch an EC2 instance with an admin IAM role attached as the instance profile. Then access the instance and steal the role's temporary credentials from the metadata service. Technique 8: iam:PassRole + CloudFormation Permissions needed: , Create a CloudFormation stack that passes an admin role. CloudFormation executes as that role, and you can have it perform IAM actions on your behalf. Technique 9: CreateAccessKey (For Another User) Permissions needed: Create a new access key for another IAM user (who has more privileges than you). Technique 10: UpdateLoginProfile (Console Access) Permissions needed: If a privileged IAM user has console access, you can reset their password and log in as them. Technique 11: iam:PassRole + Glue (CreateJob) Permissions needed: , , AWS Glue is a data integration service. Create a Glue job with an admin role and execute arbitrary Python code as that role. Full Privilege Escalation Techniques Reference | | Technique | Permissions Required | | | | | | 1 | CreatePolicyVersion → set default | | | 2 | AttachUserPolicy | | | 3 | AttachRolePolicy | | | 4 | AttachGroupPolicy + AddUserToGroup | , | | 5 | PutUserPolicy (inline) | | | 6 | PutRolePolicy (inline) | | | 7 | AddUserToGroup | | | 8 | UpdateAssumeRolePolicy | | | 9 | PassRole + Lambda CreateFunction + Invoke | , , | | 10 | PassRole + EC2 RunInstances | , | | 11 | PassRole + CloudFormation | , | | 12 | PassRole + Glue CreateJob | , , | | 13 | PassRole + SageMaker CreateTrainingJob | , | | 14 | CreateAccessKey (other user) | | | 15 | UpdateLoginProfile (other user) | | | 16 | SetDefaultPolicyVersion (existing version) | | | 17 | Delete permission boundary | | | 18 | SSM SendCommand to privileged instance | , target with admin role | | 19 | CodeBuild CreateProject (with admin role) | , | | 20 | DataPipeline CreatePipeline | , | Quick Reference — Privesc Workflow Related Notes 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals 01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks MODULE 6 — Cloud Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 1 — AWS Security/01.6 — EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager, and CloudTrail.md
title: 01.6 — EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager, and CloudTrail
body: 01.6 — EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager, and CloudTrail What This Note Covers EC2 instance attacks beyond the metadata service, Lambda function exploitation, Secrets Manager enumeration, and CloudTrail — what it logs, what it misses, and how attackers evade it. EC2 Attacks 1. Userdata Exposure EC2 userdata (the startup script) is stored and retrievable by any authenticated principal with . 2. EBS Snapshot Exposure EBS snapshots are disk images that can be shared. Publicly shared snapshots can be mounted by anyone and the full filesystem read. [!danger] Public snapshots = full disk access Any publicly shared EBS snapshot gives read access to the entire filesystem. This includes , application configs, credential files, private keys, database files, and anything else on disk. 3. AMI Sharing Misconfigurations Custom AMIs can also be shared publicly. An AMI is a full disk image of an EC2 instance. 4. Security Group Misconfigurations Lambda Attacks 1. Environment Variable Exposure Lambda environment variables are visible to anyone with . Developers frequently store secrets here. 2. Overprivileged Execution Roles Every Lambda function has an IAM role (execution role). If that role has excessive permissions, compromising the function means accessing everything the role can do. 3. Function Enumeration and Code Download 4. Invocation Testing If you have , you can invoke functions directly and potentially trigger unintended behaviour. Secrets Manager and Parameter Store Secrets Manager AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets (database passwords, API keys, certificates) and handles rotation. It's far better than env variables — but access is still IAM controlled. Systems Manager Parameter Store Parameter Store is similar but stores parameters (plain strings, SecureString encrypted with KMS). [!tip] Parameter Store access is often overlooked IAM policies for SSM Parameter Store are frequently too broad ( on ). If your identity can read parameters, iterate through all paths — you'll find credentials. CloudTrail — Logging, Blind Spots, and Evasion What CloudTrail Is AWS CloudTrail records API calls made in your AWS account. It's the primary audit log for all AWS activity. What it logs: Management events: creating/deleting/modifying resources, IAM changes, console logins Data events (optional): S3 object level access, Lambda invocations, DynamoDB operations What it doesn't log by default: S3 data events (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) Lambda invocation events Read only API calls from some services Actions taken inside EC2 instances (OS level activity) Finding CloudTrail Gaps CloudTrail Blind Spots (for Attackers) Log Disabling / Manipulation [!danger] Disabling CloudTrail is itself logged (briefly) The act of disabling CloudTrail generates a CloudTrail event — which is logged before it's disabled. In organisations with real time alerting (CloudWatch Events → SNS), this will trigger an alert. Use more subtle techniques. Stealthier Evasion Techniques 1. Use services with minimal logging — some services generate less obvious logs 2. Use for public resources — unauthenticated requests to public S3 buckets don't show in CloudTrail 3. Use read only operations — , , are often not alerted on 4. Avoid IAM operations — IAM changes are heavily monitored 5. Stay within the same region as CloudTrail trails to appear "normal" Quick Reference — EC2, Lambda, Secrets Related Notes 01.1 — AWS IAM Fundamentals 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation MODULE 9 — Cloud Persistence and Defence Evasion MODULE 5 — Serverless and PaaS Attack Surface

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.1 — Azure Fundamentals.md
title: 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals
body: 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals What This Note Covers The foundational Azure concepts every pentester must internalise before touching any Azure environment: the hierarchy of tenants, subscriptions, resource groups, and the critical distinction between Azure AD (Entra ID) and Azure RBAC. The Azure Hierarchy Azure organises everything in a strict parent child hierarchy. Permissions flow downward — access granted at a higher level is inherited by everything below it. Management Groups Optional grouping above subscriptions. Large enterprises use them to apply governance (policies, RBAC) across many subscriptions at once. Subscriptions A subscription is the primary billing and resource management boundary in Azure. Each subscription: Has a unique Subscription ID (GUID) Belongs to exactly one Azure AD tenant Can contain multiple resource groups Has its own RBAC assignments [!tip] Multiple subscriptions = multiple attack surfaces Large organisations have dozens or hundreds of subscriptions (prod, dev, staging, per team, per project). Each is a separate resource boundary. Enumerate all subscriptions accessible with your current token — don't assume you're only in one. Resource Groups A resource group is a logical container for related resources. Key properties: Every Azure resource must belong to exactly one resource group Resource groups have a region (but can contain resources from other regions) RBAC can be assigned at the resource group level — Owner of a resource group = full control of everything in it Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it Azure AD (Entra ID) — The Identity Plane Azure Active Directory (recently rebranded Microsoft Entra ID ) is Azure's identity and access management service. It is completely separate from Azure Resource Manager (ARM) — the service that manages Azure resources. This is the most important architectural concept in Azure security: They are linked but separate. A Global Administrator in Azure AD has no automatic access to Azure resources (subscriptions). A subscription Owner has full control of Azure resources but no implicit Azure AD admin rights. [!warning] This separation is where attackers get caught out — and where defenders create gaps An attacker who compromises a subscription Owner can delete VMs but can't necessarily read Azure AD user passwords. An attacker who compromises a Global Admin can control the identity plane and elevate to any subscription through Azure AD settings. Azure AD — Core Identity Objects Users Azure AD users are either: Member users — employees, internal accounts Guest users — external collaborators (B2B) Groups Security groups and Microsoft 365 groups. Used to assign permissions to collections of users. Service Principals A service principal is the identity representation of an application (or managed service) in Azure AD. When an app registration is created, a service principal is automatically created in the tenant. Service principals can be assigned: Azure AD directory roles (e.g., Global Reader) Azure RBAC roles (e.g., Contributor on a subscription) API permissions to Microsoft Graph or other services [!danger] Overprivileged service principals are common and high value Developers create app registrations for CI/CD pipelines, automation scripts, and integrations. These often accumulate excessive permissions and their credentials (client secrets or certificates) get leaked in code repos. A service principal with on the subscription = full resource control. App Registrations An app registration is the application object in Azure AD. Think of it as the "blueprint" — the service principal is the "instance" in a tenant. App registrations define: Which APIs the app can access (API permissions) OAuth redirect URIs Credentials (client secrets, certificates) Managed Identities A managed identity is an Azure AD identity automatically managed by Azure for a resource (VM, App Service, Function App, etc.). No credentials to manage — Azure handles rotation. Two types: System assigned: Tied to a specific resource. Deleted when the resource is deleted. User assigned: Standalone resource. Can be assigned to multiple resources. When a VM has a managed identity, it can get an access token from the Azure IMDS metadata endpoint — the same SSRF → token theft pattern as AWS. Azure RBAC Azure Role Based Access Control (RBAC) governs access to Azure resources (not Azure AD). RBAC assignments have three components: 1. Security Principal — who (user, group, service principal, managed identity) 2. Role Definition — what permissions (built in or custom role) 3. Scope — where (management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource) Built in Roles (Most Important) | Role | Permissions | | | | | Owner | Full access + can grant access to others | | Contributor | Full access to manage resources, cannot grant access | | Reader | Read only access to everything | | User Access Administrator | Manage access only (no resource control) | | Virtual Machine Contributor | Manage VMs only | | Storage Blob Data Owner | Full S3 equivalent access to blob storage | | Key Vault Administrator | Full access to Key Vault secrets, keys, certs | Azure AD Directory Roles (Separate from RBAC) Directory roles govern Azure AD itself — not Azure resources. | Role | What It Controls | | | | | Global Administrator | Full control of Azure AD — can take over any subscription | | Privileged Role Administrator | Can assign any Azure AD role to anyone | | Application Administrator | Manage all app registrations and service principals | | Cloud Application Administrator | Same minus on prem app proxy | | Global Reader | Read everything in Azure AD | | Security Administrator | Manage security policies and read security data | [!danger] Global Administrator = total compromise A Global Admin can elevate themselves to Owner on any Azure subscription via the "Access management for Azure resources" setting in Azure AD properties. This is the highest value target in any Azure engagement. Quick Reference — Azure Fundamentals Commands Related Notes 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks.md
title: 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks
body: 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks What This Note Covers How to enumerate Azure AD / Entra ID without credentials, how to enumerate with credentials, and the primary token based attack techniques: OAuth device code phishing, access token theft, refresh token abuse, and Primary Refresh Token (PRT) attacks. Phase 1: Unauthenticated Azure AD Enumeration Azure AD exposes some information without authentication. This is by design — federated login requires knowing the tenant configuration. Tenant Discovery User Enumeration (No Credentials) Azure AD validates whether a user account exists before checking the password. This difference in responses allows username enumeration. [!warning] Federated tenants behave differently If the tenant uses federated authentication (ADFS, Okta, Ping), the enumeration response is always the same regardless of whether the user exists — no enumeration possible via this method. Tenant Information Gathering Phase 2: Authenticated Azure AD Enumeration Once you have credentials or a token, you can enumerate the tenant using Microsoft Graph API or Azure CLI. Using Azure CLI Using ROADtools (Best for Comprehensive Enum) Token Based Attacks Azure authentication is built on OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. Understanding tokens is essential for Azure AD attacks. Azure Token Types | Token | Lifetime | Purpose | | | | | | Access Token | 1 hour (default) | Presented to APIs to prove identity | | Refresh Token | 90 days (inactive) / rolling | Used to get new access tokens without re auth | | ID Token | Short | Identity information (not for API access) | | Primary Refresh Token (PRT) | 14 days | Device level token, highest value | Attack 1: OAuth Device Code Phishing Device code phishing abuses the OAuth device code flow — a legitimate flow designed for devices without browsers (smart TVs, IoT). The attacker initiates the flow and sends the device code to the victim, who authenticates on Microsoft's legitimate site, granting the attacker an access token and refresh token. Why it's effective: The victim authenticates on — completely legitimate. No malicious URL, no fake page. Bypasses MFA if the victim has already completed MFA. [!tip] TokenTacticsV2 automates this Attack 2: Access Token Theft and Reuse Access tokens are bearer tokens — anyone holding one can use it. Where Tokens Are Found Using a Stolen Access Token Attack 3: Refresh Token Abuse Refresh tokens are valid for 90 days (or 1 year for persistent sessions). If you get a refresh token, you can generate new access tokens for any Azure resource indefinitely. [!danger] One refresh token → access to all Azure services A single refresh token lets you request access tokens for any Azure service the identity has permissions to. This is why refresh tokens are so valuable — they're persistent and broad. Attack 4: Primary Refresh Token (PRT) Attacks The PRT is the most powerful token in Azure. It's issued to Azure AD joined or registered devices and is stored in the Local Security Authority (LSASS) on Windows. It can be used to generate access tokens for any resource without MFA challenges. What Makes PRTs Special Valid for 14 days, auto renewed on device activity Includes a session key signed by the device's TPM (or not, if TPM not used) Bypasses MFA — the MFA claim is embedded in the PRT Can be used to generate tokens for any resource PRT Extraction (requires code execution on the device) Using a Stolen PRT [!warning] PRT attacks require local access PRTs are protected on devices with TPM — the session key is bound to the hardware and cannot be extracted. On devices without TPM, the PRT can be stolen with local admin rights. Always check: is TPM enforced? Quick Reference — Enumeration and Token Commands Related Notes 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 02.6 — Azure Tools — ROADtools, AzureHound, MicroBurst 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse.md
title: 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse
body: 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse What This Note Covers Managed identities are the Azure equivalent of EC2 instance profiles — they give Azure resources an automatic identity without managing credentials. This note covers how managed identities work, how to steal tokens from them via the metadata service, and how to use those tokens to move laterally through Azure. What Is a Managed Identity? A managed identity is an Azure AD identity automatically created and managed by Azure for a specific resource. The resource (VM, App Service, Function App, Container Instance, AKS pod, etc.) gets an identity it can use to authenticate to any service that supports Azure AD auth — without storing any credentials. Azure handles: Identity creation in Azure AD Credential rotation (you never see the private key) Token issuance on request System Assigned vs User Assigned | Property | System Assigned | User Assigned | | | | | | Lifecycle | Tied to the resource — deleted with it | Standalone resource, independent lifecycle | | Assignment | One per resource | Can be assigned to multiple resources | | Object ID | Unique per resource | Single object, shared across assignments | | Use case | Single resource identity | Shared identity across multiple resources | The Attack: IMDS Token Theft The Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at is accessible from within any Azure compute resource. If a resource has a managed identity, you can request an access token from IMDS — no credentials needed, just network reachability. Attack scenarios: 1. You've gained code execution on an Azure VM (via RCE, webshell, SSH brute force) 2. You've exploited an SSRF vulnerability in a web app running on App Service, Azure Functions, or a VM 3. You have direct shell access via Azure Serial Console or Run Command feature Step 1: Confirm Managed Identity Exists Step 2: Request an Access Token [!tip] Request tokens for different resources The same managed identity can have permissions across multiple Azure services. Always request tokens for ARM, Graph, Key Vault, and Storage — you don't know which ones the identity has access to until you try. Step 3: Use the Token Step 4: Enumerate the Identity's Permissions SSRF to Managed Identity Token — App Service App Service (Azure's PaaS web hosting) also supports managed identities. The IMDS endpoint is the same. Azure Functions Managed Identity Abuse Function Apps running with a managed identity can be exploited the same way: Lateral Movement via Managed Identity Once you have a managed identity token, the next step is lateral movement — using the identity's permissions to access other resources. Common Lateral Movement Chains VM Managed Identity → Key Vault → Application Credentials: App Service Managed Identity → Storage Account → Code/Config: Managed Identity → Graph API → Azure AD Enumeration: Quick Reference — Managed Identity Exploitation Related Notes 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks.md
title: 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks
body: 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks What This Note Covers Azure Blob Storage and Azure Key Vault are where organisations store their most sensitive data and secrets. Both are frequently misconfigured. This note covers public blob access, SAS token abuse, shared key exposure, Key Vault access policy misconfigurations, and secret enumeration. Azure Blob Storage — Overview Azure Blob Storage is Azure's equivalent of S3. It has three components: Access is controlled at multiple levels: Storage Account level — network rules, shared key auth, public access setting Container level — public access tier (private, blob, container) RBAC — Azure roles (Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor/Owner) SAS tokens — time limited, scoped access tokens Attack 1: Anonymous Blob Access Azure containers can be set to three access tiers: | Tier | What's Public | | | | | Private | No public access (requires auth) | | Blob | Individual blobs are public if you know the URL, but listing is not | | Container | Full anonymous listing AND downloading of blobs | Discovery Attack 2: SAS Token Abuse A Shared Access Signature (SAS) token is a URI parameter string that grants time limited, scoped access to Azure Storage resources. There are three types: | SAS Type | Scope | | | | | Account SAS | Entire storage account (all services, containers) | | Service SAS | Single service (blob, queue, table, or file) | | User Delegation SAS | Blob/container, signed with Azure AD credentials | Where SAS Tokens Are Found SAS Token Anatomy Exploiting a Found SAS Token [!warning] Account level SAS tokens are critical If a SAS token covers the entire account (srt=sco) with read+list permissions, it exposes all data in all containers. Account level SAS tokens with write/delete are catastrophic. Attack 3: Storage Account Shared Key Every Azure Storage account has two account keys — 512 bit symmetric keys that grant full access to everything in the account. They're used for legacy authentication. [!danger] Storage account keys = God mode for storage Shared keys bypass RBAC, bypass network rules, and have no IP restriction by default. Anyone with the key has full read/write/delete access to all data in the account. Treat them like root credentials. Azure Key Vault — Overview Azure Key Vault stores: Secrets — arbitrary key value pairs (database passwords, API keys, connection strings) Keys — cryptographic keys (used for encryption operations, including Azure Disk Encryption) Certificates — TLS/SSL certificates with their private keys Access is controlled by two separate mechanisms : 1. Access Policies (legacy) — Key Vault's own ACL system, separate from Azure RBAC 2. Azure RBAC (newer, recommended) — standard Azure role assignments Both mechanisms can be misconfigured. Attack 4: Key Vault Access Policy Misconfigurations Enumerate Key Vault Access Policies Common Misconfigurations 1. Wildcard permissions granted to broad groups: 2. Service principals with excessive Key Vault permissions: 3. Key Vault accessible from public internet without firewall: Enumerating and Stealing Secrets Attack 5: Key Vault RBAC Misconfigurations When a Key Vault is configured for Azure RBAC (not access policies), standard RBAC roles apply: | Role | What It Allows | | | | | Key Vault Administrator | Full access to all secrets, keys, certs | | Key Vault Secrets Officer | Create/read/update/delete secrets | | Key Vault Secrets User | Read secret values | | Key Vault Reader | Read metadata only (not values) | [!tip] Using managed identity token to access Key Vault If you've stolen a managed identity token (via IMDS) and the managed identity has Key Vault permissions, request a vault scoped token and enumerate secrets: Quick Reference — Storage and Key Vault Related Notes 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 01.4 — S3 Attacks MODULE 7 — Cloud Reconnaissance and OSINT

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation.md
title: 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation
body: 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation What This Note Covers How to escalate privileges in Azure — both within Azure AD (directory roles) and from Azure AD into Azure resources (subscriptions). Covers the Global Admin escalation path, Application Administrator abuse, Conditional Access bypass, and cross service escalation chains. The Two Privilege Escalation Planes Azure has two separate permission systems, and escalation can happen in either direction: Path 1: Application Administrator → Service Principal Owner → Escalation Permissions needed: Azure AD role: or Application Administrators can create and manage app registrations and their service principals. If a service principal has been assigned high privilege roles (e.g., Contributor on a subscription), an Application Admin can add credentials to that service principal and authenticate as it. [!danger] This is extremely impactful Application Administrator is often granted broadly ("all devs need to create apps"). But any SP in the tenant that has Contributor or Owner on a subscription is now compromisable by every App Admin. This is one of the most common Azure escalation paths. Path 2: Global Admin → Subscription Owner (The Nuclear Option) Permissions needed: Azure AD role: Global Administrators have a special capability: they can elevate themselves to User Access Administrator on all Azure subscriptions in the tenant. This is done via the "Access management for Azure resources" toggle in Azure AD properties. [!danger] Global Admin = total Azure control A Global Administrator who activates this feature can take over every single Azure subscription in the organisation within minutes. This is why Global Admin is the highest value target in any Azure engagement. Path 3: Privileged Role Administrator Abuse Permissions needed: Azure AD role: This role can assign any Azure AD directory role to any user or service principal — including Global Administrator. Path 4: Global Reader → Targeted Escalation Permissions needed: Azure AD role: Global Reader can read everything in Azure AD — including: All users, groups, and their properties Service principal credentials metadata (not values, but existence) Application registration details Conditional Access policy configurations This is valuable for reconnaissance to find escalation paths , not direct escalation. Path 5: Owner of Resource Group → Key Vault → Secrets → SP Credentials A common lateral movement / escalation chain: Conditional Access Bypass Conditional Access policies restrict when and how users can authenticate. Common restrictions: Require MFA for all users Require compliant device Block sign in from outside specific IP ranges Block legacy authentication protocols Gap Analysis Legacy Authentication Bypass Many CA policies block modern auth but don't block legacy protocols (SMTP, IMAP, MAPI, Basic Auth). If any legacy auth is still enabled: Device Code Flow CA Bypass Device code phishing (covered in 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks) bypasses Conditional Access policies that require compliant devices, because the device code flow doesn't enforce device compliance at token issuance in all configurations. Path 6: Azure RBAC User Access Administrator Permissions needed: Azure RBAC role: at subscription or resource group scope This role can assign any Azure RBAC role — including Owner — to any identity. Privilege Escalation Paths — Quick Reference Table | Starting Permission | Escalation Path | End State | | | | | | Application Administrator | Add creds to privileged SP | SP's role (e.g., Sub Contributor) | | Privileged Role Administrator | Assign self Global Admin | Global Admin → Sub Owner | | Global Administrator | Elevate access toggle | Sub Owner on all subscriptions | | Resource Group Owner | Access Key Vault → steal SP creds | SP's role | | User Access Administrator | Assign self Owner role | Subscription Owner | | Global Reader | Map all escalation paths (recon) | Intel for further attack | | VM Managed Identity | IMDS token → ARM/KV/Graph | Identity's permissions | Quick Reference — Azure AD Privesc Commands Related Notes 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks 02.6 — Azure Tools MODULE 6 — Cloud Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 2 — Azure Security/02.6 — Azure Tools.md
title: 02.6 — Azure Tools — ROADtools, AzureHound, MicroBurst, AADInternals
body: 02.6 — Azure Tools — ROADtools, AzureHound, MicroBurst, AADInternals What This Note Covers The core Azure specific security toolset: installation, configuration, key commands, and what each tool does best. These are the tools you reach for on every Azure engagement. ROADtools What It Is ROADtools by Dirk jan Mollema is the foundational Azure AD enumeration framework. It dumps the entire Azure AD tenant into a local SQLite database and provides a GUI for browsing users, groups, service principals, app registrations, OAuth permissions, role assignments, and Conditional Access policies. Install Authentication Data Collection GUI Explorer Advanced — ROADtx (Token Exchange) AzureHound (BloodHound for Azure) What It Is AzureHound is the Azure collector for BloodHound — the attack path visualisation tool. It maps Azure AD and Azure RBAC relationships into a graph database and visualises privilege escalation paths. Install Collect Azure AD Data Import into BloodHound and Query [!tip] BloodHound is the fastest way to find escalation paths What takes hours of manual enumeration in ROADtools, BloodHound shows in seconds as a graph. Run it early in every Azure engagement. The "Shortest Paths to Global Admin" query is gold. MicroBurst What It Is MicroBurst by NetSPI is a PowerShell toolkit for Azure and Azure AD security assessments. It automates discovery of exposed storage, enumeration of resources, and finding common misconfigurations. Install Key Functions [!tip] Get AzurePasswords is the fastest credential sweep This single command checks App Services, Automation Accounts, Key Vaults, and more. Run it immediately after gaining Contributor level access to a subscription. AADInternals What It Is AADInternals by Dr Nestori Syynimaa is the most comprehensive Azure AD and Microsoft 365 offensive toolkit. Covers everything from tenant recon to token attacks, PRT extraction, Golden SAML, pass the PRT, and more. Install Key Operations PowerZure What It Is PowerZure is a PowerShell framework by Ryan Hausknecht for attacking and assessing Azure environments. Focused on post exploitation once you have valid credentials. Install Key Functions Tool Selection Guide | Task | Best Tool | | | | | Initial tenant recon (no creds) | AADInternals ( ) | | Comprehensive Azure AD dump | ROADtools ( ) | | Attack path visualisation | AzureHound + BloodHound | | Find exposed storage/credentials | MicroBurst ( , ) | | Token manipulation and phishing | ROADtx, AADInternals | | Post exploitation resource abuse | PowerZure | | PRT extraction and abuse | AADInternals + ROADtx | Quick Reference — Tool Commands Related Notes 02.1 — Azure Fundamentals 02.2 — Azure AD Enumeration and Token Attacks 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 00.6 — Tool Setup — CLI and Frameworks MODULE 8 — Cloud Security Assessment Methodology

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 3 — GCP Security/03.1 — GCP Fundamentals.md
title: 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals
body: 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals What This Note Covers The foundational GCP concepts every pentester must know: the resource hierarchy, IAM model, service accounts, and how GCP's permission system differs meaningfully from AWS and Azure. GCP Resource Hierarchy GCP uses a strict parent child hierarchy where IAM policies are inherited downward: IAM inheritance: Permissions granted at a higher level are inherited by all resources below. A binding at the organisation level applies to all projects. A binding at the project level applies to all resources in that project. [!warning] Inheritance amplifies mistakes A service account granted at the organisation level has editor access across every project in the organisation. Always check what scope a binding is applied at, not just what role it grants. Organisations The root node. Tied to a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain (e.g., ). Org level policies and IAM bindings apply everywhere below. Folders Optional intermediate grouping. Large enterprises use folders for departments (Engineering, Finance, HR) or environments (Production, Development, Staging). Projects The primary boundary in GCP. Everything lives in a project: Resources (VMs, buckets, databases, functions) Service accounts APIs enabled/disabled Billing account linked [!tip] is your first enumeration command How many projects does the compromised identity have access to? Often more than expected. Each project is a separate attack surface. Enumerate them all. GCP IAM Model GCP IAM uses a binding model: you bind a member (who) to a role (what) at a resource (where/scope). Members (Who) | Member Type | Syntax | Description | | | | | | Google Account | | Individual Google/G Suite account | | Service Account | | Non human identity for applications | | Google Group | | Collection of users | | Google Workspace Domain | | All users in the domain | | All Authenticated Users | | Any authenticated Google account (public!) | | All Users | | Completely public — no auth required | [!danger] allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers are public on a Cloud Storage bucket = fully public. = any Google account in the world can access. Both are common critical misconfigurations. Roles (What) Primitive Roles (legacy, avoid — too broad): | Role | Permissions | | | | | | Full control + IAM management | | | Read/write on all resources, no IAM | | | Read only on all resources | Predefined Roles (recommended — service specific): Examples: — read GCS objects — full GCS object control — full VM management — impersonate service accounts — create tokens for any SA Custom Roles — customer defined sets of permissions. Service Accounts — The Core of GCP Identity A service account is a non human Google identity for applications and workloads. Service accounts are used by: Compute Engine VMs (attached at creation) Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE pods Any application that needs to interact with GCP APIs Service Account Types | Type | Description | | | | | User managed | Created by you in a project | | Google managed | Created automatically by GCP for internal use | | Default service accounts | Auto created when certain APIs are enabled | Service Account Keys Service accounts can have JSON key files — long lived credentials that allow authenticating as that SA from anywhere. These are the GCP equivalent of AWS access keys and just as dangerous when leaked. [!danger] Service account JSON keys = the highest value credential in GCP Unlike temporary tokens from the metadata service, SA JSON keys are permanent until explicitly revoked. A leaked key file gives an attacker indefinite access as that service account. Finding one in a GitHub repo, S3 bucket, or config file is a critical finding. Default Service Accounts — A Critical Attack Surface When you enable certain GCP APIs or create certain resources, GCP automatically creates service accounts: [!danger] Default service accounts have Editor by default The Compute Engine default SA has on the entire project. Every VM launched without a custom SA gets this identity. Compromise any such VM → steal metadata token → Editor access on the project. GCP IAM Roles for Attackers — Key Permissions to Find | Permission | Why It Matters | | | | | | Impersonate any SA — essential for privilege escalation | | | Generate OAuth tokens for any SA | | | Create permanent key for any SA | | | Modify project IAM — add any binding | | | Modify org level IAM — ultimate escalation | | | Change VM's SA — escalate via reassignment | | | Modify custom role permissions | | | Make buckets public or grant access | GCP IAM Policy — JSON Structure Org Policies GCP Org Policies are constraints applied at organisation, folder, or project level that restrict what can be done — regardless of IAM permissions. [!tip] Org policy bypass is a finding If you can modify org policies ( / ), you can remove restrictions. For example, removing re enables creating permanent SA keys. Quick Reference — GCP Fundamentals Commands Related Notes 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks 03.3 — GCP Metadata Service and SSRF 03.4 — GCS Bucket Attacks 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation 00.5 — Core Cloud Concepts for Pentesters

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 3 — GCP Security/03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks.md
title: 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks
body: 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks What This Note Covers Service accounts are the central identity primitive in GCP. Every meaningful attack chain goes through them. This note covers key exposure, impersonation, token generation, workload identity abuse, and domain wide delegation. Attack Surface Overview Attack 1: JSON Key File Exposure Service account JSON keys are long lived credentials that authenticate as the SA from anywhere. They're commonly leaked in code repositories, S3/GCS buckets, Docker images, and CI/CD configs. Structure of a Service Account Key File The tells you the SA identity. The is the RSA key used to authenticate. Finding Leaked Key Files Authenticating with a Found Key File Attack 2: Metadata Service Token Theft When a Compute Engine VM (or Cloud Function, Cloud Run) has a service account attached, it can get OAuth access tokens from the metadata service at . This is the GCP equivalent of IMDSv1. Using the Stolen Token [!warning] OAuth scopes limit token capabilities GCE instances can be launched with limited OAuth scopes (e.g., read only on GCS). Even if the SA has broader IAM permissions, the token scope may restrict what you can do. Check in the metadata response. If the scope is , you have full access. Attack 3: Service Account Impersonation If you have the permission on a service account, you can impersonate it — generate tokens as it. Check if You Can Impersonate a Specific SA Attack 4: Token Creator — Generate Tokens for Any SA The role allows generating short lived tokens for any SA without needing to impersonate it through gcloud. Attack 5: Creating a Persistent SA Key If you have permission (included in roles like and ), you can create a permanent JSON key for any SA. [!danger] This is the GCP equivalent of creating an AWS access key for another user Creating a SA key gives you a credential that doesn't expire and isn't tied to your current session. This is the go to persistence mechanism in GCP. Attack 6: Workload Identity Federation Abuse Workload Identity Federation allows external identities (GitHub Actions, AWS IAM roles, Azure managed identities) to impersonate GCP service accounts without JSON keys. Misconfigurations in WIF can allow unintended principals to impersonate SAs. Attack 7: Domain Wide Delegation Domain wide delegation (DWD) is an extremely powerful capability that allows a service account to impersonate any user in the Google Workspace domain . It's designed for admin tools that need to act on behalf of users, but when misconfigured or over scoped, it's catastrophic. Exploiting Domain Wide Delegation [!danger] DWD with broad scopes = read all email, all Drive, all Calendar for all users A service account with DWD and can read every email of every user in the company. This is an instant critical finding. Quick Reference — Service Account Attacks Related Notes 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals 03.3 — GCP Metadata Service and SSRF 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation 01.2 — IAM Enumeration and Access Key Attacks MODULE 9 — Cloud Persistence and Defence Evasion

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 3 — GCP Security/03.3 — GCP Metadata, GCS Buckets, and Compute Engine.md
title: 03.3 — GCP Metadata Service, GCS Bucket Attacks, and Compute Engine
body: 03.3 — GCP Metadata Service, GCS Bucket Attacks, and Compute Engine What This Note Covers The GCP metadata service and SSRF exploitation, GCS (Google Cloud Storage) bucket misconfigurations and attack techniques, and Compute Engine attacks including startup script exposure and OS Login misconfigurations. GCP Instance Metadata Service Every GCP Compute Engine VM has access to the metadata server at (also reachable at ). It provides instance configuration data and — critically — OAuth access tokens for the attached service account. Key Difference from AWS GCP requires a custom HTTP header: . Without it, requests are rejected. This makes basic SSRF harder to exploit than AWS IMDSv1, but not impossible — many SSRF vulnerabilities can inject custom headers. SSRF Exploitation If the target application has an SSRF vulnerability that supports custom headers: SSRF bypass techniques for the header requirement: Compute Engine Additional Attacks Startup Script Exposure Startup scripts ( or ) run as root when a VM boots. They frequently contain: Database credentials for initial configuration API keys for bootstrapping apps Commands that pull credentials from GCS buckets OS Login Misconfiguration OS Login maps GCP IAM identities to Linux users on Compute Engine VMs. When disabled, SSH is controlled by SSH keys stored in instance metadata — which any project editor can modify. Serial Console Abuse The GCP serial console provides a text based emergency console for VMs. If enabled, it can be abused for initial access or persistence. GCS (Google Cloud Storage) Bucket Attacks GCS is GCP's object storage. Bucket access is controlled by IAM policies and ACLs. The same fundamental attack patterns as S3 apply, with GCP specific tooling. Bucket Naming and Discovery GCS bucket names are globally unique. Discovery follows the same wordlist approach as S3: Public Bucket Access GCS buckets can be made public via: 1. IAM binding: → 2. ACL: bucket or object ACL granting read Authenticated Enumeration High Value GCS Targets Bucket Policy Misconfiguration Attack If you have on a bucket: GCP Firewall and Network Enumeration Quick Reference — Metadata and GCS Related Notes 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks 01.4 — S3 Attacks

title: 03.4 — GCP Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Org-Level Attacks
body: 03.4 — GCP Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Org Level Attacks What This Note Covers Serverless and container attack surfaces in GCP — Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE — and organisation level attacks including project enumeration across the org, org policy bypass, and resource manager abuse. Cloud Functions Attacks Cloud Functions are serverless, event driven functions. Each function has a service account (the execution identity). The key attack surface: Unauthenticated Invocation Cloud Functions can be configured to allow unauthenticated HTTP requests. When combined with a high privilege execution SA, this is a critical finding. Environment Variable Exposure Function Source Code Download Execution Role Abuse Cloud Run Attacks Cloud Run runs containerised workloads. Similar attack surface to Cloud Functions but with containers. GKE (Kubernetes on GCP) Attacks GKE is Google's managed Kubernetes service. Two distinct attack surfaces: the Kubernetes layer and the GCP layer (node SA, workload identity). Initial Access and Enumeration Kubernetes RBAC Misconfigurations Workload Identity Abuse Workload Identity is GKE's recommended way to give pods a GCP identity. A Kubernetes service account (KSA) is linked to a GCP service account (GSA). Misconfigured WI bindings allow unintended pods to access GCP services. Pod Escape to Node If you can execute commands in a pod (via kubectl exec or a webshell): Org Level Attacks If your compromised identity has org level permissions, or you've escalated to a role with org access, you can attack across the entire organisation. Project Enumeration Across the Org Org Policy Bypass Org policies restrict what can happen in projects. Removing or modifying them unlocks capabilities. Resource Manager Abuse The Resource Manager API controls the hierarchy. With write permissions at the org level: Domain Wide Delegation — Recap and Detection DWD is covered in 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks but detection deserves its own note here: Quick Reference — Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, Org Related Notes 03.1 — GCP Fundamentals 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security MODULE 5 — Serverless and PaaS Attack Surface

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 3 — GCP Security/03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation.md
title: 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation
body: 03.5 — GCP Privilege Escalation What This Note Covers How to escalate privileges in GCP — from low privilege service accounts and users to project owner or organisation admin. Covers the full IAM escalation technique list, Cloud Function and Cloud Run abuse, GKE node pool escalation, and org level attacks. The GCP Privesc Mindset GCP privilege escalation is almost always about service account impersonation or IAM policy modification . The question you ask at every step: "Do I have any permission that lets me act as a more privileged identity, or modify the IAM policy to grant myself more permissions?" Key permissions that open escalation paths: Technique 1: Direct IAM Policy Modification Permissions needed: The most direct path. Add yourself (or your SA) to the project as Owner. Technique 2: SA Impersonation Chain (actAs) Permissions needed: on a target SA If you can act as a service account that has higher permissions, you've escalated. Technique 3: Create SA Key for Privileged SA Permissions needed: on a target SA Creates a permanent JSON key for a SA you don't currently control. Technique 4: Cloud Function Execution with Privileged SA Permissions needed: , on a high privilege SA, Create a Cloud Function that runs as a privileged SA and executes code on your behalf. Technique 5: Modify Custom Role Permissions Permissions needed: on a custom role If you're bound to a custom role, and you can update that role's permissions, add powerful permissions to it — upgrading yourself. Technique 6: Compute Engine SA Reassignment Permissions needed: , on admin SA Change a running VM's service account from a low privilege one to a high privilege one, then access the metadata service. Technique 7: GKE Node Pool SA Escalation GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) nodes are Compute Engine VMs. They have a service account attached. If that SA is the default Compute Engine SA (with ), gaining access to any pod on the node gives you editor level access to the project. Technique 8: Org Level IAM Escalation Permissions needed: The highest possible escalation — bind yourself to at the organisation level, giving you access to every project in the entire organisation. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.1 — Docker Fundamentals and Attack Surface.md
title: 04.1 — Docker Fundamentals and Attack Surface
body: 04.1 — Docker Fundamentals and Attack Surface What This Note Covers What Docker is, how it works, and the complete attack surface — images, containers, registries, the Docker daemon, and the Linux kernel primitives that make containers work (and how they can fail). What Is Docker? Docker is a containerisation platform that packages applications and their dependencies into containers — isolated, portable, lightweight runtime environments. Containers share the host OS kernel but are isolated from each other and the host using Linux kernel features. Key Difference from VMs Containers are not VMs. There is no hypervisor. The host kernel is shared. This is why container escapes exist — the isolation is enforced by software (namespaces, cgroups, seccomp) not hardware. Misconfiguration defeats it. Core Docker Concepts Images A Docker image is a read only template — a layered filesystem snapshot containing: Base OS (e.g., , ) Application code Dependencies and libraries Configuration files Entrypoint/CMD (what runs when the container starts) Images are built from a Dockerfile and stored in a registry . Layers Every instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. Layers are cached and shared between images. Secrets added in one layer and deleted in the next are still present in the intermediate layer and extractable. Containers A container is a running instance of an image. It has: A writable layer on top of the image layers Its own network namespace (isolated networking) Its own PID namespace (isolated process tree) Its own mount namespace (isolated filesystem) Its own UTS namespace (isolated hostname) Registries A registry is where Docker images are stored and distributed. | Registry | URL | Notes | | | | | | Docker Hub | hub.docker.com | Default public registry | | AWS ECR | .dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com | AWS managed | | Azure ACR | .azurecr.io | Azure managed | | GCR / Artifact Registry | gcr.io / pkg.dev | GCP managed | | GitHub Container Registry | ghcr.io | GitHub integrated | | Self hosted | Any HTTPS endpoint | GitLab, JFrog Artifactory, etc. | Linux Kernel Isolation Mechanisms Understanding these is essential for understanding why escape techniques work. Namespaces Namespaces provide isolation — a container's processes see a different view of the system: | Namespace | Isolates | | | | | pid | Process IDs — container has its own PID 1 | | net | Network interfaces, routing tables, iptables | | mnt | Filesystem mount points | | uts | Hostname and domain name | | ipc | Inter process communication (semaphores, message queues) | | user | User and group IDs (UID mapping) | Key insight: If you can break out of a namespace — particularly the mount or pid namespace — you're on the host. The flag drops most namespace isolation. cgroups (Control Groups) cgroups limit resource usage — CPU, memory, I/O. They don't provide security isolation, but: The file is writable in privileged containers This is a container escape vector (covered in 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques) Capabilities Linux capabilities divide root privileges into individual units. Docker drops most capabilities by default, but some are dangerous when granted: | Capability | Risk | | | | | | Near root on host — many escape paths | | | Modify network interfaces, routing | | | Trace processes in other namespaces | | | Bypass file permission checks | | | Load kernel modules | seccomp seccomp filters restrict which system calls a container can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks 44 syscalls. When disabled ( ), the container can make any syscall — significantly expanding the escape surface. AppArmor / SELinux Mandatory Access Control systems that restrict what container processes can do at the OS level. Docker applies an AppArmor profile ( ) when available. When disabled ( ), the OS level MAC controls are removed. Docker Daemon Attack Surface The Docker daemon ( ) is the background service that manages containers. It listens on: Unix socket: (default — local only) TCP socket: (unauthenticated) or (TLS) Exposed Docker Socket If the socket is exposed to the internet (port 2375 with no auth): Docker Socket Mounted Inside a Container If the Docker socket is mounted into a container ( ), any process inside that container can control the Docker daemon — creating new privileged containers with host filesystem access. [!danger] Docker socket mount = immediate container escape Mounting into a container is one of the most critical misconfigurations in container security. Any process with access to it has effective root on the host. Registry Attack Surface Unauthenticated Registry Access Extracting Secrets from Docker Layers Quick Reference — Docker Assessment Commands Related Notes 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques 04.3 — Container Image Attacks 04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC 00.4 — Cloud Service Models and Attack Surface

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques.md
title: 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques
body: 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques What This Note Covers The most impactful Docker misconfigurations and the step by step container escape techniques that exploit them — privileged containers, Docker socket abuse, cgroup release agent, host networking, and capability based escapes. Escape Technique 1: Privileged Container Escape The flag gives a container nearly all Linux capabilities, disables seccomp, and removes AppArmor restrictions. The container can see all host devices. Detection (from inside the container) Escape Method: Mount Host Filesystem via Device Escape Technique 2: cgroup release agent This technique exploits the cgroup v1 file to execute a command on the host when all processes in a cgroup exit. Works in privileged containers and some other misconfigurations. [!danger] cgroup escape is highly reliable in privileged containers This technique has been reliable across many container runtime versions. Always try it in privileged containers — it works without needing host filesystem mount. Escape Technique 3: Docker Socket Abuse If is mounted inside the container (extremely common in CI/CD, Jenkins, Docker in Docker setups): Escape Technique 4: Host Network Mode + Host PID Containers launched with share the host's network namespace. With , they share the host's PID namespace. Escape Technique 5: CAP SYS ADMIN Capability is the most powerful Linux capability. With it, even a non privileged container can escape. Escape Technique 6: Writable hostPath Volume If the Kubernetes pod (or Docker container) mounts a sensitive host path: Detection Summary — Are You in a Container? Misconfiguration Quick Reference | Misconfiguration | Detection | Escape Method | | | | | | | / | Device mount + chroot, cgroup release agent | | Docker socket mounted | exists in container | Docker socket abuse | | Host network mode | shows host interfaces | Network sniffing, binding host ports | | Host PID mode | shows host processes | | | | shows sys admin | cgroup release agent | | Sensitive hostPath | shows /etc, /proc, / | Read/write host files, add users | | Exposed TCP Docker API | | Create privileged container remotely | Quick Reference — Escape Commands Related Notes 04.1 — Docker Fundamentals and Attack Surface 04.3 — Container Image Attacks 04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC 04.5 — Kubernetes Attack Techniques

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.3 — Container Image Attacks.md
title: 04.3 — Container Image Attacks
body: 04.3 — Container Image Attacks What This Note Covers How to extract secrets from container image layers, analyse Dockerfiles for vulnerabilities, scan images for CVEs, attack container registries, and understand supply chain risks in container images. Why Container Images Are a Target Container images are built in layers, and every layer is permanently stored in the image's history. Developers frequently: Add credentials in one layer and delete them in the next (the delete doesn't remove the data from the prior layer) Hardcode API keys, passwords, and tokens in environment variables (visible in image metadata) Base their images on outdated, CVE laden base images Pull images from untrusted registries (supply chain risk) Extracting Secrets from Image Layers Method 1: Docker History Method 2: docker inspect (Environment Variables) Method 3: Export and Analyse All Layers Method 4: truffleHog on Images Method 5: dive — Interactive Layer Explorer Dockerfile Security Analysis Dockerfiles contain the build instructions and are a rich source of security findings. CVE Scanning with Trivy Trivy by Aqua Security is the industry standard open source container image vulnerability scanner. Interpreting Trivy Output Prioritise: CRITICAL with a fixed version available → immediate update required. Container Registry Attacks Unauthenticated Registry Access Exposed Docker Registry (port 5000) Self hosted registries often run on port 5000 without TLS or authentication: AWS ECR — Credential Requirements Supply Chain Attacks via Container Images Typosquatting on Docker Hub Attackers publish images with names similar to popular ones: instead of instead of instead of These images often contain backdoors or crypto miners. Compromised Base Images If a base image is compromised (via a compromised registry account or supply chain attack), every image built on top of it is affected. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC.md
title: 04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC
body: 04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC What This Note Covers Kubernetes architecture from a security perspective — the control plane, worker nodes, and every component that can be attacked. Then Kubernetes RBAC — how it works, how it's misconfigured, and what those misconfigurations let an attacker do. Kubernetes Architecture Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform. It manages where and how containers run across a cluster of machines. From an Attacker's Perspective | Component | Why It Matters | | | | | kube apiserver | Every action in K8s is an API call here — main target for initial access | | etcd | Contains ALL cluster state including secrets — direct access = game over | | kubelet | Runs on every node — API on port 10250/10255 — often misconfigured | | service account tokens | Every pod gets one — frequently over permissioned | | kube proxy | Network routing — relevant for lateral movement | Kubernetes Objects — What You're Attacking Pods A pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — one or more containers running together. Namespaces Logical partitions within a cluster. RBAC can be scoped per namespace. Services Network endpoints that expose pods. Service types: — internal only — exposed on every node's IP at a static port — cloud load balancer (external) Secrets Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive data — but are only base64 encoded , not encrypted (unless encryption at rest is configured). [!danger] Kubernetes secrets are not encrypted by default Without encryption at rest configured (and only 30% of clusters have it), secrets in etcd are only base64 encoded. Anyone who can read etcd directly — or has on secrets — gets plaintext credentials. ConfigMaps ConfigMaps store non sensitive configuration, but developers frequently put sensitive data in them by mistake. Service Accounts Every pod runs as a Kubernetes service account. The token is automatically mounted at: Kubernetes RBAC RBAC controls who can do what in the cluster. Three components: Subjects — external users (managed by the authentication mechanism, not K8s itself) — groups of users — pod identities Roles and ClusterRoles A Role grants permissions within a single namespace . A ClusterRole grants permissions cluster wide (or can be bound to a namespace via RoleBinding). Critical verbs: | Verb | What It Allows | | | | | | Read a specific resource by name | | | List all resources of a type | | | Stream updates to resources | | | Create new resources | | / | Modify existing resources | | | Delete resources | | | Execute commands in pods | | | Create RoleBindings (escalation!) | | | Grant roles you don't have (escalation!) | | | Act as another user/SA | | | All verbs — admin | RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings RBAC Misconfigurations — Attack Surface Misconfiguration 1: Wildcard Permissions Misconfiguration 2: Overprivileged Service Account Misconfiguration 3: Permission If a subject can into pods, they can: Access data inside running pods Steal service account tokens Use the pod as a pivot point Misconfiguration 4: List/Get Misconfiguration 5: Verb The verb allows creating RoleBindings — granting yourself roles you don't have. Misconfiguration 6: Verb Allows acting as another user, group, or service account. The Service Account — A Common Mistake Every namespace has a service account. Pods that don't specify a use it automatically. In misconfigured clusters, this account has been granted elevated permissions — giving every pod in the namespace those permissions. Quick Reference — Architecture and RBAC Related Notes 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques 04.5 — Kubernetes Attack Techniques 04.6 — Cloud Specific Kubernetes Attacks and Tools 03.4 — Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Org Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.5 — Kubernetes Attack Techniques.md
title: 04.5 — Kubernetes Attack Techniques
body: 04.5 — Kubernetes Attack Techniques What This Note Covers Step by step Kubernetes attack techniques: unauthenticated API server access, service account token abuse, pod escape to node, etcd direct access, kubectl proxy abuse, and lateral movement through the cluster. Attack 1: Unauthenticated API Server The Kubernetes API server on port 6443 (HTTPS) or 8080 (HTTP, legacy) is the central control plane. In misconfigured clusters, it can be accessible without authentication. [!warning] Port 8080 — the completely open API The old insecure port 8080 requires no auth and no TLS. If found open, the cluster is fully exposed. Modern K8s deprecated it but old clusters or misconfigurations still have it. Attack 2: Service Account Token Abuse Every pod has a service account token automatically mounted. This token authenticates to the K8s API server. Step 1: Get the Token (from Inside a Pod) Step 2: Enumerate What the Token Can Do Step 3: Steal Secrets if Permitted Attack 3: Pod Escape to Node Once inside a pod with sufficient permissions, you can create a new privileged pod that mounts the host filesystem — escaping to the underlying node. Via kubectl (if you have permission) Via API Server Directly (no kubectl) Attack 4: kubelet API Abuse The kubelet runs on every worker node and has its own API on port 10250 (authenticated) and 10255 (read only, unauthenticated — legacy). [!danger] Kubelet with anonymous auth = exec on any pod without RBAC check If is set on the kubelet (old default), the API server's RBAC is bypassed. You can execute commands in any pod on that node directly. Attack 5: etcd Direct Access etcd is the key value store that holds all cluster state — every pod definition, every secret, every config, every RBAC policy. Direct access to etcd = complete cluster compromise. Attack 6: kubectl proxy Abuse creates a local HTTP proxy to the K8s API server. If running, it provides unauthenticated local access to the full API. Lateral Movement in Kubernetes Once inside one pod, move to other pods or namespaces. Using Stolen SA Token to Access Other Namespaces Network Based Lateral Movement By default, Kubernetes has no network policy — all pods can talk to all other pods across all namespaces. Quick Reference — Kubernetes Attacks Related Notes 04.4 — Kubernetes Architecture and RBAC 04.6 — Cloud Specific Kubernetes Attacks and Tools 04.2 — Docker Misconfigurations and Escape Techniques MODULE 6 — Cloud Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 4 — Container and Kubernetes Security/04.6 — Cloud-Specific Kubernetes Attacks and Tools.md
title: 04.6 — Cloud-Specific Kubernetes Attacks and Tools
body: 04.6 — Cloud Specific Kubernetes Attacks and Tools What This Note Covers How Kubernetes attacks differ across AWS EKS, Azure AKS, and GCP GKE — focusing on the cloud IAM integrations that create unique escalation paths. Plus the complete container and Kubernetes security toolset. EKS (AWS) — IRSA and IAM Attack Paths EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) integrates Kubernetes service accounts with AWS IAM via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) . This lets pods assume IAM roles without node level credentials. How IRSA Works Finding IRSA Misconfigurations Exploiting IRSA from Inside a Pod EKS Cluster Auth (aws auth ConfigMap) EKS uses a ConfigMap ( in ) to map IAM users/roles to Kubernetes RBAC subjects. AKS (Azure) — Managed Identity and RBAC Integration AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) integrates with Azure AD for authentication and managed identities for pod level Azure access. Azure AD Authentication for AKS Pod Identity / Workload Identity Abuse AKS supports workload identity (recommended) and the legacy Pod Identity (aad pod identity). Both let pods get Azure tokens. AKS RBAC — Azure RBAC vs K8s RBAC AKS can use either Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for cluster access. Check which: GKE (GCP) — Workload Identity and Node SA GKE integrates with GCP IAM via Workload Identity (recommended) and legacy node service account access. Legacy Node SA Access (Critical Misconfiguration) Old GKE clusters (or those not using Workload Identity) have a GCP service account on every node. Every pod can access the metadata service and steal that SA's token. Workload Identity Abuse See 03.4 — Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Org Attacks for the detailed workload identity attack chain. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 5 — Serverless and PaaS/05.1 — Serverless Attack Surface.md
title: 05.1 — Serverless Attack Surface
body: 05.1 — Serverless Attack Surface What This Note Covers What makes serverless security fundamentally different from traditional compute, the attack surface unique to event driven architectures, and how the threat model shifts when there's no persistent OS to target. What Is Serverless? Serverless computing lets you run code without managing servers. You write a function, deploy it, and the cloud provider handles: Provisioning compute Scaling (zero to thousands of instances) OS patching and maintenance Runtime environment You are responsible for: Function code and its dependencies IAM execution role and permissions Configuration (environment variables, triggers, timeouts) Input validation and output handling The three major platforms: | Platform | AWS | Azure | GCP | | | | | | | Product | Lambda | Azure Functions | Cloud Functions / Cloud Run | | Triggers | S3, SQS, SNS, API GW, DynamoDB, EventBridge | HTTP, Timer, Event Hub, Blob Storage, Queue | HTTP, Pub/Sub, GCS, Firestore, Scheduler | | Execution Role | IAM Role | Managed Identity | Service Account | | Runtime | Python, Node, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET, custom | C , Java, JS, Python, PowerShell | Python, Node, Go, Java, Ruby, PHP | How Serverless Differs from Traditional Compute What You Lose as an Attacker What You Gain as an Attacker [!tip] The attack surface moves from OS to IAM + code In serverless, you can't exploit the OS. But the IAM role, the environment variables, and the function's business logic are all entirely the customer's responsibility — and frequently misconfigured. The Serverless Threat Model Threat 1: Over Permissive Execution Role This is the equivalent of a privileged container — a function with too many IAM permissions. Threat 2: Sensitive Data in Environment Variables Environment variables are the configuration mechanism for serverless. Developers use them for: Database connection strings (with credentials) API keys for downstream services Encryption keys Feature flags with sensitive values Anyone with (AWS) or (GCP) can read them. Threat 3: Event Injection Serverless functions process events from many sources. If the function trusts event data without validation, attackers who can influence the event source can inject malicious payloads. Sources of attacker controlled input: API Gateway HTTP requests (direct) SQS messages (if attacker can write to the queue) S3 events (if attacker can write objects to the bucket) SNS notifications (if attacker can publish to the topic) DynamoDB streams (if attacker can write to the table) Threat 4: Dependency Vulnerabilities Serverless functions include third party libraries in their deployment package. The cloud provider patches the runtime (Python interpreter, Node.js) but not your dependencies. Threat 5: Unauthenticated Invocation Functions exposed via HTTP can be configured with no authentication. If misconfigured as public, any internet user can invoke them directly. Threat 6: Side Channel Information from Cold Starts Cold starts (first invocation after a period of inactivity) take longer. If timing differences are observable, this can leak whether a function was recently invoked — relevant for timing attacks on OTP verification, rate limiting bypass checks, etc. Serverless Attack Chain — General Pattern Serverless vs Traditional — Side by Side Comparison | Attack Objective | Traditional Compute | Serverless | | | | | | Initial access | RCE via CVE, SSH brute force, web shell | SSRF, event injection, public function endpoint | | Credential access | /etc files, memory dump, env vars | Environment variables, execution role via IMDS | | Lateral movement | Network pivot, pass the hash | IAM role chaining, assume role to other services | | Persistence | Cron job, rootkit, SSH key | IAM backdoor, function code modification, trigger addition | | Exfiltration | Network egress | S3 replication, SQS, API calls to external endpoints | | Defence evasion | Log deletion, process hiding | Use services that don't generate CloudTrail data events | The Execution Role — Central to Everything Every serverless function has an IAM execution role (or equivalent). When the function runs, it has the permissions of that role. This means: [!danger] Code injection in a Lambda function = acting as its IAM role If you can inject code into a Lambda function's execution flow (via event injection, dependency confusion, or function code modification), you operate with the function's IAM permissions. If those permissions are broad, the impact is account wide. Quick Reference — Serverless Attack Surface Checklist Related Notes 05.2 — Event Injection Attacks 05.3 — Serverless Privilege Escalation via Execution Role 05.4 — PaaS Attack Surface 01.4 — Lambda Attacks (covered in 01.6) 03.4 — Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Org Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 5 — Serverless and PaaS/05.2 — Event Injection Attacks.md
title: 05.2 — Event Injection Attacks
body: 05.2 — Event Injection Attacks What This Note Covers How serverless functions process events from cloud services and how attackers manipulate those events to inject malicious payloads. Covers SQS injection, SNS injection, S3 event trigger abuse, API Gateway payload manipulation, and DynamoDB stream abuse. What Is Event Injection? A serverless function doesn't receive user input directly — it receives events from cloud services. An event is a JSON document describing what happened (an S3 object was uploaded, an SQS message arrived, an HTTP request came in). Event injection exploits one core assumption: the function trusts the content of the event . If an attacker can influence the event data — by writing to an S3 bucket the function monitors, publishing to an SQS queue the function reads, or sending an HTTP request to an API Gateway the function serves — they can inject malicious payloads into the function's execution context. Attack Vector 1: API Gateway — Direct HTTP Injection Functions exposed via API Gateway receive HTTP request data. If the function passes request parameters to dangerous sinks (shell commands, SQL queries, template engines) without validation, classic injection applies. Exploitation: Server Side Template Injection (SSTI) in Lambda Attack Vector 2: SQS Injection Lambda functions often process SQS messages. If the function passes message body content to vulnerable sinks, an attacker who can publish to the queue controls the injection payload. Exploitation — publish a malicious SQS message: SQL Injection via SQS Attack Vector 3: S3 Event Trigger Abuse Lambda functions are frequently triggered by S3 events ( ). The function receives an event containing the bucket name and object key. If it processes the object without validation: Exploitation — upload a maliciously named file to the trigger bucket: Path Traversal via S3 Key Attack Vector 4: SNS Injection SNS (Simple Notification Service) publishes messages to multiple subscribers. If a Lambda subscribes to an SNS topic and processes message content unsafely: Attack Vector 5: DynamoDB Stream Injection Lambda can trigger on DynamoDB Streams (changes to a DynamoDB table). If an attacker can write to the table, they control the stream event content. Attack Vector 6: EventBridge / CloudWatch Events Functions triggered by scheduled events or EventBridge rules process the event object. If the event includes external data fed into EventBridge patterns, injection may be possible. title: 05.3 — Serverless Privilege Escalation via Execution Role
body: 05.3 — Serverless Privilege Escalation via Execution Role What This Note Covers How to use a serverless function's execution role to escalate privileges in AWS, Azure, and GCP. Covers direct role abuse, using the function as a proxy for IAM operations, modifying function code for persistence, and chaining serverless execution into account wide compromise. The Core Concept When you gain code execution inside a serverless function — via event injection, an application vulnerability, or because you have the permissions to update/invoke the function — you automatically operate with the function's execution role . This role is your actual privilege level in the cloud account. The attack question is always: "What can this execution role do, and how do I use it?" Step 1: Identify the Execution Role AWS Lambda From Inside the Function (Code Execution) Step 2: Escalate Using Execution Role Permissions High Impact IAM Permissions in Lambda Roles Scenario A: Role has Scenario B: Role has Scenario C: Role has on a powerful role Scenario D: Role has Step 3: Using the Execution Role Without Code Injection If you have or permissions (outside the function), you can update the function to execute your payload. [!danger] = code execution as the function's role If you have permission to update a Lambda function's code, you have code execution with its IAM role. This is a privilege escalation path documented in Rhino Security Labs' IAM privesc research and is detected by Pacu's privesc scanner. Step 4: Persistence via Function Modification Once you have code execution with the execution role, establish persistence that survives session expiry. Azure Function Execution Role Escalation Azure Functions use a Managed Identity as their execution identity. title: 05.5 — CI/CD Pipeline Attacks
body: 05.5 — CI/CD Pipeline Attacks What This Note Covers CI/CD pipelines are the supply chain of cloud infrastructure. They hold secrets, run with powerful IAM roles, and are frequently the path of least resistance into a cloud environment. This note covers GitHub Actions secret exposure, CodeBuild environment leakage, pipeline injection, and supply chain attacks. Why CI/CD Is a High Value Target CI/CD pipelines: Hold credentials for every environment they deploy to (dev, staging, prod) Run with IAM roles that have deployment permissions (often or ) Pull from and push to code repositories — supply chain attack surface Are often less hardened than production systems Generate verbose logs that frequently contain secret values [!tip] Compromise the CI/CD pipeline, compromise everything it deploys to A GitHub Actions workflow with on AWS can deploy anything. Compromise it and you've compromised the AWS account without ever touching the account directly. GitHub Actions — Secret Exposure Where Secrets Live in GitHub Actions Attack 1: Pull Request Injection (Untrusted Input) Workflows triggered by from forks have no access to secrets by default. But runs in the context of the base repo and does have access to secrets — dangerous for public repos. Exploitation: Submit a PR to the target repo modifying the test script to exfiltrate secrets: Attack 2: Workflow File Injection If you can push to a branch that triggers a workflow, you can inject malicious steps: Attack 3: OIDC Token Theft GitHub Actions supports OIDC (OpenID Connect) to authenticate to cloud providers without storing long lived secrets. If the OIDC trust policy is misconfigured: Exploitation of misconfigured OIDC: AWS CodeBuild — Secrets Leakage CodeBuild runs build jobs with an IAM service role. Secrets are passed via: Environment variables (plaintext or from Secrets Manager/Parameter Store) The build environment itself Enumeration CodeBuild IAM Role Abuse Triggering a Malicious Build If you can and influence the buildspec (either directly or via repo write access): Terraform State File Attacks Terraform stores state in S3 (AWS), Azure Blob Storage (Azure), or GCS (GCP). State files contain: All resource IDs and configurations Sometimes plaintext secrets (DB passwords, API keys passed as variables) SSH private keys generated by Terraform Supply Chain Attacks via Dependencies Dependency Confusion If a CI/CD pipeline installs packages from both public registries (npm, PyPI) and private internal registries, an attacker can publish a malicious public package with a higher version number than the internal one — the package manager fetches the public (malicious) version. typosquatting in CI/CD CI/CD scripts that or common package names are vulnerable to typosquatting: Quick Reference — CI/CD Attacks Related Notes 05.1 — Serverless Attack Surface 05.3 — Serverless Privilege Escalation via Execution Role 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation MODULE 7 — Cloud Reconnaissance and OSINT MODULE 9 — Cloud Persistence and Defence Evasion
