title: 06.1 — Cloud Privilege Escalation Mindset and Methodology
body: 06.1 — Cloud Privilege Escalation Mindset and Methodology What This Note Covers The mental model for cloud privilege escalation — how it differs from OS level privesc, the decision framework for every step, and how to systematically map escalation paths before acting. This is the strategic layer that all the technique notes sit beneath. Cloud Privesc vs OS Privesc In traditional penetration testing, privilege escalation means moving from a low privilege OS user to root or SYSTEM. The tools are kernel exploits, SUID binaries, writable cron jobs, weak service permissions, and password reuse. Cloud privilege escalation is fundamentally different: [!tip] Cloud privesc is always legal API calls You are not exploiting a software vulnerability. You are using permissions you legitimately have to reach permissions you shouldn't have. This is why it's harder to detect — it looks like normal administrative activity. The Core Question at Every Step At every point in a cloud engagement, ask: "Does any permission I currently hold allow me to, directly or indirectly, modify IAM — or execute code as an identity with more permissions?" If yes — that's your escalation path. If no — enumerate more, look for new credentials, find new services. The IAM Modify Hierarchy Not all IAM permissions are equal. Rank them by impact: When you have permissions in multiple tiers, always try the highest tier first . The Escalation Decision Framework Blast Radius Assessment — Before You Act Before exploiting any escalation path, mentally model the blast radius: [!warning] Minimum necessary action In a real pentest, demonstrate the escalation path clearly but don't exfiltrate real data, don't create resources that cost money, don't modify production IAM permanently. Confirm the path is exploitable, document it, and report it. Clean up any test resources created. Mapping the Attack Graph Before Acting Before firing any escalation commands, build a mental (or written) map: Cross Cloud and Cross Account Paths Escalation doesn't have to stay within one cloud or one account. Look for: Operational Security During Escalation Your actions are logged. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement/06.2 — AWS Lateral Movement.md
title: 06.2 — AWS Lateral Movement
body: 06.2 — AWS Lateral Movement What This Note Covers How attackers move laterally within and between AWS accounts — role assumption chains, confused deputy attacks, resource based policy abuse, credential hopping across services, and using BloodHound for AWS to map paths. Lateral Movement via Role Assumption (sts:AssumeRole) The primary lateral movement primitive in AWS. If an IAM identity has permission targeting another role, and that role's trust policy allows it, the identity can assume that role and operate with its permissions. Role Chaining You can chain role assumptions — assume Role A, then from Role A assume Role B, and so on. Each hop may give access to new permissions or new accounts. [!warning] Role chaining resets session duration Each AssumeRole in a chain caps the session at 1 hour. If you need longer sessions, use the access key of the original identity to re assume, rather than chaining. Confused Deputy Attack The confused deputy problem occurs when a service (the "deputy") with broad access is tricked into acting on behalf of an attacker using a resource policy. AWS Cross Service Confused Deputy When an AWS service (like Lambda, EC2, CloudFormation) acts on behalf of you, it uses the service's own authority. A resource based policy that allows the service principal without condition keys can be abused. Exploitation: Create a Lambda function in your own account, configure it to access the victim's S3 bucket (allowed because the policy trusts without restriction). Lateral Movement via Instance Profile EC2 instances with instance profiles carry IAM credentials in the metadata service. Moving from one instance to another with a more privileged profile is lateral movement. SSM Session Manager for Lateral Movement If you have or , you can access any EC2 instance registered with SSM — no SSH required, no security group changes needed. Lateral Movement via Lambda Lambda functions run as IAM roles. If you can invoke a Lambda function that has a more privileged execution role, you can use it to perform actions under that role. Credential Hopping via Secrets Manager Secrets Manager is the credential store for applications. Finding credentials for one service frequently provides access to another. Using AWSPX / BloodHound for AWS AWSPX is the BloodHound equivalent for AWS — it maps IAM relationships as a graph to find privilege escalation and lateral movement paths. Quick Reference — AWS Lateral Movement Related Notes 06.1 — Cloud Privesc Mindset and Methodology 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks 06.5 — Cross Account and Cross Cloud Movement tags: [aws, lateral movement, iam, role chaining, sts, ssm, secrets, cloudhawk] 06.2 — AWS Lateral Movement What This Note Covers Moving laterally within and between AWS accounts — role assumption chains, confused deputy, SSM for pivoting, credential hopping via Secrets Manager, and using AWSPX to map paths. Role Assumption Chains The primary AWS lateral movement primitive. If your identity has on a role, and that role's trust policy allows you, you can assume it and operate with its permissions. Chaining Multiple Roles [!warning] Chaining caps session at 1 hour per hop regardless of MaxSessionDuration settings. SSM for Lateral Movement (No SSH Required) Systems Manager Session Manager lets you access EC2 instances without open SSH ports, key pairs, or security group changes — just IAM. [!tip] SSM bypasses all traditional network controls Even if an EC2 instance has no public IP, is in a private subnet, and has no inbound security group rules — if it has the SSM agent running and IAM permissions to talk to SSM, you can reach it. This is the silent lateral movement path in AWS. Instance Profile Hopping EC2 instances carry their IAM role credentials in the metadata service. Move from a low privilege instance to a high privilege one by accessing its metadata. Credential Hopping via Secrets Manager Secrets Manager holds credentials for every downstream service. Each secret is a potential new identity. Lambda as a Lateral Movement Pivot Functions with higher privilege execution roles can be used as a proxy for actions you cannot perform directly. Confused Deputy Attack Occurs when an AWS service acts with its own authority on behalf of an attacker because a resource policy allows the service principal without condition keys. Exploitation: Create a Lambda in your account — the vulnerable policy lets it read the victim's bucket. AWSPX — BloodHound for AWS Maps IAM relationships as a graph to find lateral movement paths automatically. Quick Reference Related Notes 06.1 — Cloud Privesc Mindset and Methodology 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation 01.3 — Metadata Service Attacks 06.5 — Cross Account and Cross Cloud Movement

title: 06.3 — Azure Lateral Movement
body: 06.3 — Azure Lateral Movement What This Note Covers Moving laterally within Azure — token pivoting across resources, managed identity chaining, Key Vault as a pivot point, App Registration credential abuse, and using AzureHound to map paths. Token Pivoting Across Azure Resources A single refresh token or access token can be exchanged for tokens scoped to different Azure resources. This lets you pivot from one service to another using the same underlying identity. [!tip] One refresh token, all Azure services A refresh token from a device code phishing attack or token theft lets you access every Azure service the compromised identity has permissions on — ARM, Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Databricks, etc. Try all resource scopes. Managed Identity Lateral Movement Chain The most reliable Azure lateral movement pattern: Step by Step Service Principal Credential Abuse App Registrations in Azure AD have service principals. SPs can have credentials (client secrets or certificates) and role assignments. Finding or creating SP credentials is Azure lateral movement. Storage Account as Lateral Movement Source Storage accounts often contain application code, config files, Terraform state, and deployment packages — all of which may contain credentials for further pivoting. Azure Resource Manager — Moving Between Resource Groups If you have Owner/Contributor on one resource group, use it to reach resources in adjacent groups or access shared infrastructure. AzureHound for Path Discovery Quick Reference — Azure Lateral Movement Related Notes 06.1 — Cloud Privesc Mindset and Methodology 02.3 — Managed Identity Abuse 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 02.4 — Azure Storage and Key Vault Attacks 06.5 — Cross Account and Cross Cloud Movement

title: 06.4 — GCP Lateral Movement
body: 06.4 — GCP Lateral Movement What This Note Covers Moving laterally within GCP — service account impersonation chains, GCS as a pivot source, workload identity hopping, org level movement across projects, and using BloodHound for GCP paths. Service Account Impersonation Chains The core GCP lateral movement primitive. Each hop uses a more privileged service account as a stepping stone. Token Creator Chain GCS Bucket as Lateral Movement Source GCS buckets frequently contain credentials for other services — SA key files, Terraform state, application configs, and CI/CD artifacts. Cross Project Lateral Movement GCP projects are not fully isolated from each other when shared VPCs, shared service accounts, or org level IAM is in use. Org Level Lateral Movement If you have org level IAM visibility or permissions, you can survey and access all projects. Workload Identity Federation — Cross Environment Pivot If a GCP workload identity pool trusts an external identity (GitHub Actions, AWS IAM, Azure AD), and the condition is overly broad, an attacker with that external identity can impersonate GCP service accounts. BloodHound for GCP (via ScoutSuite + Manual Analysis) There isn't a single BloodHound equivalent for GCP yet, but the GCP IAM Privilege Escalation tool and manual analysis serve the same purpose. title: 06.5 — Cross-Account and Cross-Cloud Movement
body: 06.5 — Cross Account and Cross Cloud Movement What This Note Covers Moving between AWS accounts, Azure subscriptions, GCP projects, and across different cloud providers entirely. Covers cross account role assumption, AWS Organisations abuse, Azure cross subscription access, GCP org traversal, and multi cloud credential chains. AWS Cross Account Role Assumption AWS Organisations typically have many accounts (prod, dev, security, logging, shared services). IAM roles with cross account trust policies allow movement between them. Finding Cross Account Roles AWS Organisations — Management Account Escalation The AWS Organisations management account can apply Service Control Policies to all member accounts. Compromising the management account = control over every account in the org. [!danger] Management account = God mode across the org The OrganizationAccountAccessRole has AdministratorAccess in every member account and trusts the management account. Compromise the management account → compromise every account in the org. Service Control Policy (SCP) Bypass Research SCPs deny specific actions across all accounts. If you can modify SCPs (requires management account), you can remove restrictions. Azure Cross Subscription Movement An identity (user, SP, or managed identity) can have roles in multiple subscriptions. Finding these cross subscription assignments is the Azure equivalent of cross account movement. Azure Lighthouse (Cross Tenant Access) Azure Lighthouse allows service providers to manage customer tenants. If misconfigured, it creates cross tenant access paths. GCP Cross Project and Cross Org Movement Already partially covered in 06.4. The specific cross org scenario: Cross Cloud Movement — Real World Chains AWS → GCP via Terraform State in S3 GCP → AWS via Secrets in GCS Azure → AWS via Key Vault CI/CD as Cross Cloud Bridge Building the Attack Map When you start a multi account or multi cloud engagement, build an explicit graph before moving: Quick Reference — Cross Account and Cross Cloud Related Notes 06.1 — Cloud Privesc Mindset and Methodology 06.2 — AWS Lateral Movement 06.3 — Azure Lateral Movement 06.4 — GCP Lateral Movement 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation 05.5 — CICD Pipeline Attacks MODULE 9 — Cloud Persistence and Defence Evasion

title: 07.2 — Subdomain Enumeration and Certificate Transparency
body: 07.2 — Subdomain Enumeration and Certificate Transparency What This Note Covers How to discover cloud hosted assets via subdomain enumeration and certificate transparency logs — identifying S3 buckets, App Services, Cloud Run endpoints, and other cloud resources that are exposed through DNS. Why Subdomains Reveal Cloud Infrastructure Organisations map custom domains to cloud services via CNAME records. A CNAME pointing to reveals an S3 bucket. One pointing to reveals an App Service. Enumerate all subdomains of a target domain and you get a map of their cloud footprint. Additionally, certificate transparency (CT) logs record every TLS certificate issued for a domain — including certificates for internal subdomains the organisation may not expect to be public. Certificate Transparency — Passive Subdomain Discovery Every TLS certificate is logged in public CT logs. This means every subdomain a target has ever used with HTTPS is discoverable without any active scanning. Active Subdomain Enumeration CT logs catch historical certificates. Active enumeration finds current and additional subdomains. amass — Comprehensive Subdomain Discovery subfinder — Fast Passive Enumeration dnsx — DNS Resolution and Filtering Identifying Cloud Services from Subdomains Once you have a list of live subdomains, identify which cloud services they point to: Subdomain Takeover — Cloud Specific A subdomain takeover occurs when a CNAME points to a cloud resource that no longer exists. The attacker creates that resource and hijacks the subdomain. Detection Cloud Specific Takeover Indicators Wildcard DNS and Cloud Discovery Some organisations use wildcard DNS ( ) pointing to cloud infrastructure. This is discoverable: Cloud Specific Subdomain Patterns Build targeted wordlists using common cloud service naming patterns: Automated Cloud Recon Pipeline Quick Reference Related Notes 07.1 — Unauthenticated Cloud Asset Discovery 07.3 — GitHub and Code Repository Recon 07.4 — Shodan, Censys, and Search Engine Dorks 01.4 — S3 Attacks tags: [cloud, recon, subdomains, certificate transparency, dns, amass, subfinder, takeover, cloudhawk] 07.2 — Subdomain Enumeration and Certificate Transparency What This Note Covers Discovering cloud hosted assets via subdomain enumeration and CT logs — mapping S3 buckets, App Services, Cloud Run endpoints, and identifying subdomain takeover opportunities. title: 07.3 — GitHub and Code Repository Recon
body: 07.3 — GitHub and Code Repository Recon What This Note Covers Finding cloud credentials and infrastructure intelligence in public code repositories — GitHub dorks, automated secret scanning with truffleHog and gitleaks, Docker Hub layer analysis, and organisation wide repository enumeration. Why Code Repositories Are the Richest Target Developers commit secrets constantly. Studies consistently find that thousands of valid cloud credentials are committed to public GitHub repositories every day. Common sources: AWS access keys hardcoded in scripts Service account JSON files committed alongside application code files accidentally pushed with credentials CI/CD configuration files with embedded secrets Terraform variable files with plaintext passwords Docker Compose files with database credentials Application config files with API keys GitHub Search Dorks for Cloud Credentials GitHub's code search lets you search for specific patterns across all public repositories. Automated Secret Scanning — truffleHog truffleHog scans git history and file content for secrets using entropy analysis and regex patterns. It also verifies whether detected secrets are still active. Automated Secret Scanning — gitleaks gitleaks is a fast, rules based secret scanner for git repositories. Organisation Wide GitHub Enumeration When targeting a specific company, enumerate all their public GitHub repositories. Git History Mining Even if a secret was deleted in a later commit, it persists in git history. Full history scanning catches these. Docker Hub Layer Analysis Public Docker images may contain secrets in their build layers. Pastebin and Paste Sites Cloud credentials are also leaked on paste sites, though this is harder to monitor systematically. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 8 — Assessment Methodology/08.1 — Cloud Assessment vs Cloud Pentest.md
title: 08.1 — Cloud Security Assessment vs Cloud Penetration Test
body: 08.1 — Cloud Security Assessment vs Cloud Penetration Test What This Note Covers The critical distinction between a cloud security assessment and a cloud penetration test, how access level determines what you test and what you find, and how to structure the engagement based on the client's objective. Assessment vs Penetration Test — The Core Difference These terms are used interchangeably by clients but mean different things operationally: | Dimension | Cloud Security Assessment | Cloud Penetration Test | | | | | | Primary goal | Find all misconfigurations and risk | Demonstrate exploitable impact | | Credential access | Read only access to all configuration | Low privilege credentials (simulate attacker) | | Approach | Systematic, exhaustive, tool assisted | Targeted, creative, adversary simulating | | Coverage | Broad — all services reviewed | Focused — specific attack paths pursued | | Output | Compliance style report with all findings | Attack narrative + proof of concept chains | | Duration | Days to weeks | Days (focused) to weeks (red team) | | CloudTrail noise | High — many API calls | Variable — attacker may try to stay quiet | [!tip] Most clients need both An assessment finds all the configuration gaps. A pentest demonstrates which gaps are actually exploitable and chains them together into a realistic attack story. The most valuable engagements combine both. Access Level Determines Everything The access level granted determines what you can test and what findings you can produce. Black Box — External Attacker Simulation What you're given: Nothing. A domain name or an AWS account ID at most. What you simulate: A fully external attacker with no insider knowledge. What you find: Publicly exposed cloud storage (S3, GCS, Blob) Unauthenticated cloud services (API Gateway, Lambda URLs, App Services) Subdomain takeover opportunities Leaked credentials in GitHub, Pastebin, Docker Hub Exposed admin panels (Grafana, Kibana, Jenkins) Shodan visible cloud services Limitations: You will miss most of the actual attack surface. IAM misconfigurations, overprivileged roles, exposed secrets in Secrets Manager — none of these are visible without credentials. When to use: When the client specifically wants to test what's visible to an external attacker with no prior access. Grey Box — Compromised Credential Simulation What you're given: Low privilege IAM credentials (AWS user, Azure AD user, GCP SA with minimal permissions), equivalent to a leaked API key or a compromised employee account. What you simulate: An attacker who has obtained initial access via credential leak, phishing, or supply chain compromise. What you find: Everything in black box PLUS: IAM privilege escalation paths Over permissive roles and policies Cross account trust misconfigurations Secrets in environment variables, Parameter Store, Secrets Manager (if accessible) Lateral movement paths between services When to use: Most common engagement type. Realistic simulation of the most common attack scenario — leaked credentials. White Box — Full Configuration Review What you're given: Read only administrative access — IAM policy in AWS, Security Reader in Azure, viewer roles across all GCP projects. Architecture diagrams, list of services in use. What you simulate: An authorised security review with full visibility. What you find: Everything in grey box PLUS: All IAM policies reviewed exhaustively (not just the ones you can reach) All cross account trust relationships All network configurations (VPCs, security groups, NACLs) All logging and monitoring gaps Compliance posture against CIS benchmarks When to use: Security audits, compliance reviews, due diligence for acquisitions. Assume Breach Scenarios A specific engagement type where you start with a compromised position inside the environment: Compromised workload: You're given shell access to an EC2 instance or pod and must demonstrate what an attacker can do from there. Compromised developer machine: You're given the credentials from a developer's machine (SSH keys, AWS CLI config, kubeconfig) and must show the blast radius. Compromised CI/CD: You're given access to a Jenkins/GitHub Actions pipeline and must demonstrate what you can reach. Defining the Assessment Scope Document A proper scope document must include: Quick Reference — Engagement Type Selection Related Notes 08.2 — ScoutSuite and Prowler — Automated Scanning 08.3 — Manual Assessment Checklist by Service 00.3 — Legal and Scoping Considerations MODULE 7 — Cloud Reconnaissance and OSINT

title: 08.2 — ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, and Steampipe
body: 08.2 — ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, and Steampipe What This Note Covers The automated cloud security scanning tools used in every assessment — full command references, how to interpret output, what each tool finds best, and how to combine them for comprehensive coverage. The Role of Automated Scanning Automated tools do the broad sweep — they flag every misconfiguration against a ruleset so you don't miss anything obvious. Manual testing then confirms exploitability, finds chained paths, and tests business logic that tools can't evaluate. Rule: Always run automated tools first. Never file a finding that a tool should have caught if you skipped the tool. ScoutSuite — Multi Cloud Misconfiguration Scanner ScoutSuite by NCC Group is the most comprehensive multi cloud automated scanner. It pulls configuration data from cloud APIs and generates an HTML report with findings categorised by severity. Install and Setup AWS Scanning Azure Scanning GCP Scanning Reading ScoutSuite Output The HTML report organises findings by service. For each service: Danger (red): Immediate action required — actively exploitable or severely misconfigured Warning (orange): Misconfiguration that increases risk but may have compensating controls Good (green): Correctly configured Priority review order in the ScoutSuite report: Prowler — Compliance and Security Scanning Prowler by Toni de la Fuente focuses on compliance frameworks (CIS, PCI DSS, SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA) and generates structured reports suitable for audit evidence. Install AWS Scanning Azure Scanning GCP Scanning Key Prowler Check Categories CloudMapper — AWS Network Topology Visualisation CloudMapper creates an interactive network diagram of your AWS VPC topology — essential for understanding network architecture during assessments. What to look for in CloudMapper: EC2 instances in public subnets with direct internet access Unusual cross VPC peering connections Security groups with very broad access (thick connection lines) Database servers in public subnets Steampipe — SQL Queries Against Cloud APIs Steampipe turns cloud APIs into SQL tables. You can write SQL queries to enumerate and analyse cloud configuration. Steampipe Mods — Pre Built Query Packs Tool Combination Strategy Quick Reference Related Notes 08.1 — Cloud Assessment vs Cloud Pentest 08.3 — Manual Assessment Checklist by Service 00.6 — Tool Setup — CLI and Frameworks MODULE 7 — Cloud Reconnaissance and OSINT

body: 08.4 — Cloud Security Benchmarks and MITRE ATT&CK for Cloud What This Note Covers The CIS Benchmarks for AWS, Azure, and GCP — what they cover and how to use them as an assessment framework. Then MITRE ATT&CK for Cloud — how to map your findings and attack techniques to the official taxonomy. CIS Benchmarks — Overview The Center for Internet Security (CIS) publishes benchmarks for major cloud platforms. These are configuration standards developed by consensus among security practitioners, vendors, and governments. Two levels: Level 1: Foundational security controls, low operational impact. Every organisation should meet these. Level 2: Stricter controls for high security environments. May have operational trade offs. CIS Benchmarks are the most widely referenced cloud security standard and are directly mapped by Prowler, ScoutSuite, and Security Hub. path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 8 — Assessment Methodology/08.5 — Reporting Cloud Findings.md
title: 08.5 — Reporting Cloud Findings
body: 08.5 — Reporting Cloud Findings What This Note Covers How to write cloud security findings that communicate risk clearly — severity rating in cloud context, finding structure, remediation guidance, cloud specific severity considerations, and the full report structure. Why Cloud Finding Reporting Is Different Cloud findings often don't map cleanly to traditional CVSS scoring: A public S3 bucket containing customer PII — no CVE, no exploit, but Critical severity because the data is already exposed. Lambda execution role with — no exploit needed, but Critical because any code execution in that function = full account compromise. IMDSv1 enabled with an SSRF vulnerable application — the combination is Critical; either alone is medium. The key principle: rate cloud findings by business impact and exploitability of the chain, not just the individual misconfiguration. Cloud Adjusted Severity Framework Use a modified severity scale that accounts for cloud specific context: Critical Conditions that meet any of the following: Publicly accessible data (storage, database, API) with no authentication IAM configuration that provides direct path to account admin with no additional steps Exposed credentials (access keys, SA keys, SAS tokens) with confirmed active permissions Unauthenticated remote code execution on cloud hosted infrastructure Cross account access allowing attacker to pivot to production from compromised dev High IAM privilege escalation path with 2 3 steps available to low privilege user Sensitive data accessible to any authenticated cloud user (not just org members) Missing MFA on privileged accounts (admin, root, Global Admin) Publicly exposed admin panel (Grafana, Kibana, Jenkins) with weak/default auth RDS instance publicly accessible with known weak credentials CloudTrail disabled in regions with production workloads Medium IAM misconfiguration that could lead to escalation but requires additional factors Overly permissive security groups that increase attack surface without direct exploitation Logging gaps (CloudTrail data events not enabled, VPC Flow Logs off) Missing encryption on data at rest Unrotated secrets/access keys (90+ days) Default VPC in use for non trivial workloads Low / Informational Best practice deviations with no direct security impact Missing tags, cost allocation configuration Sub optimal configurations that don't increase risk in the current environment Hardening improvements recommended for defence in depth Finding Structure Template Every finding should include these sections: bash Get function execution role aws lambda get function configuration \ function name DataProcessor \ path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 9 — Persistence and Defence Evasion/09.1 — AWS Persistence Techniques.md
title: 09.1 — AWS Persistence Techniques
body: 09.1 — AWS Persistence Techniques What This Note Covers How attackers maintain access to AWS environments after initial compromise — IAM backdoors, Lambda persistence, EC2 userdata modification, secondary access keys, SSM agent abuse, and CloudTrail aware persistence. The Persistence Challenge in Cloud Cloud environments make traditional persistence (cron jobs, init scripts, rootkits) unreliable because: EC2 instances are ephemeral — they can be replaced any time Functions are stateless — they have no persistent runtime Credentials expire — temporary credentials last 1 12 hours Cloud native persistence therefore targets the IAM layer — the only thing that persists regardless of compute changes. If you own an IAM identity with permanent credentials, you maintain access even if the entire application is redeployed. Technique 1: Backdoor IAM User (Primary Persistence) Creating a new IAM user with an access key is the most reliable AWS persistence mechanism. Unlike role credentials, access keys don't expire. [!warning] This is the most detected persistence technique AWS CloudTrail logs CreateUser and CreateAccessKey. Any mature SOC with an alert on these events will catch this immediately. Use it only when necessary and blend the naming with existing patterns. Technique 2: Secondary Access Key (Stealthy) Instead of creating a new user, create a second access key for an existing user. Less obvious than a new user, but still logged. Technique 3: Modify Role Trust Policy (Cross Account Backdoor) Adding an external account as a trusted principal in a role's trust policy gives the attacker persistent access via cross account role assumption — harder to spot than a new IAM user. Technique 4: Lambda Persistence (Code Modification) Modify an existing Lambda function to include a backdoor trigger — every time the legitimate function runs, it also performs attacker defined actions. Technique 5: Lambda Scheduled Event (Active C2) Create a new Lambda function that runs on a schedule to beacon back to attacker infrastructure. Technique 6: SSM Agent Abuse AWS Systems Manager Run Command can execute commands on any EC2 instance with the SSM agent — without SSH, without security group changes. Technique 7: Secrets Manager Backdoor Store attacker credentials in Secrets Manager under a plausible name — retrieve them later via the API. Detection Evasion for IAM Persistence Operators with CloudTrail alerts should be aware of what events trigger alerts: Quick Reference — AWS Persistence Related Notes 09.2 — Azure and GCP Persistence Techniques 09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation 01.5 — IAM Privilege Escalation MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 9 — Persistence and Defence Evasion/09.2 — Azure and GCP Persistence Techniques.md
title: 09.2 — Azure and GCP Persistence Techniques
body: 09.2 — Azure and GCP Persistence Techniques What This Note Covers Cloud native persistence techniques for Azure and GCP — app registration backdoors, service principal credential addition, Conditional Access policy modification, GCP service account key creation, domain wide delegation abuse, and org policy manipulation. Azure Persistence Techniques Technique 1: Backdoor App Registration (Primary Azure Persistence) App registrations in Azure AD can have client secrets added at any time. If you add a credential to an existing high privilege app registration, you gain persistent access as that service principal. [!tip] New credential blends in App registrations often have multiple credentials for rotation purposes. Adding one more doesn't stand out unless Azure AD audit logs are actively monitored for events. Technique 2: Add Owner to App Registration If you can modify an app registration's ownership, you add your identity as an owner — giving permanent access to manage its credentials and permissions. Technique 3: Service Principal Key Addition (Certificate Based) Service principals can authenticate with client secrets OR certificates. Certificates are harder to detect as they require no plaintext secret in logs. Technique 4: Conditional Access Policy Modification Conditional Access policies restrict when users can authenticate. Adding an exclusion to a restrictive policy (e.g., MFA requirement) creates a persistent bypass. Technique 5: Federation Identity Backdoor (Advanced) Add a federated identity credential to an app registration, pointing to an external identity provider you control. GCP Persistence Techniques Technique 1: Service Account Key Creation (Primary GCP Persistence) Creating a JSON key file for a service account is the GCP equivalent of creating an AWS access key. The key doesn't expire until explicitly revoked. Technique 2: Create a New Service Account and Grant Roles Create a new SA under a plausible name, grant it org level roles, generate a key — persistent access that survives project changes. Technique 3: Org Policy Modification Remove org policies that restrict what can happen in projects — unlocking capabilities the attacker needs to maintain access. Technique 4: Domain Wide Delegation Addition If you have Google Workspace admin access, adding DWD to a service account gives persistent impersonation capability for all workspace users. Technique 5: Cloud Function Backdoor (GCP Equivalent of Lambda) Quick Reference — Azure and GCP Persistence Related Notes 09.1 — AWS Persistence Techniques 09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation 02.5 — Azure AD Privilege Escalation 03.2 — GCP Service Account Attacks

path: CLOUDHAWK/MODULE 9 — Persistence and Defence Evasion/09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation.md
title: 09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation
body: 09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation What This Note Covers How attackers avoid detection in cloud environments — CloudTrail blind spots, log manipulation, living off the land with native cloud services, minimising API call noise, and what detection looks like so you can understand what you're evading. The Cloud Detection Landscape Before evading, understand what defenders can see: CloudTrail Evasion — AWS Technique 1: Identify and Use Unmonitored Regions Technique 2: Use Read Only APIs (Low Alert Risk) Read only operations ( , , ) are less likely to trigger alerts than write operations. Do as much recon as possible before taking any action. Technique 3: Stop or Modify CloudTrail (High Risk — Use Only in Testing) [!danger] Never disable CloudTrail in a real client engagement Disabling CloudTrail in a production environment can cause compliance violations and hide real malicious activity from the client's security team. In pentesting, never disable logging. Demonstrate the technique in documentation only. Technique 4: Use Services That Don't Generate Management Events Some AWS service interactions don't appear in CloudTrail management events: Azure Evasion Techniques Identify Monitoring Gaps Low Profile Azure Operations GCP Evasion Techniques Cloud Audit Log Gaps Living Off the Land in Cloud Environments Using legitimate cloud services for C2 and exfiltration avoids custom C2 infrastructure that might be blocked or detected. S3 as C2 Channel SQS/SNS as C2 Cloud Functions as C2 Relay Snapshot and AMI Exfiltration Exfiltrating data via cloud native copy operations that look like infrastructure maintenance. title: 09.4 — Cloud Exfiltration Techniques
body: 09.4 — Cloud Exfiltration Techniques What This Note Covers How attackers move data out of cloud environments using cloud native mechanisms — S3 replication, cross account copy, snapshot sharing, database export, and exfiltration via legitimate cloud services that blend with normal traffic. Cloud Exfiltration vs Traditional Exfiltration Traditional exfiltration: compress data → exfiltrate over network → attacker receives file at external server. Cloud exfiltration: use cloud native features to copy data to attacker controlled cloud resources — the traffic looks like routine cloud infrastructure operations, uses HTTPS to cloud provider endpoints, and may never touch attacker controlled infrastructure at all. Technique 1: S3 Cross Account Replication S3 has a native replication feature that continuously copies objects from one bucket to another. Configure it to replicate to an attacker controlled bucket. Sync Existing Data Technique 2: EBS Snapshot Cross Account Copy Copy an EBS snapshot to an attacker controlled account. The snapshot contains the full disk image of an EC2 volume — all files, databases, logs, and credentials that were on disk. Technique 3: RDS Snapshot Export Export an RDS database to S3 in Parquet format — a full database dump accessible as files. Technique 4: Database Direct Export via Credentials If you have database credentials (from Secrets Manager, env vars, or config files), connect directly and dump. Technique 5: Data Exfiltration via Glacier Glacier is AWS's archive storage. Initiating a restore from a Glacier archived bucket to a different storage class (and then syncing) is a stealthy long haul exfiltration method. Technique 6: Data Exfiltration via DNS DNS based exfiltration encodes data in DNS queries to an attacker controlled domain. In cloud environments, DNS egress is almost universally allowed. Technique 7: Azure Storage Cross Subscription Replication Detection — What Exfiltration Looks Like Quick Reference — Cloud Exfiltration Related Notes 09.1 — AWS Persistence Techniques 09.3 — Cloud Defence Evasion and Log Manipulation 01.4 — S3 Attacks MODULE 8 — Assessment Methodology

path: GRC-GUARDIAN/MODULE-1-FOUNDATIONS/G1-01 — What is GRC and Why It Exists.md
title: G1-01 — What is GRC and Why It Exists
body: G1 01 — What is GRC and Why It Exists [!abstract] What This Note Covers By the end of this note, you will understand what GRC means, why it exists, what problem it solves, and how its three components fit together — told through real history and plain English. Why This Exists Cast your mind back to the early 2000s. Enron, one of the largest energy companies in the United States, collapsed overnight. WorldCom, a telecommunications giant, filed for bankruptcy. Both companies had been hiding billions of dollars in debt, manipulating their accounts, and deceiving investors and regulators for years. When the truth came out, thousands of people lost their jobs, their savings, and their pensions overnight. The question the world asked was: how did no one catch this? The answer was a failure of three things simultaneously: 1. Governance — The people in charge (the board, the executives) were either complicit or had no real oversight of what was happening. Nobody was asking hard questions. Nobody was accountable. 2. Risk Management — Nobody was formally tracking the risk that the company was built on fraud. There was no process to identify, assess, and escalate the danger. 3. Compliance — The company was breaking laws and regulations, but there was no robust system to check whether rules were being followed. The fallout from these scandals produced the Sarbanes Oxley Act (SOX) in the US in 2002 — one of the most significant pieces of corporate governance legislation ever passed. It forced companies to put in place proper controls, document them, test them, and certify that their financial reporting was accurate. This was one of the earliest moments where the modern concept of GRC was formalised. But the need for GRC did not start with Enron, and it did not end with SOX. Every major corporate scandal, every massive data breach, every regulatory fine, every operational disaster has at its heart a failure of one or more of these three disciplines. GRC exists because organisations are complex, and complex systems fail in complex ways — unless someone is actively governing them, managing their risks, and making sure they follow the rules. What It Is GRC stands for Governance, Risk, and Compliance . It is an integrated framework — a way of organising an organisation's approach to three fundamental challenges: Governance How decisions are made, who makes them, who is accountable, and how the organisation is directed and controlled. Think of governance as the "rules of who's in charge and how they behave." In a well governed organisation: The board sets the direction and tone Executives implement strategy within defined boundaries Policies exist to tell people what is expected Accountability is clear — if something goes wrong, there is a defined person responsible In a poorly governed organisation: Nobody knows who makes which decisions There are no policies, or policies that nobody follows Nobody is held accountable when things go wrong The left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing Risk The identification, assessment, and management of things that could go wrong — or opportunities that could be missed. Risk management is not about eliminating risk (that is impossible). It is about understanding risk, making conscious choices about which risks to accept, and putting in place controls to reduce the ones you do not want. Think of it like home insurance. You cannot prevent your house from ever catching fire. But you can: Identify the risk (fire exists and it could happen) Assess how likely it is and how bad it would be Mitigate it (fit smoke alarms, keep fire exits clear) Transfer it (buy insurance so someone else covers the financial loss) That is risk management. The same logic applies in an organisation, but for dozens or hundreds of risks simultaneously. Compliance Making sure the organisation follows applicable laws, regulations, standards, and its own internal policies. Compliance is not optional — there are laws that must be followed (like GDPR for data protection, or PCI DSS for payment card processing), and failure to follow them results in fines, legal action, loss of reputation, or loss of the right to operate. Think of compliance like an MOT for a car. The car (the organisation) must meet a defined standard (the regulation or framework) on a regular basis. An auditor (the mechanic) checks whether it does. If it fails, something must be fixed before it can keep operating. How the Three Fit Together GRC is not three separate things bolted together. It is one integrated discipline: Governance sets the direction: "We will handle data responsibly." Risk identifies the threats: "These are the ways we could fail to do that." Compliance confirms the execution: "Here is evidence that we are doing it." A useful analogy: think of a ship. Governance is the captain and the navigation plan — where are we going, and who is steering? Risk is the radar and the weather forecast — what dangers are ahead, and what do we do about them? Compliance is the coast guard inspection — are we carrying the required safety equipment and following maritime law? Remove any one of these and the ship is in danger. Governance without risk management is confident but blind. Risk management without compliance is well intentioned but unaccountable. Compliance without governance is bureaucratic theatre — ticking boxes with no real security culture behind it. How It Works in Practice Let's ground this in a real scenario. Scenario: A 300 person UK retail company processes customer credit card payments online. Governance in action: The board has approved an Information Security Policy. The CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) has been appointed with a mandate to protect customer data. There is a Security Committee that meets quarterly to review risks and approve budgets. Risk in action: The security team has conducted a risk assessment and identified that the e commerce platform could be vulnerable to SQL injection attacks — a type of cyberattack where a hacker manipulates the website's database. This risk has been documented in the risk register (a formal log of all identified risks), rated as High, and assigned to the Head of IT to mitigate. Compliance in action: Because the company takes credit card payments, it must comply with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard). An external auditor (a QSA — Qualified Security Assessor) has been engaged to verify compliance. The company has also appointed a Data Protection Officer (DPO) to manage compliance with GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation). All three are running simultaneously, and they inform each other: The governance structure (Security Committee) hears the risk assessment findings and authorises remediation spend. The risk register is used as evidence during the PCI DSS audit. The compliance audit identifies a new gap, which is fed back as a new risk. This is GRC working as intended. The Details That Matter The Business Case for GRC GRC is not just about avoiding fines. The real business case includes: | Benefit | Explanation | | | | | Avoidance of regulatory fines | GDPR fines can reach €20M or 4% of global annual turnover. PCI DSS non compliance can result in losing the right to process card payments entirely. | | Reduction in breach costs | The average cost of a data breach globally (IBM 2024) is approximately $4.88 million. Strong GRC reduces both the likelihood and the impact. | | Competitive advantage | Customers, partners, and investors increasingly require evidence of security maturity. ISO 27001 certification can be a genuine sales differentiator. | | Operational resilience | Organisations with mature GRC programmes recover from incidents faster and with less damage. | | Board confidence | Well reported risk posture gives boards the information they need to make better strategic decisions. | The Difference Between GRC as a Tick Box and GRC as a Culture This is one of the most important distinctions in the entire field. There are two types of organisations: Type 1 — Tick box compliance: The organisation fills in the forms, passes the audit, gets the certificate, and then continues operating exactly as before. Security policies exist but nobody reads them. Risk registers are updated once a year before the audit. The CISO spends most of their time on paperwork rather than actual security improvement. Type 2 — Security culture: GRC is embedded into how the organisation actually operates. Leaders visibly champion security. Employees understand why policies exist and actually follow them. Risk management is a live, ongoing process, not an annual checkbox. Compliance is a baseline, not a ceiling. The goal of GUARDIAN is to teach you the knowledge needed to build Type 2 organisations — and to recognise Type 1 for what it is. GRC vs Information Security vs Cybersecurity These terms are often used interchangeably and incorrectly. A quick distinction (covered more in G1 06): GRC is the management discipline — governance, oversight, risk frameworks, compliance programmes Information Security is broader — protecting all information, not just digital (includes physical security, paper records, people) Cybersecurity is the technical subset — protecting digital systems, networks, and data from cyberattacks GRC is the strategic and management layer. Cybersecurity is largely the technical execution layer. A GRC professional does not need to be a penetration tester, but they must understand what cybersecurity controls exist and whether they are effective. Common Mistakes and Failures 1. Treating GRC as a project rather than a programme. Organisations implement ISO 27001, get certified, and then consider it "done." GRC is never done. It is a continuous cycle of improvement. Standards evolve. Threats evolve. The organisation changes. The programme must keep pace. 2. GRC owned by IT only. GRC is an enterprise wide discipline. HR owns people risk. Legal owns regulatory compliance. Finance owns financial risk. IT owns technical controls. When GRC sits only in IT, critical risks in other areas go unmanaged. 3. No board level sponsorship. GRC without executive buy in is theatre. The board must set the tone — that security and compliance are priorities — and must actively receive risk reporting, not just rubber stamp it. 4. Disconnected silos. Many organisations have a compliance team, a risk team, and a security team that barely communicate. This leads to duplicate effort, inconsistent controls, and gaps that attackers can exploit. 5. Confusing compliance with security. Passing an audit does not mean you are secure. An organisation can be fully PCI DSS compliant and still suffer a catastrophic breach — because compliance measures what controls exist , not whether they are truly effective against real world threats. Exam Angle ISO 27001 Lead Auditor: GRC concepts underpin the entire standard. Clause 4 (Context), Clause 5 (Leadership/Governance), Clause 6 (Risk Planning), and Clause 9 (Performance Evaluation/Compliance) all map directly to G, R, and C respectively. Expect questions that test whether you understand why the standard exists, not just what it says. CISM: Domain 1 (Information Security Governance) maps to the G in GRC. Domain 2 (Information Risk Management) maps to the R. CISM tests management level understanding — how to present GRC to a board, how to align security with business objectives, how to build a governance structure. CRISC: Entirely focused on the R in GRC — IT risk identification, assessment, response, and monitoring. CRISC candidates must understand risk frameworks (COBIT, NIST, ISO 31000) and how they integrate with governance. CISSP: Domain 1 (Security and Risk Management) covers GRC concepts including ethics, governance, compliance, risk management, and legal/regulatory requirements. CISSP tests at the "manager of managers" level — you are expected to know how to design and oversee GRC programmes, not just execute them. GUARDIAN's Take After 20 years of walking into organisations of every size and sector, I can tell you that the single biggest differentiator between organisations that handle incidents well and those that are destroyed by them is the quality of their GRC foundations . The organisations that recover fastest from a breach are not the ones with the most expensive technology. They are the ones that: Already know what their assets are and what is critical (governance) Have already thought about what could go wrong and have plans ready (risk management) Have been maintaining controls and can prove it (compliance) GRC done well is not a burden. It is the organisational immune system. When it works properly, you barely notice it. When it is absent, a single incident can be existential. The organisations that view GRC as a cost centre and a compliance burden are the ones that end up on the front page of the news. The ones that view it as a genuine business enabler — a way of building trust with customers, partners, and regulators — are the ones that survive, grow, and lead. That is the mindset GUARDIAN will build in you throughout this curriculum. Module: Module 1 — Foundations | Guardian Curriculum

path: GRC-GUARDIAN/MODULE-1-FOUNDATIONS/G1-02 — Governance Explained.md
title: G1-02 — Governance Explained
body: G1 02 — Governance Explained [!abstract] What This Note Covers By the end of this note, you will understand what governance means in an information security context, why it exists, how it is structured in real organisations, and what good and bad governance actually look like. Why This Exists In 1995, Nick Leeson — a derivatives trader at Barings Bank, one of the oldest merchant banks in Britain — single handedly caused the bank's collapse by hiding £827 million in trading losses in a secret account. He had authority to both execute trades and approve his own transactions — a catastrophic failure of segregation of duties. Nobody was checking his work. Nobody had the oversight mechanisms in place to see what he was doing until it was too late. Barings Bank had been in operation for 233 years. It was destroyed in a matter of months by one person operating without proper governance. Leeson's case is extreme, but the underlying failure is universal: when nobody is watching, and nobody is accountable, bad things happen . Governance is the answer to this problem. It is the set of structures, processes, and accountabilities that ensure an organisation is directed and controlled effectively — that decisions are made by the right people, that those people are accountable for those decisions, and that there is transparency into what is happening and why. In the context of information security, governance answers the question: who is responsible for security, what authority do they have, and how do we know things are working? What It Is Governance is the system by which an organisation is directed and controlled. In the information security context, Information Security Governance is specifically about ensuring that security decisions are made at the right level, aligned to business objectives, properly resourced, and subject to oversight. It is not about technology. It is not about firewalls or antivirus software. It is about people, structures, accountability, and direction . A simple way to think about it: governance answers three questions. | Question | Governance Answer | | | | | Who is in charge? | Defined roles and responsibilities — board, CISO, risk owner, asset owner | | What are we trying to achieve? | Strategy and policy — security objectives aligned to business goals | | How do we know it's working? | Metrics, reporting, audit, management review | Without governance, even the best security technology in the world is ineffective — because nobody has decided what it should protect, who is responsible for it, or how they will know if it fails. How It Works in Practice The Governance Hierarchy Governance in most organisations operates in a layered hierarchy. Think of it like a chain of command: 1. The Board of Directors The board sits at the top. They are ultimately accountable for everything the organisation does — including how it manages risk and information security. In practice, this means: Approving the organisation's risk appetite (how much risk they are willing to accept) Receiving regular reports on the security posture Ensuring that adequate resources are allocated to security The board does not run day to day security. But they set the tone. If the board treats security as a cost to be minimised, that attitude will cascade down the organisation. If the board treats it as a strategic priority, resources and culture follow. 2. Executive Management (C Suite) The CEO, CFO, CTO, and especially the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) translate board direction into operational reality. The CISO is typically responsible for: Developing and maintaining the Information Security Management System (ISMS) Leading the security programme Reporting risk posture to the board in terms they understand (business risk, not technical jargon) Owning the relationship with regulators and auditors 3. Security Committees and Steering Groups Many organisations establish a Security Committee or Information Security Steering Group — a cross functional body that includes representatives from IT, Legal, HR, Finance, and Operations. This committee: Reviews risk register updates Approves major security investments Ensures security decisions reflect business wide priorities, not just IT priorities Provides a forum for escalating security issues that span departments 4. Operational Management and Asset Owners Individual managers and team leaders are responsible for security within their own domains. The HR Director owns people related risks. The Head of Finance owns financial data. The IT Manager owns technical infrastructure. These people are called risk owners or asset owners — they are accountable for specific risks and controls within their area. 5. All Staff Every employee is a participant in governance. Policies apply to everyone. Security training is for everyone. Incident reporting is everyone's responsibility. Governance without staff engagement is governance on paper only. What Governance Produces Good governance produces several concrete outputs: Policies Policies are formal statements of management's intent. An Information Security Policy says: "This organisation is committed to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of its information assets." It is signed by the CEO or board. It is not a technical document — it is a governance document, setting direction and establishing accountability. Roles and Responsibilities Governance defines who does what. A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is a common tool. For example, for the risk assessment process: Responsible : Security Analyst (does the work) Accountable : CISO (owns the outcome) Consulted : IT Manager, Legal (provide input) Informed : Board (receives the results) Objectives and Strategy Governance produces a security strategy — a multi year plan that defines where the organisation wants to be in terms of security maturity and how it will get there. This strategy is aligned to business objectives. Security exists to enable the business, not obstruct it. Reporting and Oversight Governance produces regular reporting upward — from operational teams to the CISO, from the CISO to the Security Committee, from the Security Committee to the board. These reports translate technical findings into business language: not "we had 4,000 failed login attempts" but "there is evidence of credential stuffing attacks targeting our customer portal; here is the residual risk and what we are doing about it." The Details That Matter Governance Frameworks Several frameworks provide structure for how governance should be designed. The most important ones a GRC professional must know: ISO 27001 (Clause 5 — Leadership) ISO 27001 requires top management to demonstrate leadership and commitment to the ISMS. This means: approving the information security policy, ensuring security objectives are set, and ensuring the ISMS is integrated into business processes. The standard explicitly requires that governance exists and is visible — you cannot delegate governance away to a junior analyst. COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies) COBIT is a framework specifically for IT governance and management. It distinguishes between governance (evaluate, direct, monitor — what the board does) and management (plan, build, run, monitor — what executives and IT do). COBIT 2019 provides detailed guidance on governance structures, roles, and processes. NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 The 2024 update to the NIST CSF added a sixth function: Govern . This explicitly elevated governance to be the foundation upon which all other security activities (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) depend. This is a significant development — it signals that the security community now formally recognises that technology controls are ineffective without governance foundations. King IV (South Africa) / UK Corporate Governance Code These are corporate governance codes that define how boards should operate. They apply to listed companies and set expectations for risk oversight, transparency, and accountability — including for information security risk. Security Strategy vs Security Policy vs Security Procedure These three are often confused. Here is the distinction: | Document | What it is | Who writes it | Who approves it | How long it lasts | | | | | | | | Security Strategy | Where we are going and why (3–5 year direction) | CISO | Board | 3–5 years, reviewed annually | | Security Policy | What we require and why (management intent) | CISO / Security team | Board / CEO | 1–3 years, annual review | | Security Standard | Specific requirements that implement the policy | Security team | CISO | 1–2 years | | Security Procedure | Step by step instructions for how to do something | Operational teams | IT Manager / CISO | Frequent updates | All of these are governance artefacts — they document decisions made by people with authority and accountability. Segregation of Duties (SoD) One of the most important governance controls. It means that no single individual should have end to end control over a critical process. If one person can both initiate and approve a transaction, there is nothing to stop fraud or error. Examples: The person who requests a new user account should not be the same person who creates it The developer who writes code should not be the same person who deploys it to production The person who processes a payment should not be the same person who reconciles the accounts This is what Barings Bank failed to do with Nick Leeson. Segregation of duties is a foundational governance control that appears in virtually every framework. The Principle of Accountability Governance only works if someone is genuinely accountable for each risk and control — meaning they bear the consequences if it fails. This is different from being responsible (doing the work) or being informed (just knowing about it). In practice, accountability means: if this risk materialises and causes harm, this named person must explain to the board what happened and why. That is why boards exist. That is why CISOs exist. That is why risk registers name risk owners. Without real accountability, governance is decoration. Common Mistakes and Failures 1. Governance by committee with no individual accountability. Security Committees that collectively own decisions but nobody is individually accountable. When something goes wrong, everyone points at the committee. Fix: every risk and every major control must have a named owner. 2. Security policy that nobody has read. The Information Security Policy is approved by the board, printed, filed, and never seen again. Employees have never been trained on it. It was last updated in 2019. This is governance theatre. Fix: policies must be communicated, trained, accessible, and reviewed regularly. 3. CISO reporting to the CTO or CIO. When the CISO reports to the technology function, there is an inherent conflict of interest — security needs are often at odds with technology speed and cost. Best practice is for the CISO to report directly to the CEO or board. This gives security a genuinely independent voice. 4. Board treating security as purely a technology problem. "That's an IT matter" is one of the most dangerous phrases in corporate governance. Every board member needs to understand that information security risk is business risk — it affects reputation, revenue, regulatory standing, and operational continuity. 5. Strategy without resource. A beautiful 5 year security strategy that was never funded. Governance must translate strategy into budget, headcount, and actual programme delivery. Strategy on paper with no resource is not governance — it is wishful thinking. 6. No management review. ISO 27001 requires regular management review of the ISMS (see G3 16). Organisations skip this because it is inconvenient. The result is a governance structure that is never updated, never challenged, and drifts out of alignment with the organisation's actual risks. Exam Angle ISO 27001 Lead Auditor: Clause 5 of ISO 27001 is entirely about Leadership (governance). Auditors will look for evidence of top management commitment — not just a signed policy, but actual involvement. Can the CISO demonstrate that the board receives security reports? Is there a management review record? Who approved the information security objectives? Key terms: top management , information security policy , roles and responsibilities , management review , security objectives . Common finding: "The information security policy has not been communicated to all relevant personnel" — a Clause 5.2/7.4 nonconformity. CISM: Domain 1 is Information Security Governance. CISM tests whether you can build and manage a governance framework, not just describe one. Expect scenario questions like: "A new CISO joins a company and finds no security strategy. What should they do first?" (Answer: understand the business context and objectives before drafting anything — governance must be aligned to business goals.) Key concepts: alignment with business objectives, board reporting, security strategy development, roles and responsibilities. CISSP: Domain 1 (Security and Risk Management) covers governance concepts including due care vs due diligence, ethics, security governance principles, and organisational roles. Due care = doing what a reasonable person would do (having the policies and controls in place). Due diligence = actively verifying that those controls are working. CRISC: Governance is the context for all risk management in CRISC. The risk framework, risk appetite, and risk tolerance are all governance outputs that CRISC candidates must understand deeply. GUARDIAN's Take The single biggest governance failure I see, repeated across every sector and every size of organisation, is this: governance exists on paper, but not in behaviour . The policy says "all systems must be patched within 30 days of a critical vulnerability." The board approved it. The CISO signed it. And yet, when you walk into an internal audit and pull the evidence, 40% of servers have not been patched in six months. Why? Because nobody with real authority is checking. Nobody is being held accountable. The governance structure exists, but it has no teeth. Good governance is not about documents. Documents are just artefacts of decisions. Good governance is about culture — whether the people at the top genuinely behave as if security matters, and whether that behaviour cascades down through every layer of the organisation. When a CEO says "I need to understand this breach because I am responsible" — that is governance working. When a CEO says "IT will handle it, keep me out of it" — that is governance failing. Your job in GRC is not just to build the governance structures. It is to make them real. To put accountability where it belongs. To make sure the board is not just informed but genuinely engaged. To make sure policies are not just written but lived. That is the difference between a GRC professional who is valuable and one who is just a document factory.
