path: OSCP-JOURNEY/STAGE-1-THM/S1-01-Penetration-Testing-Fundamentals.md
title: S1-01 — Penetration Testing Fundamentals
body: S1 01 — Penetration Testing Fundamentals What Is a Penetration Test? A penetration test (pentest) is an authorised, simulated cyberattack against a system, network, or application. The goal is to find security weaknesses before a real attacker does — and prove they're exploitable, not just theoretical. The key word is authorised . Without written permission, everything in this curriculum is illegal. With it, you are a professional doing a critical job. A pentest is NOT: A vulnerability scan (automated tool running, no exploitation) A red team exercise (longer, more covert, full adversary simulation) A security audit (compliance focused, not exploitation focused) A pentest IS: Time boxed (usually 1–2 weeks for a real engagement) Scope limited (specific IPs, domains, or applications) Evidence based (you prove impact, not just flag potential issues) Reported (written deliverable to the client at the end) Black Box, Grey Box, White Box These describe how much information you're given before you start. | Box Type | What You Get | Real World Analogy | | | | | | Black Box | Nothing. Just an IP or domain. | Cold attacker with no insider knowledge | | Grey Box | Some info: credentials, architecture diagrams, partial source | Insider threat or partner with limited access | | White Box | Everything: full source code, admin creds, network diagrams | Full transparency — most thorough, most time efficient | OSCP exam is grey/black box. You get IPs, no hints about what's running. CPTS exam is black box. You receive a brief like a real client engagement. [!tip] Which is "harder"? Black box takes longer because you spend more time in recon. White box finds more vulnerabilities because you can audit the code. For job interviews, knowing black box methodology is what matters — it's what you'll be tested on. The Legal Framework — UK (Computer Misuse Act 1990) In the UK, hacking without authorisation violates the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (CMA) . This is the primary legislation you need to understand. Three core offences: 1. Section 1 — Unauthorised access to computer material. Simply logging in without permission. Up to 2 years. 2. Section 2 — Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences. Accessing a system with intent to steal data, commit fraud, etc. Up to 5 years. 3. Section 3 — Unauthorised modification of computer material. Deleting files, installing malware, changing data without permission. Up to 10 years. Section 3ZA (added 2015): Impairing access to data causing serious damage (critical infrastructure attacks). Up to 14 years or life if endangering life. What protects you as a pentester: A signed Statement of Work (SoW) or Rules of Engagement (RoE) document Written authorisation from the system owner (not just a manager — the actual legal owner) Scope definition confirming exactly what you're allowed to test [!danger] The "I had permission" defence Verbal permission means nothing. If you're ever questioned, you need a signed document from someone with legal authority over the system. Always get it in writing before touching anything. Bug bounty programs (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) provide public authorisation within their defined scope. HTB machines are on isolated infrastructure — you're not attacking the internet. Rules of Engagement (RoE) and Scope Before any engagement begins, you establish Rules of Engagement. This is the contract between you and the client that defines: What's in scope: IP ranges / CIDR blocks Specific domains and subdomains Applications (web apps, mobile, APIs) Test types allowed (external, internal, social engineering, physical) What's out of scope: Third party systems (cloud providers, payment processors like Stripe — they need their own authorisation) Production databases (sometimes — client may want read only testing only) Denial of Service testing (almost always excluded) Specific business hours (some clients say "no testing during 9–5") What happens during testing: Emergency contact: who to call if you break something Reporting cadence: daily updates? Only at end? Handling of discovered credentials: do you use them or just report? Data handling: what do you do with sensitive data you find? [!warning] Scope creep is a real risk You find a vulnerability that leads you to a system not in scope. Stop. Document it. Report it to the client and ask for scope expansion. Do NOT follow the attack path into out of scope systems — that's where legal protection ends. The 5 Phases of a Penetration Test Every methodology — PTES, OSSTMM, OWASP Testing Guide — maps to roughly the same phases. Memorise these. The OSCP exam follows this exact flow. Phase 1 — Reconnaissance (Recon) Gathering information about the target without touching it (passive) or by interacting with it (active). Passive: OSINT, DNS lookups, Shodan, LinkedIn, WHOIS, Google dorking Active: Nmap scans, banner grabbing, web spidering Goal: understand the attack surface. What services are running? What software versions? What people work there? What subdomains exist? Phase 2 — Scanning and Enumeration Deeper interaction with discovered services to find specific vulnerabilities. Port scanning (Nmap) Service version detection Web directory brute forcing (Gobuster, ffuf) Vulnerability scanning (Nessus, OpenVAS — not OSCP exam) Manual testing of each service Goal: find specific weaknesses to exploit. Phase 3 — Exploitation Actually exploiting a vulnerability to gain access. Running an exploit against a CVE Exploiting a web application vulnerability (SQLi, LFI, file upload) Brute forcing credentials Social engineering (phishing — outside OSCP scope) Goal: get a foothold. First access is just the beginning. Phase 4 — Post Exploitation What you do after getting a shell. Privilege escalation (user → root/SYSTEM) Lateral movement (machine A → machine B) Data exfiltration (in real engagements — not in OSCP) Persistence (in real engagements — not required in OSCP) Pivoting to additional network segments Goal: demonstrate full impact, reach the crown jewels. Phase 5 — Reporting Documenting everything you found, how you found it, and how to fix it. Executive summary (non technical, for management) Technical findings (CVE references, steps to reproduce, screenshots) Risk ratings (CVSS scores) Remediation recommendations Goal: give the client something actionable. [!tip] OSCP mirrors this exactly The 24 hour exam is phases 1–4. The 24 hour report window is phase 5. The exam isn't just "get root" — the report is worth points too. No report = automatic fail regardless of machines rooted. The PTES Standard (Penetration Testing Execution Standard) PTES is the industry standard framework for structuring pentests. It expands the 5 phases into 7 formal sections: 1. Pre engagement Interactions — Scoping, RoE, legal agreements 2. Intelligence Gathering — OSINT, passive recon 3. Threat Modelling — What's valuable to an attacker? What are realistic threats? 4. Vulnerability Analysis — Identifying weaknesses (scanning + manual) 5. Exploitation — Active exploitation of confirmed vulnerabilities 6. Post Exploitation — Privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence 7. Reporting — Full written deliverable The PTES website (pentest standard.org) is the authoritative reference. OSCP, PNPT, and CPTS all implicitly follow PTES structure. CVE and CVSS 3.1 CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) A CVE is a unique identifier assigned to a publicly disclosed vulnerability. Format: — e.g., (EternalBlue/MS17 010) Who assigns CVEs? MITRE Corporation, with input from CNAs (CVE Numbering Authorities — includes vendors like Microsoft, Cisco, and Google). Where to look them up: NVD (National Vulnerability Database): nvd.nist.gov — full detail, CVSS scores, references CVE Details: cvedetails.com — good for filtering by vendor/product Vendor advisories: Microsoft Security Response Center, etc. Reading a CVE entry — the important fields: Description: What the vulnerability is and what it affects CVSS Score: Severity rating (see below) References: Links to patches, advisories, and often PoC exploits CWE: The underlying weakness category (e.g., CWE 89 = SQL Injection) CPE: Affected product versions CVSS 3.1 (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) CVSS gives every vulnerability a score from 0.0 to 10.0. You'll use this in every pentest report. Score ranges: | Score | Rating | | | | | 0.0 | None | | 0.1–3.9 | Low | | 4.0–6.9 | Medium | | 7.0–8.9 | High | | 9.0–10.0 | Critical | The 8 base metrics (you need to understand these for reports): | Metric | Abbreviation | What it measures | | | | | | Attack Vector | AV | Network (N), Adjacent (A), Local (L), Physical (P) | | Attack Complexity | AC | Low (L) or High (H) | | Privileges Required | PR | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | User Interaction | UI | None (N) or Required (R) | | Scope | S | Unchanged (U) or Changed (C) | | Confidentiality | C | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | Integrity | I | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | Availability | A | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | Example — EternalBlue (CVE 2017 0144): AV:N (exploitable over network remotely) AC:H (requires specific conditions — SMBv1 enabled) PR:N (no authentication needed) UI:N (no user interaction needed) S:U (stays within the system) C:H / I:H / A:H (full compromise) CVSS Score: 8.1 (High) [!tip] CVSS calculator Use the NVD CVSS calculator at nvd.nist.gov/vuln metrics/cvss/v3 calculator to compute scores for your reports. You don't need to memorise the formula, but you need to understand what each metric means so your scores are defensible. Report Structure Overview A professional pentest report has two audiences: the CEO (who doesn't understand TCP) and the sysadmin (who needs exact reproduction steps). You write for both simultaneously. Standard structure: 1. Cover Page — Client name, engagement dates, your name/company, classification (Confidential) 2. Table of Contents 3. Executive Summary — 1 page, no jargon, answers: "Were we compromised? How badly? What do we do first?" 4. Scope and Methodology — What was tested, what tools were used, what was excluded 5. Risk Summary — Table of all findings with severity, so management sees the big picture 6. Technical Findings — One section per vulnerability: Finding name Severity (CVSS score) Affected systems Description (what it is, why it's dangerous) Evidence (screenshots, command output) Steps to reproduce Remediation recommendation 7. Appendix — Raw tool output, full scan results, custom scripts used [!info] OSCP report specifics The OSCP report follows this structure but focuses only on successful exploitation paths. You document: machine IP, vulnerability exploited, steps to reproduce from scratch (another person must be able to replicate it), and proof screenshot (IP + whoami + cat flag.txt all visible in one image). Every failed attempt is NOT in the report — only successful exploitation chains. How the OSCP Exam Mirrors a Real Engagement The OSCP exam is intentionally designed to simulate a real external penetration test with internal access. | Real Engagement Phase | OSCP Exam Equivalent | | | | | Scope definition | You receive a list of IPs and an RoE document | | Recon and enumeration | Hours 0–2: nmap everything simultaneously | | Exploitation | Hours 2–18: exploit machines, get flags | | Post exploitation | Privilege escalation after each foothold | | Lateral movement | The AD set: Client → Server → DC | | Reporting | 24 hour report window after exam ends | The exam simulates a client who has five machines (3 standalone + 1 AD set of 3). Your job is to compromise as many as possible and prove it with evidence. The report proves you can communicate findings professionally. [!success] What passing OSCP proves You can independently find and exploit vulnerabilities on a variety of systems, escalate privileges, and document your work clearly. This is exactly what a junior pentester is hired to do on day one. Quick Reference | Concept | Key Detail | | | | | CMA 1990 | UK law governing unauthorised access — always get written permission | | Black box | No prior info given | | Grey box | Partial info (credentials, architecture) | | White box | Full info (source code, admin access) | | PTES phases | Pre engagement → Intel → Threat model → Vuln analysis → Exploitation → Post exploitation → Report | | CVE format | CVE YEAR NUMBER | | CVSS Critical | 9.0–10.0 | | CVSS High | 7.0–8.9 | | OSCP pass mark | 70/100 points | | OSCP Metasploit rule | 1 exploit module per exam, unlimited multi/handler and msfvenom | | OSCP report deadline | 24 hours after exam ends — missing this = automatic fail | Practice Resources | Resource | What to do | | | | | TryHackMe — "Jr Penetration Tester" path | Start here — this note is your foundation for everything in that path | | TryHackMe — "Pentesting Fundamentals" room | Free room, covers legality and methodology in interactive form | | PTES Standard | Read pentest standard.org sections 1–3 to see the full framework | | NVD | Look up CVE 2017 0144 and read the full entry — practice reading CVEs | | OSCP Exam Guide | Read the OffSec exam guide once before starting lab work — know the rules cold |

title: S1-02 — Linux Fundamentals for Pentesters
body: S1 02 — Linux Fundamentals for Pentesters Why Linux for Pentesting? Kali Linux and Parrot OS are Debian based. Every major offensive tool — Metasploit, Nmap, Burp Suite, Impacket, BloodHound — runs natively on Linux. The targets you'll face on OSCP are predominantly Linux machines. You will spend the majority of your exam inside a Linux terminal. This note assumes you know how to navigate a terminal. What it covers is everything a pentester specifically needs to know — the parts that directly relate to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. File System Navigation The Linux filesystem is a single tree rooted at . Everything — drives, devices, processes — is a file or directory under . Key directories and why pentesters care: | Directory | Purpose | Pentest Relevance | | | | | | | System configuration files | , , , | | | Web server document root (Apache/Nginx) | Web shells land here; find config files with DB creds | | | Log files | Log poisoning for LFI→RCE; check for creds in logs | | | Temporary files, world writable | Upload exploits and tools here — always writable | | | User home directories | SSH keys, bash history, config files with creds | | | Root's home directory | Contains on OSCP machines | | | Optional/third party software | Custom applications, non standard services | | | Kernel and process info (virtual filesystem) | for LFI tricks | | | Device files | for bash reverse shells | | | Locally installed binaries | Custom scripts, unusual SUID binaries | [!tip] MUSCLE MEMORY — run this on every engagement File Permissions — Deep Dive This is one of the most important concepts in Linux privilege escalation. You must understand permissions at a low level. Reading Permission Strings Breaking this down: | Field | Value | Meaning | | | | | | File type | | Regular file ( = directory, = symlink) | | Owner permissions | | Owner (root) can read, write, execute | | Group permissions | | Group (www data) can read and execute, not write | | Other permissions | | Everyone else can only read | | Link count | | Number of hard links | | Owner | | File is owned by root | | Group | | File belongs to group www data | | Size | | File size in bytes | Octal Notation Each permission set ( ) maps to a 3 bit binary number: | Permission | Binary | Octal | | | | | | | 000 | 0 | | | 001 | 1 | | | 010 | 2 | | | 011 | 3 | | | 100 | 4 | | | 101 | 5 | | | 110 | 6 | | | 111 | 7 | So = (owner: full, group: read+execute, others: read+execute) And = (owner: read+write, group: read, others: read) Special Permission Bits — THIS IS WHERE PRIVESC LIVES Beyond , there are three special bits that are critical for privilege escalation: SUID (Set User ID) — Bit value: 4000 When SUID is set on an executable , it runs as the file's owner rather than the user who launched it. The in the owner execute position = SUID is set. is owned by root and has SUID — so when any user runs , it temporarily runs as root (to write to ). Why this matters for privesc: If an attacker finds a SUID binary owned by root that can be abused (e.g., , , , ), they can execute commands as root. Example abuse — if has SUID: SGID (Set Group ID) — Bit value: 2000 Similar to SUID but for group. When set on an executable, it runs with the file's group permissions. When set on a directory , files created inside inherit the directory's group (useful for shared directories — less relevant for immediate privesc). Sticky Bit — Bit value: 1000 When set on a directory , only the file's owner (or root) can delete or rename files within it — even if others have write permission. The in the others execute position = sticky bit. is world writable but you can't delete other users' files. Privesc relevance: Sticky bit isn't usually exploitable itself, but world writable directories without the sticky bit ( ) mean you can delete or replace files in them — which can lead to cron job abuse. [!warning] Common mistake with SUID Beginners run and then look up every result on GTFOBins. The correct workflow is: (1) find SUID binaries, (2) cross reference against GTFOBins, (3) only spend time on binaries that have a documented abuse path. Standard system binaries like and are SUID by design — they're not vulnerabilities unless misconfigured. /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow — Format Explained These two files are the Linux local authentication database. Understanding their format is essential. /etc/passwd World readable by default. Every user account has an entry. Fields (colon separated): 1. Username — 2. Password — means the actual hash is in . If this field contains a hash (legacy systems), you can crack it directly. 3. UID — User ID. = root. UIDs ≥ 1000 typically = regular users. 4. GID — Primary group ID. 5. GECOS — Comment field. Often full name. 6. Home directory — 7. Shell — = interactive login shell. = service account, can't log in interactively. Pentest use: Find all users with interactive shells: Check if password field has a hash instead of (old/misconfigured system — crack directly) Add a root backdoor if you have write access: (empty password field = no password) /etc/shadow Readable only by root (and shadow group). Contains actual password hashes. Fields: 1. Username 2. Password hash — format: = MD5 (weak, crack fast) = SHA 256 = SHA 512 (most common on modern Linux — slow to crack) = yescrypt (modern, very slow) or = account locked/no password set 3. Last password change — days since Jan 1, 1970 4. Minimum password age — days before user can change it 5. Maximum password age — days until forced change 6. Warning period 7. Inactive period 8. Expiry date Pentest use: You need root (or shadow group) to read this If you can read it: then The hash type determines cracking speed — (SHA 512) is slow, (MD5) is very fast Users, Groups, and Sudoers The sudoers File defines who can run what as root (or other users) via . Never edit directly — use . Common sudoers entries and what they mean: = can run the command as root without entering a password. If you see this on ANY binary, go straight to GTFOBins. [!tip] MUSCLE MEMORY — run this on every engagement This is the single most important privesc check. Run it within 30 seconds of getting a shell. If you see NOPASSWD on any binary, check GTFOBins immediately. Process Management Cron Jobs — Critical for Privesc Cron runs scheduled tasks. If a script runs as root on a schedule and you can write to it, you have root. Cron syntax: Examples: Where to find cron jobs: The trick — pspy64: Many cron jobs aren't in any crontab file. They're triggered by systemd timers, scripts called from other scripts, or run by processes not visible without root. pspy64 monitors process creation without needing root: Network Commands decoded: = TCP = UDP = listening sockets only = show process name/PID = don't resolve hostnames (faster) [!tip] Finding internally listening services Services listening only on localhost ( ) are invisible from outside but accessible from the machine. A database on port 3306 listening only locally, or a web app on 8080, is often the next attack vector after getting a foothold. These internal services may have weaker authentication or known vulnerabilities. Package Managers For pentesting: Knowing what's installed on a target can reveal attack vectors. Outdated packages have CVEs. Text Processing — grep, awk, sed, cut, sort, uniq These are essential for parsing tool output during engagements. You'll use them constantly. grep — Search for patterns Pentest use cases: awk — Column based text processing Pentest use — extract usernames from passwd: sed — Stream editor (find and replace) Pentest use: cut — Extract columns sort and uniq — Sorting and deduplication Pentest use — processing Nmap output: Bash Scripting for Pentesters You don't need to be a bash developer. You need to be able to write quick scripts that automate repetitive tasks during engagements. Variables Conditionals Loops Functions Your First Recon Script Save this as . This is a minimal but useful recon script for when you land on a new machine. Key Files to Check on Every Linux Pentest Quick Reference | Task | Command | | | | | Who am I? | | | What can I sudo? | | | Find SUID binaries | | | Find SGID binaries | | | Find world writable files | | | All users with login shells | | | Listening services | | | Running processes | | | Processes as root | | | Download file to target | | | Simple HTTP server (serve files) | | | Check file permissions | | | Check capabilities | | Practice Resources | Resource | What to do | | | | | TryHackMe — "Linux Fundamentals" rooms (1, 2, 3) | Interactive exercises on every concept covered here | | TryHackMe — "Linux PrivEsc" room | Dedicated practice for the privesc techniques introduced here | | HTB — Lame, Shocker, Bashed | Easy Linux machines where these fundamentals are enough to root them | | OverTheWire — Bandit | Gamified Linux command line challenges — good for solidifying grep/awk/find | | GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) | Bookmark this. Check every SUID binary and sudo binary here |

title: S1-03 — Windows Fundamentals for Pentesters
body: S1 03 — Windows Fundamentals for Pentesters Why Windows Matters for OSCP The OSCP exam has 3 standalone machines and 1 AD set. Realistically, at least 1–2 standalones will be Windows, and the entire AD set (Client → Server → DC) is Windows. That's potentially 60 out of 100 points on Windows targets. Windows behaves fundamentally differently from Linux. The filesystem layout is different, the permission model is different, the authentication system is different, and the tools you use to enumerate and exploit it are different. The Windows File System Windows uses drive letters. The primary drive is almost always . | Path | Purpose | Pentest Relevance | | | | | | | 64 bit system binaries | , , , | | | 32 bit binaries on 64 bit OS | WoW64 subsystem | | | Temp files | Often writable — upload tools here | | | User home directories | (OSCP flag), saved creds | | | Admin's home | (OSCP flag) | | | 64 bit installed applications | Check for outdated software with CVEs | | | IIS web server document root | Upload ASPX shells here if IIS writable | | | Application data (hidden, all users) | Credential files, config files, logs | | | AD database (DCs only) | contains all domain password hashes | User Accounts and Groups Critical Built in Accounts | Account | Pentest Relevance | | | | | | Built in local admin — SID S 1 5 21 ... 500 always the same even if renamed | | | Most privileged account — this is the goal of privesc, not just Administrator | | | IIS app pools often run as this — has SeImpersonatePrivilege | | | Limited service account | Critical Built in Groups | Group | What it grants | | | | | | Full control of the local machine | | | Can connect via RDP | | | Can connect via WinRM | | | Can read any file bypassing ACLs — privesc path via SAM dump | | | Domain group — can load arbitrary DLL into DNS service → SYSTEM | [!tip] MUSCLE MEMORY — run this on every engagement Shows username, domain, SID, and every privilege and group membership. Most information dense single command on Windows. Privileges — The Windows Path to SYSTEM | Privilege | Exploit Path | | | | | | PrintSpoofer / GodPotato → SYSTEM — most common OSCP privesc path | | | Same as SeImpersonate — Potato attacks | | | Dump SAM and SYSTEM hive → extract local hashes | | | Overwrite system files, replace service binaries | | | Dump LSASS memory → credential extraction | | | Load vulnerable driver → kernel exploit | | | Take ownership of sensitive files | [!warning] SeImpersonatePrivilege is extremely common Any service account running IIS, SQL Server, or similar will typically have this. If you land as or , you almost certainly have SeImpersonate — use PrintSpoofer or GodPotato for instant SYSTEM. The Windows Registry Windows Services Three service based privesc paths: 1. Unquoted service path — has spaces but no quotes. Windows searches each segment. If is unquoted and is writable, Windows executes it. 2. Weak service binary permissions — You can write to the directly. Replace it with a payload. 3. Weak service key permissions — You can modify the registry key's value. Scheduled Tasks Look for tasks running as SYSTEM that call scripts in writable locations. PowerShell vs CMD | Scenario | Use CMD | Use PowerShell | | | | | | Basic file operations | ✓ | ✓ | | Downloading files | | ✓ (Invoke WebRequest) | | AD enumeration | | ✓ (PowerView) | | Quick one liners | ✓ | ✓ | | Constrained Language Mode active | ✓ | Limited | Windows File Permissions — icacls | Code | Permission | | | | | | Full control | | | Modify (read, write, delete, execute) | | | Read and execute | | | Write only | [!warning] The key check If , , or has or on a service binary or directory, that's a direct privesc path. SAM, SYSTEM, and NTDS.dit | File | Location | Contains | How Attackers Get It | | | | | | | SAM | | NTLM hashes for local accounts | (needs SYSTEM), VSS | | SYSTEM | | Boot key to decrypt SAM | Same — needed with SAM | | NTDS.dit | (DC only) | Every domain account's hashes | VSS on DC, or remotely | UAC (User Account Control) Even if you're in the local Administrators group, Windows gives you a restricted token by default. UAC must be bypassed to get a fully elevated token. [!danger] UAC bypass ≠ privilege escalation UAC bypass only elevates an existing Administrator token. If you're a low privilege user not in Administrators, UAC bypass won't help. You need actual privesc first, then UAC bypass. Quick Reference — Essential Windows Commands File Transfer to Windows Targets On Kali: Key Event IDs — What Your Attacks Leave Behind | Event ID | Meaning | | | | | 4624 | Successful logon (type 3=network, type 10=RDP) | | 4625 | Failed logon — brute force is visible here | | 4648 | Logon with explicit credentials (PTH, runas) | | 4672 | Special privileges assigned | | 4698 | Scheduled task created | | 4720 | User account created | | 7045 | New service installed | Practice Resources | Resource | What to do | | | | | TryHackMe — "Windows Fundamentals" (1, 2, 3) | Interactive — covers every concept here | | TryHackMe — "Windows PrivEsc" room | All techniques applied in a lab | | HTB — Blue | EternalBlue on Windows 7 — first Windows root | | HTB — Devel | SeImpersonatePrivilege via IIS upload — classic OSCP pattern | | HTB — Jerry | Tomcat WAR deploy — common OSCP pattern | | LOLBAS (lolbas project.github.io) | Windows equivalent of GTFOBins | | PayloadsAllTheThings | Windows privesc checklist section |

title: S1-04 — Networking for Pentesters (Supplement to NETGOD)
body: S1 04 — Networking for Pentesters (Supplement to NETGOD) [!info] Relationship to NETGOD Your NETGOD vault already covers networking fundamentals and protocols in depth across 13 modules. This note does NOT duplicate that content. Instead, it covers the attacker's lens on each concept — what each protocol reveals, how attackers abuse it, and what it means during a pentest. Cross reference Networking/Module 00 Foundations and Networking/Module 03 Protocols Deep Dive for the underlying theory. The TCP Three Way Handshake — At the Packet Level Understanding the handshake at the packet level is not optional. It explains how Nmap scan types work, why some scans are stealthier than others, and what "filtered" vs "closed" means. Normal Connection (Three Way Handshake) TCP flags relevant to pentesting: | Flag | Full Name | Meaning | | | | | | | Synchronise | Initiates a connection | | | Acknowledge | Confirms receipt of data | | | Finish | Gracefully closes a connection | | | Reset | Abruptly terminates a connection | | | Push | Send data immediately without buffering | | | Urgent | Data is urgent (rarely used) | | | No flags | Used in stealth scans — abnormal | What Happens When a Port is Closed (RST) A response = port is closed . The host is up, the port is actively rejecting connections. What Happens When a Port is Filtered (Firewall Drop) No response at all = port is filtered . A firewall is dropping the packets. The host may or may not be up. This is why is uncertain — it just means something is blocking. [!info] Why this matters for Nmap = SYN ACK received — something is listening = RST received — host is up, port not listening = no response — firewall dropping packets, or host down = UDP or stealth scan couldn't determine — no response but port might be open UDP — Why It Matters UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless — no handshake, no guarantee of delivery. This makes it faster but harder to scan. Why UDP matters for pentesting: Many critical services run on UDP: DNS (53), SNMP (161), DHCP (67/68), TFTP (69), NTP (123) SNMP on UDP 161 is one of the most information rich services for recon UDP scanning is slow because there's no response from open ports (only closed ports send ICMP "port unreachable") UDP port states: — a response was received (service replied) — ICMP "port unreachable" received — no response (most common for UDP — could be open or firewall dropping) [!warning] Don't skip UDP Beginners always skip UDP because it's slow. On OSCP machines, SNMP (UDP 161) has revealed community strings containing passwords. TFTP (UDP 69) has revealed config files. Always run a UDP top 100 scan in the background while you enumerate TCP services. Critical Ports to Memorise These are the ports you will encounter on every OSCP machine. Know the service, the default version, and the first thing to try. | Port | Protocol | Service | First Action | | | | | | | 21 | TCP | FTP | Test anonymous login: → user: anonymous | | 22 | TCP | SSH Oracle | — Oracle database attacks | | 2049 | TCP/UDP | NFS | Mount shares: then | | 3306 | TCP | MySQL | — try blank password | | 3389 | TCP | RDP | , brute force, BlueKeep if old Windows | | 4848 | Same as above with flag | | 6379 | TCP | Redis | — unauthenticated access | | 8080 | TCP | HTTP alt | Tomcat, Jenkins, JBoss — check manager apps | | 8443 | TCP | HTTPS alt | Same as 8080 but TLS | | simultaneously. Enumerate quick scan results while full and UDP run in background. ARP — How It Works and How Attackers Abuse It What ARP does: When Host A wants to send a packet to Host B (on the same subnet), it needs Host B's MAC address. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) asks: "Who has IP 192.168.1.50? Tell 192.168.1.1." ARP has no authentication . Any host can answer any ARP request — even if it's not the real owner of the IP. ARP Spoofing / ARP Poisoning: An attacker sends gratuitous ARP replies ("192.168.1.1 is at attacker MAC") to poison the ARP cache of victims. Traffic meant for the gateway flows to the attacker instead — Man in the Middle . ARP scanning — discovering hosts: [!info] ARP only works on the local subnet ARP broadcasts don't cross router boundaries. ARP attacks are only possible if you're on the same Layer 2 network as the victim. Once you're pivoting through a compromised host to a remote subnet, ARP attacks on that remote subnet require the pivot host to do the spoofing. DNS — Resolution Chain and Attack Vectors The DNS resolution chain (what happens when you type google.com): DNS record types relevant to pentesters: | Type | Purpose | Pentest Use | | | | | | | IPv4 address for hostname | Basic resolution | | | IPv6 address | IPv6 attack surface | | | Mail server | SMTP targets, phishing infrastructure | | | Nameserver for domain | Zone transfer target | | | Alias for another hostname | Subdomain discovery | | | Text records | SPF, DKIM, verification — reveals infrastructure info | | | Reverse lookup (IP → hostname) | Discover internal hostnames | | | Start of Authority | Zone info — reveals primary NS and admin email | | | Service location | AD uses SRV for Kerberos, LDAP discovery | DNS commands: Zone transfer attack: A DNS zone transfer ( ) is a legitimate mechanism for secondary nameservers to replicate zone data from the primary. If misconfigured to allow transfers from any IP, an attacker gets a complete map of every hostname in the domain — internal IPs, server names, development environments, everything. DNS for internal AD enumeration: Active Directory relies heavily on DNS SRV records for service discovery. On an internal engagement, querying the DC's DNS reveals the entire AD infrastructure: DHCP — How It Works and Rogue DHCP Normal DHCP process (DORA): What DHCP gives a client: IP address + subnet mask Default gateway DNS server(s) Lease time Rogue DHCP attack: An attacker runs a DHCP server that responds to DISCOVER messages faster than the legitimate server. Clients accept the first OFFER they receive. The attacker's DHCP server assigns: Legitimate IPs (so clients still work) Attacker's IP as the DNS server → DNS hijacking Attacker's IP as the default gateway → full MITM This is the basis of the attack (which uses DHCPv6, not DHCPv4) covered in the AD section. Firewalls and IDS — What They Block and Basic Evasion Firewall types: | Type | What it inspects | What it blocks | | | | | | Packet filter | IP headers, TCP/UDP ports | Traffic to blocked ports | | Stateful firewall | Connection state (tracks SYN→SYN ACK→ACK) | Unsolicited inbound connections, invalid state | | Application firewall (WAF) | HTTP content, application layer | SQLi, XSS, known attack patterns | | Next gen firewall (NGFW) | Deep packet inspection, application ID | Specific applications, encrypted traffic analysis | What "filtered" means in Nmap: A stateful firewall typically drops SYN packets to blocked ports (hence Nmap reports ). Some firewalls send or ICMP unreachable — in that case Nmap reports . Basic firewall evasion with Nmap: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) vs IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): IDS = detects and alerts, doesn't block IPS = detects and actively blocks What triggers IDS signatures: Port scans (sequential port access) Known exploit strings in payloads Unusual traffic volumes Connections to known malicious IPs Basic IDS evasion concepts: Slow scanning — space requests out so they don't look like a scan Fragmentation — split exploit payloads across packets so no single packet matches a signature Encoding payloads — base64, XOR, or custom encoding to avoid string matching Using legitimate traffic channels — HTTP/HTTPS on standard ports blends in [!info] OSCP context OSCP machines don't have active IDS/IPS that block your attacks. These evasion techniques matter more in real engagements and CPTS. For OSCP, understand the concepts — you won't need to actively evade detection. Subnetting — Quick Reference for Pentesters You need to quickly calculate subnets to understand what hosts exist on a network. CIDR notation: | CIDR | Subnet Mask | Usable Hosts | Common Use | | | | | | | /8 | 255.0.0.0 | 16,777,214 | Large enterprise | | /16 | 255.255.0.0 | 65,534 | Campus network | | /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 254 | Standard LAN segment | | /25 | 255.255.255.128 | 126 | Split /24 in half | | /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 62 | Small segment | | /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 30 | Small segment | | /28 | 255.255.255.240 | 14 | Very small segment | | /29 | 255.255.255.248 | 6 | Point to point links | | /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 2 | Point to point links | | /32 | 255.255.255.255 | 1 | Single host route | Practical calculation: For network : Network address: Broadcast: Usable range: → Wireshark — What to Look For Wireshark captures raw packets. During an internal pentest, running Wireshark for a few minutes on your interface reveals enormous amounts of information. What passive sniffing reveals in a corporate network: Hostnames via NetBIOS/LLMNR broadcasts Internal IP ranges Cleartext protocols still in use (FTP, Telnet, HTTP with Basic Auth) NTLM authentication hashes (NTLMv2) via Responder capture DNS queries revealing internal infrastructure Quick Reference | Concept | Key Command | | | | | ARP scan (find hosts) | | | DNS zone transfer | | | Reverse lookup | | | Full port scan | | | UDP top 100 | | | Fragmented scan | | | Decoy scan | | | Source port spoof | | | Subnet calculation | | | Packet capture | | | Ping sweep | | Cross References TCP/IP fundamentals and OSI model → Networking/Module 00 Foundations Protocol deep dives (DNS, DHCP, ARP, ICMP) → Networking/Module 03 Protocols Deep Dive SMB protocol specifics → S1 13 (Service Enumeration) this vault LLMNR/NBT NS poisoning → S3 02 (NTLM Relay Attacks) this vault Practice Resources | Resource | What to do | | | | | TryHackMe — "Pre Security" path | Networking fundamentals interactive labs | | TryHackMe — "Wireshark: The Basics" | Hands on packet analysis | | TryHackMe — "Passive Reconnaissance" | OSINT and DNS enumeration labs | | Wireshark sample captures (wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures) | Analyse real protocol traffic | | HackTheBox — Active | DNS zone transfer reveals all hosts on the machine | | HackTheBox — Forest | DNS enumeration for AD host discovery |

title: S1-05 — Nmap — Complete Reference
body: S1 05 — Nmap — Complete Reference What Nmap Is and How It Works at the Packet Level Nmap (Network Mapper) is the industry standard tool for network discovery and security auditing. It sends crafted packets to target hosts and analyses responses to determine: Which hosts are alive Which ports are open, closed, or filtered What services and versions are running What OS is running Whether known vulnerabilities exist (via NSE scripts) Understanding what packets Nmap actually sends is what separates someone who can read a cheat sheet from someone who can troubleshoot when scans don't behave as expected. Scan Types — Every Flag, Every Packet sS — SYN Scan (Half Open Scan) — DEFAULT for root Why it's called half open: Nmap sends SYN, receives SYN ACK, then immediately sends RST instead of completing the handshake. The connection is never fully established. Why this matters: Faster than a full TCP connect scan (no three way handshake) Stealthier — older systems/firewalls may not log half open connections Requires root/administrator privileges (raw socket access needed) Default scan type when run as root sT — TCP Connect Scan — DEFAULT for non root Full three way handshake. Uses the OS's system call — no raw sockets needed. Works without root. Downside: Slower, noisier — every connection is fully logged on the target. sU — UDP Scan UDP has no handshake. Nmap sends a UDP packet to each port: Open: Service responds with UDP data Closed: ICMP "port unreachable" (type 3, code 3) received Open|Filtered: No response (could be open with no reply, or firewall dropping) Why UDP is slow: ICMP rate limiting. The OS limits how many ICMP unreachable messages it generates per second. Nmap must wait between probes. [!warning] UDP scans require patience A full UDP scan ( ) can take hours. Always use or target specific ports unless you have a specific reason to go deeper. sA — ACK Scan Important: ACK scan does NOT tell you if a port is open or closed. It tells you whether a firewall is filtering the port. = firewall passes ACK packets (stateless firewall or no firewall) = firewall drops ACK packets (stateful firewall blocking) Use case: Map firewall rules. Determine which ports a stateful firewall is protecting vs which are open. sN — NULL Scan, sF — FIN Scan, sX — Xmas Scan These are stealth scans that exploit a quirk in the RFC 793 TCP specification: RFC 793 says: If a closed port receives a packet with no SYN/ACK/RST flags, it should respond with RST. If an open port receives such a packet, it should silently drop it. Limitation: Windows does NOT follow this RFC behaviour. Windows responds with RST for both open and closed ports when receiving these abnormal packets. These scans only work against Unix/Linux targets. Use case: Evade older stateless firewalls and some IDS that only log SYN packets. Service and Version Detection — sV Without , Nmap only knows a port is open. With , Nmap sends protocol specific probes to identify the service name and version. Intensity levels (0–9): 0–2: Only grab the banner (whatever the service sends on connection) 3–5: Send common probes for the expected service 6–8: Try additional probes for less common services 9: Try every probe — catches unusual configurations but very slow What version detection tells you: Now you know exactly what to searchsploit: , , . OS Detection — O Nmap analyses TCP/IP stack behaviour (TTL values, TCP window sizes, specific quirks in how the OS implements RFC 793) to guess the operating system. [!warning] OS detection is unreliable Firewalls, load balancers, and virtualisation can distort TCP/IP fingerprints. Nmap may say "Linux 3.x" on a Windows Server. Use OS detection as a hint, not a fact. Verify with service banners (SSH banner often shows , ; SMB shows Windows version). Timing Templates — T0 through T5 Timing templates control how fast Nmap scans — specifically, delays between probes and how many probes run in parallel. | Template | Name | Delay | Use Case | | | | | | | | Paranoid | 5 minutes between probes | Maximum IDS evasion (impractically slow) | | | Sneaky | 15 seconds between probes | IDS evasion — still very slow | | | Polite | 0.4 seconds between probes | Reduce network load — slow | | | Normal | Nmap's default adaptive timing | Balanced — default when T not specified | | | Aggressive | Assumes fast, reliable network | OSCP standard — use this | | | Insane | Maximum speed, may miss results | Labs only — unreliable on slow networks | [!tip] MUSCLE MEMORY — standard OSCP scan This is your go to first scan on every machine. Port Specification [!danger] Never skip the full port scan The default Nmap scan only checks the top 1000 ports. On OSCP machines, critical services intentionally run on non standard ports (e.g., SSH on 2222, HTTP on 8888, a custom service on 31337). Always run on every target. Start it in the background while you work on results from the quick scan. Output Formats — oN, oX, oG, oA Always save Nmap output. You will refer back to it constantly. [!tip] Always use oA This creates , , and . The file is especially useful for quick grepping: NSE Scripts — Nmap Scripting Engine NSE allows Nmap to run scripts against discovered services for deeper enumeration and vulnerability detection. Scripts are located at . Script categories: | Category | What it does | | | | | | Safe, fast, useful — enabled with sC | | | Won't crash services or be intrusive | | | Check for known vulnerabilities | | | Test authentication (default creds, anonymous access) | | | Brute force credentials | | | Enumerate services and gather information | | | Actually exploit vulnerabilities (rarely used in Nmap) | | | May crash services or trigger alerts | The most important NSE scripts for OSCP: Firewall Evasion Techniques Host Discovery — Controlling How Nmap Finds Live Hosts By default, Nmap pings hosts before scanning ports. This can cause missed hosts if ICMP is blocked. [!tip] Always use Pn on OSCP OSCP machines may not respond to ICMP. Without , Nmap assumes the host is down and skips port scanning. Always add to avoid missing machines. The OSCP Exam Scan Workflow This is the exact sequence to run at the start of every OSCP machine. Run all three simultaneously in separate terminals. Terminal 1 — Quick scan (start enumerating results immediately): Terminal 2 — Full port scan (runs in background, catches non standard ports): Terminal 3 — UDP scan (runs in background): After full scan completes — targeted script scan on all discovered ports: Reading Nmap Output — What Each Line Means Port state meanings: — SYN ACK received. Service is listening. Investigate this. — RST received. Port not listening, but host is up. Not useful now, but note for OS detection and firewall rule analysis. — No response. Firewall dropping packets. Could be open behind firewall. — Can't distinguish (common with UDP or stealth scans). Try harder probes. — Port is accessible but Nmap can't determine if open or closed (ACK scan result). Common Failure Modes and Fixes | Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix | | | | | | All ports show | ICMP blocking — host marked as down | Add flag | | Scan extremely slow | Default timing, many ports | Add | | Version detection shows nothing | Service not responding to probes | Try | | UDP scan shows all | Firewall dropping or service not replying | Increase timing, try targeted probes | | NSE scripts fail or timeout | Network latency or filtered | Add | | "You requested a scan type which requires root privileges" | Running sS without sudo | Use or switch to | | Missing services found by other tools | Top 1000 port scan missed non standard ports | Always run | Quick Reference Table | Task | Command | | | | | Quick scan with scripts | | | Full port scan | | | UDP top 100 | | | All SMB vuln scripts | | | HTTP enumeration | | | FTP anonymous test | | | Run all vuln scripts | | | Fragmented packets | | | Decoy scan | | | Source port spoof | | | Ping sweep subnet | | | OS detection | | | SYN scan | (requires root) | | Connect scan | (no root needed) | | ACK scan (firewall map) | | | NULL/FIN/Xmas (Unix only) | | Practice Resources | Resource | What to do | | | | | TryHackMe — "Nmap" room | Interactive Nmap lab — covers every scan type | | TryHackMe — "Nmap Advanced Port Scans" | NSE scripts and advanced techniques | | HTB — any machine | Run the full OSCP scan workflow on every machine | | HackTheBox — Starting Point machines | Practice the recon workflow from scratch | | / | The definitive reference — Nmap's own documentation | | nmap.org/nsedoc | Full NSE script documentation with examples |

body: S1 06 — Gobuster, ffuf, and Feroxbuster — Web Discovery What Directory Brute Forcing Is and Why It Works When a web server hosts files and directories, it doesn't advertise everything that exists. A site might have linked publicly, but also , , , , and dozens of other paths that are never linked from any page. These paths are only accessible if you know they exist. Directory brute forcing works by making HTTP requests to a target web server for every word in a wordlist: Why it works: Developers forget to unlink old files, create development/staging paths, use predictable naming conventions, and leave backup files around (e.g., , ). What you find: Admin panels ( , , ) Backup files with credentials ( , , ) Development/testing endpoints ( , , ) Configuration files ( , , ) Hidden API endpoints ( , ) Upload directories ( , ) Gobuster Gobuster is a fast, multi mode brute forcing tool written in Go. The three modes you need are , , and . Installation dir Mode — Directory and File Brute Forcing Every flag explained: | Flag | Long Form | What it does | | | | | | | | Target URL (required) | | | | Path to wordlist (required) | | | | File extensions to append to each word | | | | Number of concurrent threads (default: 10) | | | | Save output to file | | | | Follow redirects (default: off — show the redirect code) | | | | Skip TLS certificate validation (for self signed certs) | | | | Blacklist these status codes (hide them) | | | | Only show these status codes | | | | HTTP timeout per request | | | | Add custom HTTP headers (e.g., cookies, auth) | | | | Add cookies | | | | HTTP Basic Auth username | | | | HTTP Basic Auth password | | | | Route through proxy (e.g., Burp: ) | | | | Suppress banner (cleaner output) | | | | Force scan even if wildcard responses detected | | | | Don't print status codes | | | | Print full URLs instead of just paths | | | | Don't display progress | Standard usage: dns Mode — Subdomain Enumeration DNS mode brute forces subdomains by querying DNS for for each word in the wordlist. | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Target domain (required) | | | Wordlist (required) | | | Show IP addresses of found subdomains | | | Custom DNS resolver (e.g., use target's own DNS: ) | | | DNS query timeout | vhost Mode — Virtual Host Discovery Virtual hosting allows multiple websites to run on the same IP/port, distinguished by the header. A server hosting might also have , , — all pointing to the same IP but serving different content. | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Target URL (IP or base domain) | | | Wordlist of subdomains to try | | | Append the base domain to each word (e.g., → ) | Why vhost matters: On OSCP machines, you'll often find an IP serving a basic site on port 80 but with a virtual host like or that serves a completely different (and vulnerable) application. Without vhost enumeration you'd miss it entirely. ffuf — Fuzz Faster U Fool ffuf is more flexible than Gobuster because it uses a keyword that you can place anywhere in a request — URL, headers, body, or parameters. This makes it a universal fuzzer, not just a directory scanner. Installation Core Concept — The FUZZ Keyword Place anywhere in your command where you want the wordlist values substituted: All Flags Explained Input options: | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Target URL with FUZZ keyword | | | Wordlist path (use for multiple wordlists) | | | HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, etc.) | | | POST data body | | | Custom header (can use multiple times) | | | Cookie string | | | Follow redirects | | | Proxy URL | | | Request timeout in seconds | Filtering options — these are critical for removing noise: | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Filter by HTTP status code (hide these codes) | | | Filter by response size in bytes (hide responses of this size) | | | Filter by number of words in response | | | Filter by number of lines in response | | | Filter by regex pattern in response | | | Match only these status codes (whitelist) | | | Match only responses of this size | | | Match only responses with this word count | | | Match only responses with this line count | | | Match responses containing this regex | Output options: | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Output file | | | Output format: , , , , , | | | Verbose — show full URL in output | | | Silent — suppress progress bar | Performance options: | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Threads (default: 40) | | | Delay between requests (e.g., = 100ms) | | | Max requests per second | Recursion: | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Enable recursive scanning | | | Max recursion depth (default: 0 = unlimited) | | | or | ffuf Usage Examples Basic directory discovery: With extension fuzzing: Filtering out 404s (and other noise): Virtual host fuzzing: Parameter discovery (GET): Parameter value fuzzing: POST body fuzzing (login forms): Recursive scanning: Multiple wordlists (two FUZZ keywords): Rate limiting to be polite: Dealing with False Positives in ffuf The biggest challenge with ffuf is tuning filters to eliminate false positives. The workflow: 1. Run without filters first , note the response size/lines/words for a non existent path 2. Apply to filter that baseline 3. Review remaining results — check each manually in a browser or with Feroxbuster Feroxbuster is similar to Gobuster's mode but with one critical difference: it recurses automatically . When it finds a directory, it immediately scans inside it. This means it can find , then automatically scan , , etc. Installation Key Flags | Flag | What it does | | | | | | Target URL | | | Wordlist | | | File extensions | | | Threads (default: 50) | | | Max recursion depth (default: 4) | | | Disable recursion | | | Output file | | | Filter by status code (hide these) | | | Filter by response size | | | Filter by word count | | | Filter by line count | | | Proxy URL | | | Disable TLS validation | | | Custom header | | | Cookies | | | Follow redirects | | | Smart filter (auto detect and filter wildcard responses) | | | Suppress progress output | | | Output as JSON | Wordlist Selection — Which Wordlist for Which Scenario The right wordlist is as important as the right tool. Start with — fast, catches 80% of findings 2. If nothing interesting: switch to 3. Add extensions relevant to the tech stack: for PHP sites, for IIS, for Tomcat 4. Never start with a 1M+ word list — it takes too long and rarely finds things the medium list misses Extension Brute Forcing — Which Extensions to Try Knowing what tech stack the target runs tells you what extensions to try. | Server/CMS | Extensions to try | | | | | Apache (generic) | , , , , , , | | IIS / Windows | , , , , , | | Tomcat / Java | , , , , | | Nginx (generic) | , , (same as Apache) | | WordPress | primarily — but wp admin, wp login, wp config | | Django/Flask | No extensions typically — focus on paths | Always include: , , , , , (vim swap files), (macOS), Virtual Host Discovery — When and Why It Matters When to do vhost enumeration: You find an IP with a web server but the response looks like a default page or "Welcome to nginx" You see a domain referenced in SSL certificates but it resolves to the same IP The box has a or custom domain convention (add to first) The workflow: What Response Codes Tell You | Code | Meaning | Pentest Action | | | | | | | Page exists and is accessible | Investigate immediately | | | Permanent redirect | Follow the redirect — real content is there | | | Temporary redirect | Often login redirect — the destination is interesting | | | Authentication required | Try default creds, credential stuffing | | | Path exists, access denied | Still interesting — try path traversal, different methods | | | Page doesn't exist | Ignore (unless custom 404 — check size) | | | Path exists, wrong HTTP method | Try PUT, PATCH, DELETE | | | Path exists, server error | May indicate SQL injection or other vulnerability | [!tip] 403 is not the end A 403 means the path exists but you're denied. This is still valuable — you've confirmed something is there. Next steps: try different HTTP methods ( , , ), try path traversal tricks ( , ), look for misconfigured file permissions, or add the path to your notes for after you get credentials. OSCP Exam — Web Discovery Protocol [!danger] Never skip web directory brute force On OSCP, if a machine has a web service on ANY port (80, 443, 8080, 8443, 8888, etc.), you must run directory brute force. Even if you've found a vulnerability and popped the box, run it anyway — there may be additional services or credentials that help with other machines. Exam workflow for every web service: Quick Reference | Task | Tool | Command | | | | | | Quick dir scan | gobuster | | | Medium dir scan | gobuster | | | Subdomain brute | gobuster | | | VHost fuzz | ffuf | | | Recursive scan | feroxbuster | | | Parameter fuzz | ffuf | | | POST fuzz | ffuf | | | Through Burp | any | add | | Skip TLS check | any | add (gobuster/feroxbuster) or nothing (ffuf ignores by default) | Common Mistakes [!warning] Common mistakes — beginners get these wrong 1. Running only one wordlist. misses things catches. Always escalate wordlist size if initial results are thin. 2. Forgetting extensions. A PHP app that hides might expose . Always specify for PHP targets. 3. Ignoring 403 responses. They confirm a path exists — never throw them away. 4. Not doing vhost enumeration. A plain IP often has multiple virtual hosts. This is a very common OSCP rabbit hole — you stare at the default nginx page for 30 minutes when there's a full app behind . 5. Only scanning port 80. If Nmap found 8080, 8443, 8888, or any other port — run a separate gobuster against each one. 6. Not checking robots.txt. takes 2 seconds and sometimes directly reveals admin paths. path: OSCP-JOURNEY/STAGE-1-THM/S1-07-Burp-Suite-Complete.md
title: S1-07 — Burp Suite — Complete Beginner to Intermediate
body: S1 07 — Burp Suite — Complete Beginner to Intermediate What a Proxy Does and Why It Intercepts Burp Suite is an intercepting proxy. It sits between your browser and the target web server and captures every HTTP/HTTPS request and response that flows through it. Normal web request (no proxy): With Burp proxy: While Burp holds the request, you can read it, modify any part of it (headers, parameters, body, cookies, method), and then forward it. This is the foundation of all manual web application testing — you can manipulate every byte of every request. Why this matters: Web apps trust data sent by the browser. Burp lets you send data the browser would never normally send. Client side controls (JavaScript validation, hidden fields, disabled form elements) are completely bypassed — you're working at the HTTP level, not the DOM level. You can replay, modify, and fuzz requests without touching the browser. Installation and Setup Burp Suite Community vs Pro | Feature | Community (Free) | Professional (£399/yr) | | | | | | Proxy | ✓ | ✓ | | Repeater | ✓ | ✓ | | Decoder | ✓ | ✓ | | Comparer | ✓ | ✓ | | Intruder | ✓ (throttled to 1 req/sec) | ✓ (full speed) | | Active Scanner | ✗ | ✓ | | Collaborator | ✗ | ✓ | | Extensions (BApp) | Limited | Full | For OSCP: Community is sufficient for the exam. Pro speeds up Intruder attacks significantly. Installation on Kali CA Certificate Setup — CRITICAL Without installing Burp's CA certificate, your browser will reject HTTPS interception with SSL errors. Step 1 — Start Burp and configure browser proxy: 1. Open Burp Suite → Proxy tab → Proxy settings 2. Default listener: (confirm it's running) 3. In Firefox: Settings → Network Settings → Manual proxy → HTTP Proxy: , Port: Check "Also use this proxy for HTTPS" Step 2 — Download the CA certificate: 1. With proxy configured and Burp running, navigate in Firefox to: Or: 2. Click "CA Certificate" → download Step 3 — Install in Firefox: 1. Firefox → Settings → search "certificates" → View Certificates 2. Authorities tab → Import → select 3. Check: "Trust this CA to identify websites" → OK Step 4 — Verify: Navigate to any HTTPS site — no SSL warning should appear. Installing system wide (for tools that use system trust store): FoxyProxy extension (recommended over manual Firefox proxy settings): FoxyProxy lets you quickly toggle proxy on/off without diving into Firefox settings. Install from Firefox Add ons, add a profile pointing to , and toggle with one click. The Proxy Tab The Proxy tab is where all traffic flows through. It's your main workspace. Intercept On vs Off Intercept ON: Every request is held by Burp and shown to you before being sent. You must manually forward or drop each request. Use this when you want to inspect or modify a specific request. Intercept OFF: Requests flow through Burp transparently — you can still see them in HTTP History, but they aren't held up. This is the normal browsing mode. Use this 95% of the time and only turn intercept on for specific requests. Proxy → HTTP History Every request that flows through Burp (intercept on or off) is logged here. This is your audit trail. Columns: Method, URL, Params (has parameters?), Edited (did you modify it?), Status, Length, MIME type, Extension, Title, Comment, SSL, IP, Cookies Right click any request in history: Send to Repeater — most used action, sends for manual replay/modification Send to Intruder — for automated fuzzing/brute force Send to Decoder — for encoding/decoding the request or response Save item — export request/response Copy URL — copy the full URL Editing Requests Live (Intercept ON) When a request is held: 1. Modify any field directly in the Raw view — method, URL path, headers, body 2. Forward — send the (modified) request to the server 3. Drop — discard the request (browser will see a connection error) 4. Action → Send to Repeater/Intruder The Target Tab Site Map Burp builds a site map of every URL it sees traffic for. As you browse the application, it populates automatically. Use it to: Get a complete picture of all endpoints you've visited Identify areas you haven't explored yet Find parameters and forms you might have missed Scope Definition — DO THIS FIRST Setting scope tells Burp what to care about. Out of scope traffic (third party analytics, CDNs, etc.) clutters your history and wastes time. Setting scope: 1. Target tab → right click the target host in Site Map → "Add to scope" 2. Or: Target → Scope settings → Add → enter the base URL Filtering history to show only in scope traffic: Proxy → HTTP History → Filter bar → "Show only in scope items" [!danger] Set scope before spidering or scanning If you run active scanning or spidering without setting scope, Burp may make requests to third party services you don't have permission to test. On a real engagement this is a scope violation. On the OSCP exam, stay within scope always. The Repeater Tab Repeater lets you manually send HTTP requests and see responses, as many times as you want, modifying the request each time. It's your main tool for manual vulnerability testing. Workflow: 1. Find a request in Proxy → HTTP History 2. Right click → Send to Repeater 3. Switch to Repeater tab — the request is loaded 4. Modify the request (add payloads, change parameters, test injection) 5. Click Send — see the response on the right 6. Modify again, send again — iterate as many times as needed Repeater tips: Use the Inspector panel (right side) to view parameters, cookies, and headers in a structured format — easier than editing raw text Use Ctrl+Space for inline autocomplete in the request editor Right click response → "Show response in browser" — renders the HTML in your browser for complex pages Use + to open multiple Repeater tabs (name them for different vulnerabilities) Press Ctrl+R from HTTP History to quickly send to Repeater What to test in Repeater: SQL injection: modify a parameter value to , , , Command injection: modify a value to , , Path traversal: modify a filename parameter to IDOR: change an ID value from your user's ID to another user's ID Authentication bypass: modify session tokens, remove auth headers, change roles in JWT The Intruder Tab Intruder automates sending large numbers of requests with varying payloads. It's Burp's fuzzing engine — used for brute force, parameter fuzzing, and injection testing. [!warning] Community Edition throttle Intruder in Community Edition is intentionally throttled to approximately 1 request per second. For heavy brute forcing (e.g., rockyou.txt against a login), use ffuf or Hydra instead. Intruder Community is still useful for smaller targeted attacks (under a few hundred payloads). The Four Attack Types Understanding payload positions first: After sending a request to Intruder, you mark payload positions using markers. Intruder replaces the content between markers with payloads. Example — marking a parameter for fuzzing: Attack Type 1 — Sniper One payload set, one position Iterates through each payload, placing it in the marked position If multiple positions marked: cycles through them one at a time, leaving others unchanged Use case: Testing a single parameter with a wordlist (password brute force, SQLi payloads) Attack Type 2 — Battering Ram One payload set, multiple positions Puts the same payload into ALL marked positions simultaneously Use case: When you want the same value everywhere (e.g., testing if username=SAME&email=SAME triggers something) Attack Type 3 — Pitchfork Multiple payload sets (one per position), stepped through in parallel Payload set 1 item 1 goes to position 1, payload set 2 item 1 goes to position 2 — simultaneously Both lists must be the same length — they zip together Use case: Credential stuffing (username list + corresponding password list) Attack Type 4 — Cluster Bomb Multiple payload sets, tries every combination Position 1 gets every payload from set 1, position 2 gets every payload from set 2 — all combinations Request count = len(set1) × len(set2) × ... Use case: Brute force with separate username and password wordlists Intruder Workflow Example — Login Brute Force Payload Types | Type | What it does | | | | | Simple list | Plain list of strings — most common | | Runtime file | Load from file during attack | | Custom iterator | Build payloads from multiple lists with separators | | Character substitution | Apply leetspeak style substitutions to a wordlist | | Case modification | Uppercase, lowercase, toggle case variants | | Numbers | Numeric ranges with steps | | Dates | Date format iteration | | Brute forcer | Character set + length range | | Null payloads | Send the request N times with no change (useful for race condition testing) | | Username generator | Generate variations from a name | The Decoder Tab Decoder lets you encode and decode strings in various formats. Useful when you need to: Decode a Base64 cookie to read its contents URL encode a payload before inserting it Convert hex output from a tool to readable text Encoding/decoding options: URL encoding ( ↔ space) HTML entities ( ↔ ) Base64 ASCII hex Hex Octal Binary Gzip (compress/decompress) Hash (MD5, SHA 1, SHA 256 of input) Workflow: 1. Paste your string in the top box 2. Select "Decode as" or "Encode as" from the dropdown 3. Result appears below — you can chain multiple operations Common use cases: The Comparer Tab Comparer diffs two HTTP requests or responses side by side. Useful for: Comparing responses between a valid login and an invalid login (to understand what changes) Comparing two similar requests to find what parameter causes a different behaviour Identifying what changes between an authenticated and unauthenticated response Workflow: 1. In Proxy History or Repeater: right click → Send to Comparer (request OR response) 2. Do the same for a second item 3. Comparer tab → select both items → "Words" (compare word by word) or "Bytes" (byte level diff) 4. Differences highlighted — modified, deleted, inserted The Sequencer Tab Sequencer analyses the randomness (entropy) of tokens — session IDs, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens. If tokens are predictable, they can be forged or brute forced. Workflow: 1. Find a response containing a token (e.g., session cookie, CSRF token) 2. Send to Sequencer 3. Define the token location (which cookie, which response field) 4. Run the analysis — Burp captures hundreds of tokens and calculates entropy 5. Result: FIPS 140 2 test results and a visual entropy graph What low entropy means: The tokens are predictable. An attacker could enumerate session IDs or predict password reset tokens. Essential BApp Store Extensions BApp Store is Burp's extension marketplace. Accessible via Extensions → BApp Store tab. Must install for OSCP prep: | Extension | What it does | Why you need it | | | | | | Autorize | Automatically tests every request with another user's cookie | IDOR and broken access control testing — massive time saver | | Active Scan++ | Adds additional checks to the active scanner | More vulnerability patterns detected (Pro) | | Param Miner | Discovers hidden/undocumented HTTP parameters | Often finds parameters developers forgot to remove | | JS Beauty | Prettifies minified JavaScript | Makes JS source readable for manual analysis | | JSON Beautifier | Formats JSON responses | Easier to read API responses | | Turbo Intruder | High speed Intruder replacement | Bypasses Community throttle — Python scriptable | | Logger++ | Enhanced request logging with filtering | More powerful than default HTTP History | | Retire.js | Identifies vulnerable JavaScript libraries | Passive discovery of known vulnerable front end libs | | Upload Scanner | Tests file upload endpoints | Automates file upload bypass testing | Installing an extension: 1. Extensions → BApp Store → find extension → Install 2. Or: Extensions → Extensions tab → Add → load a file manually Turbo Intruder — specifically for bypassing Community throttle: Burp's Proxy Intercept — Useful Keyboard Shortcuts | Action | Shortcut | | | | | Forward request | (or Forward button) | | Drop request | (or Drop button) | | Send to Repeater | | | Send to Intruder | | | Toggle intercept | | | Search in request/response | | | New Repeater tab | button in Repeater | Practical Testing Workflows in Burp Testing for SQL Injection Manually Testing for XSS Manually Testing for IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) Bypassing Client Side Controls Community vs Pro Limitations — What This Means for OSCP | Limitation | Impact | Workaround | | | | | | Intruder throttled 1 req/s | Password brute force takes forever | Use Hydra or ffuf for large wordlists; Turbo Intruder extension for medium lists | | No active scanner | Can't auto scan for vulnerabilities | Manual testing + NSE scripts in Nmap | | No Collaborator | Can't do out of band testing (SSRF, blind XXE) | Use interactsh ( ) as free alternative | | Limited BApp extensions | Some extensions require Pro | Core extensions (Param Miner, Autorize) are free | OSCP exam allows Burp Suite Community or Professional. Either works — Pro speeds things up. Quick Reference | Task | Location | Steps | | | | | | Install CA cert | Proxy → Proxy settings → Import/Export CA | Visit http://burpsuite, download, install in Firefox | | Set scope | Target → Scope settings | Add target URL, filter history to in scope | | Capture request | Proxy → Intercept ON | Browse target, request appears in Intercept | | Replay/modify request | Repeater | Right click request → Send to Repeater → modify → Send | | Brute force (small list) | Intruder | Send to Intruder → mark position → load wordlist → Start attack | | Brute force (large list) | Turbo Intruder / ffuf/hydra | Install Turbo Intruder or use CLI tools | | Decode Base64 | Decoder | Paste → Decode as Base64 | | Diff two responses | Comparer | Send both to Comparer → Words diff | | Find hidden params | Param Miner | Right click request → Extensions → Param Miner → Guess params | | Test IDOR | Autorize | Install Autorize, set low priv cookie, browse as high priv | Common Mistakes [!warning] Beginners get these wrong 1. Not installing the CA cert. Every HTTPS site shows an SSL error and you can't intercept. Install the cert before doing anything else. 2. Leaving intercept ON while browsing. You'll be constantly forwarding requests and the browser will feel frozen. Keep intercept OFF by default, turn it ON for specific requests. 3. Not setting scope. Your HTTP History fills with Google Analytics, CDN requests, and noise. Set scope first, filter to in scope only. 4. Using Intruder with rockyou.txt in Community. At 1 req/sec, 14M passwords = 162 days. Use Hydra for big wordlists. 5. Forgetting to check the response. After sending in Repeater, actually read the response — both headers and body. The interesting thing might be in a header you're not looking at. 6. Not using the Inspector panel. Editing raw HTTP is error prone. The Inspector panel in Repeater shows parameters, cookies, and headers in a structured tree — much easier.
