What is your incident response capability — will our alerts trigger your SOC? Penetration Testing Methodologies Methodologies are structured frameworks that ensure you don't miss anything. A good pentester follows a methodology even when improvising. PTES — Penetration Testing Execution Standard The most widely used framework for commercial pentests. Seven phases: 1. Pre engagement — Scope, RoE, legal sign off 2. Intelligence Gathering — Recon (passive and active) 3. Threat Modelling — Who would attack this, and how? 4. Vulnerability Analysis — Identify weaknesses 5. Exploitation — Prove the vulnerability is real 6. Post Exploitation — What can you do after access? Lateral movement, data access 7. Reporting — Document everything with evidence and remediation OWASP Testing Guide (OTG) Specifically for web application testing. Provides a checklist of hundreds of test cases across categories like authentication, session management, input validation, and cryptography. Version 4.2 is current. Use this for every web app engagement. It's the industry standard. OSSTMM — Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual More academic/compliance oriented. Covers networks, communications, wireless, human factors. Less commonly used in commercial red teaming but appears in compliance heavy industries. NIST SP 800 115 US government framework for technical security testing. Defines four phases: Planning, Discovery, Attack, Reporting. Used heavily in US federal contracts. MITRE ATT&CK A knowledge base of real world attacker Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) . Not a methodology for running tests — it's a framework for mapping what you did to how real threat actors operate. Tactics = the goal (e.g., Lateral Movement, Credential Access) Techniques = how the goal is achieved (e.g., Pass the Hash, Kerberoasting) Sub techniques = specific implementations Used heavily in red team reporting and purple team exercises. Learn to map your findings to ATT&CK IDs. Website: https://attack.mitre.org Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin) A linear 7 stage model of how attacks unfold: 1. Reconnaissance — Gather info on the target 2. Weaponisation — Create a payload/exploit 3. Delivery — Send the payload (phishing, USB, web) 4. Exploitation — Trigger the vulnerability 5. Installation — Establish persistence (malware, backdoor) 6. Command & Control (C2) — Maintain communication with compromised system 7. Actions on Objectives — Steal data, cause damage, move laterally Useful for explaining attack chains to clients in reports. Types of Pentest Engagements | Type | Description | | | | | External Network | Attack from the internet against public facing infrastructure | | Internal Network | Attack from inside the network (simulates rogue employee or post phishing) | | Web Application | Full OWASP based assessment of a web app | | Mobile Application | Android/iOS app assessment | | API Testing | REST/GraphQL/SOAP API security assessment | | Wireless | Wi Fi security, rogue APs, WPA2 cracking | | Social Engineering | Phishing, vishing, physical intrusion | | Red Team | Full scope, goal based, long duration adversary simulation | | Purple Team | Red + Blue working together — attacker runs TTPs while defender tunes detection | | Cloud | AWS/Azure/GCP misconfigurations, IAM abuse | | Active Directory | Domain compromise path analysis | Quick Reference | Concept | Key Point | | | | | Black box | No info, full recon, most realistic | | Grey box | Partial info, most common commercial | | White box | Full info, source code review | | Legal basis | Computer Misuse Act 1990 (UK) / CFAA (US) | | RoE | Must be signed before any testing begins | | PTES | 7 phase framework for commercial pentests | | OWASP OTG | Standard for web app testing | | MITRE ATT&CK | Map techniques to real world TTP database | | Kill Chain | 7 stages: Recon → Weaponise → Deliver → Exploit → Install → C2 → Action | Related Notes 00.2 — Report Writing 00.3 — Lab Setup MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 0 — Foundations/00.2 — Report Writing.md
title: 00.2 — Report Writing
body: 00.2 — Report Writing Why Reports Matter The report is the only deliverable the client keeps . Your 40 hours of hacking means nothing if the report doesn't communicate what you found, why it matters, and what to do about it. A bad report gets filed and forgotten. A good report gets vulnerabilities fixed. Senior pentesters are judged as much on report quality as on technical skill. Report Structure A professional pentest report has two audiences: The executive — doesn't care about CVE IDs, cares about business risk The technical team — needs exact reproduction steps to fix the issue Both need to be in the same document. Standard Sections 1. Cover Page Client name, engagement type, date range Pentest firm name, lead tester, classification (CONFIDENTIAL) Report version (v1.0, v1.1 after client review) 2. Executive Summary Written in plain English — no jargon 1–2 pages maximum Answers: What did we test? What is the overall risk posture? What are the 3 most critical things to fix immediately? Include a risk rating chart (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Info counts) 3. Scope and Methodology Exact scope (IPs, domains, applications) Dates and times of testing Methodology used (PTES, OWASP, etc.) Tools used (at a high level — detailed tool list goes in appendix) Testing type (black/grey/white box) 4. Findings This is the core of the report. Each finding gets its own subsection. Finding Template: Description: What the vulnerability is, in plain terms. What is the root cause? Evidence: Screenshots, HTTP requests/responses, tool output. Everything must be reproducible. Reproduction Steps: Impact: What can an attacker actually do with this? Be specific. "Attacker can extract all customer records from the database" is better than "data breach possible." Remediation: Specific, actionable fix. Reference the developer. "Use parameterised queries / prepared statements. Do not construct SQL strings from user input. Apply input validation as a secondary control." References: OWASP: https://owasp.org/www community/attacks/SQL Injection CWE 89 5. Remediation Summary A table of all findings with severity, status, and owner. Used by the client to track fixes. | ID | Title | Severity | Owner | Status | | | | | | | | VULN 001 | SQL Injection | Critical | Dev Team | Open | | VULN 002 | Missing HSTS | Low | DevOps | Open | 6. Appendix Full tool list with versions Raw scan output (Nmap, Nikto, etc.) Detailed technical notes that don't fit the main findings Methodology reference CVSS Scoring — How to Rate Severity CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v3.1 is the industry standard for rating vulnerability severity. Every finding must have a CVSS score. Base Score Metrics | Metric | Options | | | | | Attack Vector (AV) | Network (N), Adjacent (A), Local (L), Physical (P) | | Attack Complexity (AC) | Low (L), High (H) | | Privileges Required (PR) | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | User Interaction (UI) | None (N), Required (R) | | Scope (S) | Unchanged (U), Changed (C) | | Confidentiality (C) | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | Integrity (I) | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | | Availability (A) | None (N), Low (L), High (H) | Severity Ratings | Score | Rating | | | | | 9.0–10.0 | Critical | | 7.0–8.9 | High | | 4.0–6.9 | Medium | | 0.1–3.9 | Low | | 0.0 | Informational | Use the NVD CVSS calculator: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln metrics/cvss/v3 calculator Practical Examples | Finding | CVSS Vector | Score | | | | | | Unauthenticated RCE via network | AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H | 9.8 | | Stored XSS requiring login | AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N | 5.4 | | Self XSS (affects only yourself) | AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:N | 0.0 (Info) | | Local privesc via misconfigured sudo | AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H | 7.8 | Evidence Standards [!tip] Screenshot everything before you exploit. Once you pop a shell, capture proof immediately — the session may die. A finding without evidence is a finding the client can dispute. Good evidence includes: HTTP requests and responses (from Burp Suite, use "Copy as curl command") Terminal output with the hostname and timestamp visible Screenshots of the vulnerable parameter and the impact Before and after — show the normal behaviour, then show the exploit working Always redact sensitive data that isn't needed to prove the finding (real passwords, PII, other users' data). Writing Style Passive voice for descriptions : "The application was found to be vulnerable to SQL injection." Active voice for impact : "An attacker can extract the entire customer database." Remediation is prescriptive, not vague : "Implement parameterised queries" not "fix the SQL injection." No CVE names without explanation — always describe what the CVE actually is. Severity levels must be justified. "Critical because unauthenticated attacker achieves RCE over the internet" is justified. "Critical" alone is not. Quick Reference | Section | Purpose | | | | | Executive Summary | Business risk, plain English, 1–2 pages | | Scope | What was tested, when, how | | Findings | Individual vulns with evidence + CVSS | | Remediation Summary | Tracking table for fixes | | Appendix | Raw output, tool list | | CVSS 9.0–10.0 | Critical | | CVSS 7.0–8.9 | High | | CVSS 4.0–6.9 | Medium | | CVSS 0.1–3.9 | Low | Related Notes 00.1 — What is Penetration Testing 00.3 — Lab Setup MODULE 8 — Reporting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 0 — Foundations/00.3 — Lab Setup.md
title: 00.3 — Lab Setup
body: 00.3 — Lab Setup Why You Need a Lab You cannot practice pentesting on systems you don't own or have permission to test. A local lab gives you: A safe, isolated environment to practice exploits without breaking real systems or committing crimes Full control over the target — you can reset, snapshot, and experiment freely The ability to run both attacker and victim machines on the same laptop A home lab is the single most important investment in your pentesting journey. Everything else is theory until you build one. Architecture Overview Both VMs sit on an internal/host only network — no connection to the internet from the target. This prevents your exploits from accidentally hitting real systems. Step 1 — Install a Hypervisor A hypervisor lets you run multiple operating systems (virtual machines) on your physical machine simultaneously. Option A: VirtualBox (Free, Recommended for Beginners) Download: https://www.virtualbox.org/wiki/Downloads Works on Windows, macOS, Linux Free and open source Slightly less performant than VMware but excellent for labs Install VirtualBox Extension Pack as well (USB 3.0, better networking) Option B: VMware Workstation Pro (Free since 2024) Download: https://www.vmware.com/products/workstation pro.html Better performance, better snapshot management Now free for personal use Better USB passthrough if you're testing physical hardware (Wi Fi adapters, etc.) [!tip] If you have a decent machine (8GB+ RAM, SSD), either works. VMware is faster. VirtualBox is simpler to start with. Step 2 — Install Kali Linux (Attacker Machine) Kali Linux is a Debian based distribution maintained by Offensive Security, purpose built for penetration testing. It comes pre installed with 600+ security tools. Download Kali Go to: https://www.kali.org/get kali/ Choose: Pre built Virtual Machine (saves time — it's already configured for VirtualBox/VMware) For VirtualBox: Download the file For VMware: Download the package Import into VirtualBox Default credentials: / Change the password immediately: Recommended VM Configuration for Kali | Setting | Recommended Value | | | | | RAM | 4GB minimum, 8GB preferred | | CPU cores | 2 minimum, 4 preferred | | Storage | 80GB (default 80GB is fine) | | Network Adapter 1 | NAT (for internet access — to install tools) | | Network Adapter 2 | Host Only (for attacking target VMs) | Step 3 — Network Modes Explained This is critical to understand. The wrong network mode can expose your attack traffic to the internet or prevent you from reaching your target. NAT (Network Address Translation) VM shares your host machine's IP address VM can reach the internet (to install tools, update packages) Host cannot initiate connections to VM (VM is behind NAT) Other VMs on Host Only cannot see NAT VMs Use for: Kali's internet adapter Host Only Creates an isolated network between your VMs and host machine VMs can talk to each other and to the host No internet access Perfect for attacker ↔ target communication Use for: Lab network between Kali and target VMs Bridged VM gets its own IP on your real physical network Visible to your router and other devices on your network Do not use for targets — your exploits could hit real network devices Internal Network Completely isolated — only VMs on the same internal network name can communicate Not even the host can see these VMs More isolated than Host Only Good for multi machine scenarios [!danger] Never put a target VM (Metasploitable, DVWA, etc.) on a Bridged adapter. It will be accessible from your entire home network and potentially the internet if your router is misconfigured. Step 4 — Set Up Target Machines You need something to attack. These are the best starting targets: Metasploitable 2 (Beginner Essential) A deliberately vulnerable Ubuntu VM. Contains dozens of intentionally broken services — old Samba, FTP with backdoors, PHP shells, vulnerable web apps. Download: https://sourceforge.net/projects/metasploitable/ Import into VirtualBox: 1. Create a new Linux VM, skip the disk creation step 2. Under Storage, attach the file as the disk 3. Set network to Host Only only (no NAT) Credentials: / DVWA — Damn Vulnerable Web Application A PHP/MySQL web app with configurable vulnerability levels for SQLi, XSS, CSRF, File Upload, Command Injection, etc. Run it inside Metasploitable 2 (it's included) or install it separately: Access at: http://localhost/ VulnHub Machines https://www.vulnhub.com — hundreds of downloadable CTF style vulnerable VMs, from beginner to advanced. All downloadable as or . Good beginner machines: Kioptrix Level 1 — classic SMB exploitation Mr. Robot — web + Linux privesc Basic Pentesting 1 — beginner friendly intro HackTheBox Starting Point https://www.hackthebox.com — online platform, no local setup needed for most machines. Connect via their VPN. Starting Point machines are free and walk you through concepts step by step. Step 5 — Essential Post Install Config for Kali Once Kali is running, do this before anything else: Update Everything This updates the package list and upgrades all installed packages. Run this regularly — security tools update frequently. Install Common Tools (if not present) If any are missing: Set Up Metasploit Database Metasploit uses PostgreSQL to store scan results. Set it up: Inside msfconsole, verify the DB is connected: Set Up Burp Suite Burp Suite Community Edition comes pre installed on Kali. Launch it: Or find it under Applications → Web Application Analysis. First time setup: 1. Proxy → Options → confirm listener is on 2. Configure your browser (or use Burp's built in browser) to proxy through 3. Install Burp's CA certificate in your browser (Proxy → Intercept → Open Browser → navigate to ) Install tmux (Essential for Terminal Management) tmux lets you split your terminal into panes and keep sessions alive. You'll use this on every engagement. Basic tmux commands: Install SecLists (Wordlists) SecLists is a collection of wordlists used for fuzzing, brute forcing, and directory enumeration. Essential. Key directories: Also already on Kali: Step 6 — Snapshots Take a snapshot of your Kali VM after setup is complete and before any engagement . If you break something or get infected by a sample, you can roll back instantly. VirtualBox: VMware: Take snapshots of target VMs too — before and after exploitation. Quick Reference | Component | Tool/Resource | Purpose | | | | | | Hypervisor | VirtualBox / VMware Workstation | Run multiple VMs | | Attacker OS | Kali Linux (pre built .ova) | Pentesting toolkit | | Target (network) | Metasploitable 2 | Vulnerable Linux services | | Target (web) | DVWA, Metasploitable 2 | Vulnerable web apps | | Target (online) | HackTheBox, TryHackMe | Guided practice | | Network mode (Kali internet) | NAT | Tools/updates | | Network mode (lab) | Host Only | Attack/target comms | | Wordlists | SecLists, rockyou.txt | Brute force / fuzzing | | Terminal | tmux | Multi pane sessions | | Proxy | Burp Suite | Web traffic interception | Related Notes 00.1 — What is Penetration Testing 00.2 — Report Writing MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting Active Directory Lab Setup The lab described above covers web and Linux exploitation. For MODULE 4 (Active Directory Pentesting), you need a Windows domain environment. This section extends the base lab. Why You Need an AD Lab Everything in MODULE 4 — Kerberoasting, AS REP Roasting, Pass the Hash, DCSync, BloodHound, ADCS abuse — requires a live Windows domain to practise against. You cannot simulate these against Metasploitable. Setting this up once gives you a permanent practice environment you can reset and re attack at will. Required Licences (Free Evaluation) Microsoft provides 180 day evaluation ISOs at no cost. They are fully functional — no activation required for lab use. Download the ISO files. Each is 5–6 GB. [!tip] When the evaluation expires, take a snapshot before it does. You can revert to any pre expiry snapshot indefinitely without re installing. Target AD Lab Architecture Minimum setup: 1 DC + 1 workstation + Kali . This is enough for all MODULE 4 attacks. Recommended RAM allocation: | VM | RAM | Storage | | | | | | Kali Linux (existing) | 4 GB | 80 GB | | DC01 — Windows Server 2022 | 4 GB | 60 GB | | WS01 — Windows 10 | 2 GB | 40 GB | Total requirement: 10 GB RAM. Runs on a 16 GB host. Step 1 — Create the Domain Controller VM (DC01) VirtualBox: After creation, attach the Windows Server 2022 ISO: Network configuration: Start the VM and install Windows Server 2022: 1. Boot from ISO → Windows Setup → Next → Install Now 2. Select: Windows Server 2022 Standard (Desktop Experience) — the GUI version 3. Accept licence → Custom install → select the unallocated disk → Next 4. Installation completes, VM reboots, sets Administrator password 5. Use a password you'll remember: Step 2 — Configure DC01 Network Settings After Windows installs, set a static IP on the Host Only adapter: Rename the computer before promoting to DC: Step 3 — Install Active Directory Domain Services After reboot, open PowerShell as Administrator: The server reboots automatically. After reboot, log in as with password . Verify the domain is up: Step 4 — Create Lab Users and Groups (Intentionally Vulnerable) This script creates a realistic but deliberately vulnerable AD environment for practising attacks: Step 5 — Disable Windows Defender on DC01 (Lab Only) Defender will block many offensive tools. Disable it for the lab: [!warning] Only do this in an isolated host only network lab. Never disable Defender on a machine with internet access or connected to your real network. Step 6 — Create the Workstation VM (WS01) Create a new VM for the Windows 10 workstation: Attach Windows 10 Enterprise ISO → install → set password: After install, set static IP on Host Only adapter: Rename the computer: Step 7 — Join WS01 to the Domain After reboot on WS01: After the reboot, log into WS01 with a domain account: / Add a domain user as local administrator on WS01 (for lateral movement practice): Step 8 — Disable Defender on WS01 Step 9 — Snapshot Everything Before any testing, take a clean snapshot of each VM: You can now attack the lab and restore to clean state in seconds. Step 10 — Configure Kali to Reach the Lab On Kali, the Host Only adapter should already be on 192.168.56.x. Verify: If Kali doesn't have a Host Only IP: Configure on Kali for convenience: Configure to use DC01 as DNS: Test connectivity: Step 11 — Install BloodHound on Kali BloodHound is essential for visualising AD attack paths. It requires Neo4j. Collect BloodHound Data from the Lab After uploading, use the pre built queries: Lab Attack Targets Summary With this setup, the following attacks are ready to practise immediately: | Attack | Target | Tool | | | | | | Kerberoasting | svc sql, svc web, svc backup | GetUserSPNs.py, Rubeus | | AS REP Roasting | legacyuser | GetNPUsers.py, Rubeus | | Password spraying | All domain users | kerbrute, crackmapexec | | BloodHound path analysis | Whole domain | bloodhound python | | ACL abuse (GenericAll) | legacyuser via HelpDesk | bloodyAD, PowerView | | Pass the Hash | localadmin (DA) | crackmapexec, evil winrm | | DCSync | CORP\Administrator | secretsdump.py | | ADCS (ESC1) | After installing ADCS role | certipy | | LLMNR/NBT NS poisoning | WS01 when browsing | Responder | | SMB relay | WS01 → DC01 | ntlmrelayx | Optional — Install ADCS on DC01 (for ESC Practice) To practise the attacks in , install ADCS on DC01: After installation, Certipy enumeration will show the CA and its templates: To create an ESC1 vulnerable template for practice: Troubleshooting Common Lab Issues Quick Reference — Lab IPs | Host | IP | Role | Credentials | | | | | | | Kali | 192.168.56.10 | Attacker | — | | DC01 | 192.168.56.20 | Domain Controller (corp.local) | CORP\Administrator / Lab@dmin2024! | | WS01 | 192.168.56.30 | Workstation | CORP\jsmith / Password123 | | Account | Type | Password | Attack Target | | | | | | | administrator | Domain Admin | Lab@dmin2024! | Final objective | | localadmin | Domain Admin | LocalAdmin123! | Lateral movement path | | jsmith | Domain User + local admin on WS01 | Password123 | Initial foothold | | svc sql | Service account | Service123! | Kerberoasting | | svc web | Service account | WebPass99 | Kerberoasting | | legacyuser | Domain User | Legacy2020 | AS REP Roasting |

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance/01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT.md
title: 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT
body: 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT What It Is Passive reconnaissance is the process of gathering information about a target without directly interacting with their systems . You are not sending packets to the target. You are querying public sources — search engines, DNS records, certificate transparency logs, social media, job postings — and building a picture of the target's attack surface. Why this matters: passive recon is completely undetectable by the target. No firewall log, no IDS alert, no connection. You learn as much as possible before you touch anything. What You're Looking For Before you start, define your intelligence goals: | Goal | What to Find | | | | | Infrastructure | IP ranges, ASNs, hosting providers, CDN presence | | Domains | Subdomains, related domains, old/forgotten domains | | Technology | Web frameworks, CMS, server software, cloud provider | | People | Employee names, email addresses, job roles | | Credentials | Leaked passwords, API keys in public repos | | Documents | PDFs, spreadsheets, config files accidentally exposed | | Network | Open ports visible from internet, exposed admin panels | Google Dorks Google dorks use advanced search operators to find information that normal searches miss. This is free, powerful, and entirely passive. Core Operators | Operator | What It Does | Example | | | | | | | Restrict results to a domain | | | | Find specific file types | | | | Match text in the URL | | | | Match text in the page title | | | | Match text in page body | | | | Alias for filetype | | | | Google's cached version | | | | Exclude results | | | | Exact phrase match | | High Value Dorks [!tip] Google Hacking Database (GHDB) at https://www.exploit db.com/google hacking database contains thousands of pre built dorks categorised by type (files, login pages, sensitive info, etc.). Always check it before building dorks from scratch. WHOIS Lookup WHOIS reveals domain registration data — who registered a domain, when, and through which registrar. Useful for: Identifying the organisation behind a domain Finding related domains registered by the same person Historical ownership changes Abuse contact details Key fields to note: Registrant Organisation — company name (often redacted via privacy protection) Registrant Email — can be used to find other domains registered by the same person Name Servers — tells you who manages DNS (important for later) Creation Date — old domains may have more legacy exposure Expiry Date — near expiry domains are sometimes hijackable Online alternatives (when CLI output is minimal): https://who.is https://lookup.icann.org https://whois.domaintools.com (historical records, paid) DNS Enumeration DNS records reveal the structure of a target's infrastructure. Record Types to Enumerate | Record Type | What It Contains | Why It Matters | | | | | | A | IPv4 address for a hostname | Reveals server IPs | | AAAA | IPv6 address | IPv6 exposed services | | MX | Mail server hostnames | Email infrastructure, phishing setup | | NS | Authoritative name servers | DNS provider | | TXT | Arbitrary text | SPF/DKIM/DMARC (email security posture), sometimes API keys | | CNAME | Alias to another hostname | Often reveals internal names or third party services | | SOA | Start of Authority | Zone info, admin contact | | PTR | Reverse DNS (IP → hostname) | Reveals hostnames for known IPs | | SRV | Service locator records | Internal services (SIP, XMPP, LDAP) | Manual DNS Queries with DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) A zone transfer is a mechanism for DNS servers to replicate records to each other. If a nameserver is misconfigured to allow transfers from any IP, you can dump all DNS records for a domain at once. Expected output if misconfigured: [!warning] Zone transfers are increasingly rare on modern infrastructure. But when they work, they're gold — you get the entire DNS map of the target in one query. theHarvester theHarvester is a tool for gathering emails, hostnames, IPs, and employee names from public sources including search engines, DNS, and breach databases. Core Usage Key Flags | Flag | Meaning | | | | | | Target domain | | | Data source(s) — comma separated | | | Limit results (default 500) | | | Output filename (saves .html and .xml) | | | Start result offset | Available Sources Most useful: , , , (certificate transparency), , , (AlienVault), What to Do with Output Email addresses → Use for phishing simulation (if in scope), or to check breach databases Hostnames → Feed into subdomain enumeration tools, scan for open ports IPs → Add to scope map, scan with Nmap Shodan Shodan is a search engine for internet connected devices. Unlike Google which indexes web pages, Shodan indexes banners — the responses that services give when you connect to them (HTTP headers, SSH banners, FTP welcome messages, etc.). Website: https://www.shodan.io CLI: (requires free API key) What Shodan Reveals Open ports and services on every IP Shodan has scanned Software versions (often revealing CVEs) SSL certificate details (hostnames, expiry, weak ciphers) Geographic location, ASN, ISP Industrial control systems (SCADA/ICS) exposed to internet Default credentials on devices (cameras, routers, printers) Shodan Web Search Shodan CLI [!tip] Shodan's free tier limits searches. The CLI command is extremely useful — run it on every IP you discover to see what services are exposed and what versions they're running, before you even touch Nmap. Censys Similar to Shodan but with better certificate search and structured JSON output. Particularly powerful for: Finding all IPs behind a domain's SSL cert Discovering assets the client doesn't know about Tracking infrastructure changes over time Website: https://search.censys.io Certificate Transparency Logs When a CA (Certificate Authority) issues an SSL/TLS certificate, it's logged publicly in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs. This means every subdomain that has ever had an SSL cert issued is publicly visible . crt.sh Output gives you every subdomain that has ever had a certificate — including: Staging environments ( ) Dev environments ( ) Internal tools ( , ) Historical subdomains no longer in DNS but potentially still live Maltego Maltego is a graphical OSINT tool that maps relationships between entities (domains, IPs, emails, people, organisations) visually as a graph. Comes pre installed on Kali. Free Community Edition available. Transforms (queries you run on an entity): Domain → IP addresses IP → Hostnames (reverse DNS) Email → Social media accounts Person → Email addresses [!tip] Maltego is powerful but slow for large targets. Better used for targeted investigation of specific entities (a person, a domain) than broad recon of an entire org. Breach Data & Credential Exposure Check if target email addresses appear in known data breaches. This is intelligence for phishing simulations and password spray attacks (if in scope). haveibeenpwned.com API DeHashed (paid) https://dehashed.com — search by email, username, password, IP, domain GitHub Credential Leaks Developers often accidentally commit API keys, passwords, and tokens to public GitHub repos. Building a Target Profile After passive recon, you should have: Quick Reference | Source | Best For | | | | | Google Dorks | Exposed files, login pages, error messages | | WHOIS | Registrant info, related domains | | DNS / dig | Infrastructure mapping, zone transfer | | theHarvester | Emails, hostnames, combined OSINT | | Shodan | Open ports, software versions, exposed devices | | crt.sh | Subdomain discovery via SSL certs | | GitHub search | Leaked credentials, API keys | | HaveIBeenPwned | Breach exposure of email addresses | Related Notes 00.1 — What is Penetration Testing 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap 01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration 01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance/01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap.md
title: 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap
body: 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap What It Is Active reconnaissance means directly interacting with the target's systems — sending packets and analysing responses. Unlike passive recon, this is detectable . Your IP will appear in the target's firewall logs and IDS alerts. This is why you do passive recon first: minimise your active footprint until you understand the target, and only then begin touching systems. The primary tool for active recon is Nmap — the Network Mapper. It is the industry standard for host discovery, port scanning, service version detection, and OS fingerprinting. How TCP Works (Essential Background) Before scanning, you need to understand the TCP three way handshake, because Nmap scan types are defined by how they manipulate it. Open port : completes the handshake (SYN → SYN ACK → ACK) Closed port : RST is returned instead of SYN ACK Filtered port : no response (firewall dropped the packet) or ICMP unreachable Nmap — Core Concepts Install / Verify Basic Syntax Target can be: Scan Types sS — SYN Scan (Default, Stealth) How it works: 1. Send SYN 2. Receive SYN ACK (port open) or RST (port closed) or nothing (filtered) 3. Send RST immediately — never complete the handshake Why it's stealthy: the full TCP connection is never established, so many older logging systems don't record it. Modern IDS will still catch it, but it's the least noisy scan type. Requires root/sudo (needs raw socket access). sT — TCP Connect Scan Completes the full three way handshake. Used when you don't have root privileges. Slower and more detectable — connection attempts are fully logged by the target. sU — UDP Scan Scans UDP ports. Much slower than TCP (no handshake — relies on ICMP port unreachable responses or service specific probes). Critical services run on UDP: DNS (53) DHCP (67/68) SNMP (161) TFTP (69) NTP (123) LDAP (389) [!tip] UDP scanning is slow. Target only key ports unless you have time: sN / sF / sX — NULL, FIN, Xmas Scans These exploit RFC 793 behaviour: if a port is closed , the target sends RST. If open or filtered , no response. Used for firewall evasion against stateless packet filters. Do not work against Windows — Windows sends RST for all ports regardless. sA — ACK Scan Not for finding open ports — for mapping firewall rules . RST = port is unfiltered (firewall lets ACK through) No response = port is filtered (firewall is blocking it) Useful for understanding firewall topology. sn — Ping Scan (Host Discovery Only, No Port Scan) Discovers which hosts are alive on a network. Does not scan ports. Fast — use this first on large subnets. Essential Options Port Selection Timing Templates ( T) Controls speed vs stealth trade off: | Template | Name | Description | | | | | | T0 | Paranoid | Very slow — evades IDS, 5 min between probes | | T1 | Sneaky | Slow — IDS evasion | | T2 | Polite | Slow — reduces bandwidth load | | T3 | Normal | Default — balanced | | T4 | Aggressive | Fast — assumes good network | | T5 | Insane | Very fast — likely to miss results | For labs: (fast, reliable) For real engagements: or (quieter) Service/Version Detection Output example: Service versions → search for CVEs directly. OS Detection Nmap analyses TCP/IP stack behaviour (TTL, window sizes, packet responses) to guess the OS. Requires root. Aggressive Scan ( A) Equivalent to: + NSE default scripts. Noisy but comprehensive. Good for labs. Output Formats [!tip] Always save output. creates three files. You will reference scan results constantly during an engagement. Losing them wastes time. Verbosity NSE — Nmap Scripting Engine NSE is one of Nmap's most powerful features. Scripts extend Nmap's capabilities to: Detect specific vulnerabilities Enumerate services (SMB shares, SNMP, DNS) Brute force authentication Fingerprint web applications Scripts are located at: Script Categories | Category | Purpose | | | | | | Safe, useful — run automatically with A | | | No harmful side effects | | | Enumerate services and hosts | | | Detect known vulnerabilities | | | Actively exploit vulnerabilities (use carefully) | | | Test authentication (brute force) | | | Potentially harmful — may crash services | | | Detect malware backdoors | | | Discover hosts via broadcast | Running Scripts High Value NSE Scripts SMB Enumeration HTTP Enumeration SSL/TLS Analysis FTP DNS Vulnerability Detection Practical Scan Workflow This is the standard scanning workflow for an engagement. Run these in order. Phase 1 — Host Discovery (Which Hosts Are Alive) Phase 2 — Quick Port Scan (Top 1000 Ports) Phase 3 — Full Port Scan (All 65535 Ports) Phase 4 — Service/Version + Default Scripts on Open Ports Phase 5 — Targeted NSE Scripts Based on Open Services Masscan — High Speed Port Scanner Masscan is Nmap's speed oriented cousin. It can scan the entire internet's port space in under 6 minutes (at 10 million packets/second). For large internal networks, it's much faster than Nmap. [!warning] Masscan at high rates can crash routers and firewalls . Keep below 1000 on client networks. On your own lab, 10000+ is fine. Workflow: Use Masscan for fast port discovery, then pipe results to Nmap for service detection: Netdiscover — ARP Based Host Discovery For internal networks, ARP is more reliable than ICMP for finding hosts (firewalls block pings, not ARP). Output shows: IP, MAC address, Vendor (from MAC OUI lookup). The vendor tells you a lot about a device (e.g., "Apple" = MacBook, "Fortinet" = firewall). Quick Reference | Flag | Meaning | | | | | sS | SYN scan (stealth, default) | | sU | UDP scan | | sV | Service version detection | | sC | Default NSE scripts | | A | Aggressive ( sV O traceroute sC) | | p | All 65535 ports | | T4 | Fast timing | | oA | Save all output formats | | iL | Read targets from file | | script= | Run specific NSE script(s) | Related Notes 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT 01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration 01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance/01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration.md
title: 01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration
body: 01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration Why Subdomains Matter The target's primary domain ( ) is usually hardened — it's the front door. Subdomains are the back windows. Common findings on subdomains: Staging/dev environments with no WAF, debug mode on, or outdated software Internal tools accidentally exposed to the internet (Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, GitLab) Old forgotten apps that were "temporarily" public three years ago Different attack surfaces — the main site runs React on nginx; the subdomain runs a PHP app from 2014 [!tip] Bug bounty hunters find the majority of their critical findings on subdomains. The main app is tested constantly. is not. Method 1 — Certificate Transparency Logs (Best Passive Source) Already covered in 01.1. The fastest way to get a comprehensive subdomain list passively. Method 2 — Subfinder (Fast, Multi Source) Subfinder queries passive sources (crt.sh, Shodan, VirusTotal, SecurityTrails, etc.) and returns subdomains without directly touching the target. Configuring API Keys (Significantly Increases Results) Add keys for: , , , , , Free APIs to get: VirusTotal: https://www.virustotal.com/gui/my apikey Shodan: https://account.shodan.io URLScan: https://urlscan.io/user/signup Method 3 — Amass (Most Comprehensive) Amass is the most powerful subdomain enumeration tool. It combines passive OSINT with active DNS techniques and builds a relationship graph of discovered assets. Amass Modes Useful Amass Commands [!warning] Amass is slow. For large scopes, passive mode can take 30+ minutes. Run it in a tmux session and let it work in the background while you use other tools. Method 4 — Assetfinder Simple, fast tool by tomnomnom. Great for quick passive results. Method 5 — DNS Bruteforcing The passive methods only find subdomains that are already in public sources. DNS bruteforcing tries to discover hidden subdomains by guessing names from a wordlist. For each word in the wordlist, the tool queries: — if it resolves, it's a real subdomain. gobuster (DNS mode) ffuf (DNS mode) Best Wordlists for DNS Bruteforcing [!tip] Always start with the 5000 word list for speed. Only move to larger lists if you have time or the target is large. Method 6 — Permutation & Alteration If you find , there's likely also , , . Permutation tools generate these variations automatically. dnsgen altdns Method 7 — DNSx (DNS Resolution & Validation) After you have a large list of potential subdomains, DNSx resolves them all quickly to confirm which ones are real (have valid DNS records). Subdomain Takeover A subdomain takeover occurs when a subdomain's DNS record points to a service (AWS S3 bucket, Heroku app, GitHub Pages, etc.) that no longer exists — and an attacker can claim that unclaimed service. Example: 1. → CNAME → 2. The S3 bucket is deleted 3. The CNAME record is NOT removed from DNS 4. An attacker creates S3 bucket 5. Now serves attacker controlled content How to Find Subdomain Takeover Candidates subjack (Automated Takeover Check) [!tip] Subdomain takeover is a common bug bounty finding. Even Low/Medium severity findings are easy wins if you find an unclaimed CNAME. The impact is demonstrated by serving content from the subdomain. Full Subdomain Enumeration Workflow Quick Reference | Tool | Type | Best For | | | | | | subfinder | Passive | Multi source OSINT, fast | | amass | Passive + Active | Comprehensive, graphs | | assetfinder | Passive | Quick passive results | | gobuster dns | Active | DNS bruteforce | | crt.sh | Passive | Cert transparency logs | | dnsx | Validation | Resolving large lists | | subjack | Takeover | Finding abandoned CNAMEs | Related Notes 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap 01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance/01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting.md
title: 01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting
body: 01.4 — Technology Fingerprinting What It Is Technology fingerprinting is the process of identifying what software, frameworks, and services a target is running before you start testing. Why it matters: Different technologies have different vulnerabilities (WordPress ≠ Django ≠ .NET) Knowing the version lets you look up known CVEs directly Identifies what tools and attack techniques are relevant Reveals mismatches (e.g., server claims nginx but responds like Apache — WAF in front) You're building a technology profile that guides every subsequent attack decision. What to Fingerprint | Layer | What to Look For | | | | | Web server | Apache, nginx, IIS, Caddy — and version | | Backend language | PHP, Python, Ruby, Java, ASP.NET | | Framework | WordPress, Laravel, Django, Rails, Spring | | CMS | WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento | | JavaScript frameworks | React, Angular, Vue, jQuery | | CDN / WAF | Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva, AWS CloudFront | | Cloud provider | AWS, Azure, GCP | | Analytics / third party | Google Analytics, Hotjar, HubSpot | | Programming language version | PHP 7.4 vs 8.1, Python 2 vs 3 | HTTP Headers — Manual Analysis HTTP response headers are the single most information rich passive source for technology fingerprinting. They often directly reveal the server software and version. Key Headers to Analyse | Header | What It Reveals | | | | | | Web server software and version — e.g., | | | Backend technology — e.g., , | | | CMS — e.g., , | | | .NET version | | | Security headers (or lack thereof) | | | CSP presence and configuration | | | HSTS configuration | | | Cookie names reveal tech: = PHP, = Java/Tomcat, = ASP.NET, = WordPress | | | Reverse proxy / CDN in use | | | Cloudflare is in the path | | | Varnish cache | Example Output Analysis From these headers alone: Ubuntu Linux, Apache 2.4.51, PHP 7.4.3 (end of life, multiple CVEs), WordPress. Next step: , , look up WordPress version. WhatWeb WhatWeb identifies technologies used by websites. It queries the site and analyses responses, HTML, JavaScript, cookies, and headers. Output Interpretation Each detected technology is a lead. WhatWeb knows 1800+ technologies — it's identifying them from signatures in the response. Wappalyzer Wappalyzer is a browser extension (Chrome/Firefox) that identifies technologies on any page you visit. It's the passive, point and click version of WhatWeb. Install: https://www.wappalyzer.com/ Also available as a CLI tool: Good for quick checks when browsing a target's site manually. Nikto — Web Server Scanner Nikto is a web server scanner that checks for: Outdated server software Dangerous files and directories (backup files, readme files, install files) Server misconfigurations Default credentials Known vulnerable files (e.g., , ) [!warning] Nikto is noisy — it makes hundreds of HTTP requests in a short period. It will appear in the target's web logs and may trigger IDS/WAF alerts. Use it only when active scanning is authorised. What Nikto Finds Each finding is actionable: reveals the full PHP configuration including environment variables that may contain credentials. Identifying WAF (Web Application Firewall) Before you start testing, determine if a WAF is present. If it is, your payloads may need to be obfuscated, and aggressive scanning may trigger blocking. wafw00f Output Examples Manual WAF Detection Send a clearly malicious request and observe the response: WAF indicators: Response code 403 or 406 for obviously malicious input Unusual redirect (to , etc.) Response body contains "Access Denied", "Blocked", "Security Policy" header → Cloudflare → Sucuri → AWS WAF CMS Specific Fingerprinting WordPress WPScan finds: WordPress version, installed plugins/themes with known CVEs, usernames (from ), exposed sensitive files. Manual WordPress fingerprinting: Drupal Manual Drupal fingerprinting: Joomla OS and Server Fingerprinting via TTL You can guess the operating system from the TTL (Time to Live) value in ping responses: | TTL Value | Likely OS | | | | | 64 | Linux / Unix | | 128 | Windows | | 255 | Cisco IOS / network device | [!tip] TTL decrements by 1 at each router hop, so a received TTL of 120 suggests Windows (128 8 hops = 120). Use this as a rough indicator, not a definitive identification. Building Your Technology Profile After fingerprinting, document everything in your notes: Quick Reference | Tool | Purpose | Noise Level | | | | | | curl I | HTTP header analysis | Very low | | WhatWeb | Tech stack identification | Low | | Wappalyzer | Browser based passive | Passive | | Nikto | Server misconfigs + files | High | | wafw00f | WAF detection | Low | | WPScan | WordPress full audit | Medium | | droopescan | Multi CMS scan | Medium | Related Notes 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap 01.3 — Subdomain Enumeration MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 1 — Reconnaissance/01.5 — JavaScript File Analysis.md
title: 01.5 - JavaScript File Analysis
body: test 01.5 JavaScript File Analysis Why JS Files Are High Yield Recon Modern web applications are largely JavaScript driven. The JS bundles browsers download contain far more than the server intentionally exposes: hidden API endpoints, hardcoded secrets, internal hostnames, authentication logic, and third party integrations. This step belongs in every web recon workflow immediately after directory brute forcing and routinely finds things no scanner catches. Step 1 Discover and Download JS Files Install the discovery tools first: go install github.com/lc/gau/v2/cmd/gau@latest go install github.com/tomnomnom/waybackurls@latest go install github.com/hakluke/hakrawler@latest Run discovery: TARGET="target.com" TARGET URL="https://$TARGET" echo "$TARGET" | gau blacklist png,jpg,gif,css | grep "\.js$" | sort u js urls.txt echo "$TARGET" | waybackurls | grep "\.js$" | sort u js urls.txt echo "$TARGET URL" | hakrawler js depth 3 | sort u js urls.txt curl s "$TARGET URL" | grep oE 'src="[^"]+\.js[^"] "' | cut d'"' f2 js urls.txt sort u js urls.txt o js urls.txt echo "[ ] Found $(wc l < js urls.txt) unique JS URLs" mkdir p js files/ wget i js urls.txt P js files/ q 2 /dev/null LinkFinder Extract Endpoints Install: pip3 install linkfinder Usage: Single file python3 linkfinder.py i js files/main.js o cli URL directly python3 linkfinder.py i https://target.com/static/js/main.chunk.js o cli Entire directory python3 linkfinder.py i js files/ o cli | sort u endpoints.txt Crawl page + all linked JS python3 linkfinder.py i https://target.com d o cli HTML report python3 linkfinder.py i js files/ o results.html Filter high value paths cat endpoints.txt | grep E "^/api|/admin|/internal|/debug|/v[0 9]" Example output from a React bundle: /api/v1/users /api/v1/admin/impersonate (not in the UI) /api/v1/admin/delete user /api/v2/internal/debug https://staging api.target.com/v1/ /graphql /api/v1/export?format=csv&all=true Every /admin and /internal path is a testing target. Every staging URL is a less hardened copy of production. SecretFinder Extract Hardcoded Secrets Install: git clone https://github.com/m4ll0k/SecretFinder cd SecretFinder && pip3 install r requirements.txt Usage: Single URL python3 SecretFinder.py i https://target.com/static/js/main.chunk.js o cli All JS files for f in js files/ .js; do echo "=== $f ===" python3 SecretFinder.py i "$f" o cli 2 /dev/null done | tee secrets found.txt Page + all linked JS python3 SecretFinder.py i https://target.com o cli p HTML report python3 SecretFinder.py i js files/ o report.html Detected patterns include: Google API Keys (AIzaSy...), AWS Access Keys (AKIA...), Stripe secrets (sk live ...), GitHub tokens (ghp ...), JWTs, private keys, Firebase URLs, S3 bucket URLs, Basic Auth URLs, Sentry DSNs. NOTE: SecretFinder produces false positives. Manually verify each finding before reporting. Confirm keys are active with a read only API call where possible. Never test a payment key against live transactions. Manual Grep Patterns These catch secrets that SecretFinder misses: cd js files/ Generic API keys and tokens grep rE "(api[ ]?key|apikey|api[ ]?token)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{8,}" . include=" .js" grep rE "(secret|private[ ]?key|client[ ]?secret)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{8,}" . include=" .js" grep rE "(password|passwd|pwd)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{4,}" . include=" .js" grep rE "(access[ ]?token|auth[ ]?token|bearer)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{8,}" . include=" .js" AWS credentials grep rE "AKIA[0 9A Z]{16}" . include=" .js" Firebase grep rE "apiKey\s :\s ['\"]AIza[^'\"]{35}" . include=" .js" grep rE "firebaseio\.com" . include=" .js" Internal/staging URLs grep rE "https?://(staging|stage|dev|test|uat|qa|internal|corp|admin)\." . include=" .js" grep rE "localhost|127\.0\.0\.1|192\.168\.|10\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+" . include=" .js" S3 buckets grep rE "s3\.amazonaws\.com/[a z0 9\ ]+" . include=" .js" grep rE "['\"][a z0 9\ ]+\.s3\.amazonaws\.com['\"]" . include=" .js" OAuth client IDs (reveals identity provider) grep rE "(client[ ]?id|client[ ]?secret|oauth)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{8,}" . include=" .js" Sentry DSN (reveals org/project structure) grep rE "https://[a f0 9]{32}@[a z0 9]+\.ingest\.sentry\.io" . include=" .js" JWT secrets left in config grep rE "(jwt[ ]?secret|signing[ ]?key)\s [:=]\s ['\"][^'\"]{4,}" . include=" .js" Handling Minified and Bundled JS Modern apps (React, Vue, Angular, Next.js) compile all JS into minified bundles. These look like unreadable one liners but contain all original strings. Beautify before manual analysis: Install: npm install g js beautify js beautify js files/main.chunk.js js files/main pretty.js Grep the readable version grep n "apiKey\|secret\|password\|internal" js files/main pretty.js Alternative: prettier npx prettier parser babel js files/main.chunk.js js files/main pretty.js Source Maps The Highest Yield Finding Source maps (.js.map files) are generated during compilation and contain the original un minified source code. Developers regularly forget to exclude them from production builds. When exposed they hand you the complete original frontend source. Check every discovered JS file for a corresponding .map file: while IFS= read r url; do map url="${url}.map" status=$(curl s o /dev/null w "%{http code}" "$map url") if [ "$status" = "200" ]; then echo "[!] SOURCE MAP EXPOSED: $map url" curl s "$map url" o "js files/$(basename $url).map" fi done < js urls.txt Extract the original source files from a .map: python3 << 'EOF' import json, os with open("js files/main.chunk.js.map") as f: sm = json.load(f) sources = sm.get("sources", []) contents = sm.get("sourcesContent", [None] len(sources)) for source, content in zip(sources, contents): if not content: continue clean = source.replace("webpack://", "").replace("../", "").lstrip("/") path = os.path.join("sourcemap output/", clean) os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist ok=True) with open(path, "w") as out: out.write(content) print(f"Extracted: {path}") EOF Grep the reconstructed source tree grep rE "apiKey|password|secret|token|internal" sourcemap output/ grep rE "AKIA[0 9A Z]{16}" sourcemap output/ NOTE: A source map is full source code disclosure. In a report, treat it as a Critical information disclosure finding if the app contains business logic, algorithms, or credentials in the frontend code. truffleHog Git History Scanning If the target has public GitHub repositories, truffleHog scans the entire commit history for secrets including those added and then deleted (still in git history). Install: curl sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog/main/scripts/install.sh \ | sh s b /usr/local/bin Usage: Scan a public GitHub repo trufflehog github repo https://github.com/target org/target app Verified secrets only (fewer false positives) trufflehog github repo https://github.com/target org/target app only verified Scan an entire organisation trufflehog github org target org only verified Scan a local clone git clone https://github.com/target org/target app /tmp/target app trufflehog git file:///tmp/target app only verified JSON output trufflehog github repo https://github.com/target org/target app json | jq . Finds in git history: AWS keys committed then deleted, database passwords in connection strings, SSH private keys accidentally committed, .env files committed and removed, Stripe/Twilio/SendGrid keys rotated after accidental exposure. gitleaks Alternative Git Scanner Install: sudo apt install gitleaks Usage: Scan a repository gitleaks detect source /tmp/target app JSON report gitleaks detect source /tmp/target app report format json report path leaks.json Recent commits only gitleaks detect source /tmp/target app log opts " since='30 days ago'" Nuclei Automated JS Secret Scanning Update templates first nuclei update templates Run against all discovered JS URLs nuclei list js urls.txt \ t exposures/tokens/ \ t exposures/apis/ \ severity medium,high,critical Run against the whole target nuclei u https://target.com \ t exposures/tokens/ \ t exposures/apis/ \ t misconfiguration/ Complete JS Recon Workflow TARGET="target.com" TARGET URL="https://$TARGET" 1 Discover JS URLs echo "$TARGET" | gau blacklist png,jpg,gif,css | grep "\.js$" js urls.txt echo "$TARGET" | waybackurls | grep "\.js$" js urls.txt echo "$TARGET URL" | hakrawler js depth 3 js urls.txt sort u js urls.txt o js urls.txt 2 Download mkdir p js files/ wget i js urls.txt P js files/ q 2 /dev/null 3 Extract endpoints python3 linkfinder.py i js files/ o cli 2 /dev/null | sort u endpoints.txt grep E "^/api|/admin|/internal|/debug" endpoints.txt interesting endpoints.txt 4 Hunt secrets for f in js files/ .js; do python3 SecretFinder.py i "$f" o cli 2 /dev/null done | sort u secrets found.txt 5 Manual high value grep grep rE "AKIA[0 9A Z]{16}" js files/ aws keys.txt grep rE "https?://(staging|dev|internal)\." js files/ internal urls.txt grep rE "\.s3\.amazonaws\.com" js files/ s3 buckets.txt 6 Check for source maps while IFS= read r url; do status=$(curl s o /dev/null w "%{http code}" "${url}.map") [ "$status" = "200" ] && echo "[!] SOURCE MAP EXPOSED: ${url}.map" done < js urls.txt 7 Summary echo "JS files: $(ls js files/ .js 2 /dev/null | wc l)" echo "Total endpoints: $(wc l < endpoints.txt)" echo "Interesting endpoints: $(wc l < interesting endpoints.txt)" echo "Potential secrets: $(wc l < secrets found.txt)" echo "AWS keys: $(wc l < aws keys.txt)" echo "Internal URLs: $(wc l < internal urls.txt)" Building the Technology Profile Updated Section Add JS findings to the target profile from 01.4: JS ANALYSIS FINDINGS Endpoints discovered: 47 (12 interesting /api/admin/ , /api/internal/ ) Secrets found: 2 (Google Maps API key, Sentry DSN) Internal URLs: staging api.target.com (confirmed live) S3 buckets: target user uploads.s3.amazonaws.com Source maps: /static/js/main.chunk.js.map EXPOSED (original source recovered) NEXT STEPS FROM JS ANALYSIS 1. Test /api/admin/ endpoints with regular user token (BFLA) 2. Verify Google Maps key scope is it restricted to domain? 3. Test staging api.target.com likely less hardened 4. Check S3 bucket: aws s3 ls s3://target user uploads no sign request 5. Grep recovered source for additional secrets and business logic Quick Reference Find all JS URLs echo "target.com" | gau blacklist png,jpg,gif,css | grep "\.js$" echo "target.com" | waybackurls | grep "\.js$" Extract endpoints python3 linkfinder.py i js files/ o cli | sort u Extract secrets python3 SecretFinder.py i https://target.com/app.js o cli Check for source map curl I https://target.com/static/js/main.chunk.js.map AWS key grep grep rE "AKIA[0 9A Z]{16}" js files/ Internal URL grep grep rE "https?://(staging|dev|internal)\." js files/ Beautify minified JS js beautify minified.js readable.js Git history scan trufflehog github repo https://github.com/org/repo only verified gitleaks detect source /tmp/cloned repo Tool reference: LinkFinder pip3 install linkfinder Extract API endpoints from JS SecretFinder git clone m4ll0k/SecretFinder Extract hardcoded secrets gau go install github.com/lc/gau/v2/cmd/gau@latest Discover all JS file URLs waybackurls go install tomnomnom/waybackurls@latest Archived JS URLs hakrawler go install hakluke/hakrawler@latest Live site JS crawler truffleHog curl install script Git history secret scanning gitleaks sudo apt install gitleaks Git history alternative js beautify npm install g js beautify Minified JS to readable nuclei sudo apt install nuclei Automated secret detection Related Notes 01.1 Passive Recon & OSINT 01.2 Active Recon & Nmap 01.3 Subdomain Enumeration 01.4 Technology Fingerprinting 02.1 OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite 02.4 Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic 02.5 Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting/02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite.md
title: 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite Fundamentals
body: 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite Fundamentals The OWASP Top 10 (2021) OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project) publishes a list of the most critical web application security risks. Every web app pentest is structured around these categories. Know them cold. | Rank | Category | What It Means | | | | | | A01 | Broken Access Control | Users can access resources they shouldn't | | A02 | Cryptographic Failures | Sensitive data exposed due to weak/missing encryption | | A03 | Injection | Untrusted data sent to an interpreter (SQLi, XSS, CMDi) | | A04 | Insecure Design | Fundamental design flaws — not coding bugs | | A05 | Security Misconfiguration | Default creds, open cloud storage, verbose errors | | A06 | Vulnerable Components | Outdated libraries/frameworks with known CVEs | | A07 | Auth & Session Failures | Broken login, session fixation, weak passwords | | A08 | Software & Data Integrity | Insecure CI/CD, unsigned updates, insecure deserialisation | | A09 | Security Logging Failures | No logging, no monitoring, no alerting | | A10 | SSRF | Server makes requests to internal resources on attacker's behalf | Each of these is covered in depth in the notes that follow. This note focuses on the tool you will use to test all of them: Burp Suite . Burp Suite — The Core Tool of Web Pentesting Burp Suite is an intercepting proxy and web application security testing platform. Almost every web testing task flows through Burp. Community Edition (free) is on Kali. Professional (paid, $400/year) adds the active scanner. Use Community for learning — it has everything you need. Burp Suite Architecture Step 1 — Initial Setup Configure the Proxy Listener Proxy → Options → Proxy Listeners Default: — leave as is. Configure Your Browser Option A: Burp's Built in Browser (Easiest) Proxy → Intercept → Open Browser This launches a Chromium instance pre configured to route through Burp with the CA cert already trusted. Use this for quick testing. Option B: Configure Firefox Manually 1. Firefox → Settings → Network Settings → Manual proxy configuration 2. HTTP Proxy: , Port: 3. Check "Also use this proxy for HTTPS" Install Burp's CA Certificate (for HTTPS) Without this, Burp cannot intercept HTTPS traffic — you'll see certificate errors. 1. With proxy configured in browser, navigate to: 2. Click "CA Certificate" → download 3. Firefox → Settings → Privacy → Certificates → Import 4. Import , check "Trust this CA to identify websites" Now Burp can intercept and modify HTTPS traffic. The Proxy Tab The proxy is where all traffic flows. You can: Intercept requests (pause them mid flight and modify before forwarding) Forward them as is Drop them entirely Intercept Mode Every request from your browser now pauses in Burp. You see the raw HTTP request, modify it, then Forward. [!tip] Intercept is disruptive during normal browsing. Turn it OFF during initial exploration and use HTTP History instead. Turn it ON when you want to capture and modify a specific request. HTTP History Proxy → HTTP History Every request your browser made is logged here, even when intercept is off. This is how you: Find interesting endpoints See how authentication works Identify parameters to test Right click any request → Send to Repeater (most common action) Repeater — Your Primary Testing Tool Repeater lets you manually send HTTP requests and view responses, modifying them as many times as you like. Workflow 1. In HTTP History, right click a request → Send to Repeater 2. Go to the Repeater tab 3. Modify the request (change parameter values, add headers, etc.) 4. Click Send 5. Analyse the response on the right 6. Modify and repeat What to Look For in Responses Status codes : 200 (OK), 302 (redirect), 401 (unauth), 403 (forbidden), 500 (server error) Response body : Does it reflect your input? Does it contain error messages? Is the content different from what you expected? Response length : A different length often indicates different application behaviour Response time : Significant delays can indicate blind SQLi or SSRF Keyboard Shortcuts (Repeater) | Key | Action | | | | | Ctrl+R | Send request | | Ctrl+Z | Undo in editor | | Ctrl+Shift+R | Re issue last request | | Ctrl+U | URL encode selection | | Ctrl+Shift+U | URL decode selection | Intruder — Automated Fuzzing Intruder automates sending many variations of a request — useful for: Brute forcing login forms Fuzzing parameters for injection Testing all values in a list [!warning] Community Edition rate limits Intruder to 1 request/second. body: 02.2 — Injection Attacks (SQLi, XSS, CMDi, XXE, SSTI, SSRF) What Injection Is Injection flaws occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query . The interpreter can't distinguish between the attacker's data and the intended command, so it executes both. OWASP A03:2021 — Injection covers SQLi, XSS, command injection, and others. The root cause is always the same: unsanitised user input is concatenated into a command string . SQL Injection (SQLi) What It Is SQL injection occurs when user supplied data is inserted directly into an SQL query without sanitisation. The attacker manipulates the query logic to: Bypass authentication Extract database contents Modify or delete data In some cases, execute OS commands How It Works Vulnerable PHP code: Normal request: Injected request: Step 1 — Detecting SQLi Test every input field and URL parameter with these payloads. You're looking for error messages, unexpected behaviour, or different response lengths. Signs of SQLi: Database error messages ( ) Application error / 500 response Different response length or content when injecting vs not No error but behaviour changes ( shows all records) Step 2 — Manual SQLi Exploitation (UNION Based) UNION based SQLi lets you append a second SELECT query and retrieve data from other tables. Phase 1 — Find the number of columns: Phase 2 — Find which columns display text: Phase 3 — Extract data: Step 3 — Blind SQLi When the application doesn't return data in the response — no error messages, no output — but its behaviour changes based on the query. Boolean Based Blind: Time Based Blind (when there's no visible difference at all): If the response is delayed by 5 seconds → SQLi confirmed. Extract data using conditional sleeps: SQLi by Database Type | Database | Version Query | Comment Syntax | | | | | | MySQL | | , , | | MSSQL | | , | | PostgreSQL | | , | | Oracle | | , | | SQLite | | | sqlmap — Automated SQLi sqlmap automates detection and exploitation of SQL injection vulnerabilities. Saving a request from Burp for sqlmap: 1. Right click the request in Repeater → Save item → 2. [!tip] Always try manual detection first. sqlmap is noisy and may trigger WAFs. Confirm the parameter is injectable manually, then use sqlmap for extraction. Cross Site Scripting (XSS) What It Is XSS occurs when an application includes unsanitised user supplied data in its HTML output, allowing an attacker to inject JavaScript that runs in another user's browser. Impact: session hijacking, credential theft, keylogging, defacement, redirecting users to malicious sites. Three Types of XSS Reflected XSS The malicious script is in the URL Server reflects it back in the response immediately Not stored — victim must click a crafted link Example: Stored XSS The malicious script is saved in the database (comment, profile field, message) Every user who views that content executes the script More dangerous — no user interaction needed beyond visiting the page DOM based XSS The vulnerability exists in client side JavaScript, not the server The server's response is fine — the browser's own JS reads attacker controlled input (URL hash, query string) and writes it to the DOM unsafely Example: Step 1 — Detecting XSS Test every input with a basic payload: If you see an alert box → reflected XSS confirmed. If the application sanitises , try: Check where your input appears in the response source (Ctrl+U in browser → view source): In an HTML tag attribute? → Inside a JavaScript string? → In a URL parameter? → Step 2 — Context Specific Payloads In an attribute value: Inside JavaScript string: In a URL context: Step 3 — Escalate from alert(1) to Cookie Theft just proves execution. The real payload steals the victim's session cookie: Or using : Set up a listener on your attacker machine: [!warning] Cookie theft only works if the cookie does NOT have the flag set. Check the Set Cookie header. If is present, you can still do other damage (keylogging, form hijacking, SameSite bypass) but can't directly read cookies via JS. XSS Filter Bypass Techniques When basic payloads are blocked: PayloadsAllTheThings XSS list: https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/tree/master/XSS%20Injection Command Injection What It Is Command injection occurs when user input is passed to a system shell command. The attacker injects shell metacharacters to execute additional OS commands. Vulnerable PHP: Normal: → Injected: → → runs command Detection Payloads Exploitation — Getting a Reverse Shell Once command execution is confirmed, upgrade to a reverse shell: Step 1: Set up listener on your machine Step 2: Inject reverse shell payload [!tip] Use revshells.com to generate reverse shell one liners for any language. Always URL encode the payload when injecting via URL parameters. Blind Command Injection (No Output Visible) When the app doesn't return command output, exfiltrate via DNS or HTTP: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection What It Is XXE occurs when an XML parser processes external entity definitions in user supplied XML. An attacker defines an external entity that reads local files or makes network requests, and the parser helpfully returns the contents. Basic XXE — Read Local File If you find an endpoint accepting XML: If the app returns contents → XXE confirmed. Other useful files to read: SSRF via XXE Use XXE to make the server request internal URLs: is the AWS metadata service — accessible from EC2 instances but not from the internet. XXE → SSRF → read cloud credentials. Blind XXE (No Output in Response) Set up and watch for an incoming request — confirms blind XXE. How to Find XXE Attack Surface Forms/APIs that accept XML input (Content Type: application/xml, text/xml) File upload endpoints accepting , , , (these are XML internally) SOAP web services RSS/Atom feed parsers Server Side Template Injection (SSTI) What It Is SSTI occurs when user input is embedded in a server side template and the template engine evaluates it as code. Affected engines: Jinja2 (Python/Flask), Twig (PHP), Freemarker (Java), Mako, Smarty, Pebble, Velocity. Detection Test with mathematical expressions that templates evaluate: If the response contains instead of → SSTI confirmed. Identifying the Template Engine Use this decision tree: https://portswigger.net/research/server side template injection (PortSwigger's SSTI diagram) Exploitation — RCE via Jinja2 (Python/Flask) Exploitation — Twig (PHP) Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) What It Is SSRF occurs when a server makes HTTP requests to a URL specified by the user. The attacker uses this to: Access internal services (databases, admin panels) not accessible from the internet Scan the internal network Read cloud metadata (AWS IMDSv1, GCP, Azure) Bypass IP allowlists Detection Look for parameters containing URLs: Test by pointing the URL at a server you control: Exploiting SSRF — Internal Service Discovery SSRF Filter Bypass Techniques When the app blocks direct IPs: Quick Reference | Attack | Root Cause | Key Test | | | | | | SQLi | Input in SQL query | → error / → bypass | | XSS | Input in HTML output | | | CMDi | Input in OS command | | | XXE | Input parsed as XML with external entity | | | SSTI | Input evaluated by template engine | → 49 | | SSRF | User controls URL of server side request | | Related Notes 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks 02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic 02.5 — Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation

body: 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks Why Authentication Fails OWASP A07:2021. Authentication breaks because of: weak or default passwords, no brute force protection, flawed session management, broken password reset flows, insecure token implementation, and bypassable MFA.
