title: 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking
body: 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking Why Password Attacks Matter Credentials are the skeleton key of a network. A cracked password or stolen hash often achieves in minutes what weeks of exploitation cannot. Password attacks fall into three categories: 1. Online attacks — directly guessing against a live service (SSH, RDP, web login) 2. Offline attacks — cracking captured hashes without touching the target 3. Hash relay attacks — using hashes without cracking them (pass the hash, NTLM relay) Hash Fundamentals A hash is a one way function output. You cannot reverse it directly — you crack it by hashing candidate passwords and comparing. Common Hash Types | Hash Type | Length | Example / Context | | | | | | MD5 | 32 hex chars | Old web apps, not used for passwords now | | SHA 1 | 40 hex chars | Legacy, deprecated | | SHA 256 | 64 hex chars | Modern | | bcrypt | 60 chars ($2a/2b$) | PHP/Unix password storage | | NTLM | 32 hex chars | Windows local accounts | | NTLMv1 | Challenge response | Windows network auth (old) | | NTLMv2 | Challenge response | Windows network auth (modern) | | Net NTLMv2 | Challenge response | Captured by Responder — this is crackable | | Kerberos 5 TGS ($krb5tgs$) | Long | Kerberoasting output | | Kerberos 5 AS REP ($krb5asrep$) | Long | AS REP roasting output | Identifying Hash Types Hashcat — GPU Accelerated Hash Cracking Hashcat is the fastest password cracker available. It uses GPU acceleration to test billions of candidates per second. Attack Modes ( a) | Mode | Name | Description | | | | | | 0 | Dictionary | Try every word in a wordlist | | 1 | Combinator | Combine words from two wordlists | | 3 | Mask | Brute force with a pattern (e.g., ?u?l?l?l?d?d) | | 6 | Hybrid dict+mask | Wordlist words + mask suffix | | 7 | Hybrid mask+dict | Mask prefix + wordlist words | Hash Modes ( m) — Most Common | Mode | Hash Type | | | | | 0 | MD5 | | 100 | SHA 1 | | 1400 | SHA 256 | | 1800 | SHA 512 (Unix $6$) | | 3200 | bcrypt | | 1000 | NTLM | | 5600 | NTLMv2 (Net NTLMv2 — from Responder) | | 13100 | Kerberos TGS (Kerberoasting) | | 18200 | Kerberos AS REP (AS REP roasting) | | 22000 | WPA2 (Wi Fi) | | 500 | MD5 Crypt (Unix $1$) | | 1500 | DES Crypt (Unix) | Dictionary Attack (Mode 0) Rules Based Attack Rules mutate wordlist entries — add numbers, capitalise, leetspeak, append symbols. This dramatically increases coverage beyond the raw wordlist. Mask Attack (Brute Force with Pattern) When you know the password policy (e.g., must contain uppercase, lowercase, digit): Combinator Attack Performance Options John the Ripper — CPU Hash Cracker John is slower than hashcat for GPU cracking but has useful auto detection and format support. John's Conversion Utilities John comes with tools to convert system files into crackable format: Wordlist Strategy The wordlist determines your crack rate. Use the right one for the context. Recommended Progression CeWL — Custom Wordlist Generator Kwprocessor / Keyboard Walk Wordlists Keyboard walks (qwerty, 1q2w3e) are common passwords: Online Brute Force — Hydra Covered in 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks in detail. Quick reference here: [!warning] Online brute force causes failed login logs and may trigger account lockouts. Use (4 threads) maximum on real engagements. Coordinate timing with the client. Lockouts on AD accounts lock out the actual user. Medusa Alternative to Hydra — faster for some protocols. Extracting Hashes from Windows From a Live System (requires admin/SYSTEM) From Offline Files (SAM + SYSTEM) If you have physical access or extracted these files: NTDS.dit — Domain Controller Hash Dump Rainbow Tables Pre computed hash→password lookups. Instant cracking if the hash is in the table and the password wasn't salted. Modern systems salt passwords before hashing, making rainbow tables useless for cracking. Still effective against: Unsalted MD5/SHA 1 hashes Old web applications NTLM (not salted) Pass the Hash (PTH) You don't always need to crack the hash. In Windows environments, NTLM authentication accepts the hash directly. No cracking required. Quick Reference | Mode | Hash | Context | | | | | | 1000 | NTLM | Windows local accounts | | 5600 | NTLMv2 | Responder captures | | 13100 | Kerberos TGS | Kerberoasting | | 18200 | Kerberos AS REP | AS REP roasting | | 3200 | bcrypt | Modern Unix/web passwords | | 1800 | SHA 512 | Linux /etc/shadow | Related Notes 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks 03.2 — Metasploit Framework 03.4 — Traffic Analysis MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting Hydra — Complete Reference Hydra ( / for GUI) is a parallelised network logon cracker. It works by spinning up many concurrent connections and submitting credential pairs against authentication endpoints — SSH, FTP, HTTP, SMB, RDP, MySQL, MSSQL, SMTP, IMAP, VNC, SNMP, and more. It is the standard tool for online password attacks because it supports virtually every common protocol and gives precise control over thread count, timing, and failure string matching. Core Syntax Every Important Flag Explained | Flag | Meaning | | | | | | Single username | | | List of usernames (one per line) | | | Single password | | | Wordlist of passwords | | | colon separated combo file (use instead of ) | | | Parallel tasks per target. Default 16. Use 4 for SSH/RDP to avoid lockouts and connection refusals. | | | Total parallel tasks across all targets (when using ) | | | Multiple targets — file with one host per line | | | Use a non default port (e.g. SSH on 2222) | | | Use SSL — wraps the protocol in TLS (e.g. HTTPS instead of HTTP) | | | Try =null password, =password equals username, =reversed username | | | Write valid logins to file | | | Output format: , , | | | Stop after first valid pair found (use for single user) | | | Stop after first valid pair found across all targets | | | Verbose — print every login attempt (useful for debugging form params) | | | Debug mode — even noisier than | | | Ignore previous restore file (start fresh; default is to resume from ) | | | Restore aborted session from | | | Wait time per response (default 32s) — increase on slow links | | | Wait time between connect attempts in a thread | | | Wait time between full credential pairs (slow down throttle) | | | Brute force generator instead of . e.g. = 4 6 chars, lower+digits | | | Loop users first then passwords (default loops passwords first) — useful when you have one good password and many users | Service Examples SSH is mandatory for SSH — most OpenSSH defaults reject more than 4–6 concurrent connections ( rejects probabilistically above 10). FTP HTTP POST Form (most important for web pentest) Breakdown of the third argument : = the URL path the form posts to ( ) = the POST body. and are placeholders Hydra substitutes per attempt. Other parameters (CSRF tokens, hidden fields) go here verbatim or as if dynamically grabbed. = how Hydra knows the attempt failed: — failure string. If response body contains this string → login failed. — success string. If response contains this → login succeeded (use for apps that don't show clear failure messages, e.g. response body changes after login). — match against response header (e.g. ). Tips: Use Burp to capture a real failed login first — copy the exact body and the exact failure phrase. URL encode special characters: becomes , becomes , etc. For CSRF protected forms, use with and a captured static token, or use / which handle dynamic tokens better. HTTPS POST Form HTTP Basic Auth SMB RDP for RDP — Windows TS rate limits new sessions and you'll get past about 4 concurrent attempts. Lockout policies trigger fast on RDP (often 5 fails = 30 min lockout). SMTP MySQL / PostgreSQL / MSSQL Custom Port Wordlists for Online Attacks Online attacks should use smaller, high probability wordlists — you cannot afford to test millions of candidates against a network service. [!warning] Operational Caution Online password attacks generate logs (Windows Event 4625, entries), trigger SIEM rules, can lock out real users, and may be detected by IPS/EDR with response actions. On real engagements: written approval, low thread counts, time of day windows, and notify the SOC contact. SSH Authentication & Brute Force Deep Dive SSH Authentication Methods SSH supports several authentication mechanisms negotiated during the phase of the protocol: 1. Password — client sends username + password. The password traverses the encrypted channel but is checked server side against (or PAM). Vulnerable to brute force unless rate limited. 2. Public key — client proves possession of a private key whose public key is in on the server. Mechanism: server sends a random challenge → client signs with its private key → server verifies with the public key. The private key never leaves the client. Brute forcing a strong key is computationally infeasible (RSA 2048+ or ED25519). 3. Certificate — like public key but the public key is signed by a trusted CA. Centralised, supports expiry. Used in larger orgs to avoid distributing to every host. 4. Keyboard interactive (PAM) — server driven prompts; can layer 2FA, OTP, etc. 5. GSSAPI / Kerberos — single sign on in AD/Linux mixed environments. Why Public Key Auth Is Stronger A passphrase protected private key requires: (a) the file itself (something you have), and (b) the passphrase (something you know). An attacker over the network has no path to brute force the key — there's no oracle to test guesses against. They must first compromise the client to steal the key file, then brute force the passphrase offline ( ). That two stage barrier is what makes key auth effectively immune to remote brute force. Brute Forcing SSH Thread count for SSH must stay low ( ). OpenSSH's means after 10 unauthenticated parallel sessions, new connections drop probabilistically; past 100, all are dropped. fail2ban (default jail on most distros) bans an IP after 5 failed attempts for 10 minutes. ssh audit — SSH Server Configuration Auditing What it checks: Protocol version — flags SSH 1 (must never be enabled) Key exchange algorithms (KEX) — flags (weak), (deprecated). Modern: , . Host key types — flags DSA (always weak), short RSA. Modern: , with ≥3072 bit key. Ciphers — flags , , any . Modern: , . MACs — flags , , any . Modern: . Compression — flags older (CRIME class concerns). A good output shows everything in green. Anything yellow/red goes in the report with a recommended hardening ( , , , ). SSH User Enumeration — CVE 2018 15473 Affects OpenSSH ≤ 7.7. Mechanism: the server validates the username before checking the auth packet, but only on malformed packets does it reveal whether the user exists. By sending a malformed , the server either disconnects (user does not exist) or hangs/responds (user exists). Weak SSH Key Detection | Key Type | Verdict | | | | | DSA ( ) | Always weak — fixed at 1024 bit, removed in OpenSSH 7.0 | | RSA < 2048 bit | Weak — factorable with cloud GPU clusters | | RSA 2048 bit | Acceptable; phasing out | | RSA 3072 / 4096 bit | Strong | | ECDSA P 256/P 384 | Strong, but uses NIST curves (some prefer Ed25519) | | Ed25519 | Preferred — small, fast, modern | Debian OpenSSL CVE 2008 0166 produced 32k predictable RSA keys — there are still systems in the wild with these. Tools: package, online lookup via against known bad fingerprint lists. known hosts Abuse — Pivot Discovery When you compromise a Linux host, and reveal hosts the user has SSH'd into. By default modern OpenSSH hashes hostnames ( ) — but lots of older installs and copy pasted configs disable this. Combined with ( ) and , you usually get a complete map of where the user goes. SSH Agent Forwarding Hijack (or ) forwards the client's SSH agent socket to the remote host, so the user can hop further without re typing keys. Risk: if the remote host is compromised, root on that host can read the agent socket and use it as the user. Mitigation: never use with untrusted hosts; prefer ( ) which doesn't expose the agent. authorized keys Persistence The simplest, most durable Linux persistence: append your public key. Survives password changes, survives reboots, survives most user initiated cleanups. Detection requires file integrity monitoring (auditd watch on ) or EDR telemetry on file writes to ssh paths. For root persistence: write to . For multiple users: a loop over . SSH Brute Force / Compromise Detection | Source | Indicator | | | | | (Debian/Ubuntu) | repeating, then a single | | (RHEL/CentOS) | Same, different file | | | Systemd managed log | | | Bad logins (from ) | | | Successful logins (from ) | | Windows OpenSSH | EventID 4625 (failed) / 4624 (success) — same as native Windows logon | | fail2ban log | lines in | | auditd | to alert on tampering | | Anomaly: keys that don't belong | Audit against a known good baseline | Defensive controls worth deploying or recommending in reports: fail2ban (or sshguard), enforcing keys only, (or ), allow list, MFA via PAM (Google Authenticator / Duo), TCP wrappers or firewall source restrictions, port knocking for management interfaces. Hash Cracking — Theory & Tooling Deep Dive Identifying Hash Types Recognising the format saves you from trying the wrong mode and getting . | Hash | Length | Visual Marker | Hashcat | | | | | | | MD5 | 32 hex | bare hex string | 0 | | SHA 1 | 40 hex | bare hex string | 100 | | SHA 256 | 64 hex | bare hex string | 1400 | | SHA 512 | 128 hex | bare hex string | 1700 | | NTLM | 32 hex | looks like MD5; context = Windows | 1000 | | LM | 32 hex | two halves, often for empty | 3000 | | NTLMv2 (Net NTLMv2) | long, 4 colon separated fields | | 5600 | | MD5 Crypt (Unix) | starts | | 500 | | SHA 256 Crypt | starts | | 7400 | | SHA 512 Crypt | starts | | 1800 | | bcrypt | starts , , | | 3200 | | Argon2id | starts | | 13200 (i)/13201 (id) | | Kerberos TGS (Kerberoast) | starts | huge blob | 13100 | | Kerberos AS REP | starts | huge blob | 18200 | | WPA2 PMKID | starts | from | 22000 | | MySQL5 | 40 hex with prefix | | 300 | John the Ripper — Format Coverage John auto detects the format via signatures ( , , etc.) for crypt style hashes. For raw hashes (MD5/SHA/NTLM) you must specify . Hashcat — Modes & Attacks Reference Already covered above; this is the deeper dive reference. Attack Modes | | Name | Use Case | | | | | | 0 | Straight (dict) | Standard wordlist attack | | 1 | Combination | — concatenate every pair | | 3 | Brute force / Mask | Pattern based ( ) | | 6 | Hybrid Wordlist + Mask | — append digits to every word | | 7 | Hybrid Mask + Wordlist | — prepend digits | | 9 | Association | One hash, one wordlist line — for known context cracks (e.g. password = username variant) | Mask Charsets | Token | Charset | | | | | | a z | | | A Z | | | 0 9 | | | special (space + ASCII printable specials) | | | ?l?u?d?s | | | 0x00–0xff (raw byte) | | | 0 9 a f | | | 0 9 A F | | , , , | Custom user defined charsets | Hash Modes — Pentest Cheat Sheet | Mode | Hash | Where you get it | | | | | | 0 | MD5 | CTFs, legacy web apps | | 100 | SHA 1 | Same | | 1400 | SHA 256 | Modern apps, JWTs | | 1700 | SHA 512 | Same | | 1000 | NTLM | , SAM dump, | | 3000 | LM | Pre Vista boxes; shows pair | | 5500 | NetNTLMv1 | Responder (rare nowadays) | | 5600 | NetNTLMv2 | Responder default capture | | 1800 | sha512crypt | Linux | | 500 | md5crypt | Older Linux/Unix shadow | | 3200 | bcrypt | PHP/Ruby/Django; very slow per hash by design | | 13200 / 13201 | Argon2 | Modern apps | | 13100 | Kerberos 5 TGS REP | Kerberoasting | | 18200 | Kerberos 5 AS REP | AS REP roasting | | 22000 | WPA2 PMKID/EAPOL | Wi Fi handshake | | 16500 | JWT | HS256 secret cracking | | 7500 | Kerberos 5 AS REQ etype 23 | Network capture pre auth | | 9600 | Office 2013 docx | Doc password | | 13400 | KeePass | KeePass DB cracking | | 14600 | LUKS | Linux full disk encryption | | 11600 | 7 Zip | 7z archive password | Rules — What They Actually Do A rule file is a list of mutation primitives. Hashcat applies each rule line to every word in the wordlist, multiplying coverage. Combined: applied to → . Rainbow Tables — When They Still Matter A rainbow table is a precomputed time/memory tradeoff structure mapping hash → plaintext for a fixed charset and length. Salting completely defeats them — every salt requires a new table. They remain effective against: Unsalted MD5/SHA 1 in legacy databases NTLM (Windows does not salt NTLM hashes — every user with password has the same NTLM hash) — that's why public NTLM rainbow tables work and crackstation.net is so effective for AD environments Hash collisions in (which has its own special weaknesses on top of being unsalted)

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting/03.4 — Traffic Analysis & MITM.md
title: 03.4 — Traffic Analysis & Man-in-the-Middle
body: 03.4 — Traffic Analysis & Man in the Middle Why Traffic Analysis Matters Network traffic is full of credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data — especially on internal networks where people assume safety. As a pentester, you intercept and analyse traffic to: Capture plaintext credentials from unencrypted protocols (FTP, HTTP, Telnet, SMTP) Steal session cookies from unencrypted HTTP Identify what services are being used and by whom Analyse attack patterns and understand what's happening after exploitation Man in the Middle (MITM) Attacks A MITM attack positions your machine between two communicating hosts. All traffic flows through you — you can read, modify, or inject it. How to Position Yourself: ARP Spoofing ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a LAN. It has no authentication — any machine can send a fake ARP reply claiming any IP. [!warning] ARP spoofing floods the network with ARP replies and is detectable by network monitoring tools (Wireshark, XDR, IDS). It also breaks connectivity for victims if your machine doesn't forward traffic properly. Always enable IP forwarding before running MITM attacks. Enable IP Forwarding Without this, you drop all the traffic you intercept and the victims lose connectivity (detectable and disruptive): arpspoof (dsniff suite) Classic, simple ARP spoofing tool. Bettercap — Modern MITM Framework Bettercap is the most capable modern MITM tool. It handles ARP spoofing, DNS spoofing, HTTPS downgrade, credential sniffing, and more. Ettercap — Legacy MITM Tool Ettercap is older but still functional, with a GUI option. Wireshark — Packet Analyser Wireshark is the primary tool for deep packet analysis. It captures all traffic on an interface and lets you filter, dissect, and follow protocol streams. Essential Filters Follow Streams Right click any packet → Follow → TCP Stream (or HTTP Stream, TLS Stream) This reassembles the full conversation — you see the complete HTTP request and response, FTP session, Telnet commands, etc. Finding Credentials in Wireshark Export Objects Wireshark can extract files transferred over HTTP: This saves all files downloaded by victims during your capture — images, executables, documents. tcpdump — CLI Packet Capture tcpdump is the command line equivalent. Useful on headless servers, or when piping to Wireshark. Remote Capture → Pipe to Local Wireshark When you need to capture on a remote server but analyse locally: Sniffing Specific Protocols Capturing FTP Credentials FTP sends username and password in plaintext. Capturing HTTP Login Forms Capturing Telnet Sessions Everything in Telnet is plaintext — every keystroke transmitted unencrypted. HTTPS — What You Can and Can't See When HTTPS is in use, you see encrypted bytes only. You cannot read the content without: 1. The server's private key (decrypt all sessions) 2. HTTPS stripping (downgrade to HTTP — see bettercap hstshijack) 3. SSL inspection proxy (Burp Suite for known traffic) 4. Stealing session cookies after auth (if HttpOnly is not set — via XSS) What you CAN see in HTTPS even without decrypting: Server Name Indication (SNI) — which domain is being accessed Certificate details — server identity Traffic patterns — volume, timing, packet sizes SSL Stripping / HTTPS Downgrade SSL stripping intercepts HTTPS redirects and serves plain HTTP to the victim while maintaining HTTPS with the server. The victim's browser shows HTTP — credentials are in plaintext. Effectiveness has been reduced by HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), which forces browsers to always use HTTPS. But many sites still don't implement HSTS. Detecting MITM Attacks (Defence Context) Understanding detection helps you stay stealthy and helps you advise clients. ARP Cache Poisoning Detection: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches Wireshark filter: or duplicate MACs for same IP Security tools: arpwatch, XDR/EDR agents Anomalies to look for: Quick Reference | Protocol | Port | Credential Exposure | | | | | | HTTP | 80 | Full credentials in plaintext | | FTP | 21 | Username + password in plaintext | | Telnet | 23 | Everything in plaintext | | SMTP | 25 | Often plaintext | | POP3 | 110 | Often plaintext | | IMAP | 143 | Often plaintext | | SNMP v1/v2c | 161/UDP | Community strings in plaintext | | HTTPS | 443 | Encrypted (requires stripping) | | SSH | 22 | Encrypted | | SMB | 445 | NTLM challenge response (crackable) | Related Notes 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks 03.2 — Metasploit Framework 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting IPv6 MITM Attacks — mitm6 Why IPv6 Is a Blind Spot Most enterprise networks were built around IPv4 and are defended around IPv4. Firewalls have IPv4 rules, SIEMs alert on IPv4 anomalies, and network teams focus on IPv4 infrastructure. But Windows enables IPv6 by default on every network adapter since Vista, and it runs alongside IPv4 even on networks where "IPv6 is not used." The critical insight: IPv6 has higher priority than IPv4 for name resolution on Windows . If an attacker can answer IPv6 configuration requests, they become the preferred gateway and DNS server — entirely bypassing IPv4 focused defences. mitm6 exploits this by abusing two IPv6 protocols: DHCPv6 — the attacker sends fake DHCPv6 replies assigning themselves as the IPv6 DNS server Router Advertisements (RA) — the attacker sends fake RAs advertising themselves as the IPv6 default gateway Neither of these requires breaking any encryption or defeating any authentication. Windows machines eagerly accept DHCPv6 and RA messages from any host on the local segment. How mitm6 Works Installing and Running mitm6 Basic mitm6 + ntlmrelayx Attack This is the core attack chain. Always run mitm6 and ntlmrelayx simultaneously in separate terminals. Relay to SMB (Dump SAM Hashes) Relay to LDAP — Create a New Admin User Relay to LDAP — Resource Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) This chain gives persistent access without needing to crack any password: mitm6 Targeting Options WPAD Abuse — Triggering Automatic Authentication WPAD (Web Proxy Auto Discovery) is a mechanism where Windows machines automatically look for a proxy configuration file at . This lookup triggers NTLM authentication if the WPAD host requests it. mitm6 + ntlmrelayx exploit this automatically: This triggers from: Internet Explorer / Edge opening any webpage Outlook trying to check for proxy settings Windows background update processes Any application that uses the system proxy Combining mitm6 with Responder mitm6 and Responder target complementary protocols and can run together: Reading mitm6 Output Detection and Defence Detection indicators: Unexpected DHCPv6 traffic on a network that doesn't use IPv6 Multiple DHCPv6 ADVERTISE responses from non authoritative sources DNS queries resolving to IPv6 link local addresses (fe80::) unexpectedly Windows hosts receiving IPv6 addresses from unexpected DHCP servers EventID 1080 (DHCP) in Windows Event Log showing IPv6 lease from unusual server Defensive controls: Quick Reference — IPv6 MITM | Relay Target | ntlmrelayx Flag | What You Get | | | | | | SMB (no signing) | | SAM hash dump, command execution | | LDAP (port 389) | | AD enumeration, user creation | | LDAPS (port 636) | | LDAPS relay — more reliable | | LDAP + RBCD | | Persistent impersonation | | LDAP + escalate | | Add user to Domain Admins | | MSSQL | | xp cmdshell if SA | Related Notes (Updated) 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks 03.2 — Metasploit Framework 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting 04.6 — BloodHound & AD Attack Path Analysis

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration.md
title: 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration
body: 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration Why Active Directory Matters Active Directory is the identity and access management backbone of virtually every enterprise Windows environment. If you compromise AD, you own the organisation — every server, every workstation, every user account. AD pentesting is the most impactful discipline in enterprise red teaming. A single misconfiguration — a user with delegation rights, a service account with a weak password, an ACL misconfigured years ago — can lead to full domain compromise. Core Concepts Domain Structure Forest — the top level security boundary. Multiple trees can share a forest. Domain — administrative boundary. Users, computers, and policies live here. Domain Controller (DC) — the server running AD DS. Holds the NTDS.dit database (all hashes). Compromise a DC = game over. Organisational Unit (OU) — container for organising objects. Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are applied at OU level. Trust — allows authentication across domains/forests. Bidirectional trusts are particularly dangerous. Key Objects | Object | Description | | | | | User | Domain account — has SID, can authenticate | | Computer | Domain joined machine — also has a computer account | | Group | Collection of users/computers — used for permissions | | Service Account | User account used to run services — often over privileged, weak password | | Group Policy Object (GPO) | Policy applied to OUs — controls desktop settings, software, scripts | | Service Principal Name (SPN) | Identifier for a service — used in Kerberos (Kerberoasting target) | Security Identifiers (SIDs) Every object in AD has a unique SID. Format: Well known RIDs: = Administrator (built in local admin) = krbtgt (Kerberos ticket granting account) = Domain Admins group = Enterprise Admins group Authentication Protocols NTLM Authentication NTLM is a challenge response authentication protocol. Used when Kerberos is unavailable or for local authentication. Key points: The NTLM hash (not plaintext) is used to compute the response Net NTLMv2 (the challenge response) is what Responder captures — it is crackable NTLM hash itself can be used in Pass the Hash — no cracking needed Pass the Hash only works for NTLM, not Kerberos Kerberos Authentication Kerberos is the primary AD authentication protocol. Three actors: Client, KDC (Domain Controller), and Service. Key attack surfaces: AS REP : If pre authentication is disabled → AS REP roasting TGS REP : Service ticket encrypted with service account hash → Kerberoasting TGT : If you steal a TGT → Pass the Ticket krbtgt hash : If compromised → Golden Ticket (forge any TGT forever) Initial Enumeration (Unauthenticated) Before you have credentials, these queries work anonymously or with minimum access. LDAP Null / Anonymous Bind enum4linux ng (Unauthenticated) Nmap AD Enumeration Enumeration with Credentials Once you have any domain user credentials (even a low privilege account), enumeration becomes dramatically more powerful. ldapdomaindump Dumps the entire AD structure to HTML and JSON files. PowerView (PowerShell — Run from Windows) PowerView is a PowerShell module for AD enumeration. Run it from a domain joined machine or via a Meterpreter shell with PowerShell access. CrackMapExec Enumeration (Authenticated) BloodHound — Attack Path Visualisation BloodHound is the most powerful tool for AD attack path analysis. It collects AD relationship data and displays it as a graph, automatically finding the shortest path from any user to Domain Admin. Architecture Step 1 — Collect Data with SharpHound SharpHound runs on Windows (domain joined or with domain creds). Step 1 (Alternative) — BloodHound.py (Remote, from Linux) Step 2 — Set Up BloodHound + Neo4j Step 3 — Import Data BloodHound → Upload Data → select the .zip file from SharpHound Step 4 — Key Queries In BloodHound's "Pre Built Analytics" or the search bar: Reading BloodHound Output Nodes = objects (users, computers, groups) Edges = relationships/permissions Key edges to spot: | Edge | Meaning | | | | | | User is member of group | | | User/group has local admin on computer | | | A user has an active session on a computer | | | Can RDP to a machine | | | Full control over an object | | | Can modify object attributes | | | Can take ownership of object | | | Can modify permissions on object | | | Can reset user's password | | | Full extended rights (includes DCSync) | | | DCSync rights | | | Owns the object | [!tip] Right click any edge in BloodHound → Help → shows you exactly how to abuse that relationship, with commands. BloodHound is self documenting for attacks. Password Policy Enumeration Before spraying passwords, check the policy to avoid lockouts. Key fields: MinimumPasswordLength — minimum password length PasswordHistorySize — how many old passwords are remembered LockoutBadCount — failed attempts before lockout (CRITICAL — don't exceed this) LockoutDuration — how long lockout lasts ObservationWindow — window for counting failed attempts [!danger] If , you can only try 2 passwords per account. Exceeding this locks out the user — a real user can't log in. This is visible to the SOC and disruptive to the business. Always check the policy before any password spraying. Quick Reference | Concept | Key Point | | | | | DC | Holds NTDS.dit — all domain hashes — prime target | | krbtgt | Hash used to sign all TGTs — compromise = Golden Ticket | | SPN | Kerberoasting target — service ticket crackable offline | | Pre auth disabled | AS REP roasting — no creds needed | | BloodHound | Graphs attack paths — right click edge for abuse instructions | | Lockout policy | Check before spraying — 2 guesses max if LockoutBadCount=3 | Related Notes 04.2 — Credential Attacks (Kerberoasting, AS REP, PTH) 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement 04.4 — Persistence & Impacket Suite 03.1 — Network Scanning & SMB Attacks 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.2 — Credential Attacks.md
title: 04.2 — Credential Attacks (Kerberoasting, AS-REP, PTH, PTT)
body: 04.2 — Credential Attacks (Kerberoasting, AS REP, PTH, PTT) Overview AD credential attacks exploit the Kerberos and NTLM authentication protocols to extract crackable hashes or reuse authentication material without ever knowing the plaintext password. The most powerful: you compromise one low privilege account → Kerberoast a service account → crack its hash → it has local admin somewhere → pivot → eventually reach Domain Admin. Kerberoasting What It Is Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for any service with a registered SPN. That service ticket is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash. You take it offline and crack it. No special privileges required — just any domain user account. Target: Service accounts with SPNs (SQL service accounts, IIS app pools, backup agents, etc.). These often have weak passwords because they're set once and forgotten. Step 1 — Find Kerberoastable Accounts Step 2 — Request the Ticket Step 3 — Crack the Hash Hash format looks like: If cracked → plaintext password for the service account → check what it has access to. [!tip] The most impactful service accounts to Kerberoast are those with (were once in a privileged group) or those whose name suggests high privilege: , , . BloodHound shows the shortest path from Kerberoastable accounts to DA. AS REP Roasting What It Is Normally, Kerberos requires the client to prove identity by encrypting a timestamp with their NTLM hash (pre authentication). If pre authentication is disabled for an account, anyone can request an AS REP (authentication response) for that user — the response contains data encrypted with the user's hash. Take it offline and crack it. No credentials required at all — just network access to the DC. Step 1 — Find AS REP Roastable Accounts Step 2 — Crack the Hash Hash format: Password Spraying Password spraying tries one password against many accounts — opposite of brute force. Avoids lockouts because each account is only tried once (or a few times). [!danger] Password spraying WILL lock out accounts if you exceed the lockout threshold. Use one password attempt per account per observation window (usually 30 minutes). If LockoutBadCount=5 and ObservationWindow=30min, wait 30 minutes between spray rounds. Pass the Hash (PTH) Reuse an NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext. Works for NTLM authentication — not Kerberos. Where to Get Hashes Using Hashes [!tip] PSExec creates a service on the target and is logged loudly. WMIExec is quieter — no service creation, uses WMI. Prefer WMIExec on real engagements. Pass the Ticket (PTT) Steal a Kerberos TGT or service ticket from memory and inject it into your current session. You authenticate as that user without their password or hash. Extracting Tickets with Mimikatz (Windows) Extracting Tickets with Rubeus (Windows) Extracting Tickets from Linux with Impacket Injecting a Ticket Using the Injected Ticket Overpass the Hash Convert an NTLM hash into a Kerberos TGT. Combines PTH and PTT — gives you Kerberos authentication from just an NTLM hash. Mimikatz — Windows Credential Extraction Mimikatz is the definitive Windows credential extraction tool. It reads credentials from LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) memory. [!warning] Mimikatz requires admin/SYSTEM privileges. It is heavily flagged by AV/EDR. On modern Windows with Credential Guard enabled, many features are blocked. Always check in Meterpreter first. Running Mimikatz Key Mimikatz Commands Quick Reference | Attack | Requires | Output | Tool | | | | | | | Kerberoasting | Any domain user | Crackable TGS hash | GetUserSPNs.py / Rubeus | | AS REP Roasting | Nothing (no creds) | Crackable AS REP hash | GetNPUsers.py / Rubeus | | Password Spray | Username list | Valid credentials | CrackMapExec / Kerbrute | | Pass the Hash | NTLM hash | Lateral movement | CME / PSExec / WMIExec | | Pass the Ticket | Kerberos ticket | Impersonation | Rubeus / Mimikatz | | Overpass the Hash | NTLM hash | Kerberos TGT | Mimikatz / Rubeus | Related Notes 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement 04.4 — Persistence & Impacket Suite 03.3 — Password Attacks & Hash Cracking

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement.md
title: 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement in AD
body: 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement in AD From User to Domain Admin — The Path In most AD environments, you don't go directly from user to DA. You chain attacks: BloodHound maps this path. Your job is to walk it. ACL Abuse Access Control Lists (ACLs) define permissions on AD objects. Misconfigurations — where a low privilege user has powerful rights over a high privilege object — create escalation paths. Key ACL Rights to Look For | Right | What You Can Do | | | | | | Full control — reset password, add to group, modify everything | | | Write any non protected attribute — set SPN (Kerberoast), set logon script | | | Change object owner → then grant yourself full control | | | Modify the ACL → grant yourself | | | Reset the user's password without knowing current password | | | All extended rights — includes read LAPS, reset password, DCSync | | | Add users to a group | | | Write specific attributes on yourself (e.g., add yourself to a group) | Finding ACL Misconfigs BloodHound finds these automatically and shows the attack path with abuse instructions. Exploiting ACL — ForceChangePassword If you have over a user: Exploiting ACL — GenericAll on User Exploiting ACL — GenericAll on Group Exploiting ACL — WriteDACL Exploiting ACL — GenericWrite → Targeted Kerberoasting If you have over a user, you can set an SPN on their account, Kerberoast them, and crack the hash: GPO Abuse Group Policy Objects control every domain joined machine. If you have or on a GPO, or can create/link GPOs, you can push malicious policies to machines. Finding GPO Permissions Exploiting GPO — SharpGPOAbuse (Windows) DCSync Attack DCSync mimics a Domain Controller's replication request. Instead of actually compromising the DC, you ask it to replicate specific objects' credentials — specifically, you ask for the NTLM hash of any user, including the Administrator and krbtgt. Required rights: AND on the domain object. By default, only Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and Domain Controllers have these rights. Sometimes mis granted to regular users. Run DCSync with Mimikatz (Windows) Run DCSync with Impacket (Linux — no Windows machine needed) [!tip] Once you have all domain hashes from DCSync, you own the domain. You can pass the hash as any user, create Golden Tickets, and maintain persistence indefinitely. Save everything — NTLM hashes, krbtgt hash, domain SID. Lateral Movement Getting from your initial foothold machine to other machines on the network. PsExec Creates a service on the remote machine, uploads a payload, executes it. Gives a SYSTEM shell. Noisy — service creation is logged. WMIExec (Quieter) Uses Windows Management Instrumentation — no service creation, lower detection footprint. WinRM / Evil WinRM Windows Remote Management — runs on port 5985 (HTTP) and 5986 (HTTPS). More common on servers and newer Windows. RDP Lateral Movement CrackMapExec for Lateral Movement Token Impersonation Windows uses access tokens to represent the security context of a process. If you can steal a token from a higher privileged process, you run code as that user. Incognito (Metasploit) Mimikatz Token Impersonation Unconstrained Delegation Abuse When a computer account has unconstrained delegation enabled, any user who authenticates to a service on that machine sends their full TGT along with the service ticket. If you compromise that machine, you collect TGTs for everyone who connects. Quick Reference | Technique | Requires | Gains | | | | | | ACL ForceChangePassword | ForceChangePassword right | Account takeover | | ACL GenericAll on Group | GenericAll on group | Add yourself to DA | | DCSync | GetChanges + GetChangesAll | All domain hashes | | WMIExec | Local admin creds/hash | Remote shell | | Evil WinRM | WinRM access + creds/hash | PowerShell shell | | Token impersonation | Local admin + SYSTEM | Impersonate any logged on user | | Unconstrained delegation | Compromise delegated machine | Collect TGTs, DCSync | Related Notes 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration 04.2 — Credential Attacks 04.4 — Persistence & Impacket Suite MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting Resource Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) — Full Attack Chain Delegation Types — Quick Primer Kerberos delegation lets one service act on behalf of a user when contacting a third service. Three flavours exist; only the third (RBCD) flips the trust direction. | Delegation | Trust Direction | Configured On | Attribute | Attackability | | | | | | | | Unconstrained | Trust the source unconditionally | Source machine | flag | High — compromise the source, harvest any TGT that hits it | | Constrained | Source can delegate, but only to listed services | Source machine | | Medium — compromise source, S4U abuse to the allowed services. Protocol Transition ( ) flag makes it pre auth free | | Resource Based Constrained (RBCD) | Resource decides who can delegate to it | Target/resource machine | | High — write access to that one attribute on the target = compromise of the target | The flip is what makes RBCD pentest gold: you don't need to be a Domain Admin to grant delegation; you only need write access to the target's computer object, which is given out generously in many environments (e.g., a delegated server admin role, a stale ACL from a decommissioned automation account, etc.). Why RBCD Is Attackable The attribute on a computer object is just another security descriptor. If you have any of , , , , , or over the computer object, you can write your chosen principal into that attribute. Anything you write into it is then trusted by the target's KDC ticket validation logic — that principal can request tickets impersonating any user (including Domain Admins) to any service on the target. Prerequisites Checklist You need both of: 1. Write access to a target computer object — , , , , , or . Find with BloodHound: filter for / edges where the target node type is "Computer". 2. A principal you control with an SPN — needed because S4U2Proxy demands the requester have an SPN. The two ways to get one: Create a new computer account. By default , meaning any authenticated user can create up to 10 computer accounts. The new account automatically gets two SPNs ( and ) and you choose the password. Use an existing computer account whose credentials/hash you already have. Step By Step Attack — Linux (Impacket + krbrelayx tooling) The names below: is the victim machine you want SYSTEM on; is the principal you create or already control; is whoever you want to impersonate (any user works because S4U2Self is unconstrained for protocol transition capable principals). [!important] DNS resolution Kerberos requires that the SPN host ( above) resolves correctly. If it doesn't, add the entry to and run with to dodge the standard DNS chain. If you see , your SPN is wrong (case matters: lowercase, FQDN required). Step By Step Attack — Windows (PowerView + Rubeus) Why It Works — Mechanism Walk Through 1. S4U2Self — FAKE$ asks the KDC: "Issue me a ticket to myself on behalf of Administrator." The KDC produces a forwardable service ticket ( ). Note Administrator never authenticated — this entire request is unauthenticated impersonation as long as FAKE$'s account is allowed to do it (which it is by default for any computer account with no restriction). 2. S4U2Proxy — FAKE$ presents that forwardable ticket to the KDC and asks: "Now exchange this for a ticket to ." The KDC checks: is FAKE$ allowed to act on behalf of users for TARGET? It looks at — sees FAKE$'s SID is in the list — and issues the ticket. 3. The resulting ticket is fully valid. TARGET's CIFS service decrypts it (the ticket is encrypted with TARGET$'s key), checks the PAC (which says "Administrator, member of Domain Admins"), and accepts the connection as Administrator → SYSTEM equivalent. The attack succeeds without touching the DC, without knowing Administrator's password, and without needing any high privilege beyond write access to one attribute on the target. Finding RBCD Opportunities With BloodHound The edge in BloodHound v4+ explicitly identifies the RBCD write right. Detection | Signal | Where | | | | | EventID 4741 (Computer account created) — flag if from a non admin user | Domain Controllers Security log | | EventID 5136 (Directory service object modified) where | DC Security log — high signal, low FP | | EventID 4742 (Computer account changed) referencing exhaustion patterns | DC Security log | | EventID 4768/4769 (TGT/TGS issued) with anomalous S4U flags or impersonation across unusual sources | DC Security log | | Anomalous machine creation rate from a single source IP | SIEM correlation | Hard mitigation: set ( ); restrict computer object write permissions; alert on any change to across the domain via auditing SACLs. WinRM Lateral Movement — Deep Dive What WinRM Actually Is Windows Remote Management is Microsoft's implementation of the open WS Management ( ) standard. It is a SOAP over HTTP(S) protocol for remote system management — running commands, managing services, fetching WMI data, and powering PowerShell Remoting ( , ). | Property | HTTP | HTTPS | | | | | | Default port | 5985 | 5986 | | Protocol | SOAP/XML over HTTP, body usually encrypted via SPNEGO/Kerberos | SOAP/XML over TLS | | Default state | Enabled by default on Server 2012+ ; off on Windows 10/11 client unless | Off by default — needs cert binding | | Auth | Negotiate (Kerberos/NTLM), Basic (rarely), CredSSP, Certificate | Same | For pentest purposes: WinRM on a server is your single most useful lateral movement target after SMB. PSExec drops a binary; WMIExec is fileless but logs heavily; WinRM gives you an interactive PowerShell session as a legitimate management tool, blends into baseline traffic, and is whitelisted by most EDRs as expected admin activity. Discovery evil winrm — The Standard Linux Client PowerShell Remoting From a Windows Attack Box Native equivalents — useful when you're already on a Windows host with the right creds and don't want to drop tooling. Attacker Setup — Required Group Membership A non admin user can use WinRM if they are in (granted by in some configs). Local admins can always use it. After getting a creds only foothold, check: Add yourself if you can (need admin): Detection | Signal | Source | | | | | EventID 4624 logon type 3 (network) on target with | Target Security log | | Microsoft Windows WinRM/Operational EventID 91 (WSMan session created) | Target Operational log | | Microsoft Windows PowerShell/Operational EventID 4103/4104 (script block / module logging) — captures the actual PS commands run | Target PowerShell log | | Outbound TCP to 5985/5986 from non admin workstations | Firewall / netflow | | Unusual user accounts in | AD audit | | AMSI bypass strings ( , ) | EDR / scriptblock logging | Hardening to recommend in reports: enforce HTTPS only WinRM ( ), block 5985/5986 inbound at the host firewall except from a hardened management subnet, enable PowerShell scriptblock + module logging domain wide, route logs to a central SIEM, alert on any new member of .

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.4 — Persistence & Impacket Suite.md
title: 04.4 — Persistence & the Impacket Suite
body: 04.4 — Persistence & the Impacket Suite Persistence in AD Persistence means maintaining access even after the client patches the initial vulnerability, rotates passwords, or reboots systems. In AD, the most durable persistence mechanisms are baked into Kerberos itself. Golden Ticket What It Is A Golden Ticket is a forged Kerberos TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) signed with the krbtgt account's NTLM hash . Because the Domain Controller trusts all TGTs signed with the krbtgt hash, a Golden Ticket gives you unrestricted access to the entire domain as any user — including non existent users. Persistence value: Even if every other password in the domain is rotated, a Golden Ticket remains valid until the krbtgt password is changed twice (because old tickets are cached). Most organisations never rotate krbtgt. Required: krbtgt NTLM hash, domain SID, domain name. Step 1 — Get the krbtgt Hash Step 2 — Get the Domain SID Step 3 — Create and Inject the Golden Ticket Step 4 — Verify Access Silver Ticket A Silver Ticket is a forged service ticket (TGS) — not a TGT. It's encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash rather than the krbtgt hash. Difference from Golden Ticket: Silver Ticket = access to one specific service only (e.g., CIFS on DC01, MSSQL on SQL01) Golden Ticket = access to everything Silver Ticket never touches the KDC — completely offline creation, no network traffic to DC Harder to detect (no TGT request) Skeleton Key The Skeleton Key attack patches the LSASS process on a Domain Controller to accept a master password alongside users' real passwords. Any user can then authenticate with either their real password or the skeleton key password. [!danger] The Skeleton Key only persists until the DC is rebooted — it patches memory, not disk. Also, it patches all LSASS instances — if there are multiple DCs, you need to run it on each. Detected by EDR and some AV products. DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) Password Abuse Every DC has a local DSRM administrator account — used for offline AD maintenance. This account's hash is stored in the SAM of the DC itself. If you dump it and the registry is configured to allow network logon, you have persistent admin access to the DC. AdminSDHolder Persistence AdminSDHolder is an AD object that acts as a template for permissions on privileged objects (DA, EA, etc.). Every hour, the SDProp process copies AdminSDHolder's ACL to all protected objects. If you write a permission to AdminSDHolder, it propagates to all privileged groups — and survives even if someone removes your access from Domain Admins directly. The Impacket Suite — Full Reference Impacket is a Python library with a collection of standalone tools for attacking Windows networks from Linux. It eliminates the need for a Windows machine in most AD attacks. Authentication Formats All Impacket tools accept the same auth formats: Core Impacket Tools secretsdump.py — Credential Dumping psexec.py — Remote Shell (Service Based) wmiexec.py — Remote Shell (WMI, Quieter) smbexec.py — Remote Shell (Service + Share) atexec.py — Remote Command via Task Scheduler GetUserSPNs.py — Kerberoasting GetNPUsers.py — AS REP Roasting ticketer.py — Golden / Silver Ticket Creation getTGT.py / getST.py — Ticket Requests lookupsid.py — SID Enumeration rpcdump.py / rpcmap.py — RPC Enumeration smbclient.py — SMB Shell ntlmrelayx.py — NTLM Relay Attacks If SMB signing is disabled, you can relay captured NTLM authentication to other machines instead of cracking it. Quick Reference — Full Module 4 Attack Chain | Persistence Technique | Requires | Survives Password Rotation | | | | | | Golden Ticket | krbtgt hash | Until krbtgt rotated TWICE | | Silver Ticket | Service account hash | Until service account rotated | | AdminSDHolder | WriteDACL on AdminSDHolder | Until ACL cleaned + SDProp | | DSRM password | SYSTEM on DC | Until DSRM password changed | | Skeleton Key | SYSTEM on DC | Until DC reboots | Related Notes 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration 04.2 — Credential Attacks 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.5 — ADCS Certificate Abuse.md
title: 04.5 — ADCS Certificate Abuse (ESC1–ESC8)
body: 04.5 — ADCS Certificate Abuse (ESC1–ESC8) What ADCS Is Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) is Microsoft's PKI implementation built into Windows Server environments. It issues X.509 certificates for: User and machine authentication (smart card logon, VPN, Wi Fi 802.1X) Code signing Email encryption (S/MIME) TLS for internal services In most enterprise environments, ADCS is deployed but largely unmonitored. The attack surface was systematically documented in the 2021 SpecterOps paper Certified Pre Owned by Will Schroeder and Lee Christoffersen, which introduced the ESC (Escalation) vulnerability classifications. These are now among the most reliable paths to Domain Admin in real environments. Why ADCS attacks are powerful: A certificate issued to a domain admin account is valid for authentication even after the account's password is changed Certificates persist across password resets — golden ticket level persistence via a legitimate PKI mechanism ADCS is present in the majority of enterprise Active Directory deployments Misconfigurations are extremely common because default templates are overly permissive The Attack Flow Authentication from a certificate: PKINIT — Kerberos pre authentication using a certificate → get a TGT Schannel — TLS client authentication using a certificate Shadow Credentials — add a certificate to a user's attribute Tools Certipy (Linux — Primary Tool) Certify (Windows — Alternative) Step 1 — Enumeration Always enumerate before attempting any ESC. You need to know: Which Certificate Authorities (CAs) are in the environment Which certificate templates exist and their permissions Which templates are enabled and enrollable Reading Certipy Output Key fields to look for in the enumeration output: ESC1 — Enrollee Supplies Subject (Most Common) What It Is A certificate template is misconfigured to allow the enrollee to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN). Combined with Client Authentication being enabled, this means any user can request a certificate that claims to be any other user — including Domain Admin. Conditions Required Exploit ESC2 — Any Purpose EKU or No EKU What It Is A template has the "Any Purpose" EKU or no EKU at all. This means the certificate can be used for any purpose — including client authentication — even if Client Authentication isn't explicitly listed. Conditions Required Exploit The exploit is identical to ESC1 if the template also has . If it doesn't, use ESC3 chaining (see below). ESC3 — Certificate Request Agent (Enroll on Behalf of Another User) What It Is ESC3 abuses the Certificate Request Agent EKU. A certificate with this EKU allows the holder to enroll in other certificate templates on behalf of another user . This is a two step chain: 1. Enroll in a template with the Certificate Request Agent EKU 2. Use that agent certificate to enroll in a second template (one with Client Auth) on behalf of a Domain Admin Conditions Required Exploit ESC4 — Vulnerable Certificate Template Access Control What It Is A low privilege user has Write permissions over a certificate template object itself — not just the ability to enroll. This allows modifying the template's properties to introduce ESC1 conditions, then enrolling. Conditions Required Exploit [!warning] In authorised engagements, always use and restore the template after exploitation. Leaving a template misconfigured is a permanent change that affects the client's production PKI. ESC6 — EDITF ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Flag on CA What It Is The Certificate Authority itself has the flag set. This flag allows any template — even those without — to accept a user supplied SAN. Combined with any template that has Client Authentication, this gives ESC1 equivalent exploitation against all templates. Detection Exploit ESC7 — Vulnerable CA Permissions What It Is A low privilege user has or rights on the CA itself. ManageCA → can enable flag → converts to ESC6, then exploit as above ManageCertificates → can approve pending certificate requests → useful when a template requires manager approval Exploit (ManageCA → Enable ESC6) Exploit (ManageCertificates → Approve Pending Requests) ESC8 — NTLM Relay to ADCS HTTP Enrollment Endpoint What It Is ADCS Web Enrollment ( ) uses HTTP by default without enforcing HTTPS, and does not require signing. This makes it vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks. If you can coerce a domain controller or high privilege machine to authenticate to you, you can relay that authentication to the ADCS Web Enrollment endpoint and obtain a certificate for that machine account. A Domain Controller's machine certificate can then be used to perform a DCSync equivalent via PKINIT. Conditions Required Authentication Coercion Methods Exploit [!tip] ESC8 is often the fastest path to Domain Admin in environments where ADCS Web Enrollment is enabled — which is a significant proportion of enterprise deployments. Combine with PetitPotam for an unauthenticated (or low privilege) → DA chain. Pass the Certificate — Using Certificates for Authentication Once you have a certificate, you have two authentication paths: Path 1 — PKINIT (Kerberos) Path 2 — Shadow Credentials (When PKINIT is Unavailable) If Kerberos PKINIT isn't available (no DC supporting PKINIT, or certificate doesn't match), Shadow Credentials is an alternative — it adds a certificate to the target account's attribute, which Windows Hello for Business and PKINIT can use for authentication. ADCS for Persistence (Post Domain Compromise) Once you have Domain Admin, certificate based persistence outlasts password resets. Forge Certificates as Rogue CA (Golden Certificate) [!warning] A forged certificate signed by the compromised CA is valid as long as the CA certificate itself is trusted by the domain. To fully remediate this, the organisation must revoke the CA certificate and reissue it — a significant operational undertaking. This is extremely persistent.
