title: 09.1 — Labs & Practice Resources
body: 09.1 — Labs & Practice Resources How to Build Practical Skill Reading notes is passive. Skills are built by doing. This module maps out the best free and paid resources to practice every module covered in this curriculum, from beginner to advanced. The fastest path to competency: solve one machine per week, write a full report for each one. Online Platforms HackTheBox (HTB) https://www.hackthebox.com The gold standard for practical pentesting practice. Real machines, realistic vulnerabilities, no hand holding. Free tier: Starting Point machines (guided) + active free machines VIP ( $14/month): Access to retired machines (thousands) + official walkthroughs Progression path: HTB Academy: https://academy.hackthebox.com — structured learning paths with labs. Covers most topics in this curriculum with hands on exercises. TryHackMe (THM) https://tryhackme.com More guided than HTB. Better for complete beginners — rooms explain concepts as you go. Free tier available. Recommended learning paths: Specific rooms to prioritise: PortSwigger Web Security Academy https://portswigger.net/web security Free. The best web application security training that exists. Created by the makers of Burp Suite. Every topic in Module 2 has a dedicated lab track: Do every lab in a topic before moving to the next. PortSwigger labs are the most effective web security practice available. Local Vulnerable Machines (VulnHub) https://www.vulnhub.com — download as OVA, run in VirtualBox/VMware. No internet needed. Good for network situations where you can't reach HTB. Deliberately Vulnerable Applications Run locally for focused practice on a specific topic. DVWA — Damn Vulnerable Web Application https://github.com/digininja/DVWA PHP/MySQL web app with configurable vulnerability levels (Low/Medium/High/Impossible). Covers: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, file upload, command injection, IDOR, file inclusion. Metasploitable 2 Deliberately vulnerable Ubuntu VM. Covers network service exploitation (Module 3). Metasploitable 3 (Windows) Windows Server 2008 version with dozens of vulnerabilities — better for Windows attack practice. VulnHub — OWASP WebGoat Guided web app training with embedded hints. Good for step by step learning. bWAPP — Buggy Web Application Over 100 web vulnerabilities in one application. Reference Resources PayloadsAllTheThings https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings The single most useful offensive resource repository. Contains: Payload lists for every injection type (SQLi, XSS, SSTI, XXE, SSRF, LFI, etc.) Bypass techniques for every filter Methodology notes for each category Tool syntax and examples Bookmark this. Use it every time you test an injection point. HackTricks https://book.hacktricks.xyz The offensive pentesting wiki. Contains detailed notes on: Every service attack (by port number) Linux and Windows privesc AD attacks Cloud attacks (AWS, Azure, GCP) Container escapes File type exploitation Treat it as your live reference during engagements. Something weird on port 5985? Go to HackTricks and search "5985". GTFOBins https://gtfobins.github.io Covered in 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference. Every Unix binary's abuse potential. LOLBAS https://lolbas project.github.io Covered in 06.3 — PrivEsc Tools Reference. Every Windows binary's abuse potential. Exploit DB / SearchSploit MITRE ATT&CK https://attack.mitre.org Map every technique you use to a TTP (Tactic, Technique, Procedure). Use this for report writing — "This attack corresponds to T1558.003 (Kerberoasting)" shows professional depth. Wordlists SecLists The definitive collection of security wordlists. Key Wordlist Recommendations | Purpose | Wordlist | Notes | | | | | | Dir brute force (fast) | | Good balance | | Dir brute force (thorough) | | Classic | | API endpoints | | Module 2 | | Subdomain brute | | Module 1 | | DNS brute (thorough) | | Community favourite | | Password spray | | Spray carefully | | Hash cracking | (at ) | Essential | | Parameters | | Module 2 Arjun | | XSS payloads | | Fuzzing | | SQLi payloads | | Fuzzing | Practice Methodology — How to Use These Resources Effectively The Right Way to Practice a Machine Structured Weekly Schedule (If Starting from Scratch) Certifications (Context for Your Career Path) | Cert | Level | Content | Cost | | | | | | | eJPT (INE) | Beginner | Network + web basics | $200 | | CEH (EC Council) | Beginner Mid | Theory heavy, you already have this | — | | PNPT (TCM Security) | Mid | Practical, AD focus, great value | $400 | | OSCP (OffSec) | Mid Senior | 24h practical exam, industry gold standard | $1,500 | | BSCP (PortSwigger) | Mid Senior | Web only, Burp Suite mastery | $150 | | CRTO (Zero Point Security) | Senior | Red team, Cobalt Strike, AD | $450 | | CRTE (AlteredSecurity) | Senior | Advanced AD | $250 | OSCP is the most recognised cert for junior penetration tester roles in the UK. It validates practical skill, not exam memorisation. Target it after you're consistently solving HTB Medium machines. title: Active Directory Pentest Mindmap (Orange Cyberdefense)
body: Active Directory Pentest Mindmap (Orange Cyberdefense) This is not my work. It was made by Mayfly277 and the team at Orange Cyberdefense , and is published free under GPL 3.0. Full credit and thanks to them. Everything below is just my notes on how to use it. Source: <https://github.com/Orange Cyberdefense/ocd mindmaps Live, zoomable: <https://orange cyberdefense.github.io/ocd mindmaps/ What This Note Covers Where to find the mindmap, what is on it, and how to actually use it during an AD engagement rather than just admiring it. The map Version v2025.03 , the current release. Stored in this vault so it is available offline: It is 19150 x 7623, so the embed above is only useful as an overview. Open the SVG directly and zoom, or use the live version which pans and zooms properly. Why it is worth keeping Most AD cheatsheets are a flat list of commands. This one is a decision tree : it starts from what you currently have (no credentials, a username, a password, an NT hash, a shell) and shows what each of those unlocks next. That is the actual shape of an AD engagement, and it is the part that is hard to hold in your head. What is on it Branches worth knowing by name, because they are what you scan for when stuck: Recon and enumeration — from unauthenticated through to domain admin Credential access — LSASS, LSA, SAM, DPAPI, NTDS.dit, backup keys Kerberos — roasting, delegation (unconstrained, constrained, RBCD), S4U2self abuse ADCS — vulnerable templates, misconfigured CAs, certificate mapping, web enrolment ACL and ACE abuse — on users, groups, computers and OUs; DCSync; writes; GPO and DNS Admin paths; LAPS and gMSA reads Trusts — parent to child, child to parent, external, MSSQL links SCCM — a whole branch of its own, credential and takeover paths Lateral movement — what each credential type actually gets you Persistence — golden and silver tickets, diamond and sapphire tickets, golden certificate, DSRM, skeleton key, custom SSP, DC shadow Known CVEs — PrintNightmare, Certifried, ProxyNotShell and others, placed where they fit in the chain rather than listed separately How to use it 1. Start from what you hold, not from the top. Find the box matching your current access and read outward. The map is built around that question. 2. Use it as a checklist when stuck. If a path is exhausted, the adjacent branches are the things you have not tried yet. 3. Keep the live version open on a second screen. The offline copy here is for when there is no internet; the hosted one zooms better. Licence GPL 3.0. The full licence text and the attribution notice sit beside the file in . It is redistributed unmodified, as that licence requires. That licence covers the mindmap only, not my notes.
